14636.name: Comment-start markers in source code (//, #, ///, ##), particularly inline or line-leading comments that introduce a natural-language explanation of the following code. There is weaker activation on similar transitions from code or formatting into explanatory prose (e.g., "Now", "We" after headings).

14638.name: Words about crowds and mass public gatherings, especially protests and demonstrations: rallies, protesters gathering, petitions, protest votes, days of action, parades, celebrations, applause and cheering crowds, plus collective nouns such as multitude, groups and armada. The strongest responses are on explicit protest or demonstration terms, with weak scattered firing on surrounding context words.

14647.name: Weak activation on non-initial words or pieces inside fixed multi-word proper names and boilerplate labels, mainly journal titles (PLoS ONE, JAMA Network Open, Cell Reports), institutions, courts, committees, degree names, license codes (BY-NC-ND), and metadata or website labels. These tokens continue a conventional title or name that is already underway.

14698.name: Binary operator tokens in math and code, mainly exponent operators (^, **, )^, ^{, ).^) placed just before a power such as 2. Weaker hits on other operators and casts (as, >=, -, /, <<) and on a few stray punctuation and whitespace tokens.

Exponentiation operators ("^", "^{", "**", ")^", Math.pow's comma) placed between a base and its exponent in math/code, especially polynomial terms like x^3. Weaker hits land on other binary operators (%, >=, >>) and on list-separating commas.

Exponentiation operators: the caret (^, ^{, ^\) or ** that raises a base to a power, especially right before an exponent like 2 or 3 in math, LaTeX or code. It also fires weakly on other operators and separators (/, ::, -, commas, periods, spaces).

14708.name: The second item in a paired or binary construction, usually the token right after "and"/"or" in phrases like "between X and Y" or "both X and Y" (e.g., young and old, transmitting and reflecting, crop and animal). Activation is strongest on the final word of that second conjunct, especially when it completes a contrast or relationship between two entities.

14724.name: The first piece of a compound noun or multi-token word, i.e. a modifier or word fragment whose meaning depends on what follows (scale→ups, rain→forests, coast→ers, transcription→factors, wind→farms, best→practices). It is often a noun used attributively in technical or domain-specific terms. Activation is generally weak.

14769.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on structural boundary and delimiter tokens in semi-structured text: line breaks after headers, labels or metadata fields, punctuation closing a sentence or citation, colons after field names, URL pieces (".org", "://", "/io"), HTML tag closings, and code or shell prompts ("In [", "$"). These are points where one segment or field ends and the next begins.

14814.name: Connective or punctuation tokens that come right after a question, computation or quantity has been stated. They mark the shift to a qualifying constraint, an output format or the result, as in 'according to' the text, 'as a' set 'in' interval notation, 'using', '=', '?' or '@'. They appear mostly in Q&A and math or code contexts.

1483.name: Fires on the final subword pieces that complete a word split across several tokens (e.g. bellig-erents, Repet-ition, non-perturb-ative, Crockp-ots), often spilling onto the next one or two tokens of the same noun phrase or name. It shows up mostly in technical terms, proper names, acronyms and version or code strings, and peaks on the token where the multi-token word is resolved.

A diffuse, weak feature. It fires most strongly on subword pieces that finish a word split across several tokens, such as "ude" in Jean-Claude, "ers" in man-agers, "ship", "eness", "ical" and the Cyrillic and Korean endings. It also often fires on the next one or two tokens that continue the phrase. This is common in noisy, garbled, code, multilingual or repetitive text, and it is not tied to any clear meaning.

14858.name: Titles, offices and role nouns for people (President, Minister, Prime Minister, CEO, director, chief, Gov., Queen, coach), typically right before a person's name. Activation is strongest for political leadership titles such as President, Prime Minister and Gov.

Titles of positions, offices and ranks (President, Prime Minister, Pope, Chancellor, Sheriff, Queen, director, mayor), firing most strongly on high-ranking political, religious or royal titles placed just before a person's name.

1487.name: City and town names (and other place names), with activation strongest on the final token completing the name (e.g. 'sburgh', 'sha', 'Angeles') and sometimes the comma after it in datelines or addresses. Weak firing on other proper nouns or generic place words like 'city'.

14893.name: A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires weakly on function words and punctuation at phrase or clause junctions, such as prepositions, conjunctions, articles, auxiliaries, commas and sentence or paragraph breaks. These are positions where the sentence is about to continue into a new constituent (e.g. 'is the ability to', ', which we have', 'and has').

A diffuse, weakly selective pattern with no clear semantic theme. It mostly fires on function words and clause connectors such as "to", "of", "that", "the", "was a", "yet you have a" and "with the". It also fires on sentence boundaries and paragraph breaks. These tokens tend to sit at points where a new clause or the main content of a phrase is about to begin.

14954.name: Final token of a proper name (usually a person's surname or last subword piece of a name, also ships, Pokémon, products), marking completion of a multi-token named entity.

14964.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires across scientific and technical expository prose, especially biology/biomedical research writing such as abstracts and papers. It activates on scattered content words, word-piece fragments and function words, peaking on explanatory claims about mechanisms or capabilities (e.g. "can", "can be", "resulted in", "which eventually").

15067.name: The "=device" token inside the HTML viewport meta tag (content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0"). It fires strongly and consistently there, with only faint, scattered activations on unrelated tokens elsewhere.

15095.name: Tokens at boundaries within web-page boilerplate and metadata, such as the newline ending a field value (IDs, ISBNs, DOIs, dates, namespaces, "pages on⏎this wiki") just before the next label, and the word "navigation" in wiki "Jump to: navigation, search" headers. Generally marks where one structured, templated element ends and the next begins.

Weak, diffuse feature that fires on boundary tokens ending a segment in structured or boilerplate text, just before a new field or line begins. Typical spots are line breaks between header or diff lines (strongest after an #ifndef include-guard line), the final digit of an ISBN, URL fragment words like 'comments' or 'respond' that precede a timestamp, and punctuation or delimiters in code, URLs and metadata. It fires only rarely on ordinary prose.

15108.name: A diffuse, weak feature with no single dominant token. It fires mostly at structural boundaries in text, such as sentence-ending periods, commas separating clauses or list items, paragraph breaks and closing tags like "</". It also fires on the words immediately after these boundaries, typically sentence or clause openers like "In addition,", "Coming up," and "However,". Within running prose it picks up scattered content words, often nouns and verbs describing events or outcomes such as "losses", "progress" and "lost a bunch of".

15113.name: Descriptions of research study design and data sources in scientific or academic writing, especially methods-section details about who or what was studied, where, when and how. Typical phrases cover participants and cohorts, sites, protocols, surveys, screening, monitoring, measurements, models and date ranges. The strongest activations fall on participant and sample descriptions such as 'children were screened', 'participants', 'protocols' and 'sites in'.

15273.name: Definite article "The"/"the" (occasionally other determiners like "These"/"A") at the start of a new sentence, paragraph, or clause, opening a fresh noun phrase that introduces the next topic. Activation is strongest right after a period or paragraph break.

Sentence-initial definite determiners (mostly "The", sometimes "the"/"This") that open a new sentence or clause and begin a noun phrase referring back to something already introduced. Activation is strongest right after a sentence break or paragraph break in news-style prose.

15355.name: Opening punctuation of in-text citations and references, mainly the bracket "[" (often fused with a period, ".[") before a reference number in academic or Wikipedia-style text. It also fires weakly on other citation pieces such as "(", superscript braces, the space before a year in author–year citations, separator dots in section or figure numbers, and words like "Figure" or "page".

15373.name: Tokens in citation or cross-reference markup that come just before a reference number or label: \ref, \cite{ / \citep, "Ref"/"Source", opening brackets and superscript markers, the commas or spaces separating numbers in citation lists like [2,3,5], and "image" in markdown image links such as (image2). The feature fires on the scaffolding of numbered references rather than on the numbers themselves.

15401.name: The opening words of a subordinate or adverbial clause, mostly right after conjunctions like "when", "if", "after", "since" and "while": the subject plus verb ("they start", "we have") or a participle or gerund ("camping with", "being heated at"). Activation peaks on the main verb, the start of the clause describing the condition or time of an event.

The subject and verb (or verb phrase) right after a subordinating conjunction such as "when", "if", "while", "as" or "using" that begins a conditional or temporal clause, e.g. "when you run it" or "if the list is empty". The strongest activations fall on pronoun-plus-action pairs like "you attempt" or "we looked".

15423.name: Separator and delimiter tokens (spaces, hyphens, periods, slashes) placed immediately before a number or code segment inside structured strings such as DOIs, URLs, dates, file names, version numbers, and metadata like ratings or word/page counts, where a name or word gives way to digits.

Separator tokens, mostly hyphens and bare spaces, that link two alphanumeric segments in URLs, slugs, dates, IDs, product codes and metadata strings. They usually come right before a number, e.g. "Words 3 Pages" or "line 32". A few weak activations fall on ordinary words in prose.

1546.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires across the continuation of an ongoing phrase, clause, or list. It marks the middle and tail tokens that elaborate or complete a structure begun earlier: the remaining list items, argument fields in code, the rest of a purpose or relative clause. It appears in prose, code, citations and dates alike. Activation usually builds toward the end of the unit and stops at sentence or line boundaries, without clear dependence on topic.

A broad, diffuse feature that fires on predictable continuations of text, especially where content repeats or follows an established pattern. It responds most strongly to copying earlier material: repeated phrases, recurring identifiers, lists and sequences (RC17 RC18…, "String #", 666…, "/ / /"), repeated code calls or tags, and formulaic structures like SQL conditions, lambda chains and key-value dicts.

155.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires on content-bearing words across varied text, including code. It is strongest on the head nouns and final subword pieces of specialized or technical noun phrases, especially medical and scientific terms such as 'eye movements', 'saccades', 'syncope' and 'DBS', and on product or entity names. Function words get little activation.

A diffuse, weak feature with no single clear trigger. It fires broadly across structured or technical text (code, markdown tables and lists, math variable definitions, problem statements, garbled or noisy text). Its peaks fall on key content noun phrases or technical terms being specified or defined, such as "throwing exceptions", "Faraday rotation", "tan"/"cot", "MFA" and "Athletes' Association". Secondary activity appears on surrounding formatting tokens like pipes, newlines, brackets and whitespace runs.

15561.name: Fires weakly on tokens that repeat or continue a pattern already in context, an induction-like copying signal. Typical cases are repeated words or strings (Image Image…, true true…, Why? Why? Why, abcabc, Omnomnom, eewwwwwww, JcakJcak), continuations of ordered sequences (alphabet letters, CDEFGABC, 12345678) and pieces of random or ID-like character strings.

15569.name: Language about self-perception, ego and status: people regarding themselves as superior, in charge or entitled, plus related notions of power, dominance, hierarchy, arrogance and ambition. The strongest cases are explicit attitude phrases such as "a superior attitude towards" and "see themselves as in charge." Weaker hits are scattered words about self-regard, confidence or how one thinks of oneself.

15583.name: Fires most strongly on backtick characters, both single inline-code backticks (e.g. around `Webhooks`, and backtick-like transliteration marks in Arabic) and triple-backtick code-fence closings. It responds weakly to other markup or formatting delimiters such as closing LaTeX math (}$, $), markdown asterisks and angle brackets. Activations on ordinary words are faint and scattered.

15677.name: Main predicates in news-style lead sentences announcing a new event or development, especially the verb phrase right after the subject (e.g. 'has begun production in', 'has launched', 'filed a lawsuit', 'have identified a', 'announced that'). Weaker activation falls on surrounding prepositions, dates and objects in these factual report or headline sentences.

News-style announcement language: the main predicate of a lead sentence reporting a new event or development, typically right after the subject (said/voted/secured/launched/has begun), often with time words (Wednesday, yesterday, this week), 'new', and the clause punctuation that follows. Strongest in press releases and news ledes.

15708.name: A diffuse, weakly activating feature. It fires on subword fragments and later pieces of multi-token names, technical terms and compounds, such as surnames, mid-word pieces, list items and equation terms. It is strongest when the span repeats or copies something already seen in the context, e.g. Edward Snowden, Erez Winner, Bletchley, Plaintiff/Defendant, 4x + 3x.

15746.name: Diffuse, low-level activation across scientific and technical expository prose. It peaks on phrases describing how something works or what it does, especially biological mechanisms and causal roles (e.g., "genome-wide control of gene expression", "alter regulatory function", "play a critical role", "responsible for", "pathogens that can cause", "other physiological functions"). Function words in these explanatory clauses also fire, such as "which are", "they are", "to" and "of the".

15805.name: Promotional or descriptive text about companies, brands and products. It fires most strongly on brand or company names (Graco, Samsung, ADATA, Philips, Goodrich) and on the words right after them that describe the company, such as "is known for its commitment", "is an awful brand", "from top brands like", "created the" and "Based in… is proud to". It also fires weakly on general marketing or press-release wording.

Mentions of companies, brands, manufacturers and makers (e.g., Patagonia, Nissan, LEGO, Google/Asus, Les Baer Custom, Avid Carp), plus the surrounding text describing what they make, design or do, especially promotional or company self-descriptions ("we produces/designs", "designed by ... built by").

1587.name: A diffuse, weakly activating feature. It fires mostly on structural and formatting tokens at line or section boundaries: newlines after headers, HTML/LaTeX markup (e.g. '<table>' followed by a newline, '\begin{align*}'), separators, ellipses and code braces. It also fires on highly predictable words inside boilerplate or formulaic phrases, such as 'stay tuned', 'be sure', 'every reasonable effort to ensure', 'hello there and welcome', 'Received:' and 'Subscription'.

15899.name: Tokens about the final or positional part of a number or string, such as digits, units, place value, endings and suffixes. Common forms are "last digit", "end in", "endswith", file extension and rhyme, plus modulo operations like "% 10" and "mod" that extract the final digit. Activation is strongest on "digit(s)".

Tokens about inspecting a specific part of a number or string, especially its final or individual elements: digits, digit sums and digital roots, last or lower bits, parity (odd/even, n&1, % 10), and endings ('ends in/with', endswith, [-1]). Strongest on 'digits' and on 'in'/'with' after 'ends'.

1593.name: A diffuse feature that fires weakly across ordinary prose on function words and parts of fixed multiword phrases, collocations and formulaic constructions (e.g. "is just one of the", "nowhere to be found", "may play a role", "managed to", "seconds away", "did the world a favor"). It peaks on the predictable middle or continuation tokens of these set expressions, typically modifiers, quantifiers, light verbs and prepositions, rather than on content-heavy nouns.

A diffuse, weak feature that fires on ordinary function words and clause-continuation tokens (auxiliaries such as do/does/did/is/are, and words like 'that', 'the', 'in', 'if', 'best', 'final') in the middle of fluent explanatory or instructional prose, especially assistant-style answers, tutorials and code comments. The strongest activations fall on predictable multi-word phrase continuations ('in place at', 'if they are', 'can't seem to stay', 'you want information') rather than on content-specific words.

15977.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly in code, HTML tables and structured text. It peaks on the token that finishes a name, identifier or field value right before a delimiter or closing element. Typical hits are closing tags such as and , the ends of variable or ID names (_USER, ATIONS, relay, Cause), and closing quotes or commas around string keys. In prose it fires on scattered nouns or punctuation that end a term or clause.

16061.name: Language about technological or scientific progress and advancement, such as words like "advancements", "progress", "new technologies", "cutting-edge", "high-tech", "improved" and "modern", plus phrases like "progress has been made in recent years". Activation is strongest on explicit progress/advancement nouns and their following "in [field] technology" phrases.

Language about technological progress and advancement, such as "developments", "technology", "advancements", "improvements", "evolved over time", "state-of-the-art", "newer more accurate devices", and the capabilities or limits these bring. It is strongest on nouns like developments, improvements and technology.

1607.name: Marks plural noun phrases that refer to sets of several items (representatives, witnesses, presentations, books, museums, disorders, games, models), along with the words tied to them: quantifiers and counts (all, both, five, three, "of these"), plural pronouns (they, them, their, these) and plural verbs (are). Activation often extends to the following comma or period, or to list-ending brackets in code.

16079.name: A diffuse, weakly firing feature on discourse pivot points: clause or sentence boundaries (commas, periods, question marks, line breaks) and the words just after them that introduce contrast, debate, criticism or differing viewpoints. Typical triggers are "However, its use has also been criticized", "open to debate", "Experts debate", "some leading experts" and rhetorical questions. It fires most strongly when text shifts toward controversy or evaluation.

Weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly at clause and sentence boundaries, such as periods, paragraph breaks, and the opening words of the next sentence. It is strongest at discourse pivots that introduce a contrast or shift, like "but come up against", "although not without controversy" and "there is debate". It also fires lightly on function words and auxiliaries (has, been, the, ’t) in running prose.

16161.name: A diffuse, weakly activating feature that fires on content-bearing noun-phrase tokens (often the start or subword pieces of rare, technical, or proper-noun terms) such as place and organization names, product codes, scientific and technical vocabulary, and the head nouns of the topic being discussed, typically right after a determiner, preposition, or verb.

16175.name: The word "County"/"county" (and "counties"), especially as the final part of a place name like "Lake County" or "Orange County". Weaker activation on other words or word-endings that complete a geographic or institutional name, such as River, Creek, Township, district, Province, City and University.

16209.name: Discourse transitions right after a statement ends, especially after an enumerated list ("A, B and C"). Activation falls on the closing period or line break and the opening words of the next sentence or clause, such as "The", "It", "This", "For example," or "Out of these three". These openers often refer back to or elaborate on what came before. Activation is weak and diffuse.

16219.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly within narrative clauses about motion, travel or journeys. Typical contexts are going along a way, road or route, walking past, heading somewhere, reaching an altitude or destination, and objects popping out or being carried along. It also fires on related nouns such as roads, vehicles, paths and streams, and on the clause connectors or commas inside these event descriptions. The strongest hits are phrases like "on the way I said to" and "driving down a rural road at".

16258.name: A diffuse feature with weak activation on many ordinary mid-sequence tokens, such as function words, list items, dates and phone-number digits. It fires most strongly inside arithmetic or mathematical expressions, peaking on operators like ÷ and minus, parentheses and numeric operands (e.g., "÷ 2 - ( 8 - 6 )", "+(-3)", "C/360").

Weak, diffuse activation on tokens in noisy, low-coherence or highly structured symbolic text. It fires mostly on numbers, arithmetic operators and other symbols inside math expressions, number lists, code and garbled strings. Mid-sequence tokens in a pattern of digits or operators trigger it, especially in arithmetic expressions such as ÷ or fractions. It also fires occasionally on random words within incoherent prose.

16265.name: Highly predictable tokens inside rigid repetitive or templated sequences, such as runs of repeated characters, whitespace or newlines, code indentation, and the opening quote before "object" in JSON schema "type": "object" fields.

16298.name: Structural and formatting punctuation in document scaffolding. It fires most on periods in abbreviations and section numbers ("Fig.", "Jan.", "1. Introduction", "12.1.1") and on commas between citation numbers ("[7, 8]", "{1,2}"). It also fires on bullet-list leading spaces, section headers ("Abstract", "INTRODUCTION", "Index Terms"), superscript markup and boilerplate like "advertisement" or "navigation".

1641.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires across long stretches of ordinary running prose rather than on any single word. It is strongest on content words in descriptive or explanatory passages that spell out concrete details: physical objects and their parts (control panels and bulbs, ceramic fibers and matrix, duct tape, sword), mechanisms and processes (reacts with, cleared out, determines how), and features or properties (editing tools, simplicity of the shape). Function words, punctuation and newlines inside these descriptive clauses also activate weakly, while names, framing words and boilerplate tend to drop out.

A broad, diffuse feature that fires across technical and instructional content (code, comments, math derivations, format specifications, CLI/config explanations), often in noisy or garbled text. It is strongest on explanatory noun phrases that describe what something is, how it is structured or how it works, such as 'the hollow part of', 'the affine expression', 'sequence of bytes' or 'Module Replacement plugin'. Weaker activation spreads over whitespace, newlines and code punctuation.

16427.name: In code, the opening token right after a control keyword (if, switch, while, echo, [ ) that starts the condition or argument expression, usually a variable sigil or opening paren like ' "$', ' ${', ' $', ' (', '($'. It fires most strongly on shell test brackets such as `if [ "$var"`.

16439.name: Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences: repeated numbers, symbols, separators and code lines (e.g., 30, 31, 30…; -*-*; ~~88~~88; repeated '; ' lines; 16x16x16). The token itself repeats an earlier element in the same run, and activation is strongest in highly regular, predictable repetition. Weak, scattered activation on ordinary words elsewhere.

Tokens inside long runs of repeated tokens or symbols (whitespace/newlines, emoji, arrows, letters, code fences, filler strings). Activation builds as the same token or short pattern keeps repeating, firing on the later repetitions of a degenerate repetitive sequence.

1644.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature that spans ordinary running prose, especially the predicate parts of clauses: verb phrases, their complements, and descriptive or evaluative modifiers ('can present a few extra problems', 'revolve around instant gratification'). Activation rises somewhat in emotionally weighted or reflective statements ('can no longer face the tragedy', 'could signify that'). It largely skips names, numbers and technical labels.

A diffuse, weak feature that fires across running clauses in explanatory, instructional, or assistant-style prose (code comments, math, Q&A, narrative). It tends to activate on function and content words in the middle of elaborating or qualifying phrases (e.g., "not sure about the value", "mind playing tricks", "claimed to have", "very broad from just"), rather than on any specific token type. Activation peaks inside hedging, reasoning, or descriptive continuations.

16461.name: Strongest on the '>' + newline token that ends HTML/XML closing tags (, , , ), especially in runs of nested closing tags. It fires more weakly on connective or punctuation tokens that open or sit inside parenthetical asides and examples, such as '(', 'e.g.,', 'of' in 'the case of', and 'let' in 'let's'.

1648.name: Line-break tokens (newline, often merged with the preceding punctuation such as period, semicolon, brace, colon or quote) that end a line, sentence, heading or code statement, across prose, lists, metadata, LaTeX and code. A single newline tends to activate more strongly than a double newline.

Line-break tokens, often merged with preceding end-of-line punctuation (periods, colons, brackets, backticks, spaces), that end a line of text, code, or a list item. Single newlines fire most strongly, while multiple newlines fire a bit less.

16494.name: Final tokens of the content words in image captions, photo credits and alt-text descriptions, such as places, names, dates and the objects shown. The text often sits just before a line break, a credit like AP or Getty, or the start of an article. Activation is strongest at the end of caption phrases describing location and date, e.g. 'airport in Thailand', 'Festival in France in 2012', 'Oct. 5, 2020'.

Content words in photo-caption-style descriptions of a scene, especially where the event, location (venue, city, country) and date are given (e.g. "speaks at the funeral of… in Tokyo on Saturday"). The strongest activations fall on place names, venue nouns and date tokens in these captions.

16495.name: The word "conformal" (and related forms like conformable, quasiconformal), with the strongest activation on its final "al" piece. It fires most in math/physics settings (conformal field theory, conformal maps and transformations) and also in conformal radiotherapy and coatings. Weak activations occur on related scale and symmetry terms (scale, scaling, invariance, modular, Weyl) and on stray tokens such as bullet points.

16514.name: Arguments of C socket API calls (accept, connect, bind), especially the comma and the cast to (struct sockaddr *)& before the address variable. It also fires weakly on scattered tokens in code and prose.

1654.name: The first subword fragment (often one or two letters) of a word that the tokenizer splits into multiple pieces, most often rare proper nouns, names, acronyms or unusual words (e.g. "M"+"ikhailov", "Qu"+"inoa", "D"+"CLC"). It fires most strongly on capitalized name or acronym starts.

16568.name: Tokens that mark the start of unit-test code. The strongest is the ".junit" token in Java imports such as "import org.junit...", especially its first occurrence in a file. It also fires more weakly on "(test" in Rust's #[cfg(test)] attribute before a tests module. Scattered faint activations on ordinary prose and HTML tokens appear to be noise.

1657.name: Content nouns and noun phrases (often multiword compounds or technical/domain terms) that name the key topic entity or concept in a clause, typically the head noun after a preposition or determiner, e.g. object-of-preposition or subject noun phrases. Function words are rarely marked.

Content-word nouns (and noun-modifier compounds) that name the topic, object, or entity being talked about, often the head of a noun phrase after a preposition or determiner (e.g. "the polygon", "chord chart", "team names", "error message"). This shows up across prose, math, and noisy or garbled code and multilingual text, and activation is weak and diffuse.

16570.name: A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires on scattered tokens (function words, digits, operators, identifier suffixes, separators) in technical, mathematical, scientific, code and structured web text. It is strongest mid-exposition, just before a specific variable, value or quantity is introduced, as in "the number…", "is calculated as" or "v01 for this… close to v1".

16585.name: Mostly very weak, scattered activations on glitchy or garbled mixed-language text, code fragments and list markers ("-", "1.", "="). The one clear, strong trigger is the odd token "INFRINGEMENT", especially in the form "-INFRINGEMENT", appearing as a non-sequitur inside noisy or nonsensical text.

16606.name: Scientific and technical prose, mostly physics, astrophysics, chemistry and earth science, describing physical processes and mechanisms. Activation lands on the nouns and verbs that name physical entities and what they do: particles, photons, electrons, emissions, growth, transport, collisions, migration, form, accumulate. It is strongest inside causal clauses such as "photons are needed for ionizing", "scattering of seed photons off the electrons" or "would have been trapped there by".

Tokens within scientific explanations of physical processes, chiefly particles or bodies moving, colliding, interacting or exchanging energy (e.g. 'bounce against each other', 'gain energy from', 'interaction between the particles', 'moves… directed against'). The marked words are usually the verbs, prepositions and nouns that spell out what the moving entity does or acts on. Activation is strongest in dense particle/energy descriptions and weak or scattered on unrelated text.

16610.name: The "UTF"/"utf" token naming a character encoding (as in UTF-8), strongest in HTML meta charset declarations and weaker in Python coding headers and encode/decode calls.

16712.name: Fires on string-length functions in code, most strongly on C/PHP "strlen" and also on "len", "nchar", ".length" and "LEN", including when they show up in garbled text. It also fires weakly on long runs of dashes in markdown table separator rows and on a few scattered code tokens.

16741.name: Separators and boundaries inside lists of people's names, as in committee rosters, meeting attendee lists, signature blocks, and editor or author credits. It fires on the commas, newlines, colons and parentheses between names, and on titles and degree abbreviations (Prof., Dr., Ph.D., Chair). It is strongest where one listed person ends and the next begins.

16764.name: Language tied to to-do lists, checklists and task management: lists, items, tasks, things to do, prioritizing, getting work done, pending items, check marks and checkbox brackets. It fires most strongly on "to-do" and an empty checkbox "[ ]".

16786.name: Dashes (em/en dashes, hyphens, double hyphens) used mid-sentence after a complete clause to introduce an elaboration, aside, or continuation. Occasionally semicolons, colons, or ellipses serve the same role, and the word right after the dash (when, but, from, albeit) is sometimes included.

16803.name: The acronym "DRM"/"drm", whether it means Digital Rights Management in media and tech discussions or the Linux Direct Rendering Manager graphics subsystem in code. It fires most strongly on the lowercase kernel/driver usage and also catches split forms such as "DR"+"M" and random strings containing "drm".

16806.name: The final subword token that completes a Latin binomial species name (the species epithet's ending, e.g. "aure-us", "cerevis-iae", "lipoly-tica"), most often for bacteria, fungi and other microbes. It also fires weakly on the endings of other multi-token technical terms such as disease and drug names.

16810.name: The "Override" in Java's @Override annotation. It fires most strongly when the annotation sits inside an anonymous inner class created inline, such as new View.OnClickListener() { or new Runnable() {. It is weaker on ordinary class-level method overrides like toString or onCreate.

The Java @Override annotation (the "Override" token after @). It fires most strongly when the annotation sits inside an anonymous inner class, such as new View.OnClickListener() { @Override ... }, Runnable, or Comparator. It fires more weakly on top-level class method overrides. Activations on unrelated prose words are negligible.

16822.name: Tokens immediately preceding a reference number such as a page or line number: the <td> cell before page numbers in table-of-contents HTML, "p." before a page, "line" or the colon after a filename in stack traces, and the line/column digits themselves. Weaker activations on scattered prose tokens appear to be noise.

16830.name: Double-backtick tokens (``), mostly the opening part of Markdown code fences (```) or inline code delimiters, and also LaTeX-style opening quotation marks (``). Activation is strongest at the start of a code block or quoted span. Weak activations appear on other opening delimiters such as „ and $$.

16875.name: The word "data" (any casing), mostly in scientific and technical writing where it starts a compound or heading such as "data analysis", "data processing", "Data extraction" or "Data source".

16894.name: Tokens inside loop and conditional control flow, mostly in code: the closing parenthesis, brace, colon, or indentation right after a while/if/else/except condition, and the loop body that follows (continue, break, increments, join, print, endl). Prose matches are weaker and come from analogous conditional or repetition phrasing, such as the comma after an "if" clause or words like "twice", "retry a total of 5 times", "every single", and "keeps".

16910.name: Tokens in code (and technical prose) that name or declare handles and pointers to system resources, such as file pointers and descriptors (FILE *fp, FileDescriptor, FreeFile), thread and window handles (m_hThread, hwnd, Hdl hdl) and the word "handle" itself. Activation is strongest on pointer-or-handle prefixes and type markers. Weaker activations fall on generic type and identifier fragments in variable declarations.

16931.name: Strategic moves and tactical play in competitive games, most strongly chess (forcing positions, threats, pawn sacrifices, breaking a defense). Weaker activations come from poker hand analysis, card drafting, sports and wargame scenarios. Isolated low activations on generic tokens in unrelated text are noise.

16940.name: Tokens in the middle of predictable, repetitive structured sequences, mostly runs of dot leaders in tables of contents between an entry title and its page number. Also fires on similar mid-pattern spots in HTML table tags, numeric lists, and citation dates.

16951.name: Code annotations and attributes that bind or map method parameters and fields to external data, mainly Java/Spring ones like @PathVariable, @RequestParam, @JoinColumn, @Param and @ModelAttribute, plus C# [FromBody]. The closing quote-parenthesis after the annotation's name argument (e.g. ("id")) also fires. Weaker activity appears on request-parameter accessors such as .getParameter and .params.

16958.name: A diffuse feature that fires weakly on assorted tokens in structured, technical, or web-scraped and boilerplate text (lists, tables, LaTeX, report front matter, word lists). It peaks on the hyphenated token "-sidebar" in CSS-style class names and leftover web-page markup, such as "qode-content-sidebar" and "mma-sidebar".

16963.name: Weak, diffuse activation on biology and biochemistry vocabulary, mainly words and word pieces about organisms producing or secreting chemical compounds and their biological roles (metabolites, pheromones, antibiotics, signaling, pigments, acids, hydrocarbons). The strongest activations fall on 'secondary metabolites', pheromones and microbial production. Scattered activations on name and word fragments in scientific text are low.

16970.name: The first subword token of a proper name (usually a surname or brand) when it is repeated after appearing earlier, as in citation keys, parenthetical author references, handles, URLs, emails and speaker labels. Activation peaks at the opening fragment of the reused name, especially in citations like \cite{kre…}, [Sch92] and (Pres…kitt et al.).

16988.name: Tokens that open a parenthetical or nonrestrictive modifier attached to a just-named noun (often a person or organization): relative pronouns like "who", "which" and "whose" after a comma or dash, plus the comma or dash itself and appositive starters such as "a" or "the". These signal that extra descriptive information about the entity is coming.

16995.name: Language about buildings, facilities and physical structures being built, extended, renovated, destroyed or replaced. It fires most strongly on parts and additions of structures (wings, extensions, new parts) and on words like "new", "building" and "renovations", plus the function words and punctuation near these descriptions.

17021.name: The first coordinate pair (x y numbers) right after a curve command letter (especially "C", also Q/T) in SVG path data, i.e., the first control point of a Bézier curve; weak on other coordinate-like numbers.

17024.name: Highly predictable tokens inside stock boilerplate, chiefly "WARRANTY" in the GPL license phrase "WITHOUT ANY WARRANTY". Weaker activations land on the colon in repeated wiki diff headers ("Line N: Line N:") and on other formulaic continuations.

17036.name: Positions where a specific answer or value is about to be given. The clearest case is the colon after "Answer" in multiple-choice quizzes, just before the letter choice. It also fires on tokens just before a predicted value, such as " $" before a number or "the" inside quiz-style questions, and on sentence ends just before a new "Question:". Overall it tracks quiz/QA formatting and anticipation of an answer.

17049.name: Final subword pieces that complete a person's surname, usually an unusual multi-token one, in author lists, citations and bylines. Activation is strongest on the closing fragment of the name and sometimes carries onto the next punctuation, affiliation superscript or line break.

17065.name: Primarily the method-call token ".invoke"/".Invoke" attached to an object or delegate in code and stack traces (e.g. MouseDown.Invoke, getCommandMap.invoke, _ZoneDelegate.invokeTask). Other activations are weak and scattered, falling on spaces before numbers, domain suffixes and common function words.

17095.name: Variables and other terms in the middle or later part of a math expression, most strongly a variable right after a coefficient in a polynomial's linear term (e.g. the "x" in "2x" in x^2 + 2x + 1). Weak activations also appear on occasional non-math tokens such as sentence-ending periods and commas.

17105.name: Head nouns that close the name of an award, prize, contest, grant, fund, exam, or project (e.g. "Award", "Prize", "Cup", "Fund", "competition", "grant"), usually right after a proper-name or descriptive modifier. "Award" and "Prize" in honor or recognition contexts activate most strongly.

17106.name: Unusual Unicode dash and line characters, mostly the hyphen (U+2010) and horizontal bar (―, U+2015), plus non-breaking hyphens, en dashes and box-drawing lines. They appear singly or in long repeated runs, usually inside garbled, code-like or mixed-language text rather than as ordinary ASCII hyphens.

17134.name: The "h" token (often fused as "<h") that opens an HTML heading tag like <h1>–<h4>, strongest inside HTML/markup code. It also fires weakly on related mentions of headings (the word "headings", H1/H2, html.H1, HBox) and on the "h" in LaTeX commands such as \hline and \hfill.

17138.name: Words that introduce an aggregate statistic, mostly "average" and also "mean", "Total", "per", "common" (a spun synonym for average). They usually sit before the measured quantity (price, rating, salary, lifespan, cost), often in data headers or in phrases like "The average X is…". Activation is strongest for average prices, ratings and usage figures.

17142.name: A diffuse, non-semantic feature that fires on boundary tokens marking a transition into the next phrase or structured field: closing punctuation (periods, commas, "\$", ").") right before metadata such as citations, DOIs, IDs, usernames or dates; articles and prepositions ("the", "a", "of", "in") just before their noun phrase; separator spaces before values; and discourse openers ("Please", "Well", "however"). It tracks where one segment ends and a new, often formulaic, one begins rather than any particular word meaning.

17159.name: The subject at the start of a conditional clause: determiners, pronouns or nouns ("the", "a", "this", "any") right after "If", "when", "where" or "unless". These mostly appear in boilerplate license, copyright and instruction text. Weaker hits include "copy of" in license phrases.

17162.name: A comma that closes a long introductory or descriptive clause and comes right before the main subject of the sentence, here in product-description text.

17181.name: Words for defense (defense/defence, defensive, defender, defending, the D in D-line), strongest in team sports, especially American football and basketball (defensive coordinator, defensive tackle, a team's defense). Weaker for defensive meanings in military, gaming, biology or workplace contexts.

Words built on the root "defen-" (defense/defence, defensive, defending, defender, defensively, defenseman), mainly in sports contexts describing a team's defensive unit, positions, or play. Activation peaks on "defensive" used as a modifier for football positions or team units (defensive lineman/end/back/line/front) and on team defenses, is weaker for soccer "defence," "defending champion," and non-sport or psychological uses.

17207.name: The token "sh", usually with a leading slash ("/sh"), firing hardest on the shell path in shebang lines ("#!/bin/sh") and other references to the sh shell (execv("/bin/sh"), "env sh", "sudo sh"). It fires weakly when "sh" is just the start of an unrelated word or path segment (e.g., "shipping", "shoves", "sys/shm.h").

17226.name: Second-clause verbs and conjunctions in boilerplate disclaimers and notices, mostly the "and" after a negated or qualifying statement and the modal or verb that follows it (may, should, is, are used, could). Typical contexts are "does not constitute X and should not…", "is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged", "not passed on… and are used solely" and "does not purport… and shall be used". Activation is strongest on the modal or verb in these legal/disclaimer phrasings.

17229.name: The "function" keyword opening an anonymous/IIFE-style JavaScript function, especially right after an opening parenthesis like "(function" or "$(function". "(()" arrow-IIFE starts fire similarly. Final closing braces or tags that end a code file fire weakly.

17235.name: Internal parts of structured classification and registry codes, most strongly Enzyme Commission numbers ("EC x.x.x.x") after enzyme names. Weaker hits fall on the hyphens and digits inside CAS registry numbers, patent classification codes (e.g. G01, C07), protein family numbering and gene family names (SLC18). Activation peaks on the middle separators and digits of these hierarchical identifiers.

17239.name: Phrases in scientific or academic writing that introduce the authors' own work and its contributions, such as "Here we", "In this study,", "We show", "this paper", "the present work", and "herein". The signal is strongest on "Here", "we", "study" and "show", especially where an abstract turns from background to what the authors did.

17246.name: Head nouns, or the final subword of a noun, naming a technical device, instrument, component or functional unit, often an agent noun ending in -er/-or/-ator/-iter. Examples include modulator, saturator, mixer, switch, amplifier, limiter, controller, telescope and balancer. Activation is strongest on the suffix that marks the word as a device.

17247.name: Month names (full, abbreviated, or capitalized) in the second or later date of a publication or revision timeline, coming right after words like "Accepted", "Revised", "Updated", or "Published". These appear mostly in academic manuscript headers. The strongest activations come when the month directly follows the keyword. Weaker activations fall on the space before the day number in day-month formats.

17252.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires in mostly technical or instructional text about storing, passing, embedding or protecting data and information (secrets, input, URLs, strings, keys, text fields). It picks out the words for the data item, the container or location, or the method of conveying it (e.g. "carry it on-board as", "save data using", "in brackets", "as input").

17257.name: Separators and numbers in academic citation references marking the transition from volume/issue to page numbers: the colon, space, or parenthesis after a volume/issue number, the first page number, and the dash in page ranges (e.g. "243:646–648", "82, 65-82").

17265.name: Mathematical algebraic-structure terminology, especially group and Lie theory: words like "group", "reductive", "Lie algebras", "subgroup", "SU(2)" and quantum groups U_q(g). Activation is strongest on the head nouns and qualifiers in phrases naming algebraic or Lie groups. Weak, scattered activation occurs elsewhere on other math or technical tokens.

17269.name: Speech-attribution phrases for quoted or reported statements: verbs of saying or thinking (said, says, explained, claims, admits, added, continues) and the speaker reference attached to them (pronoun, name ending, 'according to X', interview speaker labels). Activation is strongest right after a closing quote, as in “...,” she says.

17298.name: Concessive hedging: modal verbs (especially "may be"/"might") and "while/though" clauses that grant something as possibly true before a contrasting "but". Activation is strongest on the concession itself ("may be X,") and on the comma just before "but".

17323.name: The "style" property token, strongest as ".style" accessed on a DOM element in JavaScript (el.style.display/position/color). It fires more weakly on other styling or configuration accessors such as a style attribute, getStyle, plt.style, .config/.configure, .classList and .css(.

17326.name: The program or executable name at the start of a shell command line (e.g. python, php, ruby, gcc, curl, cat, npm), especially interpreters invoked to run a script file. Activation is strongest for interpreter names like python/php/ruby, weaker for flags and subcommands that follow.

1733.name: The final word or token of a short noun phrase that ends a parenthetical, appositive, or list item, i.e. the token immediately before a closing parenthesis, comma, dash, or period, such as "(the loop)", "(3.6 m)", "Google Chrome," or "de facto standard,". It marks the completion of an inserted or clarifying phrase.

17342.name: Mainly fires on "kinase" and the final "K" of "PI3K" in phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase signaling pathway text. It peaks on the "K" in PI3K/Akt. It responds more weakly to other enzyme-name endings such as "-ase", "-ases", PTEN's "EN" and PP2A's "A".

17385.name: Tokens in passages describing the past or history, such as historical eras, events, dates and past figures (World War One, the Nixon administration, 1984, Sept. 11, Truman/Eisenhower), childhood memories, and origins or first occurrences. The strongest activations fall on named historical periods and events that anchor a 'back then' timeframe.

174.name: A diffuse, weakly firing pattern on content words that complete a phrase, mostly head nouns serving as the object of a verb or preposition (e.g. "raising money", "pet stores", "on walls"). It also fires on some predicate adjectives and participles and on following commas or conjunctions at phrase boundaries. There is no single topic, so it looks like a general marker of a phrase's main noun or argument completion.

Content-bearing words that complete a phrase or clause, mostly the head noun of a noun phrase (often after "the", "a" or a preposition) naming the object of discussion, such as question, code, input, variable, file, help. The text is mostly technical, programming or assistant-style. Weaker activations fall on verbs or participles that end a clause, like done, failed, provided and help.

17403.name: The Android method name "findViewById" in Java code, usually after a cast like (Button) or after a view object with a dot, e.g. "= (TextView) findViewById(R.id...)". Weak, scattered activations show up on spacing and boilerplate tokens in templated web text.

17413.name: The day number in a written calendar date, usually right after a month name (e.g. "On April 3,"), often with an ordinal suffix like st/th. It fires most strongly in sentence-opening "On [Month] [day]" phrases introducing an event. Where the day comes first ("13 May", "19th November"), the month name is marked instead.
The day-of-month number in a date that follows a month name or numeric month, usually in narrative phrases like "On [Month] [day]" that introduce when an event happened.

17427.name: Word-initial tokens that form the first piece of a larger compound or multi-token word, such as "high" in the hyphenated "high-speed" or the Turkish stem "iç" in "içeriğe" (from "skip to main content").

17464.name: Input-direction markers in code, chiefly the keyword "in" (also "IN", "inout", "in:") used as a parameter-passing mode or input flag, e.g. Ada "in out", Swift "inout", C++ ios::in. Activation is strongest for these parameter modes. Weaker activations occur on related parameter terms such as "input", "parameter", "ByVal", "ref" and the file-mode 'r'.

17474.name: Separators placed right before line numbers in error stack traces, such as the colon after a filename in JS/C++ traces (file.js:123:45) or the " line " text in Python tracebacks.

17490.name: In code, the indentation whitespace and closing braces (or else/dedent lines) that come right after a block ends with return, break or pass, i.e. the dedent where nested scopes close. It fires most strongly on leading spaces/tabs before '}' and on following 'else'/'return' lines. There are weak, sporadic hits on line breaks and structural tokens in non-code text.

17502.name: Names and descriptions of specific physical locations or venues where something happens or is situated (buildings, arenas, parks, plazas, centers, landmarks). It fires mostly on the head noun of the place name (Center, Arena, Plaza, Palace, Zone, garden), often after prepositions like 'at' or 'in', and sometimes carries through to a following 'in [City]'.

17507.name: The "sec" prefix inside LaTeX \label{} or \ref{} keys (e.g. sec:intro), strongest right after \section{Introduction} or Acknowledgments headers; weaker for in-text section references and other label prefixes like "tab".

17508.name: Adjective-forming suffix tokens (mostly "-imal" in proximal and "-al" in distal, also "-ical" in apical, "-inal" in luminal, "-ateral", "-ral") completing anatomical or positional terms that say where something lies relative to a body, cell or structure. Activation is strongest for proximal/distal in anatomical contexts. Weaker hits include standalone positional words (upper, top, basal) and other "-al"/"-imal" words (primal, optimal, final).

17513.name: Opening tokens at the very start of a code or markup block, typically "<!" beginning a DOCTYPE or HTML comment, or a docstring opener, appearing right after a header such as "assistant", a code fence, or a repeated DOCTYPE line. A few activations fall on odd symbol tokens in garbled code.

17516.name: Tokens in references to earlier or related documents, publications, filings and events: words like published, issued, filed, "application No", "related articles/tests", "my review", "see the prints", links (http), and the final digits of dates/years. Together they point to prior records, citations or dated releases.

17518.name: Section-boundary tokens in academic paper front matter, mainly the "Abstract" heading or paragraph breaks that come right after author affiliations and before the main body (abstract, keywords, received dates). There is also some weak activation on similar structural tokens in web or search metadata, such as ":true" and "Tickets".

17525.name: Software installation and filesystem terms, especially names of directories, folders and file types where programs get installed or stored (e.g. /sbin, /bin, install, binaries, executables, dll, runtime, dev files, scripts, tmp, Applications, program_files). Activation is strongest on path segments and install targets in build or setup instructions. Weak, scattered activations also appear on list punctuation and structural tokens.

Category/type words that classify a resource or component, chiefly in software and computing contexts: directory names in file paths (template, Bin, usr, var, headers, init.d), and modifiers naming a kind of file, code or build element (DLL files, system apps, read-only sections, compile dependency, library path, classpath). It fires more weakly on similar classifier nouns elsewhere (staff, books, assets, parking, stationery).

17540.name: The digit "3" as a standalone number token in numeric, mathematical, code, or tabular contexts (coefficients, decimals, operands, list items). It fires most strongly when 3 is a coefficient or term in an algebraic expression. It rarely fires on the word "three".

17541.name: Headers for metadata and classification fields in scholarly paper front matter, usually right after the abstract. These include "Index Terms", "PACS numbers:", "JEL Classification:", "Key words:", "OCIS codes:", "MSC:" and "AMS subject classifications". The feature fires on the label word and its following colon or separator, and on punctuation between the classification codes. It peaks on "PACS numbers:". It also fires weakly on the "I." before INTRODUCTION and on similar labeled code fields such as HS Code, CAS Number and CPT Codes.

17543.name: Junctures in procedural or technical text (instructions, API docs, code) where one action or step ends and its result or the next step follows: sentence and clause boundaries after an action, step numbers, "and"/"will" connectives, and especially the hand-off to a response or output (e.g. "Response from the API:", closing parentheses or braces after a call).

Tokens in process or step-by-step descriptions at the point where an action has been performed and its outcome or next stage follows. Typical cues are waiting, a response or feedback, results, success or failure (e.g. 'If your request fails', 'sit back and wait a few minutes', 'a call succeeded') and sentence or step boundaries leading into the next step.

17545.name: Imperative task verbs that open the question in a math or problem statement, mostly "Find", "Calculate" and "Compute" (also "to find"), typically right after the givens and just before what is being asked for. Weaker activation on "of" in "the value of". Strongest when a sentence starts with the verb after a math setup.

17554.name: Null or disabling values assigned to properties or parameters in code and markup, mostly "none" in CSS declarations (strongest for list-style-type: none, border: none, text-decoration: none), plus similar values such as off, false, null, 0, None and transparent that switch a setting off or clear it.

17567.name: Abbreviated honorifics and titles placed before a person's name, such as Dr, Prof, Mr, Mrs, Ms, Sen, Rep, Gov, Gen and Lt, usually followed by a period. 'Dr' fires most strongly, especially when it introduces a named expert after verbs like 'said', 'by' or 'contact'. Weak activations also appear on other short abbreviations, such as 'St' for saint and 'Re'.

17583.name: The word "absolute" as a CSS positioning value, chiefly in "position: absolute" declarations and style.position = 'absolute' assignments, plus prose mentions of absolute(ly) positioned elements. "fixed" as a position value and unrelated filler words fire only weakly.

17587.name: Nonlinear activation and transfer functions, especially in neural networks: ReLU, sigmoid, softmax, tanh, logistic, plus words like "activation", "nonlinearity", "link function" and "hidden" layers. ReLU and sigmoid tokens activate most strongly. Weaker activations occur on related math functions (hyperbolic, sinh, clipping, max(0, …)) and on generic "function" or "layer" terms.

17591.name: Formal institutional and bureaucratic language: official bodies (Board, Committee, Commission, Executive Director) acting on matters such as approving, investigating, electing, licensing, enforcing, and reviewing complaints, plus the structure of legal rules, meeting minutes, and official reports. Activation is weak and diffuse except for the strongest case, "The Board became aware of" in a disciplinary context.

17592.name: Tokens that sit right before a link, value, or worked example. The strongest are HTML attribute names, especially " href" after "<a", plus " src", " type" and " uri". Weaker hits are introducer punctuation such as the comma in "So," or "For example,", "e.g.,", colons before answers or URLs, and "://".

17607.name: Mathematical language of correspondence and structure-preserving mapping: strongest on "isomorphic/isomorphism" and the ≅/≃ symbols, and also on "bijection", "homomorphism", "one-to-one correspondence", "mapped to", "equivalent to" and "images of". It fires more weakly on the relational prepositions that follow such terms ("to", "with", "as") and diffusely on technical or explanatory text.

17625.name: Sentence or line boundaries, mostly periods and newlines, that close one segment and lead into a new one. It fires most often at the end of boilerplate or website text, such as ad-blocker notices, license and copyright statements, and publisher or attribution lines, just before the next notice or paragraph starts. It also fires weakly on the final token of repeated UI labels like "Chat Online" and "Hire writer".

17638.name: Role, position, or title nouns used as descriptors right before a person's (or ship's) name, e.g. "guitarist Anthony", "point guard Neil", "hooker Julien", "Coach Jalal". Activation is strongest on sports positions and band roles, often on the final subword such as "-er", "-ist" or "-man".

17651.name: Spreadsheet and Excel vocabulary, chiefly the words "cell", "cells" and "range" (strongest in VBA code such as .Range(" and .Cells). Weaker activations fall on related terms like formulas, fields, tables and other object or property names in code; scattered unrelated tokens fire only faintly.

Mentions of grid or spreadsheet cells, most often the word "cell"/"cells" (also Chinese 单元格). It also fires on related spreadsheet references such as VBA `Range("`, `.Value`, `(range` in formulas, and cell addresses like "D2". The strongest activations are on Excel or VBA cell references.

17658.name: The denominator unit in compound "per" measurement expressions, strongest for "/kg" in dosages (mg/kg, g/kg body weight); also fires on other per-unit denominators (/g, /ha, m², ⁻¹, per kilogram) and the following "body weight".

17686.name: Tokens that close a reference to a project-local module or base type in code, chiefly the file extension of a quoted local include ("foo.h", ".hpp", ".c", ".php") and also the terminator after a using, package, import or use line, or the base-class name after extends. Weak, sporadic activations occur on prose tokens and on newlines that end header lines.

17691.name: Two-digit (abbreviated) year numbers inside citation keys or references, e.g. \cite{Granot02}, [Bryant 86], [Neu73], typically after an author name in academic writing. Weaker on years in standard codes or dates (GOST R 50817-95, '16) and sporadic unrelated tokens.

17693.name: Nouns or phrases that name a limit, boundary or capacity that something reaches, runs out of or goes past. These usually follow words like "beyond the", "more than", "greater than the", "end of the", "edge of the", "out of", "exceeds" or "run down the". Typical targets are edge, radius, battery, number of items, maximum allowed, duration and limit; code examples mark the bound variables (lim, $late, payload length).

A limit, capacity, or available amount that something exceeds, drains, or overruns, usually right after words like "exceed", "more than", "greater than", "over the", "off the", "drain the" or "<=". Examples include battery, budget, quota, max, available space, capacity, size of the volume, and .length. Activation is strongest on code bound checks (e.g. ".length" in a length comparison) and on "available" or "capacity of".

17706.name: Diffuse, weak activation on journalistic/news-style narration, especially the words that report factual events and their context: past-tense reporting verbs (announced, released, disclosed, convicted, died, says), time expressions (in March, earlier this year, recently, yesterday) and the sentence boundaries or commas joining such factual statements. It tracks the flow of encyclopedic or news exposition rather than any single word.

A diffuse, weakly selective feature that fires on scattered tokens in fluent, explanatory, assistant-style prose. It tends to land on the word that completes a phrase or clause, often a content noun or adjective (e.g., 'year', 'mathematics', 'secure', 'compassion'), or on boundary tokens such as commas, opening parentheses and line breaks just before the text continues with elaboration. It has no clear semantic theme.

17707.name: The verb "issue" in all its forms (issued, issuing, issuance, Japanese 発行), meaning to officially put out or distribute a document, statement, warning, certificate or product. It often extends to the following article (a/an), and fires more weakly on synonyms like "released" or "uttering" and on the look-alike "ISS".

Forms of the verb "issue" (issued, issuing, issuance, issuers), meaning to officially release or distribute something such as statements, warnings, documents, cards, currency, or stamps. A following "a" or "of" is sometimes included. Other tokens show only weak, sporadic activation.

17716.name: The "usr" token in Unix paths, especially in shebang lines (#!/usr/bin/python, #!/usr/bin/env) at the very start of scripts. It fires most strongly when the shebang opens the file and much more weakly for mid-text or non-shebang paths like /usr/share.

The "usr" directory token in Unix paths, firing most strongly right after the shebang "#!/" at the start of scripts ("#!/usr/bin/env ..."). It is weaker when the slash is a separate token (" /usr") and very weak for "/usr" appearing elsewhere in text.

17721.name: Words that switch a feature or condition on or off, mostly in code and config: enable/disable, use, allow, show/hide, has, include, require, and "no"/"without". They appear most strongly as the leading part of flag or option names (ENABLE_LZ4, HAS_SITE, USE_JACOBS, --enable-, showAlpha) and in conditional or optional-inclusion phrasing.

17738.name: A diffuse feature for forward-looking or prospective content: tokens within statements about future events, plans, predictions or possibilities, such as modals (will, would, may, could, should), 'future', 'expected', 'possible', 'longer term', 'lasting implications' and upcoming-time phrases ('this summer', 'for the weekend'). It often fires on the sentence boundary or conjunction that introduces such a clause, and activations are mostly weak and scattered.

17741.name: Tokens in the middle of a multi-token word, name, or fixed phrase (word fragments like 'un|sc|athed', 'Nan|op|ore', 'Aix|-M|arseille', or function words in set expressions like 'point of view', 'piece of paper', 'all the time', 'up to date', 'U.S.'), where the following token is highly predictable. Activation is often strongest when the phrase repeats earlier text.

Tokens in the middle of a fixed collocation, name, or split word whose continuation is highly predictable: word fragments and first pieces of multi-token words (Obi-W|an, LOS AN|GELES, U|.S., 4 p|.m.), and connecting words in set phrases (more or less, all of a sudden, first of all, exactly the same, shapes and sizes).

17748.name: Digit chunks in the middle of long multi-digit numbers, mostly after a decimal point or the first few digits (decimal expansions, conversion constants, IDs, DOIs, ISBNs, phone numbers). The strongest cases are long mathematical or physical constants and precise decimals.

17756.name: Diffuse, low-intensity activation at syntactic boundaries: where a phrase or clause completes and the next constituent begins. Typical spots are the end of a subject noun phrase or the verb right after it ("builder remain liable", "division reported", "Edward is"), and commas closing introductory or subordinate clauses. Sentence-final periods and question marks also fire, as do connectives such as because, and, as, when and that. The same behavior appears in Japanese at topic and clause particles (は, が、).

17757.name: Names of third-party or standard library packages, classes and tools in code, especially in import/using statements and constructors. The strongest cases are serialization, JSON, parsing and formatting utilities such as Newtonsoft, serde, Gson, ObjectMapper, JsonSerializer and SimpleDateFormat. It also fires weakly on similar brand-like name fragments in prose.

17775.name: Mainly the colon (or the first word right after it) in "Question:" lines of synthetic reading-comprehension Q&A text, at the point where a new question begins after a passage. It fires more weakly on other junctions where a new clause or expression starts, such as math variables, closing parentheses, opening parentheses, sentence-ending periods and "However".

17779.name: File extension tokens for structured data/config formats (mainly .json, .xml, .yaml; weaker for .csv, .txt, .html) attached to filenames, strongest for config/manifest files like package.json, config.json, AndroidManifest.xml. Also fires weakly on format names alone (xml, Json) and on .json method calls.

17833.name: The first word or two right after an opening article (mostly "The", sometimes "A") at the start of a title, heading or sentence. These are usually the head noun or modifier of a noun phrase, often in a "The X of Y" construction (e.g. Importance, Art, Essence, history).

The first content word (noun or modifier) right after a determiner like "The", "An" or "This", most often at the start of a title, headline or sentence. It marks the head of the opening noun phrase, e.g. "The Power of…", "The film…", "The syndrome…".

17853.name: Tokens inside verbatim repeated text. The feature fires on words or phrases that recur several times in close succession (repeated lines, chants, list items, code lines, table cells, boilerplate such as "Invalid Input" or "Show more"), usually from the second or third repetition onward, as the model predicts a copy of earlier text. Activation is strongest in long, highly regular loops of identical multi-token lines.

Tokens inside repetitive, looping text, where the same word, phrase, symbol or number sequence is repeated many times in a row. The feature fires on later repetitions, where the next token can be predicted by copying the earlier pattern. It is often strongest on the start of the repeated unit or on tokens that begin a slight variation of it.

17863.name: Line breaks, indentation and opening '<' tokens at the very start of an HTML document, chiefly the '>\n' that ends a <!DOCTYPE html> declaration and the newline after ```html, anticipating the next tag such as <html> or <head>. It fires most strongly on malformed or unusual doctype/tag sequences.

17885.name: Words inside the condition or triggering circumstance of a rule, contract, law or policy (after 'if', 'in the event that', 'when', 'during any period', 'would be counted as'), i.e. the hypothetical event or situation under which a provision applies. It peaks in legal and contractual conditionals such as 'In the event that the vessel…', 'or has violated…' and 'when medical proof is given', with weak scattered activation elsewhere.

17898.name: A diffuse, mostly positional pattern rather than a semantic one. It fires on tokens sitting inside a fixed, highly predictable structure, where the next token is strongly constrained. These include separators inside phone numbers, the first halves of split compounds or set phrases ("game" before "pad", "in order" before "to", "w" in "w/w", "Program" before "Coordinator"), and double newlines after section titles or headings in technical and academic documents.

17925.name: Tokens made of one repeated letter, chiefly runs of 'e'/'E' ("eee", "eeee", "EEEE"). These appear in hex color codes (#eee, #eeeeee, #bbbbbb, #cccccc) and in long strings of repeated letters within garbled text or hex dumps. Activation is strongest at the start of a CSS color code or a long all-caps E run. Weak, scattered activations on ordinary words are noise.

17943.name: The word "pool" (and related forms such as "Pool", "pooling", "ThreadPool") in programming contexts naming a managed collection of reusable resources, especially thread pools and connection pools. It fires most strongly on "thread pool"/"ThreadPool". Similar resource-group names like "ThreadGroup" also fire, and there is weak noise on unrelated tokens such as indentation and bold markers.

17957.name: The final (head) word or suffix that completes a multi-word category label, tag, keyword or title, especially in comma-, semicolon- or line-separated lists of topics, skills, genres and hashtags (e.g. 'Behaviour therapy', 'puzzle games', 'Australian players'). It is usually a plural or generic category noun closing a compound term.

17969.name: The word right after "obtain" (almost always " a" in the Apache License boilerplate "You may obtain a copy of the License at"); fires weakly on other tokens following "obtain" or in similar boilerplate.

17981.name: Mostly the opening parenthesis that follows a Slashdot-style username in a "by <user> (ID)" comment header. Weaker activations land on words that introduce following examples or specifics, mainly "like", and also "source"/"cause".

18036.name: Newline tokens fused with closing delimiters, chiefly the last backtick of a ``` code fence plus a line break ("`⏎"), also triple quotes ("""⏎, '''⏎) or $ followed by a newline. These mark the start or end of a code/quoted block, often in messy, repetitive or garbled text.

18039.name: The unit word that a number is rounded or converted to, overwhelmingly "integer" (also "whole", "minute"). It fires most strongly in "to the nearest integer", more weakly in "is an integer"/"convert to an integer". There is also weak activation on the "|" column dividers in markdown table separator rows.

18040.name: The last token of an answer option in a multiple-choice list (e.g., the final digit, unit, suffix or word of options like "(C) 7/10", "D) 30 km"), marking the end of a candidate answer before the next option label or line break.

18041.name: Separator tokens (commas, 'and', 'while', 'with', newlines, semicolons, opening parentheses, periods) that occur between entries in a list of people, mostly cast or credit lists. They usually fall just after one person/role description and right before the next person's name, so they predict that a new proper name is coming.

18055.name: Present-tense speech/reporting verbs (especially "says"/"say") attributing statements or claims to a source, e.g. "he says", "researchers say", "results show", typically introducing or interrupting a quotation or reported clause; strongest for "says" after a named person in news-style attribution.

18059.name: Fires on a partial-word token, usually the first or a middle subword piece of a word split into several tokens. These are mostly rare proper nouns such as surnames, places and institutions ('Beck'→man, 'Urb'→ana, 'Wat'→ertown, 'Lie'→berman, 'Id'→so), plus technical terms and URL or path fragments. The fragment leaves the word incomplete, so the next token is a predictable completion. Occasionally it fires on whole words that commonly begin a fixed compound or phrase (e.g., 'partial' → fulfillment).

18067.name: Fires on the token right after a number, mostly a percent sign fused with following punctuation ("%)", "%,", "%.", " percent"). It is strongest on "%)" closing a parenthetical statistic, as in "(13%)". It also fires weakly on closing parentheses or other punctuation that end a parenthetical aside or measurement.

18074.name: Words describing a person's (often an athlete's or performer's) participation, tenure, or career with a team, organization, league, or venue, such as joining, playing for, returning to, leaving, or future with. Activation peaks on the prepositions and nouns linking the person to the institution ("in Pittsburgh", "future in the Reds organization", "at Man Utd", "at the club since").

18084.name: The argument or subscript token right after a function or variable name in math and code notation, most often an opening bracket fused with a variable, as in f(x, a(n, R(t, x_i, row[i. It marks the start of a function's argument list or an index.

18104.name: Subword tokens inside non-English words or phrases (Spanish, German, French, Danish, Bosnian, Lithuanian, transliterated Russian) that appear within English text, often as translations, titles, or parenthetical glosses. Activation is strongest on the continuation pieces of foreign words, such as German terms in philosophy or a Spanish translated abstract title, and weak on odd fragments in URLs or rare English words.

18106.name: Tokens right after a shell text-processing command name (sed, grep, awk, tr, head, curl, echo, perl) that open its arguments: option flags like -e, -E, -i, -n and the opening quote ' or " (or '{) that starts an inline script or regex. Strongest on the flag plus quote that begins a sed substitution expression.

18126.name: The status value given to an exit or return statement in code, such as the 1 in shell "exit 1", exit(0), EXIT_FAILURE/EXIT_SUCCESS, or return 0/1/false. It fires most strongly on "exit 1" after error or usage messages, and weakly on other error codes like HTTP 500 or exception values.

18130.name: Unit words that follow a number to state a size, mostly in digital and computing settings. The strongest are "-bit" and "bit" in phrases like 32-bit or 8-bit. Weaker hits include bits, bytes, digit, character, pin, syllable, note, hour and ounces, typically in compound measure phrases such as "N-unit".

Unit or measure words placed directly after a number, typically as compound modifiers like "32-bit", "4-digit", "15-pin", "140 characters", "Gigabit". It is strongest for "bit"/"bits" in computing contexts (bit width, encryption strength) and weaker for digits, pins, ounces, characters and similar units.

18139.name: Inner word-piece tokens of pathogen and infectious-disease names, mostly parasites, fungi and bacteria (Toxoplasma, Histoplasma, Trypanosoma cruzi, Chagas, Lyme, Borrelia burgdorferi, Coccidioides). The strongest activations are in biomedical contexts. Weaker activations appear on the same fragments in unrelated or garbled text.

18141.name: Mostly fires on operators and separators inside formal notation, strongest on the " +" joining terms on the product side of chemical equations (after an arrow, e.g. "→ C + D", "CuO + 2H2O") and on rewrite-rule outputs. It also fires on algebra joins like ")(" or ")f", minus signs and list commas in math. Weaker activations appear on generic tokens in reasoning text ("Answer:", "Wait,", "the").

18173.name: The "(R" token opening an Android resource reference (R.layout, R.id, R.string, etc.) as a method argument. It fires most strongly in setContentView(R.layout...) inside onCreate, strongly in inflater.inflate(R.layout...), and more weakly in findViewById, getString and getColor calls. It is near zero for unrelated "(R" uses like RetentionPolicy or RpcService.

18184.name: The token "pthread" (the POSIX threads library, e.g. pthread.h, pthread_mutex_lock, -pthread), firing strongest in C code. Weaker activation on related threading terms like "POSIX" and "thread", plus faint noise on LaTeX \text commands and citation punctuation.

18262.name: Nouns, usually the final token of a proper name, for geographic places and political entities (countries, states, cities, regions) and, less strongly, organizations or groups tied to them. Typical contexts are locative ones like "in X", "from X", "around the world" and "abroad". Country names that stand for a national government or actor activate most strongly.

18263.name: Separator tokens right before a page or section number, mostly in tables of contents: the last dot leaders, spaces, or table-cell tags between an entry title and its page number (e.g. "Introduction ....... 1"). Weaker hits come from similar spots before equation numbers, running page headers and footers, and timestamps.

18267.name: On the right-hand side of an assignment (mostly in code, sometimes math), a variable name that repeats the name being assigned on the left, as in self-referential updates like `x = x + 1`, `cur = cur->next`, `df = df[...]`, or `n = n;`. The token that completes the repeated identifier (e.g. "ref", "_max", "1") is what is marked.
