The signal is strongest when the right-hand reference exactly matches the assigned variable, and weaker for near-matches like `tVal = trueVal` or `num = int(num)`.

18276.name: The final token that completes a clause or sentence, typically just before punctuation or a boundary. These are often predictable phrase-closing words: sentence-final adverbs and particles ("too", "though", "respectively", "rn", "eh"), tag-question pronouns ("shall we", "aren't you") and fixed-phrase endings ("for example", "as follows", "over time"). It also fires on clause-final verb or particle endings in other languages, such as German verb-final suffixes ("-ellt", "-legt", "haben") and Chinese/Japanese sentence-final markers (了, 吗, です). These non-English endings activate most strongly.

Clause- or sentence-final tokens, mostly in non-English or code-mixed text: verb endings, copulas, and sentence-final particles (Chinese 吗/呢/啊/的/了, Japanese ん, Hindi है, Telugu ది, Russian/Persian suffixes, German sind) that sit just before punctuation or the end of a phrase. Occasionally English phrase-final words or closing punctuation.

1829.name: Locations and spatial descriptions: place names (cities, regions, states, countries, landmarks), street addresses, and prepositional phrases describing where something is ("in the valley", "down the block from", "to the north of"). Activation is strongest on proper geographic names and spatial-relation words inside location phrases.

18296.name: A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no clear semantic theme. It shows up on varied structural or boundary tokens, most strongly on delimiters in code, markup and lists: closing quotes, comma or semicolon followed by a newline, colon plus line breaks, and units like "px". It also fires faintly on function words and connectors mid-phrase (of, the, and, who, on, "(").

18297.name: GUI widget class names in code, especially button types (JButton, QPushButton, tk.Button, wx.Button) plus related components like JLabel, JFrame, ComboBox, CheckBox and QLineEdit, often in Swing/Qt/Tkinter declarations or imports. These fire even in garbled text, strongest on JButton. Weak, scattered activations also appear on variable-declaration keywords (let, var) and stray commas.

1831.name: A diffuse feature firing on content words (mostly nouns, plus some verbs and adjectives) that head a new phrase. These are typically the first meaningful word after a determiner, sentence start or list bullet. The strongest cases are abstract or relational head nouns followed by 'of' (shape of, graph of, effects of, limits of, timing of, interior) and participles opening a clause (Planted, Holding, identified, observed).

A diffuse feature that fires on content words (mostly abstract or generic nouns, plus some verbs and adjectives), typically right after a determiner, preposition or line break. Examples are 'values', 'reception', 'medium', 'concentration' and 'pairs'. It activates sparsely across many tokens in ordinary, and often garbled or spammy, prose. The strongest activations come on nouns that head a noun phrase, such as 'The ___ of' or 'a ___'.

18327.name: The word "artist" and its variants (artists, artiste, artistic, artistry), meaning creative practitioners such as painters, musicians or performers. Activation is strongest on the noun "artist(s)" and weaker on the adjective forms and on related creator words like author, comedian or creative.

18356.name: Verbs and determiners in calls to submit or send something to someone, such as a comment, message, question, email, or information (e.g. "Leave a", "Send us an email with", "submit questions", "register your"). The phrases often appear in reader-engagement or contact prompts, and the feature fires most strongly on the verb and the following article or possessive, just before the item being sent.

Verbs and following determiners in requests or calls to action asking the reader to provide, send, or contribute something (leave a comment, send photos, email, submit your, bring a, give me your), typically after "please", "you can", or "by".

18373.name: The last token of a genus name in Latin binomial species names (word-final suffixes like -us, -ium, -rum, -a, or the period of an abbreviated genus such as "S."). The genus name sits right before the species epithet, and activation peaks just as the epithet is about to follow.

18381.name: Fires on the ".ComponentModel" namespace token in C# using directives ("using System.ComponentModel", including .DataAnnotations and .Composition sub-namespaces). The similar ".ObjectModel" token in "System.Collections.ObjectModel" triggers it only weakly, and other activations elsewhere are negligible noise.

18405.name: Tokens tied to hyperlinks and web markup: URL and path pieces (://, ../, /, .html, .md, domain fragments), Markdown link syntax (](, [), HTML tags and attributes (<thead, alt, quote marks), and boilerplate link or navigation text such as 'see more' in several languages (Ver mais, Zobacz więcej), 'view all', 'click here to' and 'for more information'. Stray whitespace tokens in scraped page layouts also fire.

18407.name: Diffuse, weak activation across expository scientific/technical prose, strongest in dense biomedical text describing how entities (hormones, cytokines, genes, factors) function or relate. It fires on subject nouns, linking verbs and connective phrases that state a mechanism or causal role, such as "is associated with", "promote … by the respective activation of", ", leading to the induction of" and "are the main … subtype", along with nearby commas and periods.

18418.name: The TAG identifier used for logging in Android/Java code, both where it is declared ("private static final String TAG = ...") and where it is passed as the first argument to Log.d/i/e ("(TAG"). Literal tag strings in Log calls (e.g. "DEBUG", "MainActivity") activate weakly, and unrelated prose activates only faintly.

18419.name: Fires weakly and diffusely in technical, code-like, config/markup, or garbled mixed-language text. It tends to land at structural boundaries where a new element begins: attribute or key names after quotes, words that start the next field, opening parentheses before clarifying examples, colons, list dashes, and clause-ending punctuation. It seems to track segment or field transitions in structured or noisy text rather than any specific word.

18444.name: Fires weakly and diffusely in formal technical and scientific prose, such as research abstracts, patents and product specs. It mostly lands on structural and connective tokens rather than content: sentence-ending periods and the sentence starts that follow them ('The', 'A'), clause commas, 'and', 'to' and 'that', and reporting or methods verbs ('was measured by', 'results show a', 'showed that', 'can be achieved'). Activation is strongest at sentence and clause transitions in academic-style writing.

A diffuse feature with no single lexical trigger. It fires on scattered tokens in synthetic, LLM-style instructional or technical text: markdown step headings ("### **1."), docstring openers in generated Python problems, "Output:" lines in coding problems, scripted student/participant dialogue ("Yes", "Right"), and boilerplate or pseudo-technical prose. Activation is strongest at points where a new clause, step or answer begins.

18446.name: The start of an explanatory annotation, chiefly code comment markers (//, #, ', bullets) at the beginning of a comment, plus the first few words after them. Weaker hits fall on verbs and function words inside descriptive or explanatory prose, such as captions, documentation and technical explanations.

18459.name: Highly predictable continuation tokens in formulaic, structured text. The clearest case is Question/Answer reading-comprehension boilerplate that refers back to a source passage: "text" in "according to the text" and "in the given text", "context of", and "not specified" or "provided". Weaker activations land on predictable tokens in math and LaTeX (spaces after "=", braces, backslashes) and on line breaks in markdown lists.

18493.name: The first token of a new segment or entity right after a structural boundary, such as a newline, bullet, comma, open parenthesis, equals sign or LaTeX command (e.g. the brace after \frac or \text). These tokens open a label, name, identifier, hash value or argument. Activation is strongest on boilerplate field labels like "Article" in "Article Rating" and "Story" in "Story Length".

18494.name: A diffuse feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires on single tokens inside formulaic, highly predictable text: the middle of a recurring URL, a standard code keyword argument, separators such as the line break between an author list and its affiliations, and words in stock technical phrases (e.g. "biological membranes", "positive saturation"). It may track tokens the model can confidently predict from context or that set up a predictable continuation.

18506.name: Function words and phrase content within adverbial or prepositional phrases that set the temporal or circumstantial backdrop for the main event (e.g. 'at a time when…', 'as the national debate shifts from…', 'on the eve of an election', 'during', 'after', 'following a', 'due to the', 'delayed by a fire drill'). Activation is strongest on extended 'when/as…' context clauses describing ongoing situations.

18511.name: Structural tokens inside code documentation comments (Javadoc /** * @param/@return, C# /// <summary>/<value> tags), especially the newlines, indentation, comment markers and tag names near the end of the doc block just before the method signature. Weak, scattered firing elsewhere on getter/setter parameter names and miscellaneous punctuation.

18513.name: A weak, diffuse signal in lofty, idealistic or inspirational passages about purpose, virtue, God, country, humanity, democracy, the earth or the world. It fires on function words and nouns within these grand statements rather than on any single token type. The strongest activations are on phrases expressing a higher calling or universal scope, such as "God. What would the world", "put on this earth to be", "Country, we advocate" and "activist on the planet".

18514.name: Universal/quantifier keywords used as parameter or option values in code and config, most strongly "all" after CSS "transition:" and "both" after "clear:". Other cases include media="all", notify_all, fill=BOTH, include='all', restart: always, needs: none, and wildcards like * or */*. Plain prose quantifiers fire only weakly.

18539.name: First-person pronouns (mainly "we", plus "We", "our", "us", "I") used by authors to introduce their own work in scientific or technical writing, such as abstracts and papers. They usually begin a clause stating what the authors did, propose, or present, and often follow framing phrases like "In this study,", "Herein,", or "To address this,".

18544.name: The first token of two-word proper names that are nearly always followed by a fixed second word, chiefly "Rhode" (Island) and "Notre" (Dame). Activation is strongest when the name refers to the U.S. state or the university/football team. It is weaker for French uses of "Notre" (churches, ordinary French text) and for related names like Providence.

18550.name: Whitespace and line-break tokens at structural boundaries, mostly the indentation spaces that open a new line after a heading, title or YAML-style field ("author:", "description: |-"), and newlines after a title or sentence. It also fires weakly on an occasional function word ("the", "a", "y") or number right before the next content word.

1857.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires across content-bearing spans in ordinary prose, mainly noun phrases and predicates naming the specific subject, setting or domain of the passage (places, organizations, products, technical or medical terms). Activation peaks on the key topic nouns, such as 'quantum dots', 'Boquete', 'carcinoma' and 'Academic Decathlon', and stays weak on function words and generic connectives.

Diffuse, weak activation over multi-word descriptive noun phrases and their prepositional complements (often following 'the', 'of', 'in'), spanning entity/domain descriptions such as places, organizations, technical items, and groups of people. It peaks on content head nouns and compound modifiers (e.g., 'network security', 'automobile industry', 'stores', 'places'), and on code it fires loosely on identifiers and paths.

18573.name: Words for letting someone or something go, leave or return from custody or an institution, such as being released, discharged, paroled, sent or taken home, or leaving hospital. The strongest cases involve people released from custody or discharged from hospital or the army. Weaker activations cover related ideas of release, issuance or approval.

18576.name: Word pieces in compound scientific terms for physical effects that couple one quantity or stimulus to another, such as magneto-, thermo-electric, piezo-resistive, photo-refractive, electro-optic, and voltage-operated. Typically the connecting or middle fragment (e.g. "eto", "oe", "ores") fires, along with property words like resistivity, resistance and coefficient.

1859.name: Mostly weak, diffuse activations on words about errors, failures and problems. The strongest are on "error" and related terms (error messages, error handling, error reports, errors, crash, failed, alerts, rejection, misconduct, caution/emergency). The feature also fires faintly on error-reporting code and system-message contexts such as print statements and log-like text.

18610.name: Fires on the first fragment of a word that the tokenizer splits into several subword pieces, usually a word-initial piece (often capitalized), and mostly for rarer words, proper nouns and technical terms. It tends to appear after a quote mark or within a title or name.

18612.name: The subword token "yst" (including "myst"/"syst") inside a longer word, e.g. crystalline, polycystic, systolic, mystic/mystique, demystify, cholecystectomy. Activation is highest in medical and biochemical words (polycystic, cholecystectomy, homocysteine).

18615.name: Whitespace runs (indentation/padding) and line-drawing characters (\, /, |, #, _) in ASCII art diagrams and text-based drawings, especially the leading spaces before slanted or vertical stroke characters.

18619.name: Tokens inside dense structured or symbolic content, chiefly operands, operators, brackets and function names within math equations (the strongest is \sin^2 in a LaTeX formula), plus dot-leader runs in tables of contents and fragments of chemical names and formulas. It also fires weakly on odd, out-of-place words in garbled or unusual prose.

18639.name: Tokens that complete a highly predictable code identifier or API call, especially the second part of a compound method name (strongest on "FragmentManager" in Android's getChildFragmentManager(); weaker on localStorage.setItem, add_module). The remaining activations on prose, hashes and DOIs are faint and look like noise.

18655.name: Fires most strongly on the variable term ("*p") in a simple algebra problem like "Solve -96 = -9*p for p", i.e. the multiplied unknown being solved for. Elsewhere it gives only weak, scattered activations on arbitrary tokens in code, math or garbled technical text.

18683.name: Words describing a bad fate that befalls someone, especially punishment, capture and loss of freedom (arrested, prison, sentenced to death, banishment, detained, imprisoned), plus related misfortunes such as being trapped, chased, evicted or laid off, foreclosure, or injury. Arrest and imprisonment terms activate most strongly.

18684.name: The final token of a noun phrase (often the object of a prepositional or modifier phrase: a place, specimen, tissue, cell type, or title) that closes off a constituent, marking the boundary right before the sentence continues with a verb, comma, conjunction, closing parenthesis or period.

18710.name: Structural boilerplate in source code (mostly C#/Java), firing on indentation whitespace, comment closers (*/, ///), XML doc tags (summary, param) and the tokens right around them. It peaks at the transition from a doc comment to the next member declaration (annotations, access modifiers, method signatures and braces, e.g. Dispose()). It also fires weakly on formulaic structure in templated documents such as safety data sheet section breaks and spacing in nutrition labels.

18713.name: Tokens of the word "large" and its forms (larger, largest, enlarge, Large), marking great size, scale or quantity. Activation is strongest for the base form "large" used as a plain adjective (e.g. "a large number", "large-scale") and weaker for comparative and superlative forms.

18730.name: The comma that separates a city name from its following state, region or country in a location or address (e.g. "St. Louis, MO", "Copenhagen, Denmark"). It is most common in academic affiliations, supplier credits and citations, and is strongest in manufacturer parentheticals such as "(Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO)". It occasionally fires weakly on similar connectors like "in" after an institution name.

Function tokens (a preposition "to" or a comma) placed right after a complete phrase, such as a math instruction or an institution/location name, marking the point where the text pivots to a continuation like a purpose clause or an abrupt shift in content.

18745.name: The word "District" (or its "RICT" fragment from all-caps "DISTRICT") in U.S. federal court names in legal case headers, e.g. "United States District Court". Other activations on punctuation and function words are weak and scattered.

18752.name: Mainly fires on "LGPL", the software license name, in a licensing statement following "Modified". Other activations are weak and scattered over word fragments in technical or boilerplate text, such as code namespaces, placeholder Latin and split words.

18759.name: Layout and grid class names or style values in HTML/CSS/UI code, firing most strongly on "row" as the first class in a div class attribute (especially in Bootstrap-style container > row > col markup). It also fires on "flex", "grid", "card", "-center", and Row/Col components. There are weak, scattered activations on unrelated prose tokens.

18775.name: Tokens in multiple-choice quiz/test text where the correct answer is about to be revealed: answer labels like "Answer:", "the correct option is", "Option" and "【答案】", the line break after the last listed choice, and the separators in answer keys (e.g. "3.", "B)", "6~10"), all of which come right before an answer letter or value.

1880.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires across many genres (prose, code, technical, legal, recipes) on content-bearing tokens, mainly nouns and noun phrases naming key entities, technical terms, proper names and list items, together with the punctuation or line breaks that close those items. It seems to track salient topic or entity spans rather than any single word or meaning.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no sharp semantic focus. It fires on scattered tokens in structured, often synthetic-looking or slightly garbled text such as code, CSS, math and calculations, tables, lists and logic puzzles. It tends to land on key nouns or terms (identifiers, units, named entities like 'root beer', 'MJD', 'container') and on line-ending punctuation or newline/whitespace tokens that close a clause or list item.

18805.name: Mostly the subword "shiv"/"Shiv", strongest inside Indian names (e.g. Sshivada, Shivdas) and phonetic spellings. It fires weakly on other mid-word fragments in compound names, URLs and code identifiers (e.g. 'warehouse', 'cks', 'on', '/max').

18848.name: The "bin" directory token in Unix paths, firing most strongly in shebang lines at the start of scripts (#!/bin/sh, #!/bin/bash, #!/bin/env), and more weakly in other /bin/ paths inside commands or code.

1887.name: Opening parenthesis tokens (" (", "(", "[(", ">(", "(('") that start a parenthetical, such as an abbreviation, citation year, clarification, enumeration, count, or math/code argument. Activation is often highest when the parenthesis begins a line or opens a standalone aside.

18935.name: Words that refer to a person's or group's positions, beliefs, views, policies, stances or commitments, often political, plus verbs and phrases of expressing or committing to them (said, signed on to, committed to, vote for). The strongest cases are nouns such as 'stances', 'policies', 'beliefs', 'comments' and 'commitments'.

18955.name: Word pieces containing "add"/"addle" (often preceded by s), the strongest being "saddle", "sadd" in saddened/saddled, "Saddle River", and "saddle thrombus". Weaker on similar pieces such as straddle, swaddle, paddle, cradle, madden and Saddam, and on other horse-riding or straddling terms (stirrup, astride, bridle).

Word pieces containing the letter sequence "add"/"addle", strongest for "saddle"/"saddled"/"saddening" (also Saddam, Saddleworth, straddle, swaddle, paddle, maddening). Weak activation on similar-sounding fragments like astride, buckle, ashtray.

18979.name: The final part of a module or library name in import/include statements, most strongly the ".h" extension in C/C++ system #include <...> headers (math.h, time.h, stdlib.h). Weaker activation on the terminating ";" of C#/Java using/import lines and the "2" in "import cv2", plus faint hits on colons after dates or citations.

18988.name: Opening bracket or parenthesis (mostly " [", also " (" and superscript "(^") that begins a numbered citation reference in academic/scientific text, typically right after a claim or author name. Weaker activation on periods or commas that directly precede superscript citation numbers or separate citation numbers.

19004.name: In algebraic expressions, the exponent or variable of the leading term (e.g. the "2" in x^2, the x in 3x) right after a coefficient or caret, usually just after an equals sign or simplification step where a new expression begins. Weak secondary firing on periods after multiple-choice letters (A., b.).

19006.name: A diffuse, weak feature tied to document structure in encyclopedic or wiki-style text. It fires most strongly on wiki boilerplate and lead-sentence phrasing ("From The … Wiki⏎⏎The", "Not to be confused with", "also known as", "Jump to navigation / search"). More commonly it fires weakly on transitions between sections: sentence-final periods followed by paragraph breaks, header and title boundaries, and the first token after a heading.

1902.name: Fires on the first token of a document and, most strongly, on the first break after the opening title or header line: the newline, comma or space that ends a headline, file header or shebang. It also fires on tokens whose next token is nearly certain, such as " don" before 't, "201" or "200" before a year digit, " able" before "to", " such" before "as", "Figure " or "Chapter " before a number, and "utf-" before "8".

A position-based latent with no consistent meaning. It fires moderately on the very first token of a text and peaks on one token shortly afterward, usually within the first several tokens. That peak token is typically a function token such as a period, comma, newline, space or "the", regardless of content or language.

19051.name: Fires most strongly on the token " affid", the first piece of the word "affidavits" in legal or document contexts. Weaker, scattered activations fall on other word-fragment or noun tokens, such as Japanese 記事 ("article") and " data".

19076.name: Numeric coefficients or constants in polynomial or algebraic expressions, mainly the third-position term after a plus or minus sign (e.g., the "6" in x³ − 4x² + 6x). It fires most strongly on the coefficient of the linear x term in cubic polynomials. Weaker activation appears on other numbers within sums or sequences.

19081.name: The assignment or definition operator that comes right after a function, sequence, or indexed term and introduces its formula or value. This is mostly "=" in forms like f(x) =, a_n =, A[1]=, but also includes lambda colons, arrow functions (=>), "to be"/"be" in "define f to be", and Chinese 为.

19093.name: Repeated punctuation or symbol tokens in long runs of the same character, such as dashes, asterisks, pipes, backticks, colons, dots, quotes, zero-width characters and tabs, often forming separators or decorative lines. Activation sits in the middle of the repetitive run, after the pattern is established, and is strongest for spaced asterisks and dashes.

19098.name: Diffuse, weak activations on connective and structural tokens (arrows, 'if', 'when', 'then', 'because', commas, colons, parentheses, newlines) inside step-by-step, rule-based calculations or code that adjust a value or score (add/subtract, increase by X% only if, 'No → 0'), strongest on arrows marking a computed result.

19105.name: Fires on a token inside formulaic boilerplate where the continuation is highly predictable. It is strongest on "Respond" (completed as "Respondent") in legal case captions. It also fires moderately on "published" in header phrases such as "Originally published at" and "Received and published:". Weak, scattered activations appear on tokens in fixed multi-word names and phrases, such as Pride Rock, data bases and "amount in".

19142.name: Names of bibliographic and literature-search databases, especially the completing subword tokens of names like EMBASE, MEDLINE, CINAHL, PsycINFO and Scopus, plus the word "database(s)" and similar index names, mostly in systematic-review search descriptions. The strongest activation is on "ASE" in EMBASE. Weak activations also appear on stray list or formatting tokens.

19153.name: Affiliation markers placed right after author names in academic paper bylines: superscript numbers, letters, Roman numerals, or symbols (*, †, ⋆) that point to institutional affiliations. Activation is strongest for the first affiliation marker (especially "1"/"¹"/"a") and when the same marker repeats across several authors, and weaker for later or secondary indices.

19177.name: Mostly fires on Android boilerplate code, peaking inside the auto-generated onCreateOptionsMenu(Menu menu) method: the parameter, the opening brace and indentation, the "// Inflate the menu; this adds items to the action bar" comment, and getMenuInflater().inflate(R.menu..., menu). Related Android template lines ("Inflate the layout for this fragment", getSupportActionBar()., import android.view.Menu;) fire weakly. Elsewhere it gives very weak activation on predictable tokens in stock phrases ("on the other hand", "As a result", "However", "enables you to").

19180.name: The "cdnjs" subdomain token in Cloudflare CDN script URLs (https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...) inside HTML script/link tags. Other tokens activate only weakly.

1922.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires at the end of a multi-token term or name, such as the head noun of a compound phrase after a rare or technical modifier ("schedule", "Environment", "framework", "effect", "option") or the final subword of a split word ("ging", "escence"). It also fires on the punctuation, parentheses or newlines that close that phrase. In short, it marks phrase-boundary completion rather than any particular meaning.

A diffuse, low-intensity feature active on garbled, incoherent or degenerate text, such as mixed-language fragments, nonsense pseudo-code, repetitive token loops and broken markup. It fires weakly across many tokens. The strongest activations tend to fall on punctuation, delimiters, colons, closing brackets and line breaks that end a fragment.

19274.name: Standalone symbol tokens, mostly '#', plus '*', '$' and similar, especially when backslash-escaped or repeated inside noisy, garbled, code-like or markup-heavy text. Activation is strongest for escaped or repeated '#' sequences such as '\#' lines and '#'-prefixed hex or ID values.

19275.name: The word "Franklin" in the Free Software Foundation's address (51 Franklin Street, Boston) from GPL license boilerplate, following the street number. Rare weak firing on unrelated function words or punctuation.

19288.name: Structural boundary tokens in web-scraped text, mainly sentence-final punctuation fused with newlines (".⏎⏎", "⏎⏎"). These mark where one section or block ends and a new, often unrelated one begins, such as a heading, byline, review, list item or boilerplate. Weaker activations fall on delimiters inside metadata like author lists, dates, prices, IDs and usernames (commas, parentheses, colons, bullets, quote marks). The strongest cases close a quoted testimonial before a new date or entry.

1929.name: A weak, diffuse feature spread across ordinary running prose. It shows no single lexical trigger and mostly fires on function words, clause boundaries (commas, periods, "but", "however", "that", "which"), and the content words that continue a clause. It is strongest mid-sentence in expository or narrative text, where the next phrase elaborates, contrasts, or adds a result (e.g., "result in", "contribute to", "downside of").

A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires across long runs of ordinary tokens (function words, nouns, punctuation, code) rather than on any specific word. It is strongest in rambling, semantically incoherent or machine-generated-sounding text, where sentences are grammatical but lose meaning (for example "outcomes befall as a result of human-cetera interaction"). It also appears on garbled code and mixed-language snippets.

19327.name: The first digit chunk of an article, page or grant ID number in citations, DOIs and funding notes, usually right after a volume number, period or dash. It fires most strongly on Physical Review / APS-style article numbers such as PhysRevB.94.245… or "Phys. Rev. Lett. 126, 045…", and fires weakly on page ranges and grant numbers.

19339.name: The word "General" in "GNU (Lesser) General Public License", mostly in software license boilerplate inside code comments. Activation is strong there, and weak, scattered firing elsewhere is negligible.

19346.name: Numeric suffixes and version numbers attached to cryptographic, hashing, and encoding algorithm names (the 256 in SHA-256 or AES-256, the 5 in MD5, the 2 in Argon2 or WPA2, CRC32, uuid v4), strongest for SHA-family digest sizes. It also fires weakly on related identifier codes like ISBN13 or EAN13 and on stray bullet tokens.

19359.name: Commas inside postal addresses and place names. They most often separate a city from its state, country, or postcode (e.g. Boston, MA), and also street parts like suite or floor. Activation is strongest in full mailing addresses.

19364.name: Tokens marking the start of a new question, problem, or list item, typically after a line break or numbering. These are numerals and their following period or colon, bullets, and the first words of a question or problem statement (e.g., "What/Which/How/Is", "A", "If", "Consider"), common in quiz, homework and Q&A text.

The opening token of a new item, entry, or segment, typically right after a paragraph break, a list/question number ("2.", "Problem 2.", "Q:") or another separator. It fires most strongly at the start of numbered questions, exercises and problems ("A person travels...", "You are shrunk...") and on the numbering itself. The activating words are mostly function words or sentence-starters such as The, A, How, There and I.

19372.name: Fires strongly on the token " OF" in the boilerplate license phrase "WITHOUT WARRANTIES OR CONDITIONS OF ANY KIND" (Apache License header). Other activations are weak and scattered on miscellaneous tokens.

19391.name: Weak, diffuse activations on function words, punctuation and clause boundaries in expository or scientific prose. The feature fires most strongly where the text introduces, names or defines a novel kind of thing, as in phrases like "known as … a new type of … that is so new and special", "a new type of organism" and "such a 'liquid glass' … has not yet been explored".

19395.name: Fires on a mid-phrase token whose continuation is strongly predictable, such as an auxiliary or function word inside a fixed verb construction ("how much you are [prepared]", "might be [willing]", "need to [file]", "want to [make]", "is [being]"). It also fires on the space before a number in base-conversion listings ("Octal 6256...") and on the middle syllable "ak" of foreign names (Di-ak-onia, Dun-ak-la).

19396.name: Tokens that close off a formatting or separator element, often fused with a newline: the final dashes, hashes, quotes or comment markers of a divider, banner or header line (e.g. -----, ####, //, ''', -->), and line breaks after such lines. This fires mostly in code comments, markdown and tables. Weak, scattered activations also appear on stray tokens in prose.

19407.name: Marks the end point of a time span: the closing date, time, or year of a range, plus the words that introduce it (until, thru, to, into, end on, dashes between start and end). The strongest activations come right after range connectors, as in 'thru January 15' and 'into early January'. The pattern occasionally carries over to the end point of spatial ranges, as in 'mouth to anus'.

19434.name: Tokens immediately after a newly introduced term, name, or acronym (often technical, quoted, or parenthesized), at the point where its definition or description begins. Typical spots are a closing parenthesis or quote, a relative pronoun like "which"/"who", or a copula such as "is a"/"are".

19455.name: A diffuse feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires on the first token of a new word or item that directly follows a long modifier or list element, as in 'insoluble DNA', 'Satisfaction guar(anteed)', 'unanswered question' and 'MSN, O(CN)'. It is strongest in dense, list-like or boilerplate text such as spam ads, username lists, tag lists and credentials.

19459.name: Fires mainly on "appeal" after "On" or "under", most strongly in the court-document header "On Appeal from…", and on "request" in formulaic headers like "On request from". These mark the procedural origin of a legal or official document. Activations on other tokens are weak and scattered.

19480.name: Words for people or channels that covertly or confidentially supply information, such as sources, informants, contacts, tips/tip-offs, whistleblowers, undercover/double agents, and anonymous reports. Activation is strongest on "informant" and "tip-off".

19503.name: The token that ends a specialized name or term, usually a closing delimiter such as italic asterisks, a parenthesis, a quote mark or a LaTeX $/}$, and sometimes the final subword of a name. Activation is strongest at the asterisk closing an italicized Latin species or gene name (e.g. *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*). Other triggers include closing parentheses after acronyms or binomials, closing quotes around titles, and the last fragment of a taxonomic name.

19520.name: A closing parenthesis, often space-prefixed, that has no matching opening parenthesis, appearing in garbled, noisy, multilingual or pseudo-code text. Rarely the feature also fires on similar stray symbols such as an isolated "#" in a run of separators.

19537.name: Subword pieces and abbreviations inside medical disease names, especially cancers: the 'oc' in hepatocellular, 'carcinoma', 'cancer' after an organ word (liver, renal, lung), and acronyms such as HCC, RCC, NPC, BPH. HCC fires most strongly. Weak, scattered activation also occurs on other technical subwords like PMCID and HBase.

19539.name: A diffuse feature with no single semantic theme. It fires on highly predictable, context-determined tokens that complete a fixed pattern or structural boundary. These include function words that a verb or phrase calls for ("to" after "asked" or "start", "a" after "such as") and clause-separating punctuation (commas after introductory phrases, semicolons in legal lists). It also covers formulaic code and name completions such as "ControllerBase" after a controller class declaration, "VM" in MVVM, and the blank line after import statements.

19562.name: Weak, diffuse activation on phrases that describe what something can do or enables: its capabilities, advantages, uses, or functional properties. Typical cases are "can slow down... and sort on any field", "capable of reaching an enormous amount of users", "the ability to manage", "which let you control" and "starts up from rest". Activation is strongest on verbs and prepositions of capability or action and their objects, often in lists of benefits or features.

19567.name: Words naming definitive physical or procedural interventions, mainly surgery and curative treatment (surgical, surgery, resection, transplant, cure, remove surgically, intervention). It fires most strongly on tokens that present surgery or removal as the treatment option. Weaker activations occur on other physical removal or engineering methods, such as removal by hand and hydropower. There is also faint noise on DOI labels.

19578.name: The all-caps word "COPYRIGHT" in legal notices, license headers, and code comment blocks (e.g., "COPYRIGHT AND LICENSE", "CONCERNING COPYRIGHT RESTRICTIONS", "COPYRIGHT (c)"). There is weak activation on other line-initial tokens such as list dashes and quote markers.

19590.name: Fires on a token inside a formulaic or set phrase, where the next word is highly predictable. It is strongest on "POSSIBILITY" in the legal boilerplate "ADVISED OF THE POSSIBILITY OF SUCH LOSS OR DAMAGES". Activation is weak elsewhere, e.g. "leading to", the comma before a citation year, "Earth–ionosphere" and "call(igraphy)".

19631.name: The base quantity or denominator in a rate or ratio expression, typically a round number (100, 1,000, 10,000, 1) or unit word (dollar, thousand, kW) following "per", "for every", "each", or "/". Strongest on "100" in phrases like "for every 100 people" or "per 100 grams".

19644.name: Shell output redirection operators (>, >>, >&2) that send a command's output into a file or stream, usually right after an echo/cat string. Weaker hits are other output-directing constructs such as Python's print(..., file=), fputs(..., stdout), pipes, and file-creation commands like touch.

19668.name: Non-semantic formatting and filler tokens: whitespace runs, separators, symbols, box-drawing/ASCII-art characters, table delimiters, emoticon/kaomoji pieces, mojibake, and paragraph breaks within layout-heavy or garbled text. Kaomoji and decorative symbol strings activate most strongly.

19677.name: The token "/android" as a path segment inside URLs, file paths or repository names (e.g. docs/android, repository/android-releases). Activation is strongest in web URLs and much weaker in local file paths. Other tokens in the examples (commas, spaces, function words, digits) fire only faintly and look like noise.

1969.name: A diffuse, weakly activating feature on formatting and separator tokens rather than words. It fires mostly on the space before a number ("January 1995", "n = 3"), decimal points and digit chunks inside numbers, DOIs and IDs, and on paragraph breaks or punctuation at section boundaries. The strongest activations are in numeric tables, equations and headings.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires most clearly in numeric contexts. It peaks on the space token before a number (e.g. 'last 26', 'the 762'), on hyphens in scores and vote tallies (53-46, 3-0), and on thousands-separator commas (26,616). It also fires sporadically and weakly on unrelated tokens.

19721.name: Bodily functions and their disorders, chiefly digestion and elimination: bowel, constipation, fiber, bloating, digestive tract, bladder, insomnia, secretion and congestion. Strongest on constipation, fiber and bowel. It also fires weakly on related ideas of flow, blockage or release in non-medical settings, such as clogging drains, stagnant energy and releasing tension.

Words about digestion and bowel function, firing most on constipation and laxatives, then on intestines, bowel habits, digestive disturbances and urination. Weaker activation on other bodily-function or body-care terms involving blockage, release or clearing, such as flossing, exfoliation, clogging, cleansing, cramping and stiffness.

19734.name: Separator punctuation inside structured classification or identifier codes, firing on the delimiter just before the final segment. It peaks on the '.Letter' token in PACS codes (e.g. 36.40.Gk), and is weaker on hyphens in CAS registry numbers and Japanese addresses, slashes in patent Int. Cl. codes (e.g. 48/00), and brackets in ACM subject codes.

1976.name: Abstract, purpose- or benefit-oriented phrasing typical of mission statements, marketing, and formal expository prose. It is strongest on extended clauses describing goals, capabilities, and outcomes, such as "to help you…", "enabling X to deliver…", "emphasize the importance of…", or lists of verbs like "manage costs, mitigate risks, and maintain…". Activation is spread across whole clauses rather than single words.

A diffuse, low-intensity feature that spans whole stretches of generic, abstract, buzzword-heavy explanatory or corporate prose, such as mission statements, lists of services, benefits, processes and goals (e.g. 'create safer cars', 'protection of… promotion of…', 'Planning, Budgeting, and Project Execution'). It peaks on polished, formulaic phrasing and fires weakly on scattered tokens in incoherent, mixed-language or garbled synthetic text.

19762.name: A diffuse feature active across source code and technical/mathematical text, peaking in machine-learning and statistics code and prose (building or returning a model, activation functions like sigmoid, loss and likelihood functions, logistic regression, fitting and predicting). It fires mostly on structural tokens: indentation whitespace, line breaks, closing parens or braces, "=" assignments, "def"/"self", and variable names. Elsewhere it shows only weak, scattered activation on ordinary words.

19763.name: Integer part of a decimal number in a sequence of numeric coordinates, chiefly the second number of a pair (y-value) following a space or command letter in SVG path data (e.g. after C/V/H). It is strongest on the leading digits and the decimal point, and is weak on scattered numbers and words elsewhere.

19764.name: Connectors placed between personal names in author lists and citations, mostly "and"/"&" (also commas) right after a surname and before the next author's name. Activation is strongest in in-text academic citations such as "(Xiong and Kupski, 1999)" or "Lavidor and Ellis".

19770.name: Restrictive or exclusive focus words, mainly "only" (strongest when "Only" starts a sentence, e.g. "Only those" or "Only now"). They also fire on the determiner or quantifier that follows, such as "only the" or "only a few". Activation is weaker on related limiting or exceptive words like "except", "unless", "not until", "even" and "anything but".

The restrictive/limiting focus word "only" (strongest when it starts a clause, e.g. "Only then" or "only the"), plus the tokens right after it. Weaker hits fall on similar limiting words ("just", "merely", "not every", "even") and on the word following "only" or "just".

19786.name: The word "future" and its variants (futures, futurist, futuristic, Tomorrow), including capitalized names. Activation is strongest on financial "futures" and "futurist", and weaker on everyday uses such as "sustainable future" or "future-proof".

19807.name: The "jdk"/"DK" token in Java Development Kit names (JDK, OpenJDK), firing most strongly on lowercase "jdk" right after "open" in URLs and package names such as openjdk.java.net, mail.openjdk.org and openjdk-11.

19880.name: The "<!" token, almost always the start of an HTML "<!DOCTYPE html>" declaration. It fires most strongly when the declaration opens a code block or template string after a newline, and more weakly at the very start of a document. It also fires weakly on other "<!" uses, such as regex negative lookbehind "(?<!".

19884.name: The space token right before the second operand in an arithmetic expression, after an operator like by, *, ÷, /, × or "% of", where the model is about to produce the number to be computed with. It also fires weakly on "Answer" labels that follow multiple-choice options.

19888.name: Connective function tokens and punctuation (periods with paragraph breaks, dashes, colons, commas, 'to', 'has') at the junction right after a completed phrase, where the text pivots to a highly predictable continuation. This is especially common in formulaic or boilerplate text such as product blurbs, metadata fields, lists and DOIs.

19914.name: The word "cell" (also cells/cellular, "Cell" capitalized, or as a fragment like sub-cell-ular) in biological contexts. It is strongest when "cell" acts as a noun modifier in compounds such as cell death, cell division, cell contact, cell cycle and cell viability. Related biological units (neuronal, plant, brain, particle) activate weakly.

The word "cell" (usually singular, lowercase), strongest in biological contexts, especially as a modifier in compounds like cell death, cell growth, cell culture, cell function and cell biology. It fires weakly on "cells", on non-biological senses (cell phone, prison cell, the place name Cellardyke), and on a few other nouns that modify a following noun, such as "plant growth" and "company voluntary".

19927.name: Sentence-ending punctuation fused with line breaks (".⏎⏎", ".⏎", "?⏎⏎") and bare paragraph breaks, firing most strongly at abrupt boundaries in spammy, incoherent or auto-generated web text where the next line begins an unrelated heading, ad or topic.

Sentence- and paragraph-ending boundaries (periods, newlines, especially ".

" and "

") in low-quality, spammy or incoherent web text (SEO/casino/pharma spam, machine-generated gibberish), firing where the text abruptly switches to an unrelated sentence, heading, or boilerplate. Strongest after nonsensical sentences.

Sentence- or line-ending punctuation and newline breaks (especially ".\n\n") that close off a segment in incoherent, spammy or keyword-stuffed web text (SEO spam, casino ads, gibberish), right before an abrupt shift to an unrelated topic or heading. Weaker activations land on other boundary tokens such as runs of spaces, closing brackets, and menu or boilerplate words.

19967.name: Fires densely and broadly across whole clauses of machine-translated Chinese web-novel prose (xianxia/cultivation stories with sects, Qi, Immortal Kings, Great Emperors), strongest in narrative and explanatory clauses such as 'it was clear how strong…' or 'realize how difficult it was…'. It is especially strong where the passages are scraped or spam-injected with unrelated keywords like 'cbd gummies'. Elsewhere it gives only weak, scattered activations on ordinary function words and phrases in awkward or translated-sounding English.

19993.name: Word-internal subword fragments, usually mid-word pieces right after the first token, in rare or unfamiliar words split into several tokens: proper names, foreign-language words, technical terms, acronyms and misspellings. The word's identity is not yet determined at that point.

20012.name: Scientific and technical process descriptions, mainly physical or chemical, that involve supplying, moving or treating substances. It responds most to phrases about introducing gases, reagents or particles into a system, such as feeding a hydrocarbon gas or admitting gases. It also responds to related process vocabulary like temperature, transport, solutions, baths, material removed from surfaces and dissolving agents.

20018.name: Mainly the " ?" plus newline token that follows the dictionary-site header "References in periodicals archive" or "References in classic literature", marking the jump from a definition page to an unrelated quoted excerpt. It also fires more weakly on a few function words or word fragments mid-sentence in technical or explanatory text, such as "with", "for" and "met".

2002.name: Later items in enumerated lists or series (comma/and/or-separated, or run-on menus and tags): the final items, the separators and conjunctions leading up to them, and the closing element of the enumeration. Activation rises toward the end of the list.

20032.name: Separators and connectives that come right after a negative or lower-bound number and lead into the next value. These include range words such as "to" and "and", commas, semicolons, inequality signs, and LaTeX integral bound markers like "}^{". Activation is strongest for range expressions running from a negative number to a positive one, e.g. "-5° to 36°" or "-1,1".

20039.name: Tokens inside long runs of the same repeated character or token (e.g. "zzzz", "````", "OOOO", "啊啊啊"), typically in garbled or noisy text. Activation picks up after a few repetitions and stays on through the middle of the run.

20047.name: Opening delimiters that begin a value right after a key or assignment, e.g. an opening quote following '=' or ':' in code, config and JSON/YAML (sometimes '{' or '['), and opening <td>/<th> tags that start an HTML table cell.

20072.name: Segment boundaries (periods, question marks, newlines, colons, commas) that end a sentence, title or line just before an abrupt topic shift or disjointed continuation. Activation is strongest in incoherent, spun or spam-like text where consecutive sentences are unrelated, and weaker at ordinary sentence ends or list and heading breaks.

20073.name: Function words, chiefly prepositions (for, to, in, of, with, at, de), plus articles, colons and bold markers, that link a noun or verb to its complement, especially after request or demand words such as "request for", "asks for", "allowed to" and "adhering to". It fires most strongly on colons that introduce a definition or message, as in "any number of times:" or "ZeroDivisionError:".

20078.name: The token "fed"/"Fed" (also "edor"/"ed" after F), whatever it means: the Federal Reserve, "fed up", Fedora, the Fed Cup, and name fragments such as Fedorov, Federico, Feddic and Fedele. Activation is highest for capitalized "Fed" as an abbreviation or the start of a name, and weaker for the verb "fed".

20089.name: Words for soft, moldable, kneadable substances, chiefly "dough" (including "dough" within doughnut, sourdough, and the name Dougherty), along with batter, crust, clay, slurry, pulp, papier-mâché and paste. The "kne" token of knead/kneel also activates. Activation is strongest on "dough" in baking contexts.

The word "dough" (strongest, even in garbled or odd contexts like "doughnuts"), plus weaker activation on related malleable or kneadable substances and baking terms ("kne" from knead/kneel, pastry, clay, batter, sourdough, crust, Chinese 粉/胶).

20095.name: Punctuation or spacing immediately following a weekday name in date headers/timestamps (the comma after "Monday", "Friday", etc., or the space after "Tuesday,"), typically right before the day/month in blog or article dateline metadata; weakly also "Posted on"/"Updated:" lead-ins to dates.

20118.name: Tokens inside long runs of the same repeated character or token (dot leaders, dashes, spaces, nbsp, -*, ;\, repeated letters or symbols). Activation is strongest deep in the run, and a few sequence positions stand out as peaks. There are weak, sporadic activations on ordinary tokens, mostly prepositions like "in".

Tokens inside long runs of the same repeated symbol or short token (pipes, slashes, dashes, colons, asterisks, underscores, tabs, dots, arrows, etc.). The feature fires on interior repetitions once the repeating pattern is established, not on ordinary prose.

Tokens inside long runs of the same repeated character or symbol, such as whitespace, tabs, dashes, pipes, dots, invisible or zero-width characters, emojis, or repeated letters. The feature fires on tokens deep within these monotonous repetitive sequences (separators, padding, filler), not on the first occurrences.

20129.name: Superlatives of proximity, mostly "closest" and sometimes "nearest" or "closer", used when picking the value or answer option that best approximates a target. This typically comes after "the" in math or multiple-choice reasoning, e.g. "the closest option/integer/answer".

20149.name: Negation tokens ("not", "n't", "neither", "non", "no longer", "un-") and, more weakly, the verb or condition word where a state is being checked or failing. These usually fall in descriptions of conditions or outcomes such as a file not being linked, something that wouldn't fit or work, "if not given", or "check whether X is".

20150.name: The ".h" extension token immediately after "string" in C/C++ #include directives (the string.h header), strongest in angle-bracket includes and weaker in quoted ones.

20154.name: Fires on the first token of a tag name right after an opening '<' or closing '</' in HTML/XML-like markup. It is strongest for framework component prefixes such as <ng, <el, <ion and <app, and weaker on namespace separators like '::' or ':' in code. Most examples are noisy, garbled mixed-language code.

20162.name: HTTP request type tokens in web code, strongest on "HttpServletRequest" (in javax.servlet.http imports or as a servlet method parameter), with weaker activation on related request/context/session types (Request, HttpContext, HttpSession) and other framework parameter types such as JoinPoint, Model and CancellationToken. Non-code text is near zero.

20169.name: Mostly the second (or later) variable or factor in a multiplicative math term or product, such as the y in x*y, xy, x²y, c3*z, or a·b. It fires on the token right after a multiplication sign, cdot, or juxtaposed coefficient, and is strongest in multi-variable algebraic expressions. Weak activations also land on mid-sentence continuation words like "let", "it", or "or" after a clause break.

20180.name: Pieces of technical and code-like text, mostly in shell commands, file paths, URLs and Python imports: filename extensions (.py, .sh, .cpp, .gz), path parts (/bin, usr, ~/), URL parts, flags and arguments following a script name, and "import" after a module name. Activations are weak and scattered, with a few stray hits on ordinary prose words like "the".

20184.name: Tokens in the middle of long random-looking alphanumeric strings, such as hex hashes, IDs, API keys, URL tokens and GUIDs, plus separators (dashes, spaces) inside codes and numbers. Activation peaks deep inside these unpredictable character sequences.

20190.name: Affirmative or "on" values assigned in code, chiefly the CSS/JS display/visibility value that makes an element shown ("block", "visible"), with weaker activation on similar true/Yes/enabled/solid settings.

20215.name: Structural delimiters at the start of a formatted item or output: mostly the comma (and space) right after the first number in a printed list or sequence, plus colons after 'Assistant'/'Reverse', markdown list dashes, '###' headers, table '|' separator rows, and 'separated by' phrases. It responds to the point where a list, answer, or structured output begins.

20223.name: Contexts about layoffs, job cuts and cost-cutting (e.g., 'pink slips to employees', 'laid-off workers', '1,000 employees… affected', reducing waste). Activation peaks on words in these workforce-reduction phrases, such as employees, workers and slips, and on the surrounding function words. Elsewhere there are weak, diffuse activations on ordinary function words in news or expository prose.

20232.name: Positive aesthetic or admiring adjectives (and related nouns/adverbs) such as "wonderful", "beautiful", "lovely", "delightful", "marvellous" and "beauty". The strongest activations are on "wonderful"/"wonderfully", weaker on "beautiful"/"lovely", and weakest on "beauty" used as a product or category noun.

Positive aesthetic/admiring words, chiefly "wonderful" (strongest), "beautiful", "beauty", and "lovely", plus similar terms like "delightful", "amazing", and "magical", used in any context to praise or describe something pleasing.

20235.name: Mentions of scheduled or time-bounded events (conferences, festivals, tournaments, ceremonies, elections, seasons, trips) and the words giving their timing, duration, or venue, such as dates, weekdays, 'two-day', 'held at', 'ends', 'last day of', 'opening'. It is strongest where an event's occurrence or ending is stated, e.g. 'The conference ends Thursday'.

20248.name: Separator tokens that close one entry in a code data literal (a dict, list, JSON object or array) before the next key or element starts. These are mostly fused punctuation such as "],", "'},", "\"," or "," and sometimes the indentation whitespace before the next key, typically right after a value ends. The strongest cases are closing brackets or quotes merged with a comma.

2025.name: Relational/classifying adjectives (often ending in -al, -ic, -ical, -ological) placed before a noun to specify its domain or type (e.g., financial, legal, optical, emotional, medicinal, political), including word-piece suffixes that complete such adjectives.

20267.name: The final subword of a Latin scientific (binomial) species or genus name, such as the -us, -um, -a, -ensis or -ii epithet ending, a closing italic asterisk, or the closing parenthesis of a parenthetical author. It fires at the point just before the taxonomic author citation (e.g., Linnaeus, Walker, L.) follows. Weak, sporadic activations occur on unrelated tokens.

2028.name: The preposition "of" (including capitalized "Of" and fused forms like "numberOf"), mostly in noun-phrase constructions that link a head noun to its complement, such as possessive, part-whole, attribute or title relations ("President of", "benefits of", "squares of"). Activation is highest when "of" follows a specific, technical or title-like noun.

The preposition "of" (and its equivalents such as "Of", "-of", or Chinese "的"). It fires most often where "of" links a head noun to its complement ("the Sword of", "a table of", "the odds of"), and also on the "Of" in "Of course".

20285.name: The word "special" in any casing or split form (special, Special, SPECIAL, S+PECIAL), mostly in formal or boilerplate phrases such as safety data sheet headings ("special treatment needed"), legal damage disclaimers ("indirect, special, consequential"), NASA "SPECIAL PUBLICATION" lists, and labels like "Special Collaborator"/"Special Members". Activation is strongest on the all-caps and standalone label forms.

20294.name: Subword suffix pieces completing technical names inside code, URLs, and config filenames, most strongly "-ci" in CI service names such as travis-ci and gitlab-ci, and weakly "ypi" in pypi. Isolated filler tokens in technical text activate only faintly.

20305.name: Clause and sentence boundaries in fluent, generic expository or SEO-style web prose. Activation peaks on sentence-ending periods, especially those followed by paragraph breaks, and is somewhat lower on bare newlines before headings. Weaker activation falls on commas, conjunctions like "and" and "or", and the words that begin the next sentence (It, In, She, If you, The). When the feature is strong, it spreads across many function words and pronouns (your, her, the, to), tracking the flow of formulaic text from one phrase to the next.

20314.name: Structural tokens at the start or end of a line that open or close a block or list entry: closing braces and HTML tags in code, indentation before numbered list items, section/chapter headers, and labels preceding a colon. The common thread is boundaries in structured text, where the token marks a transition between elements.

20317.name: Legal entity suffixes that end company names, chiefly "LLC" (strongest, especially after a comma or in copyright, applicant and manufacturer lines). "GmbH" and other forms such as L.L.C., PLLC and PLLP activate more weakly.

20330.name: Fires most strongly on names of space missions, spacecraft and large science/engineering projects, often on the token that completes the name (Apollo, Mariner 10, Helios, HERMES, Opportunity, SLV-8, CANDU, DUNE, CERN). It also fires weakly on the leading pipe of markdown table separator rows (|---|) and on scattered tokens in noisy technical text.

20342.name: Tokens that repeat an immediately preceding item in a run of identical elements, typically the third or later occurrence of a repeated number in lists, arrays, tables or sequences (e.g. "9, 9, 9", "10, 10, 10"). It also fires on repeated words, characters or HTML cells, and is strongest for repeated numbers in comma-separated lists.

20351.name: The first word of a message string, most strongly when that message is an error, warning, or status report. This shows up in program output and code string literals (print, log, and raise calls), and in log or error lines just after a colon. The strongest cases are error-description words right after an error prefix, like "Specified driver could not be loaded", "Unrecognized", "No suitable", and "No issue". Weaker activations land on sentence-initial words of notices or list items.

20352.name: Word-internal subword fragments in unusual or rare words, such as names, URLs, domain names, code identifiers, acronyms and technical terms. The fragment usually sits mid-word, where tokenization splits the word at an unnatural point that is not a morpheme boundary, and the word continues after it. Examples include 'pag' in pagelines, 'ib' in Unibet and 'fs' in rsfsocialfinance.

Subword fragments in the middle of an unusual, made-up or compound identifier (variable names, code tokens, odd words) that the tokenizer splits into pieces. They fire mostly on the continuation piece just after the first chunk (e.g. h|to|ffline, m|ym|ail, skill|sc|olumns), often when the identifier is a repeat of one seen earlier in the context. Common in noisy code and garbled text.

20359.name: Modifiers naming a type of document or publication series, especially the preliminary or unpublished kind found in boilerplate notices: "working" (papers/drafts), "discussion" (papers), "interim", "preliminary", "Internet-Drafts", "Tech Brief", "Recommended Practice", "Research Papers" and "Editorial BOARD". Activation is strongest on "Discussion" and "Working" right before Papers/Drafts.

20376.name: The last token of a parenthetical abbreviation/acronym that directly follows its spelled-out term, right before the closing bracket. It fires most strongly on the plural suffix ("s", "Fs", "Os", "'s") of a pluralized acronym and weakly on the final piece of singular acronyms or units.

20400.name: Prepositions and connectives inside fixed multi-word legal or formal phrases, firing most strongly on "of" in "arising from, out of or in connection with" in license and disclaimer boilerplate (also "in relation to", "in, upon, or adjoining"). It responds weakly to discourse connectives like sentence-initial "However" and "as a result of".

2044.name: Fires on unnatural, low-quality or garbled text. It is strongest in spun, machine-generated word salad and essay-mill prose, where it covers long runs of incoherent phrasing. It fires weakly on isolated anomalies such as typos, wrong word forms ("critical acclaimed", "filling to", "there me"), odd fragments and artifacts like "[email protected]" or mojibake.

Fires on incoherent, garbled or machine-spun text (word salad, SEO spam, gibberish identifiers), marking tokens that don't fit their context semantically or grammatically. It is strongest on long runs of fluent-sounding but nonsensical prose.

20451.name: Closing delimiters and separators that end an item in a repetitive, list-like or templated sequence, such as closing brackets, parentheses, braces (especially \boxed{} endings), backticks, quotes, pipes, and the newlines between repeated entries. These fire on the token that finishes one repeated unit just before the next copy begins.

20458.name: Words in decision, approval or voting actions, especially verbs like approved, voted, signed into law, allow or permission and the prepositions or "to" that follow them, right before the object of the decision. Activation peaks on official approval by a governing body ("commission approved to").

Words describing a decision or official action by an authority, board, council, court or voters, especially "approved", along with words like "voted to", "decided to", "consider", "reject", "support", "grants" and the prepositions or articles that introduce the thing being acted on (a measure, budget, plan, project).

20459.name: Single capital letters embedded inside alphanumeric classification or identifier codes, typically following a number. The strongest cases are the letter in Mathematics Subject Classification (MSC/AMS) codes such as 34A30 or 55P42. Weaker cases include the letter after the dot in PACS codes (03.67.Bg), JEL codes (C22), patent IPC classes (G06F), and letters in part, grant or gene identifiers.

20461.name: Generic type parameter declarations in code: strongest on the "typeparam" tag in C# XML doc comments, plus the opening "<" (and commas) of generic parameter lists like <T, E> or <'a, T> in Java and Rust and in Javadoc @param <T>. Activations on ordinary prose tokens are weak and scattered.

20469.name: Fires where a specific answer or value is about to be given or has just been determined, mostly in math, code and Q&A text. This covers numeric operands and values in equations, lists and computations, especially results such as the maximum or a selected element. It also covers the "Answer" label and the colon after "Question" in quiz-style formats.

20517.name: Opening punctuation or markup tokens (quotes, brackets, asterisks, #, parentheses, HTML tags) placed right before the first word of a title, heading, quotation, or other delimited span. These usually appear at the start of a line or after a colon or label.

20563.name: Object pronouns (him, them, me, us, you, it, herself), and occasionally nouns that refer back to one, placed right after a verb or preposition. They point to a previously mentioned person or entity, usually one receiving the action (e.g., "given to us", "betray him").

Object-case personal pronouns (me, him, us, them, you, itself, myself; also Russian/Chinese/Yoruba equivalents) appearing as the object of a verb or preposition, especially after 'to', 'by', 'for', 'with'.

20572.name: Pieces of the SVG XML namespace URL in xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg", strongest on "://", "www", ".org" and the year digits. There is weak firing on predictable boilerplate tokens in code and markup (e.g. the quote in `from 'react'`), often in noisy or garbled text.

20613.name: Placeholder or toy values in code, math, and examples. These are typically the first in a sequence: single-letter variable names (a, x, A), sample literals (1, 'a', "hello", 'bob'), and first elements of arrays or tuples. They appear in demo code, function parameters, and abstract statements ('state A', 'if A ⊢ B').

20624.name: Surname tokens, usually the final subword piece of a multi-token last name (Scalia, Alito, Gorsuch, Ginsburg, Breyer, Posner, Sowell). Activation is strongest for U.S. Supreme Court justices and other judges or legal figures, especially after "Justice" or a first name. Weak, scattered activations also occur on unrelated function words and markup.

20628.name: Function words and punctuation that come right after a topic's subject or title is introduced, usually at the start of a definition or description ("X is a…", "X refers to…", "X has…", a comma or period closing the first descriptive clause). It fires on the verbs, relative pronouns, commas and periods that build an expository opening sentence about a named entity or term, often one just given as a heading.

Function words and punctuation immediately following a just-introduced topic or entity name (usually right after a title or heading), especially the copula/verb that begins its definition or description ("X is a…", "X has…", "X (also known as …) is"). It also fires on the commas and periods that end such introductory, encyclopedic statements.

20631.name: Volume numbers in bibliographic or serial citations: the word "volume"/"Vol." and especially the number (plus surrounding period, space, comma) that follows it. Weaker activation for similar part, season, issue, edition, or book numbers in a sequence, and for the word "volume" meaning a book.

20641.name: Tokens naming or marking a number base/representation (e.g., "decimal", the digit after "base", subscript base digits, modulus values) where a following conversion or value is expected; also fires on "Answer" headers after multiple-choice options, i.e. points just before a determined answer or value is given.

20642.name: Surnames of famous wealthy financier/banking dynasties and philanthropists (Rockefeller strongest, plus Rothschild, Sachs, Soros, Goldman, Vanderbilt), often in Goldman Sachs or Rockefeller Foundation contexts; other tokens only weakly.

20653.name: A weak, diffuse feature that mostly fires on discourse connectives and formulaic multi-word phrases that link clauses, such as "on the other hand," "moreover," "however," "then," "in such a way that," "at the time of" and "further I will." It is strongest at the completing word of a fixed expression, for example "hand" in "on the other hand." It appears especially in SEO-style, promotional or non-native web English. It also fires on transliterated Hindi/Urdu words and scattered sentence-ending punctuation.

Markers of Indian/South Asian English: characteristic phrasings and non-native constructions (e.g. 'on basis of', 'keeping in view', 'as per your requirement', 'till date', 'as compared to', 'since…, so', redundant 'then' after 'if', 'etc'). It also fires on South Asian names, terms and contexts (Singh, Jhabak, garam masala, Rs., Sri Lanka, Delhi '011' phone codes).

20657.name: Words or symbols that link two quantities in a rate or ratio, mostly "per" (miles per hour, cost per click). It also fires on "/", "to" (debt to EBITDA), "vs", "in", "on" (return on investment) and "Per" in identifiers like samplesPer. Activation is strongest for "per" following a measured quantity.

20687.name: Mostly the final period closing an answer sentence in synthetic Q&A text ("Question: ... Answer: ... ."), i.e. the end-of-answer/sentence boundary where a new segment would begin. Weaker activations land on structural junctions in math, code and step-by-step text, such as the space after "by", the brace after \frac or \text, colons after step labels, and indentation.

A diffuse, non-semantic feature that fires on single tokens where the text is highly predictable. Typical spots are function words such as "the", "an", "is" and "they", spaces before numbers in equations, LaTeX braces, and word fragments that complete a known term ("X-ian-xia"). It also fires strongly on sentence- or document-final periods and newlines, especially at the end of boilerplate ("...Terms of Service apply.") or just before a section or document break.

20711.name: Mainly fires on the "/runtime" path segment in GitHub URLs for the dotnet repository (github.com/dotnet/runtime). Other activations are weak and scattered over unrelated tokens.

Fires most strongly on the repository-name segment of a GitHub URL path ("/runtime" after "github.com/dotnet"). It also fires weakly on a scattered range of tokens that are highly predictable continuations in their context, such as function arguments, prepositions, line breaks and common collocations.

20718.name: The colon (or the assignment opening quote in JS style code) right after CSS property names, chiefly "position" and "display", where a layout keyword such as absolute, relative, fixed, flex, none or inline-block comes next. It fires most strongly for position. Weak activation also occurs on colons after similar words outside CSS.

2072.name: The word "WITHOUT" in software license warranty disclaimers, firing hardest on the GPL "but WITHOUT ANY WARRANTY" line and strongly on the Apache "AS IS" BASIS, WITHOUT WARRANTIES" line. Lowercase "without" in other "as is" disclaimers is weak, and scattered newlines and punctuation give only faint activation.

20742.name: Separator tokens (newlines, spaces, commas, semicolons) that end one option in a multiple-choice or option list and come right before the next option label (e.g., before "B.", "(C)", "- item"). Activation is strongest after the first or second option.

20751.name: Fires on JavaScript's hasOwnProperty method (".hasOwnProperty", "OwnProperty", "hasOwn"), most strongly in for-in loop guards like obj.hasOwnProperty(key). Very weak activations appear on bullet-list dashes and minor punctuation in technical text.

20754.name: The end of author-affiliation addresses in academic papers. It fires mainly on the country name that closes an address (Italy, USA, France, UK, etc.) and on the newline, comma, semicolon or 'and' right after it, where the next affiliation or section begins. It fires more weakly on other line-ending punctuation in scholarly text, such as the end of a reference or caption.

2076.name: Tokens in passages where the writer announces or frames the main contribution or topic of a text, as in abstract-like openers ("this paper proposes a method", "in this paper, the authors present", "this study investigates", "we here describe a case of", "To tackle this problem", "today announced"). The strongest activations fall on these framing verbs and nouns and on the sentence boundaries just before them. Weak, scattered activations also occur on transition words and the content that follows the framing.

20763.name: The opening double quote fused with a dollar sign ("$ or "${), which starts a quoted variable expansion like "$var", "$1" or "$@". It fires most strongly in shell scripts (echo, test brackets, case, cd/cp arguments) and also in Perl or other code. A handful of unrelated tokens fire weakly.

20773.name: Tokens that are highly predictable continuations of the immediately preceding context, i.e. the expected next word in fixed collocations or syntactic frames. Examples include function words after a word that demands them ("during the", "because of", "consists of", "relationship between"), set phrases ("EDITORIAL BOARD", "ship[wreck]", "public class") and repeated code indentation whitespace.

20777.name: The ".Web" token in code namespaces and imports. It fires most strongly on C# "using System.Web" (including System.Web.Mvc, .UI, .Http). It is weaker for other packages such as Java/Android imports (webkit.WebView, WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter) or project namespaces like SpotifyAPI.Web. Scattered prose tokens get only negligible activation.

20784.name: The noun "person" right after a universal or indefinite quantifier ("any", "any other", "every", "no other"), mostly in legal, licensing and disclaimer boilerplate. It fires strongest on "to any person obtaining" in software licenses. Weak scattered hits include "class" after "public" in code.

20814.name: Units of measurement and quantity labels that come right after numbers, especially scientific or technical units (mol, mL, A, J, GB, g, oz, rpm). Activation is strongest on the unit token and often carries onto the slash or "per" of a compound rate unit (mol/m², mL/min, flops/MB). Weaker activations fall on counted nouns after numbers and on parts of ratio or fraction expressions in math and code.

20817.name: Academic citation markers, mainly the final digit of the year in author-year citations (e.g. "et al., 201[1]") and the numbers and opening brackets of numeric references like [18] or (10–12). It also fires weakly on 'et al.' and author names inside citations.

20847.name: Keywords that close a code block or function body, mostly Ruby-style "end" on its own line (strongest when ending a method before the next def), plus VB "End Sub" and Python placeholder "pass" in empty method bodies.

20848.name: Separator punctuation (mainly colons, occasionally underscores) between numbers in repetitive, structured sequences such as indexed lists or identifiers.

20855.name: File extensions in URLs and links, especially ".php" (and occasionally ".html") after a page name like index, viewtopic or doku. Activation is strongest when the extension is followed by a query string or more path. Other tokens activate only weakly.

20918.name: A token that repeats one appearing just before it in a highly repetitive sequence (lists, loops, degenerate or glitchy text). It is strongest on placeholder, empty or negative values such as null, NaN, None, False, Empty, wrong and error.

20924.name: Terms for health and well-being outcome measures, peaking on "quality of life" (especially "life") and its abbreviation QoL. It also fires on related outcome constructs and instruments (disability, health perceptions, EQ-5D, QALY, VAS), on parts of similar acronyms like QoS/QoE, and weakly on scattered other tokens.

Strongest on words naming measured well-being or outcome constructs, such as the 'life' in 'quality of life', 'happiness', 'life satisfaction', 'outcome', 'sentiment' and 'indices'. Weaker, diffuse activation falls on structural tokens in formatted or technical text, like markdown bold markers, colons after step labels, acronyms in parentheses and 'convert'.

20931.name: Java event-listener interface names, especially the ".OnClickListener" token in Android's View.OnClickListener (strongest in new View.OnClickListener() anonymous classes and imports). Weaker for AdapterView.OnItemClickListener, DialogInterface.OnClickListener and Swing's java.awt.event.ActionListener. Activation on other text is negligible.

20992.name: A diffuse, position-like feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires on single tokens in the middle of a phrase where the continuation is strongly predictable. These are often connectors such as "of", "de", "the", "his", ":" and line breaks that lead into a following noun or value. It also fires on the last word of a set noun phrase ("country-level reports", "course assignments"). Many examples come from templated or semi-structured web text such as listings, metadata, bylines and review fields.

21011.name: Nouns for a gathered group or assortment of items, chiefly "collection"/"collections", plus related words such as selection, compilation, catalog, archive, library, range, variety, collector, treasure, and curated. Activation is strongest for "collection" itself, especially for museum, library or artist collections and in the phrase "collection of".

Collective nouns for a group of gathered or owned items, chiefly "collection" (strongest, especially a personal or museum collection), plus near-synonyms such as selection, set, line, range, fleet, library, archive, stash and assortment, often followed by "of" plus the items.

21015.name: The three-digit number chunk immediately after "10." in a DOI prefix (the publisher registrant code, e.g. 1103 for APS, 1109 for IEEE). Activation is strongest for the token "110" and weaker for other prefixes like 101, 103, 108 or 109. It also fires weakly on "110" appearing in other numeric IDs such as ISBNs or user IDs.

21022.name: Diffuse, weak activation across technical/scientific and product-description prose about devices, materials, light and energy. It fires mostly on function words and descriptive tokens in phrases that characterize a device's or material's properties and performance, such as high brightness, low power consumption, long-lived, perfectly sinusoidal output, and does not suffer from. It is strongest in LED/lighting and efficiency descriptions.
