24360.name: Numeric indices inside Lie/symmetry group names, especially gauge groups like U(1), SU(2), SU(3), O(3) (the number and its closing parenthesis/subscript), with strongest activation on U(1) and Standard Model gauge groups; weaker activation on related physics concepts such as electromagnetism, conserved quantum numbers (baryon/lepton number, R-parity) and other group subscripts.

Tokens in technical math/physics contexts, chiefly small numeric parameters inside group or interval notation (SL(2,Z), SO(2,1), Z_2, (-1,1)), plus physics terms about charges and forces (charge, electromagnetism), with the strongest activation on 'electrom'.

24361.name: The word "Question" that opens a synthetic reading-comprehension Q&A block ("Question: ... Answer: ...") following a passage after a blank line. More generally it marks the boundary where a passage ends and appended QA or boilerplate content begins. It also fires weakly on a few similar section breaks, such as double newlines in website boilerplate.

24367.name: Fires on the Go standard-library package name "sync" in import blocks (strongest when tokenized together with its opening quote, "sync); weakly related tokens like "mutex" get low activation. Other scattered weak activations, e.g. on list dashes, look like noise.

24439.name: Words about explaining or accounting for something, giving a cause or reason for a phenomenon. "explain" is the strongest, especially after modals or hedges ("may explain", "partly explain", "would explain"). Related forms ("explanation", "explained"), "account for", "understand", "makes sense", "reason" and "why" activate more weakly.

24441.name: Binary operators that combine sets or functions, mostly set intersection: the LaTeX \cap token (strongest), the ∩ symbol, and the words "intersection" and "union". Weaker activations go to related operators such as \cup/∪, \circ (function composition), ∧, Python & between sets, and .intersection. Isolated non-math tokens (e.g. "Pages", "the") activate only faintly.

24442.name: Separator tokens (colons, equals signs, opening quotes or braces, spaces) right after a property, parameter or field name and just before its value is written, especially color values in CSS, plotting and code (e.g. 'color:', "col = '", 'background-color: #'). It also fires more weakly on the space before a number in prose.

24448.name: The final token(s) of long alphanumeric strings such as IDs, hashes, URL shortener codes, hex addresses, part/serial numbers and numeric values. The activation lands on the last chunk of these random-looking sequences, right before a delimiter like a slash, quote, newline or space.

24451.name: Tokens inside long, degenerate repetitive sequences where the same token or short pattern (digits, letters, symbols, punctuation, spaces, words) repeats many times in a row. Activation grows as the repetition continues, and is strongest in long uniform runs such as repeated zeros, bullets or OO.

24463.name: The space token placed right before a year's digits in a date, after a month, day, or preposition such as "in", "during" or "of" (e.g. "June 2006", "March 26, 1964", "in 1989"). It marks the point where a year is about to follow.

24496.name: Punctuation and markup tokens that sit between or right after numbered citation references, such as "),", "][", "]-", ");" and ")\" between superscript or bracketed citation numbers, plus LaTeX delimiters like "\[" and "\". It fires mostly in academic or technical text, with a few weak hits on ordinary words.

245.name: Weak, diffuse feature on the token immediately following a number or completed noun phrase, usually a connector or separator leading to the next item: range and comparison words ("to", "and", "than", "more"), math operators (+, =, ×, )/( ), dashes, spaces, commas, newlines, and units. It is most common right after numeric values in ranges, equations, dates and measurements.

Separator or connector tokens that come right after a number (or a numeric or other item) and link it to a following value. Typical cases are hyphens, dashes, slashes, plus signs, ±, commas and line breaks in scores, records, ranges, page spans and table cells, e.g. 3-0, 15 - 10, 9st 4lb / 130lb. Weaker activations fall on short words that play the same linking role after an item (in, and, at, than, for).

24516.name: Fires mainly on "regulatory" and "enhancer" (especially the "enh" piece), most strongly in genetics and molecular-biology contexts such as gene regulatory elements, networks, proteins and enhancer activity. It responds more weakly to related words (regulation, control, promoter elements) and to "enh" in non-biological uses like flavor or frame enhancer. It also fires weakly on the boilerplate phrase "Available On Air Stations".

24573.name: Content of formal, journalistic or official-report prose, especially clauses reporting attributed claims or findings about government, military, intelligence or security actions (e.g. sources saying an attack was intended to cause harm, that malware was used against agencies, or that officials attempted/created a program). Weaker activation is spread across function words in similar documentary/historical report text.

24632.name: Website metadata and labeling boilerplate, mainly the tagging of posts. It fires most strongly on "ged" in "Tagged", especially in "Posts Tagged" archive headers. It fires weakly on "Tags:", "tagged", "Tagged as/with", "Filed Under", "Posts by" and "archive for", which introduce the category, tag or author labels of a blog or forum page.

24647.name: Number chunks (usually three-digit tokens like "000", "130", "700") inside the suffix of DOI identifiers. They tend to fall in the middle of the article number after the journal or year prefix, not at the start or end.

24653.name: In academic citations, the space, opening parenthesis, or bracket right after an author name (e.g. "et al.," or "Smith and Jones") together with the first digits of the publication year that follows ("200", "199", "201"). In short, the point where an author name gives way to the citation year. Activation is highest in lists of several references.

The space (or opening parenthesis) right before a year number, and the first digits of that year ("198", "200", "201"). It fires most strongly inside academic author–year citations such as "et al., 2013" or "Smith (1994)". It fires more weakly on years in dates and in lists.

24660.name: Terms for biological or physical specimens collected for testing or analysis, chiefly "blood" and "samples" (blood tests, blood work, serum, saliva samples, specimen, biopsy, tissue, swab), plus verbs of collecting or sampling. Activation is strongest on phrases like "blood samples" and "saliva samples".

24671.name: Mainly the word "plural", especially in dictionary-style word-form notes ("noun, plural ...", "Word forms: plural") and in software pluralize/pluralization contexts. Weaker activations fall on the indentation space before bullet-point list items and on scattered formatting or parameter tokens such as "delays=", "BYDAY" and "<td>".

24714.name: A diffuse, weakly selective feature. It fires most strongly on the exception name in a Python error message ("OSError"). Elsewhere it activates weakly on scattered function words, punctuation and word fragments. These often occur in structured or technical text such as code, citations, product lists, dictionary entries and command lines, usually just before a name, number or continuation of the listed item.

24738.name: The "pom" letter sequence across words and languages: whole tokens like "pomp" (pompous), "Pom" (Pomodoro, Pompidou, pom-pom) and Czech/Slavic "pom" (pomalu, pomáhají), plus "om/ome/omer/um" pieces right after a split-off "P/p" (Pompeo, pomegranate, Pomeranz, pummeled). Activation is strongest on "Pom"/"pom" tokens.

Word-piece tokens for the sound "pom"/"om" (and similar "um"/"omm"), mostly right after a "P" (or L/G) at the start of a word. Activation is strongest for a capitalized " Pom" opening a proper noun (Pomona, Pomsky, Pompidou, Pomodoro, Pomc) and for "Pompe"/"pomp", and weaker for mid-word fragments like p-ome-granate, p-um-meled, L-om-ax and G-om-el.

24740.name: The letter pair "GL" (any casing or prefix: " GL", ",GL", "/GL") as a token, nearly always in an uppercase acronym, abbreviation or code: GLP, GLUE, GL(n) groups, GLaDOS, GLA, postcodes, IDs and random strings. It is strongest when GL begins an acronym or follows an opening parenthesis. There is weak firing on similar tokens such as "GH" and "gh".

24747.name: The subword token "uz" (and close variants such as "Suz", "Luz", "uzz", "z"), mostly found inside proper names and foreign words like surnames, place names and brands (Suzuki, Soyuz, Fuzhou, Kreuz-). Activation is strongest when it falls mid-word in an unfamiliar name.

The subword "uz" (and close variants like " Luz", " Suz", "uzz", "z", "Z", "ž", Cyrillic "з") appearing inside words, mostly proper nouns such as surnames, given names and place names (e.g. Kuznets, Guzman, Luzon, Suzie), plus slang spellings like "cuz"/"duz".

24795.name: Weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly inside credit lines and lists of proper names: venues, institutions, foundations, galleries and places (e.g., "at the … Center in Fullerton CA", "Photo by", "Photography:"). It lands on the connective tokens and punctuation that join these names (by, at, in, commas, parentheses, "Foundation", "Center"). It also fires consistently on the "<tr" / "<th" tokens that begin a table header row.

24819.name: The category noun (head of a reference class) in classifying or superlative statements like "the most common X", "one type/form of X", "X% of all X", saying where something ranks within or belongs to a class. It fires most strongly on disease terms, especially "cancer", "tumor" and "malignancy".

24822.name: Scientific taxonomic and type names, mostly Latin genus and species names of bacteria, fungi, plants and animals (e.g. Streptococcus, Aspergillus, Quercus). It also fires on words that introduce members of a category in lists, such as "including", "like", "other", "type" and "and". Activation peaks on the subword pieces inside these names.

24829.name: Ball-possession mistakes and changes in sports, chiefly turnovers, fumbles, interceptions and turning the ball "over", plus weaker hits on errors, forced fumbles, dribbling and catches. It also fires weakly on general words for blunders or fumbling.

24849.name: Job titles and occupational roles, especially the head noun completing a position name after a modifier (e.g., editorial assistant, acquisitions officer, security guard, Audit Senior, DevOps expert), plus occasional work-related nouns or activities.

Job titles, occupations and professional roles, with activation on the head noun or final subword that completes the role (e.g. clerk, driver, designer, attorney, gunner). It also fires weakly on related work or field nouns (management, design, instruction). Activation is strongest in job-posting or hiring contexts.

2485.name: Separators and coordinating conjunctions (commas, "and", "or", "&", "/or", "such as", "including") that join items in coordinated lists or pairs of nouns, especially enumerations of proper names, platforms, or technologies. Activation is strongest late in longer lists, at the final ", and" or "and".

24864.name: Mainly a numeric-chunk feature: three-digit number tokens at the start of, or inside, long digit strings. Typical contexts are accession IDs (S-EPMC...), IP-address octets, base-conversion outputs, OEIS sequence counts and other large numbers. It also fires weakly on scattered word pieces or function words that continue a partially started word or phrase.

24887.name: A weak, diffuse feature with low activation that does not track any particular word. It fires on tokens inside clauses that express contrast, comparison, negation or evaluation, such as "but we weren't the only ones", "not even", "instead of", "more real than", "easier and more likely", "right or wrong" and "aren't". It also picks up some of the function words that carry these argumentative turns.

24898.name: Words that name an intervention or change in something's presence or level (loss, lack, knockdown, lesions, blockade, addition, overexpression, suppression, removal, deficiency). They usually take an "of" object and set up a cause-effect claim about what that manipulation does, mostly in scientific or experimental writing. The strongest are phrases like "Loss of", "knockdown in" and "blockade of".

24923.name: Subword fragments inside personal names, mostly non-English given names (especially Chinese, Korean, Thai and other Asian names) in author lists and bylines. It fires most strongly on the middle or later pieces of multi-token or hyphenated given names (e.g. "-Ki", "-Ho", "ih", "h").

24931.name: A weak, diffuse feature firing on structural boundary tokens where one unit ends and a new one begins: sentence-final periods, paragraph and line breaks, stray spaces, list and line numbers, markdown and closing markup such as ** and , and code delimiters such as ```, $$ or (['. It peaks slightly in code and markup contexts, but overall reflects text-segmentation positions rather than specific meaning.

24936.name: Words naming prisons and the penal/correctional system, especially as part of facility or agency names (Correctional, Corrections, correction officers, jail, prison, penitentiary, Shawshank, San Quentin, Department of Justice). The strongest are 'correction(al)' forms. Other institution-name heads (Hospital, Convalescent, College of Education) fire weakly.

24954.name: Tokens that are a name or identifier stem immediately preceding an index-like suffix, usually a digit (e.g. value→3, decorator→1, Part→2, R→1, Profile→7), but also Roman numerals, letters or subscripts (Walker B, Science IV, Villa Wagner II, n_i). Common in code variable and function names, labels, part or section numbers and model/catalog codes. The feature anticipates an upcoming number or label.

24957.name: Line breaks, bullets, spaces and closing punctuation that separate fields in boilerplate or structured web and document text, such as metadata, HAL IDs, radio player widgets, bid listings, HTML tables and citation footers. Activation peaks at the newline that ends one metadata item and comes right before the next item.

24967.name: Dot leaders (runs of periods/ellipses, sometimes spaces or table cell tags) that fill the gap between an entry title and its page number in tables of contents, indexes and similar listings. Activation is strongest on the final dot tokens just before the page number.

25005.name: The word "by" after passive verbs in website boilerplate and legal/license text, chiefly "governed by" (license/terms clauses) and "powered by" (footers such as "comments powered by Disqus"); strongest on "is governed by a" in source-code license headers.

25012.name: Scientific journal names and their abbreviations in citations, especially the "J" in ApJ/EPJ bibcodes and "Journal" after "Astrophysical"/"Astronomical". Also fires on other journal abbreviation fragments (Sci, Natur, PhysRevLett, RMP, CQG, ApJS).

25038.name: Logical negation operators in code and code-like text, mostly the keyword "not"/"NOT", especially in conditions such as "not in", "is not", "if not" and SQL "NOT NULL". Symbolic forms like "!", "!=", "~" and "unless" fire more weakly.

25050.name: The suffix token "atitis" completing inflammatory disease names, chiefly pancreatitis and hepatitis. Pancreatitis gives the strongest activations. Weak activations on unrelated function words are noise.

25058.name: Words that refer back to a set of several items named earlier, often quantifiers or demonstratives such as "these/those", "both/all of which", "respectively", "the two", "each" and "the latter". The activating words are anaphoric or distributive and point to multiple entities already introduced in the text.

25070.name: Mostly function words and delimiters in the middle of a phrase or clause, such as articles, prepositions, auxiliaries, "to", "including/like/without", and colons or bullets in spec lists. Each typically sits just before the content word or value that completes the phrase (e.g. "even the [largest]", "forgets to [wear]", "Power Assist: [5 levels]"). The feature seems to mark connective tokens that anticipate a following complement rather than any specific meaning.

25120.name: Statistical uncertainty terms, chiefly "interval" in "confidence interval" (strongest) and its abbreviation "CI"/"CIs"; "error(s)" in "standard error" activates more weakly.

25131.name: The "type" element of the programming term "data type" and similar compound type identifiers (datatype, DataType, data_types, dtype, ValueType, EventType, fileType). It fires mostly on the "type/types/atype" piece that follows "data" or "dat", and more weakly on non-code labels such as "Document Type" or "Resource Type".

25132.name: Tokens inside URLs, file paths and web addresses (domains like .com/.org/.uk, github.com, path segments such as /blob/master, /uploads/2018/05, relative ../ paths), especially image/link sources in markdown or HTML. Strongest on domain names and path components. Weaker hits fall on source or credit attributions (website, publisher or organization names, e.g. 'CBC', 'Facebook', 'Survey').

25173.name: Words for entry points and ways in or through: entrance, entry, gate, door, access, portal, gateway, intake, ingress, mostly physical but also figurative. Activation peaks on "entrance", especially "the entrance (of/to)", and the following "of" or "to" also fires.

Words for entry and threshold points of a place, such as entrance, entry, gate, gateway, door, lobby, foyer, exit, front and access, plus verbs like enter. It is strongest on "entrance", especially "entrance to/of" a physical place like a mine, tunnel, station or restaurant.

25179.name: Highly predictable space-prefixed tokens that complete a strongly constrained collocation or template slot (e.g. 'aims to', 'in honor of', 'x and y', 'guarantee that', 'ounces [', 'art. 3'), usually a function word or bracket that opens the continuation of a phrase.

25182.name: The ".Linq" token in C# using directives ("using System.Linq;", also System.Linq.Expressions / System.Xml.Linq), within the import block at the top of a file. Activation is strongest for the plain System.Linq import.

25201.name: The word "agreements" in the Apache license boilerplate phrase "contributor license agreements", where activation is strong. Activation is weak elsewhere, mostly on sentence-ending periods, especially in spammy gambling and lottery text.

25207.name: Words naming mathematical structures, chiefly spaces from functional analysis and topology: the 'bert' in Hilbert, the 'ach' in Banach (strongest), 'metric', 'space', 'topological', 'norm', 'functional' and similar terms. These usually come right before 'space' or a similar structure noun. Unrelated tokens get only weak, scattered activation.

25214.name: Initial tokens of proper names, chiefly Scottish/Irish "Mc" surnames and brands (strongest on "McDonald", especially the restaurant chain; also McKinsey, McLaren, McCormick). Weaker hits on other name-start pieces like "Maurit" (Mauritius/Mauritania), Kellogg, Tiffany and Suzuki, and on fast-food words.

Strongest on the name "McDonald", especially the fast-food chain McDonald's, and weaker on other "Mc"/"Mac" surnames (McConnell, McKinsey, McGuire). It also fires on related fast-food words ("fast food", Happy Meal, burger) and on brand or place names that look like surnames (Tiffany, Kellogg, Buckingham, Coventry).

25217.name: Special/sigil variables and placeholder tokens in code, mostly the symbol right after a sigil like $ or @: shell/Perl built-ins ($@, $#, $_, $!, $0, $1, ${#@}, @_) and Python/Rust "{}" format placeholders. Strongest on "@" in "$@"/"${@...}". Also fires on symbol-heavy censored swearing (#$%@).

25249.name: Nouns for retail establishments, mainly "store"/"stores", plus "shop(s)", "retailer", "bookstore", "supermarket" and Chinese 店. They often follow a modifier naming what is sold (grocery, toy, comic book) or a brand name (Honeywell Store). Activation is strongest for "store", weaker for "shop", and also fires on the idiom "in store".

Nouns for retail establishments, mainly "store" and "shop" (plus plurals and compounds like bookstore, storefront, boutiques, in-store). They cover physical and online stores (App Store, iTunes store), and occasionally storage senses such as evidence stores, ammunition store, or the code term Store/load. Activation is strongest for "store"/"stores" in the retail sense and weaker for "shop".

25260.name: Tokens that begin a continuation line in multi-line math derivations: new display-math openers (\[, $$) or alignment characters (&, &=) and line breaks (\\) immediately after a previous equation closes, usually followed by '=', '\le', '+', or '⇒' chaining the next step.

25263.name: Separator or lead-in tokens in structured lists, sequences, equations and numbered answer options (commas, spaces, "=", ".\n\n", "$\\") that come right before the next item. That next item is usually a number or math value.

25266.name: Names or abbreviations of regulatory codes and official legal publications in citations, especially "CFR" (Code of Federal Regulations) after a title number, plus "Federal Register"/"FR", "C.F.R.", NYCRR, Minn. R., Gov. Code and §. Other tokens activate only weakly and sporadically.
Legal citation terms for U.S. federal regulations, chiefly "CFR" (Code of Federal Regulations) when it follows a title number, and "Register" after "Federal" (Federal Register).

2528.name: Binary operators and operands inside mathematical or code expressions (=, +, -, %, /, ==, <=, \times, \cap, \implies, closing braces, numbers). It fires at the point where an operation links two terms, including prose phrasing of arithmetic such as "by 2", "from 360" and "60 times".

25290.name: Tokens that act as separators or filler inside tabular, grid-like or column-aligned layouts. Typical cases are whitespace padding between columns, table cell tags (<td>), LaTeX alignment and spacing commands (&, \quad), dashed separator lines, and numbers or labels arranged in grids. Activation is strongest on aligned numbers and spacing in ASCII layouts and on repeated delimiter runs.

Repeated punctuation, symbols, and whitespace runs in ASCII art, text-drawn tables, diagrams, and grid layouts, especially column separators like pipes, hashes, X's, slashes, and spacing tokens that are aligned across lines.

25311.name: Sentence- and segment-ending boundaries (periods, period+newlines, double newlines) in incoherent, spammy or machine-generated text, especially at an abrupt topic shift where the following text doesn't follow from what came before. Activations are uniformly weak.

25328.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on surprising or irregular tokens, typically glued directly onto the preceding text without the expected space. Typical cases are encoding artifacts (Â, â), typos or stray letters (your<<r>>, of<<A>>ustralians), and citation and markup symbols († ~ {{ <p). It also catches code or parameter tokens right after a colon, comma or equals sign, and odd punctuation or whitespace. It reflects broken formatting and unexpected token boundaries rather than any particular meaning.

25348.name: Separator tokens (commas, spaces, newlines, '=', ';', ':', '>' of table cells) in numeric lists, sequences, tables and citations, at the point just before the next number is expected. It fires most strongly in patterned number series such as 1978, 1987, 1996…, where the next value is predictable. Activation is weak on prose lists and other non-numeric text.

25350.name: Whitespace tokens that combine leading spaces (or a short mark like ---, —, ###) with a double newline, giving blank, empty-looking paragraph breaks. These usually appear in runs of repeated blank lines, between separator or code-fence marks, or just before a new section, question or heading. Activation is highest after code fences or other repeated separators.

25365.name: Punctuation or delimiter tokens placed right before a forthcoming answer, label or list item. It is strongest on the colon after "Answer" in multiple-choice questions, just before the chosen letter. It also fires on "e.g.,", commas in keyword lists and table separators where content is about to follow.

25366.name: The word "Gaza" (mainly as the Palestinian territory/Gaza Strip, especially in Israeli–Palestinian conflict contexts). Activation is weaker for unrelated uses or partial matches (a comic character named Gaza, "GAZA", "Gazel"), and other tokens fire only weakly.

25397.name: The word "clot" (blood clot, clotting, clots, including split tokens like "cl"/"ots"/"ot"), with weaker firing on related coagulation terms such as thrombus/thrombo- and scab. It is strongest in medical contexts about blood clots blocking vessels or about the clotting process.

254.name: Fires on non-English text (Danish, Dutch, Russian, Greek, Bengali, Japanese, Azerbaijani, Spanish, French, German), mostly on word-continuation subword pieces, inflectional endings and short function words, and most strongly in longer foreign-language passages. It fires weakly on foreign fragments inside English text, such as names ("du Pont de Nemours", "Chateau de"), loanwords and domains, and only rarely and weakly on ordinary English tokens.

Tokens inside foreign-language (non-English) words and phrases embedded in English text, especially Romance or Latin function words and word endings in titles and names (e.g. "de la", "pour le", "come", "en el", Latin inflections). It fires weakly on unusual or all-caps English text.

25411.name: Currencies and foreign exchange, peaking on currency names (dollar, yen, USD, Sterling, Euro) and words like currency, forex, and exchange rates, especially when a currency's strength or value is discussed. Weaker activations fall on related value and conversion words (devaluation, value, converter) and on scattered unrelated tokens.

25444.name: The ".createElement" method token right after "document" in JavaScript DOM code. Weaker activation appears on other code that creates elements or HTML tags, such as "('<" in jQuery or BeautifulSoup calls, ".create" methods, and the word "elements" in "DOM elements".

25482.name: An opening parenthesis placed right after a Latin scientific (binomial/genus) name. It typically introduces the naming authority (e.g. "(L.)", "(Greene)", "(Linnaeus, 1758)") or a higher taxon such as order or family (e.g. "(Coleoptera: ...)"). Activation is strongest when an author citation follows, including after "Species Authority:".

25486.name: The closing period (often with a newline) right after the boilerplate "All rights reserved" in copyright notices, where the text ends and new, often unrelated content begins. Weaker firing occurs on other sentence or segment boundaries and stray tokens in noisy or code-like text.

25541.name: The separator (" and" or comma) placed between the two operands of a binary number relation, above all the arguments of GCD/LCM or common factor/denominator expressions (e.g. "gcd(x, y)", "GCD of 21 and 28"), in both math text and code.

25557.name: Declarations of generic type parameters and bound variables in code and math, mostly single-letter names like T, U, V, N inside angle brackets in Rust, C++, Java, Swift or C# generics (e.g. impl<T>, template<class T>), plus type-class constraint variables and quantified or summed variables. Activation is strongest on later parameters in a list. Scattered weak activations appear on unrelated tokens.

25596.name: Tokens in garbled, noisy or atypical text: OCR errors, broken or misspelled word fragments, random character strings, odd capitalization or spacing, and spam-like or formatting junk. The strongest activations fall on dense OCR gibberish (stray letters, numbers and punctuation from scanned documents); weaker ones on single malformed subword pieces.

25621.name: The space (or separator like period, hyphen, "Op.", "of") right after an identifier label and just before its number, e.g. street names, "Suite", "P.O. Box", "RFC", "No.", "Proposition", "Flight", "Op." or grant and patent codes. It fires on the gap that joins a name or category to its numeric designation, mostly in addresses, citations and catalog codes.

25644.name: Dependency-injection annotation names in code, chiefly Spring's "Autowired" (after or including "@") placed above class fields, constructors or setters. Related annotations that mark a member for injection or binding (Inject, InjectMocks, InjectView, SerializeField, FXML, PersistenceContext) activate more weakly. Prose tokens show only negligible activation.

25656.name: The first argument of a function call in code, usually a short context or handle variable fused with the opening parenthesis. It fires most strongly on Go test calls like assert.NoError(t / require.Equal(t, and also on Rust write!(f, Graphics (g, (this, (null and (c. Activations on scattered prose tokens are weak and inconsistent.

25662.name: The word "License"/"license"/"Licence" (and occasionally "Terms"), mostly in copyright and licensing notices for software, articles, and media, e.g. section headers, metadata fields, or names like MIT/Creative Commons/Apache License. It is strongest when it stands alone as a heading or label.

25670.name: The separator (mostly a lone space token, sometimes a comma or ×/*) placed between numbers in a list or product, most strongly in sequences of small primes or prime factorizations (e.g. "2, 3, 5" or "2 × 3") and space-separated numeric outputs. It typically fires just before the second or third item. Occasional weak hits occur on unrelated filler tokens.

25681.name: A diffuse, weak feature of scientific and technical expository prose (abstracts, papers, explanations in physics, materials science, biology, and math). It fires on scattered tokens within explanatory sentences: function words (the, of, that, is, with), clause-ending punctuation, and key technical nouns or phrases such as range, distance, phase transition and temperature dependence. It peaks on phrases describing physical quantities, conditions, or findings.

25683.name: Code tokens tied to while-loops, mainly the condition's closing part (":\n", "0", ")", "]") and the indentation at the start of the loop body, plus loop-variable updates like "current = ..." when traversing paths or pointers. In prose it also picks up words about following links or paths ("follow", "following").

25700.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on structural tokens beginning a new element in formatted or list-like text. Most often this is the "</" of the closing </tbody> tag that follows </tr> at the end of an HTML table. It also fires on " =" in equations (the strongest case), on the first fragment of usernames in comma-separated name lists, and on indentation whitespace or bullet markers that start a new line.

25701.name: The boundary that closes a conditional or temporal subordinate clause (if/when/once/in that case/by default/when not needed) and opens the main clause. Most often it is the comma at that point, but it can also be the first word of the consequent, such as "then", "so", "otherwise", "it" or "the". The same pattern appears in other languages, for example Chinese 就 and 时候，. Activation is strongest when the condition has just ended and the result is about to begin.

25706.name: Words about losing a spouse, parent or loved one and the marital or family status that follows, such as widow, orphan, bereaved, mourning, grieving, divorce, single, and phrases like "lost his" or "died when". "Widow" and "orphan" activate most strongly. Weak activations also appear on look-alike fragments ("wid", "Div") and related ideas such as inheritance, succession, vacancy and remains.

25761.name: A diffuse, weakly activating feature with no single clear trigger. It mostly fires on syntactic junctures where a sentence pivots into further elaboration or consequence. These junctures include commas, relative "which" and "that", conjunctions such as "and" and "but also", colons, opening quotes and paragraph breaks. It also fires on some head nouns and verbs that introduce such continuations (failure, violation, dedication, aided, commenced). It appears often in news, legal or narrative text, frequently about wrongdoing or its effects.

25776.name: Punctuation or symbol tokens (underscore, $, @, *, /, ., -) that act as a prefix glued to the start of a following identifier, path, handle or word, as in _name, @user, $scope, .NET, /dev, -1. Most common in code, URLs and file paths, and strongest for leading underscores such as ._ and __.

25780.name: Separators and numeric parts inside bibliographic and citation identifiers (DOIs, journal volume/issue/page fields, URL paths, ISBN/ORCID/phone numbers). It fires on the punctuation and digits that delimit volume and issue numbers, firing hardest on the hyphen-number-hyphen segment within BMC-style DOIs (e.g. 1471-2350-11-77) and on issue-number labels.

25786.name: The separator between the two bounds of a numeric range, strongest within confidence intervals (e.g. "95% CI 0.54–1.01"). It fires on the dash/en-dash, " to " or comma between the lower and upper values, and secondarily on the decimal point of the upper bound. It is weaker for general ranges ("range 8–60", "from 30 to 100") and fires only faintly on unrelated punctuation.

25791.name: Long runs of repeated dashes (a 28-character "----------------------------" token) used as horizontal separator or divider lines in code, docs, comments and tables. It fires weakly on other repeated-character filler such as table-of-contents dot leaders and indentation whitespace.

25818.name: The final digit of the DOI registrant prefix (e.g. the last digit in "10.1371", "10.1109", or the "/j" after "10.1016"), i.e. the point where the publisher prefix ends and the slash begins the suffix in DOI citations.

25827.name: The combined token '=".' (an equals sign, opening quote, and period), typically an attribute value that begins with a dot, like a relative path or class name (e.g. tools:context=".MainActivity"). It is strongest in real XML/Android markup and weaker in noisy or garbled text.

25846.name: Words within a prompt's output or format instructions that say what the reply should be or contain, mainly imperative verbs and response nouns. Typical cases are "give", "provide", "output only", "show" and "return", plus "response" and "final answer" in phrases like "in your response" or "your answer must contain". Activation is strongest on "output only" and "give" directives about the answer format.

25864.name: Assignment/separator punctuation (=", :, ":", =') that comes right after an attribute or key name in code and markup, just before its value. It is strongest after "role" (role=", role=') and is also common after the CSS "cursor:" property and HTML attributes such as type, rel and aria-label.

25878.name: Strongest on the line-initial " at" in .NET/Java stack traces ("at System.Windows.Forms..."). Weaker on connectors that introduce a following identifier, location or name in formulaic text: " in" in error messages and "X in Region, Country" place lists, and colons after labels like "Species factsheet:". It also fires weakly on boundaries in templated text, such as paragraph breaks after addresses and sentence ends in intros.

25898.name: A diffuse, position-based feature with no single lexical trigger. It fires on tokens that sit just before, or inside, a specific identifying detail. Typical cases are separators and determiners leading into a name, institution, value or date: " -" before an author's affiliation or a location, "the" after "funded by", table <td> cells, "=" before a number, and year or date digits. It also fires on parts of proper names or codes.

25944.name: Multiplication operators in math and code expressions, mostly '*', plus '\times', '\cdot', '·', '×' and 'x'. They usually sit between two operands, often right after a number, variable or closing bracket, and the token sometimes includes the attached bracket (e.g. ')*', ']*'). A few weaker hits are implicit multiplication, such as juxtaposition in LaTeX or a parenthesis following a coefficient.

25945.name: Fires on the token that completes a name or phrase at a boundary before the next item, most often inside lists of named entities such as drug and product names, places, or book titles. Typical cases are the last subword of a drug name, a closing parenthesis ending a title, or a connective like "including" or "from" right before the list or source is named.

25952.name: The "al" token in "et al." in academic author citations (e.g., "Smith et al. (2010)"). It is strongest when the citation is the grammatical subject of a sentence reporting what the authors did. Weaker activation on other citation markup such as LaTeX \citet/\cite.

25959.name: The closing bracket plus newline (">\n") that ends an opening HTML structural tag at the top of a document, strongest right after <head> and weaker after <html> or lang="en". It fires very faintly on other block-opening line ends such as Python "try:\n" or <ul>.

25966.name: Language describing selection, qualification, or allocation rules: who or what gets chosen, ranked, or advances (top teams, largest party, most votes, minimum/maximum limits, fractions of a group, candidates picked). The strongest activations fall on ranking and qualifying phrases in electoral, competition, and admission procedures.

A diffuse feature with no single trigger word. It fires on scattered tokens (articles, prepositions, sentence breaks, plural nouns) inside rule-like, procedural or puzzle-statement text. That text describes groups, counts and conditions: which candidates qualify, how many of the N items, who gets a prize, how a winner is determined. It is often slightly garbled or synthetic. Strongest on nouns for members of a set (contestants, candidates, numbers, dialects, governments) and on connectives that set out selection criteria.

25985.name: Technical and scientific writing about observation, measurement and data collection, especially astronomy: instruments such as telescopes, cameras, filters, spectrographs and CCDs, observing sessions and patterns, survey cycles and phases, date ranges, and units or quantities. Activation is diffuse and weak, spread over nouns and phrases that describe observational setups or measurement procedures and parameters. It peaks on astronomy terms like observing patterns, observation cycles and instrument names.

260.name: A dense, broadly active feature over ordinary flowing prose (and even code), firing on most content tokens but typically skipping articles and short function words like "the", "a", "and". Activation peaks around sentence and paragraph boundaries, on the opening words of a new sentence or paragraph and on key topic nouns there (e.g. "concept", "mechanism", "variation", "limitations").

A dense, nonspecific feature that fires on nearly every token across diverse text (prose, code, instructions, puzzles, multilingual and garbled text), with notable gaps on articles and short function words like "the", "a" and "of". It peaks on content nouns and verbs that open a new sentence, section or explanation (e.g. "phrase", "dominance", "breakdown", "examples", "Testing").

2602.name: A diffuse feature for generic expository or promotional prose, strongest at the start of a document's body or section (right after a title, heading, or line break) and in summary sentences that define or describe what something is or does (e.g. "X is an online retailer that offers…", "It is essential to…", "These attitudes can vary…"). Weaker activations fall on heading markers, colons, and structural tokens that introduce such content.

A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires broadly across runs of tokens in LLM-style or synthetic instruction/assistant text: chatbot answers, code with comments, math and word problems, task prompts, and formal explanatory prose. It does not track any particular word. It is somewhat stronger at clause boundaries, punctuation, newlines and transition words (e.g. 'However', 'To get', 'Yes'), and nearly absent in casual human writing.

26021.name: Fires most strongly on "resolve" as the first parameter of a JavaScript Promise executor callback (new Promise((resolve, reject) => ...)), and moderately on "levelname" in Python logging format strings. It also fires weakly on scattered tokens, such as "Question" headers in Q&A text and ".," after "e.g".

26026.name: Historical and biographical narration about scientists, inventors and notable figures, with the strongest activations on scientist names and roles, dates and attribution phrases ("discovered", "invented in 1947 by", "developed by", "was first known as") that credit a person with a discovery or achievement. Weak activations are scattered over function words in nearby scholarly or historical text.

26038.name: Closing-parenthesis tokens combined with a preceding symbol, mainly "*)" (as in C pointer casts like (char *) or stray "*)" in garbled, multilingual text) and long repeated runs of escaped quote-paren "\")"; activation is strongest on isolated "*)" in noisy or code-like contexts.

26043.name: Concurrency and thread-synchronization terms, mostly in code. The strongest activations are on the "synchronized" keyword and "lock" statements in Java/C# blocks. Weaker activations fall on related words such as Lock objects, synchronize, and thread objects, with faint noise on unrelated tokens.

26062.name: The "CL" token (and the trailing "C") inside medical acronyms, strongest for NSCLC (non-small-cell lung cancer) and weaker for lymphoma acronyms such as DLBCL and ALCL. Weak activations also appear on scattered formatting tokens like newlines and HTML tags.

26088.name: Word-piece tokens beginning with a consonant cluster plus "re/ren" and ending in "nt" or similar, mostly in proper names and name fragments (Trent, Brent, Brett, Laurent, Trev, Bren, -rent), along with "torrent". Activation is strongest for "Trent" and "Brent".

26092.name: Tokens that complete highly predictable fixed phrases or boilerplate, especially repeated website template text (e.g. 'Green Image', 'Registration Dossier', 'Other female celebrities', 'Previous article') and set collocations ('such as', 'like', 'kata atau frase', 'Alberta, Canada'). The feature fires on the second or last word of these formulaic word pairs.

26097.name: Whitespace and newline tokens (mostly double newlines, sometimes fused with punctuation like ",", "{", ":", "]") that close a header, metadata line, salutation or code declaration and come right before the main body text or code block. Code-fence backticks and markup tokens at the start of a block fire more weakly.

26098.name: Words about how parties choose their candidates, peaking on "primary"/"primaries" as a party nomination contest (e.g., "Republican primary", "The primary is Aug. 12"). It fires more weakly on related terms like caucuses, preselection, nominee/nominate/nominations, candidate, party ticket, delegates, debates and leadership election, and faintly on other contests such as award nominations.

26107.name: Operations that combine or split sequences around a separator. In code this covers join and aggregation calls (.join, StringJoiner, implode, sum, collect, fold, reduce, split, sep=/delimiter=/axis= arguments); the strongest activation is on "join". In prose it covers phrases like "separated by", "separated with" and "with commas" that describe how items are delimited.

Concatenating or delimiting sequences of items. The strongest case is string join calls in code, such as the 'join' token and the separator string before it (''.join, '\n'.join). It also fires on prose and code describing how items are separated or formatted in output: 'separated by (a)', 'one per line', 'join with', 'sep=', 'end=', and split/format calls.

26127.name: The suffix token "j" (or "J") that closes Java library names built on a number or prefix, such as slf4j, log4j, neo4j, aspectj and twitter4j. It fires most strongly on "slf4j" inside import statements like org.slf4j.Logger. Similar suffixes such as log4net or retrofit2 produce weak activations.

26128.name: Words marking the endpoint of a process or movement, such as the final destination, recipient, or end-use stage where something ends up or gets used (e.g., 'before installation', 'prior to utilization', 'distribution to individual people', 'end users', 'to those who need them', 'returned to their homes'). The strongest activations fall on use and consumption stages like installation, utilization and feeding.

26140.name: Words expressing fractions or proportions of a whole (third, half, quarter, fifth, tenth, percent/%), usually after quantifiers like "one", "about", "over", "less than" and followed by "of". Activation is strongest on fraction denominators such as "third" and "fifth"; multiples ("fold", "times", "dozen") fire weakly.

26171.name: Tokens at structural breaks in web text, usually right after a paragraph break, where the main prose stops and boilerplate or navigation takes over. Typical cases are section headers, labels with colons, calls to action and link text. Examples include "Click here to…", "Related Stories", "READ:", "Note:", "Contact Us", "Spoiler alert" and "Continued on page". Activation is strongest on promotional or cross-reference phrases that redirect the reader.

26190.name: Separator tokens (a space after "p.", "at", or "page", or a colon, slash, period, or hyphen) that sit just before a page number or similar numeric locator in citations, tables of contents, legal references, patent classifications, and timestamps. They mark the spot where the number is about to appear.

26209.name: The divisor in a division expression: the number (or variable or closing parenthesis) that comes right after "divided by", "÷", "/", or a fraction's denominator brace. It fires most strongly on the digits of that number, including both parts of a decimal divisor. Weaker activations appear on the second operand of subtraction.

26231.name: Paragraph-break newline tokens (often fused with preceding punctuation like '.', ')', '-*-', '+', '#') that end a header, comment block, license notice, or boilerplate section and come right before a new section. They fire most strongly when the next part is code such as imports, includes, use statements or a function definition.

26235.name: The token "Super" in legal citations, abbreviating "Superior" (court) after a state reporter abbreviation like "N.J." (e.g., "N.J. Super.", "Pa. Superior Ct."). Other activations are weak and scattered.

26243.name: Institutional affiliation markers following a person's name: the tokens linking an author or researcher to their organization ("of", "at the", "from the", commas, newlines, footnote numbers, "Professor of", "Department of", "University of"), as seen in paper author lists, bylines, and descriptions of where someone works.

26261.name: The ".apache" token in the Apache License URL (http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0) found in license header boilerplate. Weak activations occur on scattered tokens, such as the " (" after Slashdot usernames and surname fragments in citations.

26262.name: Timestamp and date fields in structured or machine output, firing most strongly on the size/date/time columns of Unix directory listings (ls -l), such as "40 Apr 20 13:03". It also responds to clock times (hh:mm:ss), the spaces between date parts and times, and year fragments like "200". Activations on ordinary prose are weak and scattered.

26282.name: Fires on garbled or invisible text, mainly empty/zero-width tokens, mojibake (�) fragments and stray combining diacritics inside corrupted, mis-encoded or binary-like text. It is strongest on runs of empty tokens in Cyrillic-looking binary garbage and only weak elsewhere.

26308.name: Mostly source code, especially beginner-style or student-written programs. It fires on structural tokens such as declarations (int/String/float, def, class, struct), imports and includes, assignments ('=', '[]'), newlines, indentation and punctuation, with the strongest response on variable declarations and initializations. Weak scattered hits in prose fall on connectives like 'through', 'via' and commas.

26317.name: Strongest on the "(name" token, and to a lesser degree the following "=", in ORM column annotations in code (@Column(name=…), @JoinColumn(name =…)). Otherwise it gives only faint, diffuse activation. The most frequent weak cases are the indentation space before bullet (•) or numbered list items and line breaks inside lists. It also fires faintly on scattered words such as "Casinos" and "DirectX".

26353.name: The first token of a new row, line, or cell in repetitive, structured, or garbled text (number sequences, tables, grids, code, repeated lines). It fires where a repeating pattern restarts, typically right after a newline, pipe, or separator, as the model predicts the next repeated element.

26355.name: In code and shell scripts, the final token of a variable or expression naming a directory or base path (e.g. _dir, _path, DIR, Folder, HOME, __dirname, _root), placed just before a path separator, a '/'-starting string or a concatenation operator that appends a subpath or filename. Activation is strongest on explicit directory or path suffixes.

26362.name: Whitespace-only tokens, mostly runs of several newlines (often with indentation spaces or tabs), that form blank gaps between sections of code or documents. Activation grows with the length of the run, so long stretches of consecutive blank lines fire most strongly.

26367.name: Color values in code, especially hex color codes (the leading "#" and the trailing hex digits) used as gradient stops inside CSS linear/radial-gradient lists, along with color stop endpoints like "transparent" or Tailwind from/via/to color shades. Activation is weak on other list arguments and code tokens.

26406.name: Diffuse activity in code-like or garbled text, strongest on tokens that open a module or package reference in import/require statements (e.g. the bracket opening a Clojure :require vector, require('@, package/pkg/Library/plugins). It also fires moderately on the 'Answer' label after multiple-choice options and on scattered structural tokens that precede a value or name (closing braces, '**', TODO).

26419.name: Scientific words for things obtained or extracted from a source, chiefly 'isolated', 'isolates' and 'isolation' (strongest on the 'isol' of 'isolates'). Weaker activations fall on related terms for collected biological or material units, such as samples, strains, specimens, clones, cultures, recovered and sera.

26426.name: A diffuse, weak feature that fires mostly on function words and punctuation (prepositions like of/at/in/over, articles, commas, periods) right before an upcoming noun phrase. It is strongest when the next words are a specific entity such as a title plus name (President, Gov.), a place, an acronym (HTML, NIL) or a named person. It also fires on subword pieces inside proper names (Chen, Dalberg, Hacohen).

A diffuse, weakly activating feature with no single token identity. It fires mostly on function words and punctuation (the, of, to, for, in, commas, periods, 'says') at phrase or clause boundaries. These are typically the positions just before a new noun phrase or named entity, such as a person, organization, place or title, gets introduced.

26433.name: Structural and boilerplate tokens in web-scraped text, such as delimiters between list items (commas in username lists), paragraph breaks after headers or UI text, and wiki/markup elements ("folder:", "[edit]", "+x", "#region", "BOOKMARK"). Activation is strongest on template and navigation markup, with weak activation on scattered ordinary function words.

26435.name: The "bytes" package name as the first entry in a Go import block ("bytes" right after `import (`). Other tokens in the examples get only trace activation.

26436.name: Tokens immediately before the answer to a computed numeric result (GCD, min, common factor, output), such as '=', ':', 'is', or a trailing space, where the model is about to state the resulting value.

26446.name: Words for stealing: "theft" (strongest, including split pieces like "the|ft" and "thefts"), "thief/thieves", and weaker hits on "stealing", "burglaries", "shoplifting" and "heist".

Words denoting stealing: chiefly "theft"/"thefts", plus "thief", "thieves", "thievery", "steal(ing)", "shoplifting", "heist", "embezzlement" and "loss" in loss prevention. Literal crimes, identity/data/copyright theft and titles like Grand Theft Auto all count. The plain noun "theft" activates most strongly; verb forms are weaker.

26453.name: The noun "Information" (sometimes "material") right after "Supporting" or "Supplementary" in the scientific-paper phrase "Supporting/Supplementary Information". It fires most strongly after "Supporting", especially when the phrase serves as a section header. Weak scattered activations appear on tokens that follow other modifiers.

26461.name: Technical or scientific nouns and verbs that name the process, quantity, or outcome being measured or changed. They typically come right after words for effect or change such as 'decreased', 'reduces', 'induce', 'increased', 'high', 'stable' or 'to', and the strongest cases are biomedical, e.g. 'PEPCK transcription' or 'induce TDCC activity'.

26466.name: Glitchy, out-of-place code-identifier tokens (UI/framework class names like .ToolStrip, .labelControl, JNIEnv, sourceMappingURL, groupBox, AssemblyTitle, interopRequire) dropped into garbled, mixed-language or nonsensical text where they don't belong. Runs of whitespace and odd symbols in the same noisy context also fire.

26480.name: Fires within low-quality SEO-style web prose, especially article-spinner or machine-paraphrased text. The strongest activations land on awkward synonym substitutions and unnatural phrasing, such as 'in consequence', 'along with your moniker', 'our very own sounds' and 'aptitudes'. Weaker activations hit stock discourse connectors and filler words like 'However', 'Nevertheless', 'Moreover', 'Additionally', 'In fact', 'you' and 'very'.

26499.name: Academic degree and graduation contexts, especially the tokens describing when, where, or what degree was earned (e.g., "degree in", "graduated from … in", "for the degree of"). It fires most strongly on the final digit of a graduation or award year ("B.A. degree in 1928"), and weakly on similar completion or award dates and on thesis boilerplate.

26506.name: Words naming a location or site, mostly body parts and anatomical regions (groin, thigh, neck, abdomen, pedicles, epidermal) plus bodily samples (blood, saliva, urine). Activation is strongest where the word gives the place where something is applied, inserted, taken from or felt, often after prepositions like through, from, over or around. Weaker activation appears on geographic places (rural, onshore, New Jersey).

Words naming a physical location or site, mostly body parts and anatomical regions (skin, hand, chest, nose, forehead, artery, finger), usually the object of a locative preposition saying where something is applied, inserted or taken from. Strongest on anatomical phrases in medical or procedural contexts ("the back of a patient’s hand", "transcervical access", "pars plana"). Weaker on non-body locations like a wall, coast or firewall.

26543.name: Words naming algebraic or structural properties, mainly operation and symmetry properties: commutative/commutativity (strongest, especially "comm", "mut" and "ut" pieces, sometimes firing on similar non-math "commut-" words like commuter), symmetric, distributive, associative, idempotent, abelian, Hermitian, unital, transitive and undirected. Activation usually falls on the word's suffix or middle subword tokens.

26553.name: A diffuse, weak feature found in expository scientific, technical and health writing. It fires on scattered function words, punctuation, list separators and content words, most strongly within explanatory clauses that describe mechanisms, roles or effects (e.g., "nutrients may play a role", "vitamin E utilization", "filters and … technology remove").

26566.name: Scientific measurement and characterization contexts: names of analytical techniques and instruments (spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, SEM-EDS, spectra), phrases introducing how something was measured or confirmed ("carried out by", "evaluated by", "indicated by", "confirmed by"), and labels for physical/chemical property fields in data sheets (pH, density, melting point, properties).

26575.name: The word "reasonable" and its variants ("reasonably", the "able" in "Reasonable"), most often in legal, contractual or policy phrases such as "reasonable doubt", "reasonable efforts/steps", "reasonable adjustments" and "reasonably believe". It fires weakly on related evaluative words like "fair" and "equal".

26591.name: The word "Intent"/"intent", firing most strongly on the Android Intent class in Java code, especially the constructor in "new Intent(...)" and the type in "Intent intent = ..." declarations. It fires more weakly on getIntent() and on ordinary uses of "intent" in prose, such as Letter of Intent or intent data.

26599.name: Highly predictable tokens inside boilerplate or templated web text. The clearest cases are "navigation" in the Wikipedia header "Jump to: navigation, search" and "profiles" in "N profiles already created". It also fires weakly on other near-deterministic continuations, such as "order" in "in order to" and "the" after prepositions.

266.name: Words tied to electricity and electromagnetism, firing hardest on "electrical" and "electro-" forms (electronegative, dielectric) and somewhat on magnetic, battery power, wire and similar physics/engineering terms. It also fires weakly and diffusely on scattered technical or scientific words and on loosely related senses such as connection, charge, voting and Magn- word pieces.

26613.name: Separator or boundary tokens in highly repetitive, templated text that mark the start of the next item in a predictable sequence: opening quotes after "or" in unit-conversion lists, <td> cells in tables, commas in lists, and the "BASIS" in boilerplate license text ("AS IS" BASIS). The token is fully predictable from the repeated pattern.

26640.name: ASCII pointer and annotation markers in code or plain-text diagrams, such as carets (^, ^^^^), arrows (<--, ←, ↑, →), pipes and the runs of whitespace used to align them under or beside the text they point at. Caret underline runs and compiler-style ^~~~ markers activate most strongly.

26644.name: Class-name tokens at the end of Java import statements, especially string and text utility classes (StringUtils, TextUtils, Strings), with weaker firing on other utility or type classes like BigDecimal and FileUtils. Activation elsewhere is faint and scattered.

26654.name: The word "the" right after a formulaic past-participle-plus-preposition phrase in front-matter or boilerplate text, such as "licensed/distributed under the" in license and copyright notices or "submitted to the" on thesis title pages. It is strongest in code-header license lines like "Licensed under the Apache License".

26671.name: Field names or keys in structured metadata (key: value headers, YAML front matter, catalog/record fields), i.e. the label tokens just before a colon/value, strongest for 'ms.' prefixed docs metadata keys like ms.service, ms.custom, ms.author.

26695.name: Fires on tokens in structured data and dataset contexts, such as table markup and cells (HTML td/th, LaTeX tables), CSV filenames and column names, lists of numeric values or categories, and phrases introducing data ("were as follows:"). It is strongest on HTML table tags and cell contents like "Age" and on number sequences in tables or charts.

26701.name: Fires on unpredictable tokens in noisy, incoherent or low-quality text, such as spun/SEO spam word salad, OCR garbage, DNA sequences, symbol/ASCII art, username lists, number lists, URL fragments and archaic or foreign scripts. It is strongest in long runs of nonsensical text. In otherwise normal sentences it fires weakly on a single oddly placed function word or noun.

26728.name: Sentence-ending punctuation (periods, often merged with closing brackets/citation markers or newlines), and occasionally clause-ending commas, that close a descriptive or technical statement, especially in academic or expository writing just before a new sentence or a shift in topic.

26735.name: Tokens inside personal names, chiefly in author lists and bylines of academic papers and reports, along with the separators between names: commas, initials, affiliation markers, superscripts and parenthetical native-script names. It fires most strongly in dense, multi-author lists. It also fires weakly on names and roles of researchers quoted in science news (e.g. 'postdoctoral research fellow') and on email domains near author blocks.

26748.name: Final or later tokens of organization and publication names, especially news outlets, magazines, websites, universities and institutes (e.g. Post, Tribune, Slate, News, Journal, Institute, Stanford). They often come right after 'writer for', 'told', 'at' or 'of', in bylines, attributions and affiliations. Activation is strongest on news-outlet names.

26781.name: The standalone space token that precedes a number following an operator or comma in math expressions, number lists, and code arguments. It is strongest for the constant or later term of a polynomial, as in the space after "+" or "-" in "3x^2 - 10x + 8".

2679.name: The attribute name "class" inside HTML/JSX tags (e.g. <div class="...">) is by far the strongest trigger. It fires weakly on related styling and selection words such as style, id, setStyleSheet and getElementsByClassName, on "class" used as a code or programming concept, and on a few scattered unrelated tokens.

26795.name: The word "modification", firing most strongly in the license boilerplate "with or without modification" and more weakly as a column header ("Modification") in version tables. A few unit tokens and nouns in product or spec listings fire only faintly.

26814.name: Repeated separator or operator tokens inside chains of three or more items, usually the second or later " +" in a running sum. It also fires on other repeated joiners such as *, x, /, commas, spaces and LaTeX \right)\left(. Activation tends to grow the longer the sequence of repeated operations runs.

26833.name: Mainly the "d" in legal reporter citations such as "F. Supp. 2d" or "A.D.3d" (the edition/series suffix right after the digit, before the page number). Activation is strongest in "F. Supp. 2d". Other tokens, like fragments inside identifiers, usernames, and numbers, fire only weakly.

26861.name: Boilerplate web-page insertions that break into article text, such as ad labels, "READ MORE"/"RELATED"/"See also" links, "Sponsored:", "Recommended" and "Loading". They usually start a new line after a paragraph break. The strongest response is to "Advertisement" in the "Advertisement - Continue Reading Below" pattern.

26866.name: Geology, earth-science and paleontology writing. The feature is strongest on phrases that place a rock unit, fossil bed or formation in space and time. Typical triggers are words like "beds", "dike swarms", "Basin" and "Island", and the prepositions and relative clauses around them ("from the late Rupelian of the Mainz Basin", "dating from the Cretaceous, which runs", "in these beds"). Elsewhere it fires weakly on scattered tokens across scientific and technical text.

A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires on function words, prepositions, punctuation, section markers and transition words such as 'However' and 'In contrast'. It appears mostly in technical, expository or synthetic, LLM-style text (science, math, code, markdown headings). It is strongest in descriptions of geology and earth processes, such as a scarp formed by folding and faulting, stratification patterns in core samples, or volcano and fault hazards, where it fires on the connecting words of the description.

26883.name: The "Question" label that begins a synthetic reading-comprehension Q&A block ("Question: ... Answer: ...") right after a passage ends with a blank line. It also fires weakly on other section breaks that move from a passage to appended meta content, such as a "Note:" after an answer.

26889.name: The subword token "fony" (and the weaker variant "phony") completing words, chiefly the chemical prefix "sulfonyl" (methylsulfonyl, sulfonylurea) and the PHP framework name "Symfony". Weak, scattered activation on unrelated word fragments.

26923.name: Month and hour fields in date/time format strings (e.g. the "-MM" after "yyyy", "HH", "%m", "%H" in SimpleDateFormat/strftime patterns), strongest on "-MM" in "yyyy-MM-dd". Weaker activation on time-unit words like "hours" and "month".

26937.name: Words about remembering and honoring people or events, especially "memorial"/"Memorial" (strongest when it is a noun or part of an institution name like Memorial Hospital/Stadium/Library). Weaker on related forms such as commemorate/commemoration/commemorative, monument, remembrance, centennial and "In Memoriam".

26942.name: Tokens within formal proper names of organizations and institutions, especially academic author-affiliation lines (Department/Institute/Laboratory of …, University of …, Academy of Sciences), along with nearby author names, titles, and award or agency names, often in Chinese or East Asian contexts. Activation is strongest on the connecting words and descriptive words inside long multi-word institution names.

Fires on the tokens that make up proper names of organizations, institutions and places, especially generic name-forming words. Examples include County, town, Academy of Sciences, Ministry of Foreign/Culture, University of, Cloud Inc, Museum, City, Center and Act. Chinese company-name suffixes like 电子科技有限公司 also trigger it. The strongest activations come from administrative and organizational names. Elsewhere there is weak, scattered activation on formatting and noisy tokens.

26947.name: Diffuse, low-specificity activation, mostly in code, comments and structured text, at the token that closes a short label, type or annotation just before a clarification follows. Typical spots are colons after labels ('Example data:', '// max-heap:'), closing parentheses, and nouns finishing a type description ('opponent object', '0/1 ints'). It also fires on transition words ('and then', 'for') and on 'Why did the' joke setups.

26958.name: Tokens that come right before a cited or listed item: opening quotation marks, colons, "like", "namely", "=", bullets, opening parentheses and list commas. They usually follow a metalinguistic or definitional cue ("the word", "the predicate", "misspelled", "Model:") and signal that a specific term, string, value or example comes next. Activation is strongest on opening quotes after "the predicate" or "the word".

Tokens that open a mention of a literal word, phrase, name or value, i.e. where the text starts quoting or citing something as a string rather than using it normally. They are mostly opening quotation marks after words like "word", "the lyrics", "named" or "searched for". Related tokens are colons, slashes, "=" and delimiters that introduce a quoted term, label or field value.

27008.name: Tokens that begin or repeat an element of a repetitive, list-like or patterned sequence (repeated nonsense strings, list bullet dashes, recurring labels), firing where the token is predictable from an established repetition pattern.

27055.name: Attribution of information to unnamed or generic sources, especially news-style phrases like "people familiar with the matter", "sources close to", "officials said", "spokesman" and "granted anonymity". Activation peaks on "familiar with" and anonymous-source wording.

27061.name: Middle subword fragments of anatomical/medical adjectives, typically the piece right before an "-al" suffix. The strongest is "ne" in "corneal"/"cornea", followed by "nge" in "pharyngeal"/"laryngeal", plus "oden" (duodenal), "ange" (phalangeal) and "he" (diarrheal). It also fires weakly on "Cor-ne" inside names.

27065.name: The finite verb right after a sentence's subject, nearly always a form of "have" (has/have/had), mostly as a perfect-tense auxiliary ("has found", "have been") but also as possessive "has the right". Sometimes it is a form of "be" or a following "been". The strongest cases follow subjects like "I", "this study/research" or "the undersigned" in reporting or formal contexts.

Perfect-tense auxiliaries ("have", "has", "'ve", and the "been" that follows them) placed right after the subject, where a past participle is coming next (e.g. "we have developed", "Microsoft has released", "has been treated"). Activation is strongest for first-person "I/We have" in reporting or research statements.

Finite verbs (mostly auxiliary "have"/"has"/"'ve", also "had", "were", "been", "made") immediately after the clause subject, typically marking the present perfect or the start of the predicate in a declarative statement (often first-person "I/We have…" reporting actions or findings).

27144.name: Words about processing, transforming or cleaning data (clean, parse, convert, encode, clip, format, hash, anonymize, sanitize, translate, wrap). These appear mostly in code or technical prose, often as method names. The feature also fires weakly on code block endings such as closing braces, parentheses and newlines.

27152.name: Formatting/structural tokens that open a new labeled item in structured documents: markdown bold "**" before Proof/Example/Definition/Figure headings, HTML "<td" opening table cells (esp. in tables of contents or figure lists), list numbering punctuation before "Theorem" entries, and separators like newlines, citation brackets, or "and" right before a theorem/figure/section reference or title.

27161.name: Fires in physics and spectroscopy text about quantum or particle states and energy levels. It is strongest on the noun "states" and its descriptors (narrow, excited, bound, quasi-bound), on resonances and levels, and on particle masses such as the Higgs mass M_h = 125.7 GeV. Weak activations spread diffusely across other scientific and technical text.

27185.name: Exponent values in math and code: the numbers, fractions and negative signs right after a power operator (^, ^{, ^{-, **, superscript digits like ³). Activation is strongest for superscripts, fractional exponents and negative exponents. Weaker hits land on other math operands (denominators, function arguments) and on sentence-ending periods in word problems.

27193.name: Mostly code. Fires on the token right after a variable, field, or member name: the assignment operator (strongest, especially " =" assigning an object or value such as "= new"), or a member access or method call (.Add, .set, .Size), a colon in struct-field initializers, or a closing bracket. Prose activations are weak and sporadic.

27213.name: Tokens inside structured, list-like or quantitative content, most often numbers, variables and math operators. These include equation steps, prices, dates, units, format specifiers and answer options such as Yes/True/Never. Activation peaks at the start of a new line or item that restates or continues a calculation, e.g. "4x +" or "x > -5".

The first token at the start of a new line or list item, especially after a line break or a heading/question/colon. It is most often a number, list label (A., (B), a) or short answer word beginning an answer, list, or data row. Weaker activations occur on line-ending punctuation just before a newline.

27223.name: The word "rounded"/"rounding" in numeric rounding contexts, especially right after a number (e.g., "490.024 rounded to the nearest tenth"). Other activations are weak and scattered.

27225.name: Tokens that specify or convert a data type in code, strongest on NumPy-style "dtype" keywords and ".astype" casts. Weaker activations come from other type-casting syntax ("as" casts in Rust/SQL, "::", np.uint8 / tf.float32 arguments) and the word "type" in technical documentation.

27258.name: Mostly the " =" sign right after a derivative or other math expression on the left side (f''(x) =, y' =, ∂w/∂y =), the spot where the result is about to follow. It also fires on other tokens that come just before an expected continuation: colons, the opening brace of \frac, prepositions in set phrases (role of, rhyme with, such as), and "Yahoo" in lists of usernames.

27259.name: Boilerplate, machine-generated technical strings, chiefly browser user-agent strings (AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko), rv:, Gecko, OS/version numbers). Activation peaks on the predictable version numbers and punctuation inside them. Weaker activation appears on other templated metadata, such as forum profile fields (Posts:, Schools:, Followers), website-stats lines, DOI fragments, software version numbers and NASA/JPL-Caltech credits.

2726.name: A weak, diffuse feature on ordinary prose tokens (content words, prepositions, commas and periods) within the first sentence or clause after a paragraph break or heading. It seems to track the progression of a new paragraph's opening statement, with mild peaks at clause boundaries and key nouns or verbs rather than at any specific word.

A diffuse, low-intensity feature with no specific lexical target. It fires on ordinary tokens in running prose, mostly in news, informational and descriptive text. Activation tends to land at phrase and clause boundaries: the head noun ending a noun phrase, the preposition or conjunction linking two phrases, and the comma, period or question mark that closes a clause. It is slightly stronger on clause-final punctuation and on key words in the opening statement of a sentence.

27266.name: Short, non-word fragments forming abbreviations, symbols, or code-like identifiers: variable names (h, diff, lr_qi), chemical symbols (Cs, Pb, Ca/Al), acronyms (MF, LAR, FDA, USDT), codon strings (atc, atg), and digit pieces of numbers or dates. They often sit in parallel lists of similar items, and the strongest activations are on single-letter or very short suffixes that complete a compact code.

2727.name: Quantifiers and scope words that set how much of a group is covered, chiefly universal ones such as "all", "every", "any" and "no one". It also fires, more weakly, on other totality or extremity words like "complete", "completely", superlatives and "main"/"primary", and on the nouns they modify. Activation is strongest on "all" and "every" before a noun phrase.

27271.name: The head noun of a clause's grammatical subject, right before its verb (e.g. 'officials talk', 'Google will add', 'the FBI has been'). Activation is strongest for named organizations, institutions, governments and companies acting as agents (Supreme Court, Google, Sony, MTV, Fed, Congress). It also fires on generic subject nouns such as customers, consumers, God, money and teeth.

Nouns or names that are the subject or agent of a general statement about how something works or behaves, usually at the start of a clause (after 'In', 'The', a colon or a bullet). Common examples are programming languages, tools and platforms (Python, JavaScript, SQL, Excel, iOS, browser), institutions (government, schools, board) and fields (physics, nature) that the sentence then says 'will', 'often' or 'does' something.

27302.name: A determiner (almost always "the", sometimes "this"/"an"), usually right after a preposition like "in", "within" or "of", that opens a noun phrase naming a domain, field or sphere of activity (industry, market, realm, world, field, process, area). Activation is strongest when an industry or market phrase follows.

27340.name: A diffuse, weakly firing feature found mostly in technical or scientific explanatory prose (math, physics, computing, cryptography). It lands on mid-sentence function words and connective tokens (the, and, with, of, is the, by, into) and on verbs or nouns that introduce the object of a described operation or process (takes, produce, finding, state, outcome). These tokens tend to sit just before the key object or result, as in step-by-step descriptions of how something is done or transformed.

27345.name: The first token of a multi-token proper noun, mostly place names (towns, regions, islands, institutions, businesses), especially after locative words like "in", "at" or "of the". It marks the start of a rare or foreign name that the tokenizer splits, such as the "Ge" in Geelong or the "Hal" in Halcyon.

27349.name: Combinatorics and number-sequence concepts, peaking on binomial coefficients (\binom, Binomial, Binomialkoeffizient, Trinomial) and also firing on Pascal's Triangle, C(n,k), Fibonacci/F_n, pow/power and factorial-style formulas. Weak, scattered activations appear on LaTeX/code fragments such as \cite, \frac and \varphi.

2736.name: Fires on the later pieces of multi-token technical names, mostly biochemical ones such as hormones, growth factors, cytokines, vitamins and chemical formulas. It typically lands on a word-internal fragment (lept|in, prol|act|in, interle|uk|in) or on letters and numbers inside an acronym (TGF, HIF, BDNF, SO₄). It is strongest on growth-factor terms ("growth factor", "TGF").

Tokens within names of biochemical molecules (and some other technical terms and acronyms), strongest for inflammatory cytokines and growth factors like interleukins (IL-1, IL-6), tumor necrosis factor (TNF) and growth factors (TGF, IGF), especially the final 'factor', number or letter. It fires weakly on chemical formulas, enzymes and tech acronyms.

Inner or final subword pieces of technical names, mostly biochemical and biomedical (cytokines, drugs, chemicals, vitamins), less often acronyms and technical terms. Activation is strongest for inflammatory cytokine names, especially the 'F' in TNF and the parts of interleukin-6/IL-6.

27361.name: A diffuse, weak feature centred on literalness, identity and sameness: things taken as-is or left unchanged. It fires most strongly on phrases like "matches any literal character" and on immediate or trivial outcomes ("return 500", "starts immediately", "F = 0", "the theorem is trivial"). It also responds to equality and identity expressions ("=1", "equals unity", "the same as", "equal width", "sameRoot") and to echo or unprocessed meanings ("repeat it back", "just copy and paste", "served raw", "face value", "literal translation"). Activations appear in both prose and code or math.

27371.name: References to a document element or visual artifact: the number after "Figure/Fig./Table/Eq./Chapter/line/Sect." or the noun itself (figure, table, plot, graph, paper, screenshot, movie) after "in the/this/your", typically where the text points the reader to that item.

27372.name: Language about collections, repositories and access to stored information or content (archives, libraries, databases, digital records, scanned documents, PDFs, images, datasets), especially phrases describing what a resource contains, provides, or makes available ("access to", "including", "collection of", "available for").
