33896.name: The final digits of a ZIP code (the "10" or "11" in 02110/02111) in the Free Software Foundation's Boston address found in GPL license headers, right before the "-1301"/"-1307" extension. Activation is strongest for the old Temple Place 02111 address. Other tokens show only weak, scattered activation.

33911.name: Stray whitespace tokens (a lone space, or spaces plus a newline) at line or paragraph starts after line breaks, marking a section or content shift. Whitespace-only lines in Markdown and code fire most strongly.

33913.name: Words referring to letter case, such as uppercase, lowercase, capitalization, caps, case-sensitive, camelCase, .upper(), and equivalents in other languages (mayúscula, maiúsculas, регистр). Strongest on 'uppercase' and 'capital(ized)' in password, naming, or formatting rules. Weak hits on loosely related words like 'capitalize on' or 'capitalists'.

33927.name: The word "Question" used as a label after a double line break, opening a synthetic reading-comprehension Q&A pair that follows a passage (usually trailed by ": ... Answer:").

33931.name: A diffuse, weak feature found mostly in AI-assistant-style responses, strongest near their conclusions. It fires on the "'m" in sign-off offers like "I'm here to help" or "I'm happy to clarify", on final "!" and trailing newlines, on the closing "\]" or "}" of boxed final answers, and on the "()" after a closing main() call. It also fires on scattered formatting and filler tokens such as "**", "e.g.," and " р". The highest activation is an anomalous code token, " printk".

33933.name: Fires on the token "embry-" and its forms (embryo, embryos, embryonic, embryology), peaking on the "embry" piece in "embryonic". The match is by spelling, so it also fires on unrelated "Embry"/"emb" fragments. Weaker activation on related early-life and developmental terms: developmental/development, neonatal, fetal, blastocysts, trimester, seedlings, larval, intrauterine.

33941.name: Prepositions and prepositional phrases that introduce a topic, meaning "concerning/with regard to" (e.g., "as to", "with respect to", "in regard to", "in relation to", "about", "regarding", "of"). The strongest activations fall on the topic-introducing word itself, especially "to" in "as to" and "respect"/"relation".

33943.name: Words for transforming data into another format or representation, chiefly "encoded", plus serialize/serialized, stringified, encrypted, compressed, compiled, and "(string) representation". Activation is strongest on serialization terms ("serialized", "stringified", "serializes").

33960.name: Academic and research administrative boilerplate covering funding acknowledgments, ethics and review approvals (ethics committees, IRBs, IACUC), regulatory and supervisory bodies, trial registrations, and author/affiliation metadata. Activation lands on the function words and nouns that link to the approving or funding body ("approved by the", "funded", "support from", "Council", "Ethics Board") and is strongest on ethics and oversight terms.

33962.name: The second term in a slash-joined pair or alternative (X/Y), marked on the word or word-completion right after the slash. These are usually closely related alternatives or co-equal options such as left/right, arrival/departure, iPhone/iPad and elements/words. Weaker activations appear for similar pairings joined by hyphens, 'and', or commas in a list.

33998.name: Tokens that begin a new component inside a compound identifier or multi-part term, typically right after an underscore, hyphen, or camelCase boundary (e.g. in snake_case function or variable names, file paths, API names), and often only a partial-word subtoken. Activation is strongest in code identifiers; in prose it fires more weakly on the next word of a multi-word compound or name.

34011.name: Numeric coordinates and parameters in vector graphics path data, mainly SVG path "d" strings (M/C/A/H/V commands), with weaker hits on Asymptote drawing coordinates. The space-separated numbers and the spaces between them activate most strongly, especially inside arc and curve command arguments.

34023.name: Function words and connective tokens in the middle of a phrase where the next word is highly predictable, chiefly prepositions like "of" following a math noun ("derivative of", "range of", "stability of"). Also fires on fixed-expression slots ("stay on", "side by side", "mistaken for") and on number or LaTeX delimiters (thousands commas, opening \( or $).

34025.name: The noun "point"/"points" (and similar discrete-location nouns like "dots", "node" 点), especially in the geometric/mathematical sense of a location or data element (each point, a single point, data point, at point A). It is strongest in technical contexts and weaker for score points or other senses.

The noun "point"/"points" (incl. midpoint, timepoints, -point), mostly meaning a location or position, as in geometric, data, or physical points in space, also other senses like point guard, decimal point, stock points. Weak firing on similar nouns (dots, pin, notes). Strongest in mathematical/geometric contexts ("another such point", "about a point").

34045.name: Chess move notation: fires most strongly on square coordinates and captures (e.g. 'e6', 'dxc4', 'xf2', 'g5', 'O-O-O') in game records. It also fires weakly on moves and actions in other play-by-play accounts (card games, poker, board/war games, sports, fights).

34048.name: A diffuse, low-specificity feature firing on mid-sentence connective tokens, mostly prepositions, determiners (especially "the" after a preposition or verb) and verb/preposition complements, that open or continue a phrase leading to an upcoming noun object (e.g. "in the development of", "targeted by the", "find out the"). It has no clear semantic theme.

A diffuse, weakly selective feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires on ordinary mid-sentence tokens, mostly function words such as determiners, prepositions, pronouns and auxiliaries, and occasionally on a content word. Many of these sit right after a verb, preposition or connective and begin the complement or noun phrase that continues the clause (e.g., "after a", "exposure to this", "resulted in", "difference from"). The contexts are typically expository or explanatory prose.

34055.name: Mostly in math formulas and code, the token that completes a binary operation, i.e. the right-hand operand directly after an operator such as /, *, ^, + or %. This is typically a denominator, divisor, multiplier or exponent (numbers, variables, slash-variables like /n or /M). Activation is strongest when that operand ends a parenthesized or bracketed sub-expression, just before the closing ) or }. There are a few weak, scattered activations on ordinary prose words.

3407.name: Discourse transition points where a new clause or section begins, most strongly the contrastive connective "However/however" (sentence-initial or parenthetical between commas). Weaker hits fall on other boundary tokens that open new content: sentence-starting "There" or "Let", the comma after "said" before a quote, numbering periods, list-item spaces, and structural markup such as "thead" or "\begin".

34099.name: Fires on the first token of the complement that immediately follows a governing word or operator, such as an exponent marker after a base ("^{", "^"), the space before a numeric value after "is equal to", "that" after "know" or "knows", and the word right after "from". The strongest activations are on math exponents and on numbers in unit conversions.

34100.name: Fires on the last word of a verb or noun phrase (e.g., happen, received, take place, overexpressed, stable, thrive, -inch) when it is immediately followed by a locative or temporal prepositional phrase such as 'in X', 'at X', 'during X', 'off X' or 'near X'. In effect it anticipates a 'where/when' modifier coming next.

34116.name: Binary operators and similar connectors (+, -, ^, *, %, ==, ->, :) placed right after a variable or operand in code and math expressions, marking the point where a second operand follows.

34124.name: Terms for isolated software or development environments, chiefly "virtual environment", "virtualenv"/"venv" and "Python/dev environment", with weaker activation on related concepts like chroot, sandbox, dev-container, VirtualBox and requirements files. The strongest activations fall on "environment" and "env".

34126.name: Citation and footnote markers placed directly after a word or punctuation, such as superscript reference numbers in scientific papers, author affiliation numbers after names, and opening brackets of Wikipedia-style citations ([, ,[, ^{). Activation is usually on the first number or opening bracket of the marker, especially when it comes after a comma or period at the end of a clause.

34127.name: The subword fragment "material" ("aterial", "-material", "/material") attached to a prefix to form compound terms like nanomaterials, metamaterials, and biomaterials, usually in the plural. The feature also fires weakly on a space before a number (e.g. "age 63", "= 100") and on scattered function words.

34143.name: Markers that begin a separate block set apart from the main text, usually at the start of a new line. Most are footnote or affiliation symbols (asterisks, ∗, numbered notes such as "3" or "7."), as in "* Corresponding author". Others are figure or table numbers in captions and web page boilerplate such as "Leave a Reply" or "Scroll to Top". Footnote numbers and asterisks activate most strongly.

34149.name: Places where a term, symbol, variable or abbreviation is being defined or expanded. It fires on the defined symbol or acronym and on the linking token that follows it ("=", "means", "where", "is", a dash, comma or parenthesis), as in glossaries, table footnotes, keyword lists and variable definitions in equations. The strongest case is "SD = standard deviation".

34153.name: Closing punctuation tokens (closing brackets, braces, parentheses, bold markers **, periods, question marks), usually merged with trailing newlines, that end a segment or block. They mark the boundary just before a new section, list, code block or paragraph begins, and fire most strongly on empty or closing bracket pairs such as "()" or "}".

34160.name: A diffuse, low-specificity feature. It fires most strongly on separators between items in enumerations, especially commas and "%," in lists of specs, terms or categories. It also fires weakly on mid-phrase fragments that lead into a predictable continuation: subword pieces of names and acronyms (GR-AC-O, AB-USE, 0xAB) and function words (of, an, a, which).

34173.name: Newline and indentation tokens that end a Python traceback frame header ('File "...", line N, in <function/module>'), just before the indented source code line. Activation is strongest right after the function name (or 'module>'). Other code and table whitespace gets only weak activation.

3419.name: Words about creating or initializing something, strongest on programming object lifecycle terms (constructor, destructor, initialization, created, setter). It also fires weakly on sign-up and registration wording and scattered tokens in technical text.

Object-creation vocabulary, mostly in programming: by far the strongest on "constructor(s)", and weaker on related terms like create/creating, instance, instantiate, builder, factory and copy. Faint, noisy activations also appear on unrelated words, such as section headers and "Commentary".

34200.name: Narrative news-report prose describing events, scenes and reactions in the past tense (who did what, where, and how people responded). The strongest activations fall on main-clause verbs, auxiliaries ("were", "was", "had"), collective subjects such as people, groups or communities, and scene-setting phrases about circumstances or aftermath. Sentence boundaries followed by paragraph breaks also activate.

A diffuse syntactic-boundary feature: it fires on the token that completes a phrase or clause just before a new constituent begins. These are often the head noun closing a noun phrase (e.g. streams, basin, echoes, members), clause-ending punctuation or commas, and, in code, line-ending tokens such as ':⏎' after except/if statements or '.")⏎' closing a print call. It appears across prose, code, lists and non-English text, with no clear semantic theme.

34205.name: Clause and sentence boundaries in expository, documentation- or tutorial-style prose. It fires on transition points such as punctuation and paragraph breaks, and on clause openers that set up an explanation ("You can", "To access", "If", "Whether you are", "As a", "The syntax of… is"). These tokens mark where the text moves from stating a topic to explaining how something works or what the reader can do.

Clause and sentence boundaries in explanatory, technical or instructional prose. It fires most on periods, commas and line breaks that end one statement, and on the words that open the next one ("This is", "In this case", "If", "A", "You", "However"). It also fires on linking verbs and connectives inside definitional or descriptive statements ("are called", "is", "will", "that", "to").

34206.name: Diffuse, low-strength activation on the content of embedded verb-phrase complements that spell out an intended action, purpose or effect. These tokens typically follow a setup word such as "to", "of", "through", "efforts", "willingness" or "help". Examples include "to provide users with", "efforts to develop a field-based test", "to figure out how to make" and "how climate change will affect sea level". The strongest activations fall on the verbs and objects in the middle of these purpose or goal clauses.

34211.name: Subject-field words or word fragments, often abbreviated or split into subword tokens, within the names of academic journals, scientific societies, conferences and research departments in citations and affiliations (e.g. "Immun", "Micro", "Astr", "Endocrin"), especially the discipline term that follows "Journal of", "Frontiers in" or "and".

34218.name: Language about audience size and media performance metrics, especially TV ratings and viewership (Nielsen, household rating, viewing rate, audience share, record-high ratings). Peaks fall on words like "ratings", "rate" and "share", with weaker activation on the surrounding statistics (numbers, percentages, counts of viewers, followers or players).

34219.name: The word "property"/"properties" (also Chinese 属性), firing most strongly on its programming sense of an object attribute or field (code, XML, config, APIs). It fires more weakly on scientific or mathematical attributes and weakest on real-estate or proper-name uses.

34234.name: Fires on tokens that sit mid-construction, where the next token is highly predictable. Most are function words or connectors inside fixed phrases ("with regard to", "together with", "patterns of", "there is"). Others are word fragments ("inter"+vision), year digits, or code indentation.

34290.name: The element name in closing HTML table-row tags (the "tr" in </tr>). It fires more weakly on other table-structure markers such as </tbody>, vc_row, and LaTeX \hline, and only faintly on unrelated words.

34300.name: Personal names, especially first names (and the start of full names), of authors, reporters, photographers, or people being quoted. These often appear in bylines, credits, or contact lines after cues like "By", "Author:", "Photo:", or "said". Activation is strongest on the given name, weaker on surnames and on surrounding punctuation or initials.

Personal names, chiefly first names and the early part of full names, in author/byline or attribution spots (after "By", "—", "@author:", "name:", photo credits, or a name standing alone on its own line before text). Feminine first names often activate most strongly. There is weak activation on list/answer starters such as "1.", "**", "*".

34304.name: Leading indentation whitespace (spaces/tabs) at the start of a code line, especially the first line of a newly indented block after a colon, brace, or control statement; weaker activation on line-break/delimiter tokens that separate statements or sections in code and math text.

Whitespace indentation tokens (runs of spaces or tabs) at the start of code lines, especially inside nested blocks, along with line-ending punctuation plus newlines (e.g. ");\n", " {\n"). In prose it fires weakly on clause or sentence boundaries such as commas and periods, essentially marking structural boundaries where a new statement or line begins.

34305.name: Whitespace runs and filler/separator tokens in structured or tabular text (column padding, alignment spaces, empty HTML table cells like , LaTeX & separators, underscores/dots), plus boilerplate web text such as "Sponsored" and "Jump to"; strongest for long space runs that pad columns.

Runs of whitespace (spaces, tabs, sometimes followed by newlines) used for alignment or padding inside code, tables, ASCII art, and other formatted or structured text. Activation is strongest for long space runs separating symbols in ASCII diagrams and aligned columns.

34307.name: Header or label words in boilerplate web and metadata layouts, most often "Authors" (as in "Authors:", "Famous Authors", "Yonsei Authors") and "Question" after a programming-language tag in Q&A pages. Weaker hits include publication names (Post, Sentinel), "-review" in URLs, and newlines before "Title:" fields. These are labels that introduce a list of names or the main content that follows.

34322.name: Mentions of a class/struct's own type name inside its definition or methods in code, e.g. constructors and destructors (Command(), Game::~Game), return types (-> Self, -> Scorekeeper), self-typed parameters (const Rational&, Node*), and impl headers. It also fires weakly on recursive self-references such as a function calling itself or d[i] = d[i-1].

34334.name: The word stem "electric" (electric, Electric, electricity, electrician, electrically), strongest for the adjective "electric" in technical or physical senses (electric field, current, charge, motor, grid). It is weaker for "electricity" and weakest for the figurative "electr-" in "electrifying".

34335.name: A weak, diffuse signal on words in reporting and attribution frames, where the text says how information is known, sourced or conveyed. It covers attribution and evidence phrases such as 'according to', 'officials have told / declined', 'later identified', 'identified from records', 'mentioned', 'we learn', 'we will see', 'it's theorized', and 'evidence' or 'information'. It also includes the auxiliary or verb right after a subject that is about to report a fact ('has been', 'is', 'have').

34337.name: Words for a first public appearance, launch or introduction, most strongly "debut" (especially debut novel, album or film), along with premiere/premiered, breakout, inaugural and opener. More weakly, related words for a leading or notable start such as flagship, career and opening.

3437.name: Word-initial fragments beginning with a vowel plus p/b (mostly "hyp"/"Hyp", with weaker "imp", "hip" and "yp"), firing on the first subword of words like hypotension, hypertrophic, hyperspectral, impressive and impacts. "hyp" fragments activate most strongly; whole words and unrelated tokens activate only weakly.

34378.name: The first word (usually an adjective) of a fixed multi-word proper name or technical term, which predicts the word that follows. Typical cases are agency and department names such as Internal Revenue, Social Security, Environmental Protection Agency and Internal Medicine, plus anatomical or technical phrases like internal carotid or internal combustion. Activation is strongest for Internal Revenue and Social Security.

34448.name: Line-initial comment/marker symbols, almost always "#" (occasionally "//" or indentation), at the start of a new line in code-like or garbled list text where earlier lines began with the same prefix. It fires most on repetitive, structured sequences of prefixed lines.

34455.name: The "Answer" label (and its colon) placed after the lettered options of a multiple-choice question, right before the correct letter is given. It also fires more weakly on "Question" labels and on scattered tokens in synthetic, quiz-like or explanatory text.

34462.name: The first three-digit chunk of a four-digit year (e.g. "164" in 1645), firing most strongly on pre-modern dates (11th–18th centuries) in historical prose and weakly on 19th–20th-century years or other numeric strings.

34524.name: A diffuse, mostly structural pattern. It fires on tokens at segment boundaries or at the start of a new unit: paragraph breaks after a sentence (the strongest), bullets, table and line-break tags, and statement-initial code keywords inside a namespace or class block ('using', 'internal', 'private'). It also fires on sentence-opening connectives ('However', 'Furthermore', 'If', 'The company'). Isolated tokens such as 'assigned' or 'mathrm' also activate, with no clear semantic theme.

A diffuse, low-level feature firing on structural boundary tokens, mostly in code or noisy/garbled text. Typical hits are line-start indentation, newlines, braces and parentheses that open blocks, sentence- or line-ending punctuation, list bullets, and tokens that begin a new statement or clause (e.g. "However", "In addition"). It is strongest on C# "using" directives at the start of lines inside a namespace, and on opening "((" in JavaScript.

34532.name: Tokens in code that open a block body: the closing parentheses, arrow, opening brace or colon (often with a trailing newline) right after a function, lambda, namespace, loop or condition header. Strongest on anonymous JavaScript function/IIFE openers such as "function(){" and "(function($){".

34539.name: Fires most strongly inside PHP strict-standards warnings of the form "X::method(args) should be compatible with Y::method(args)". The peaks are on "with", the parent class name, "::", the method name and the argument list. It also fires strongly on ".ops" in code identifiers (bpy.ops, org.ops4j). There is weak, diffuse activation on scattered tokens in code, error messages and noisy or spammy text.

34541.name: Mainly the "ellant" suffix completing "Appellant" in legal case captions (e.g., "Defendant-Appellant"), which activates strongly. Other hits are weak and scattered, mostly on boilerplate tokens in templated text such as the "!)" after the OEIS header, "Icon" after "RSS", and the space after "slug:".

34556.name: Inner subword pieces of medical/anatomical terms, firing most strongly on the 'ch' in bronch- words (bronchitis, bronchial, bronchodilator) and on 'b'/'bo' in thromb- words (thrombosis, thrombocytopenia). Weaker activations occur on similar mid-word fragments (papill-, glomerul-, cervix) and on the '<tr' tag that starts each new HTML table row.

34563.name: Numeric values (often the final digits or result) in math equations and word problems, especially numbers right after "=", "+", "-", or "exactly", i.e. constants and computed results. It fires weakly on a few non-numeric tokens in math/technical contexts, such as "the", "it" in "I hope it is correct", and variable names.

34577.name: Words describing fullness, crowding, or capacity: something being packed, clogged, congested, cluttered, flooded, overstretched, backed up, busy, filled to the brim, or in high demand (and occasionally its opposite, emptiness or lack of space).

Words about capacity, fullness, and limits: being full, filled, crowded, empty, sold out, maxed out, capped, overloaded, limited, or taken. The feature fires on adjectives, verbs, and particles that describe how much something is occupied or saturated, with the strongest activations on words like 'full', 'sold out', and 'capped'.

34580.name: Android Java superclass names after "extends" in class declarations, firing hardest on "AppCompatActivity" and more weakly on "Activity", "BaseActivity" and the "Activity" suffix of names like FragmentActivity. Activations on non-code text are rare and weak.

34631.name: Dental problems and treatments, the strongest being cavities, tooth decay, root canals and crowns/bridges, plus enamel and caries-causing bacteria. It also fires weakly on general damage, decay and repair terms such as corrosion, rot, cracks, structural repair and minor surgical procedures.

34663.name: Words that set up a comparison or matching criterion, typically in questions or selection phrases like "which/the one that best describes, fits, matches" or "closest/nearest/similar to". The feature fires on the relational word, most often "to" after closest/nearest/equal, "than" after comparatives, or verbs such as fits, matches, describes and makes true. It is strongest for "equal to" and "nearest/closer to".

34665.name: The word "divided" in the arithmetic phrase "X divided by Y", usually right after a number or quantity. Activation is strongest in explicit numeric calculations. There is weak activation on other operator-like separators between numbers.

34718.name: Punctuation right before a color value, mostly after color, fill, stroke or background attributes in CSS, SVG, HTML, LaTeX or plotting code. Typical tokens are ="#, : #, ='#, a bare # before a hex code, or { after \color. Activation is strongest on ="# ahead of hex color codes.

34778.name: Tokens where arguments or inputs are being specified. Activation is strongest inside function and method signatures and parameter lists, such as C, C#, Java and Perl prototypes. It peaks on opening parentheses, parameter types and names, and the commas or newline indentation between parameters. It fires more weakly on usage-syntax option brackets. It also fires weakly in procedural instructions where the user is told what to supply or choose ("choose the", "fill in the", "add the recipient", numbered step markers, bullets).

Tokens marking a slot where an input, argument, or parameter is expected next. The strongest cases are function signatures and parameter lists ("=function(e", "open(", "(enum mode, uint", "(int"). The pattern also covers API descriptions such as "expects an", "takes a" and "given by the arg". It appears in UI instructions to supply a value ("Enter your", "enter a name", "type in a number for", "Choose a") and in form field labels followed by a colon or asterisk.

34787.name: Function words and connective tokens (the, of, and, that, which, in, by, is) in scientific or technical expository prose, peaking in dense biology abstracts that describe mechanisms, structures and functions (e.g. "is mediated by the glycoprotein complex", "domains responsible for interaction are formed during"). Activation is weak and diffuse elsewhere.

34788.name: The word "Question" opening a synthetic reading-comprehension Q&A label ("Question: ... Answer:") placed right after a passage of text, usually following a blank line. Weak secondary firing on other structural label/delimiter tokens such as "=" or "Error".

34790.name: Fires in garbled, nonsensical or corrupted text (broken code, random symbols, mixed scripts, encoding junk), mostly on tokens that repeat an earlier fragment in a repetitive pattern, such as a repeated bracket tag, URL-encoding piece, number or suffix. It does not track any particular word meaning.

34799.name: Fires weakly and diffusely on tokens, often mid-word subword fragments or function words, in text that is non-English (French, German, Spanish, Romanian, Polish, Korean, Persian, Greek, Welsh, Russian) or unusual and nonstandard English (archaic or Scots spelling, Shakespearean contractions, ungrammatical or machine-translated phrasing). It seems to respond to language or orthography that departs from ordinary modern English rather than to any particular meaning.

A diffuse feature that fires on tokens where the English is unexpected or non-standard, often right after a verb or preposition. This covers misspellings and odd word splits (sup-r-ised, b-ing, anounce), awkward machine-translated, non-native or spun text ("tour to Odisha", "I am purchase the Find"), and foreign-language words. It also fires on stiff, formal announcement or notification phrasing ("has the honor to enclose", "I inform the House", "glad to announce you, that").

34800.name: Fires mainly on the ".net" domain suffix in URLs, most strongly in jsfiddle.net, and more weakly in blog.csdn.net and cdn.jsdelivr.net. Elsewhere it gives only faint, scattered activations on random tokens in noisy code or technical text, and none on Telugu script.

34834.name: The token "submit" in code, especially as an HTML input/button type value (type="submit"), with weaker activation in identifiers, event handlers, and keys built from "submit".

34875.name: Website navigation and boilerplate UI text, such as links for Previous/Next post or page, Home, Return/Back to, page-number lists (1 2 3…), arrows and separators, skip-to-content and table-of-contents links. These typically sit between or after main content.

Website navigation and boilerplate text, such as "Home", "Previous", "Next", "Back to Gallery", "Page X of Y", "«", "Jump to", and "You are here". These usually appear at line starts between scraped page content and the main text. It also fires on similar words like "Previous" or "Home" in ordinary prose at the same positions.

34894.name: References to the US Republican Party and its members: "Republican(s)", "GOP", and the "R" party abbreviation after politicians' names. Activation is strongest for US political uses and weaker for other right-leaning or "republican" terms (Tory, "bipartisan", Irish Republican Army, Turkish CHP, Portuguese "republicano") and for the coincidental string "GOPATH".

34911.name: The abbreviation "No" (number) after a document-type label such as Appl., Report, Contract, Docket, Investigation or Bill, introducing an identifier in formal headers like patents, technical reports and legal filings. It is strongest in patent "Appl. No." lines. Weaker activations fall on similar label words such as "Version".

34921.name: Weak, diffuse activation on boilerplate web text such as site descriptions, cookie and browser notices, newsletter or subscription prompts, repository and access notices, and product blurbs. It fires on function words and generic service phrases like "to ensure you have", "for the latest updates", "with your name and password", "uses ... that" and "for further information".

34968.name: A weak, diffuse feature found mostly in personal, profile-style or promotional text such as bios, dating or classified ads, and self-descriptions. It fires on list connectors (commas, "and", "or") and on first-person words ("I", "am", "your") in enumerations of hobbies, traits or interests, e.g. "hiking, adventuring, and cuddling" or "hardworking, motivated and determined".

3497.name: Opening markup tag names and commands, mostly HTML table cell tags (<td, <th) plus <p, <strong, <br, <sub and LaTeX commands like \frac, \caption and \textsuperscript, marking the start of a formatted element just before its content.

34972.name: Tokens inside long random-looking alphanumeric strings such as hex hashes, UUIDs, session IDs, URL query tokens, DOIs, and other identifier codes. Activation is strongest in the middle of high-entropy character sequences, especially mixed letter-digit runs.

34975.name: Descriptions of a person's or entity's body of work or output, especially counts of creative or scholarly works produced (e.g., "authored more than 700 papers", "author of six previous books", "his films include", "third novel"). The strongest activations fall on the quantity phrase and the work noun ("more than 30", "articles", "papers", "books"); weaker ones appear on general catalog or listing language about works, publications, or items.

34984.name: Newline tokens that end a short, isolated line (often a single word, label, or fragment) in incoherent, list-like, code-block, or repetitive text, frequently right after an odd/out-of-place word or the "assistant" role marker, just before the next line begins.

3501.name: Separator tokens that sit between two paired or listed values: commas between coordinates, function arguments, or list items; hyphens in ranges; ' x' in resolutions; slashes and colons in ratios; 'and', 'to', or 'of' joining two terms. Most often numbers, especially in code and technical text. It is weak, firing a little more on commas inside coordinate or argument pairs.

35061.name: A diffuse feature that fires on function words and punctuation at clause boundaries where a statement continues into a qualifying or elaborating segment. Typical triggers are prepositions (of, to, at, per), conditionals (if), an opening parenthesis, "e.g.," or a colon or newline. It shows up mostly in technical writing and code comments ("as per input convention", "Use actual weighting if known", "(e.g., ..."), but also on stray tokens in noisy or garbled text.

35068.name: The last word (or final subword piece) of a short heading, section title, or page/UI label, usually a generic noun like Information, Details, Reviews, search, content or features. It typically follows a newline and comes just before another line break or colon, as in web boilerplate and document headers.

35073.name: Numeric result tokens: the number given as the computed answer or output of an arithmetic expression, code evaluation, or problem (after '=', '# Output:', '//', 'boxed{', 'Output' sections, answer choices).

35092.name: The closing quotation mark that ends an attribute value inside HTML meta tags, especially right after name="viewport" or http-equiv="Content-Type"/"X-UA-Compatible" and just before content=. It fires weaker after charset="UTF-8" and on similar header-key quotes.

35117.name: Mainly the long run of leader dots in a table of contents, usually the first dot chunk right after a section title and before the page number. A weaker secondary pattern is the word right after 'reproduce' or 'reproducing' (the, this, them, through).

35169.name: Words for rounding numbers (round, rounds, rounded, rounding, round off/up/down to), used for numeric approximation in math, programming and data reporting. Related terms like 'nearest', 'approximation' and the Russian 'округление' fire weakly.

35196.name: Function words and punctuation (prepositions, conjunctions, articles, commas, relative pronouns) that come right after a complete noun phrase or clause and introduce a continuation such as a modifier, appositive, prepositional phrase or list item. The activation marks the boundary where the sentence is extended beyond a finished constituent.

35205.name: Diffuse, low-level activation across formal scientific and technical prose such as abstracts, papers, reports and specifications. It fires most on structural and functional tokens: sentence-ending periods, paragraph breaks, citations and reference numbers, and section headers like Introduction. It also picks up methodological phrasing in the body text, such as "we developed an analysis method", "newly developed", "these tools are developed within" and "basic design".

35210.name: A diffuse, low-level feature that fires in technical prose about web development and programming, such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, markup and rendering. It mostly lands on function words, clause boundaries and punctuation in explanatory sentences around those mentions, not on the technical terms themselves. It is strongest where the text describes writing or needing code to make a page work, e.g. 'CSS will be needed… This is some simple CSS that will' and 'code it up and'.

35214.name: The top-level domain and the following collection/series path in institutional repository URLs, strongest on ".edu" and the slug after it in "Follow this and additional works at:" boilerplate (e.g. digitalcommons…edu/etd). Other parts of academic URLs and DOIs, such as year digits and path pieces, activate only weakly.

35223.name: Mostly weak activations on discourse connectives and transition words that begin a new clause or sentence ("However", "In addition", "As a result", "There", "so that"). The one strong activation is ".org" in the "mozilla.org" URL of the Mozilla Public License boilerplate header.

35251.name: Newline tokens and other separator tokens (spaces, pipes, @@, often fused with punctuation like '%', ')', ':', '`') that delimit items in repetitive, list-like, tabular or garbled/structured text, firing at boundaries between repeated units.

35265.name: Tokens in formulaic, semi-structured or boilerplate text (spec sheets, safety data sheets, taxonomies, bullet lists, page templates), usually the final token of a field label or value that sits right at a boundary before the next value, list item, or line break, where the continuation is highly predictable.

35297.name: The word "coupling" and its variants (couplings, coupled, decoupling, split forms like "cou-pling"). It fires most strongly on the physics sense of an interaction strength between fields, particles or systems (e.g. strong coupling constant, Higgs–top coupling). It fires more weakly on mechanical, chemical (silane coupling agent) and instrument-linking senses. Faint activity appears on a few unrelated technical nouns such as damping and crosstalk.

35317.name: A weak, diffuse feature on structural and formatting tokens. It fires most strongly on decorative comment banners and boxed headers in code: runs of # or *, "//" and "|" borders at line ends, and "<!--" openers. It also fires weakly on markup scaffolding such as HTML table tags (td, tbody, br, p), LaTeX commands, markdown fences and dividers, and line breaks between list or table items.

35327.name: Language about climate change and global warming: terms like "warming", "climate", rising temperature, CO₂ emissions, sea level rise and human-induced environmental change. It is strongest on "warming" and "temperature increase" phrases, and weaker on general change or increase words (prices, risk, losses) in scientific contexts.

35349.name: Path-segment tokens that begin with a separator (mostly a backslash, sometimes a dot or slash) inside hierarchical names. The strongest activations are on PHP namespace segments in use/namespace statements (Illuminate\Support, Symfony\Component\Validator, App\Repositories). Weaker activations come from Windows file paths, Java/C# package imports and URL path parts. Rare faint hits fall on ordinary function words or spaces.

35352.name: Responds most strongly to the word "override" in code, especially the @override annotation before a method in Dart/Flutter or Kotlin, and sometimes the indentation token after it. Also fires weakly on "overrides" and on other code keywords and function words such as final, if, _, using and that.

35379.name: Words describing investigation, discovery and evidence-gathering, such as searching, finding, examining, tracking down, suspecting, proving or identifying something. These show up mostly in police, crime, legal or detective contexts, e.g. interviewing, finding sufficient evidence, or information leading to identification. Activation is strongest on the action verbs and on 'evidence/information' phrases.

35387.name: A diffuse, weakly firing feature found mostly in technical text such as math, physics, code and data tables. It fires most on named variables or quantities being defined or compared: the variable name in a definition like 'R =', a repeated 'width' in a ratio, symbols like rho and mu, indices and subscripts, and parameter or field names like 'x:', 'href' and 'Unit'. It also responds weakly to surrounding syntax and to some ordinary words in explanatory prose.

35396.name: Diffuse, mostly structural feature that fires on boundary or separator tokens just before a new segment begins. Typical spots are sentence-final periods followed by blank lines before a heading, spaces or indentation before list numbers, dates and citation page numbers, and markup or delimiter pieces (td>, $$, ):, backticks, opening quotes). It also fires weakly on some mid-sentence function words (the, than, including, make) that introduce a predictable continuation.

35403.name: Tokens in boilerplate or legal, regulatory and technical text (licenses, copyright notices, safety data sheets, terms) that introduce additional, supplemental or exceptional conditions. Typical forms are "additional/further/other/supplemental" + noun (information, data, hazards, usage rights), "except (where)", "with the exception of" and "see also", plus restrictions such as "may not further distribute" or "restrictions apply".

35412.name: The word introducing a reference to a numbered figure in scientific/technical writing ("Fig", "Figure", "figure", "Figures"), typically after phrases like "as shown in", "see", or at sentence start before a figure number. It fires more weakly on similar references to tables or equations ("Table", the "(" in "Eq. (1)").

35424.name: The noun "notice" right after "copyright", peaking in the standard license boilerplate "The above copyright notice and this permission notice shall be included". Weaker activation falls on similar boilerplate head nouns such as "address" in "Your IP address will be recorded", with scattered noise elsewhere.

35426.name: The word "you" that begins the clause "you may not use this file except in compliance with the License" in Apache License 2.0 boilerplate headers, right after (the "License");. It fires most strongly when "you" opens a new comment line (after *, //, #); activation elsewhere is weak and sporadic.

35431.name: The subword token "raf" inside words, firing most strongly on the middle of "zebrafish" (zeb-raf-ish). It fires only weakly on "raf" in other words such as Musharraf, Ashraf, Trafalgar and dabrafenib, and weakly on other fragments of model-organism or fish names.

35440.name: Repeated symbol/character runs, strongest on box-drawing horizontal lines (─) in ASCII tables, diagrams and separators. Weaker on other long repetitive sequences such as backticks, Z's, arrows, dashes, spaces and odd Unicode glyphs.

35474.name: Mentions of saints and other revered religious figures: "Saint", "Blessed", "holy Elder", guru and canonization, feast days and devotion/commemoration. Activation is strongest on the title words themselves ("Saint", "canonization", "Feast Day"). Weaker activation spreads to the honorific and hagiographic context around such figures, including piety, mystics, honoring legacies and the names of revered people.

35476.name: The word "continent" and its forms (continents, continental, subcontinent, Continental), plus weaker activations on related large landmass terms like peninsula, mainland, plains, and planet.

35554.name: The "/or" token in the phrase "redistribute it and/or modify it" from free-software license boilerplate (GPL/LGPL/Perl headers); other tokens fire only weakly.

3557.name: Language reporting quantitative changes and statistics, especially in financial or news reports: words and phrases describing increases, decreases, or levels ("dropped by 3.4 per cent on last year", "increased to", "stood at", "down almost 5%"), together with the attached numbers, percentages, currency amounts and reporting-period dates. Weaker activation appears on scattered numeric or technical tokens such as years and spec figures.

35576.name: Concepts of legitimacy and formal recognition of status or authority: words in contexts where something or someone is acknowledged, declared, installed, elected or proclaimed (a leader, government, spouse, heir, independence), or where legitimacy is questioned (illegitimate, illegally occupied, annexation). The strongest activations are on 'legitimacy', 'acknowledge … independence' and 'installed … government'.

3558.name: Code annotations, attributes and decorators that modify following declarations, such as Java @Subscribe (strongest), Rust #[derive(...)], #[allow], #[test], Blade @if and mentions of decorators. Weaker activations fall on boilerplate page and document metadata labels, e.g. 'Skip to content/navigation', 'Corresponding author', 'Open Access', 'Opinion' and 'Location', plus similar header or structural tokens in code.

35594.name: Gravitational lensing, firing most strongly on "lens" (and "ensing" in microlensing) in astrophysics text. Weaker activations appear on related light-distortion and astrophysical terms such as bend/bent, mirage, mirrors, redshift, shear, Shapiro delay, curvature, polarization and clusters.

35595.name: The word "Question" opening a generated Q&A section ("Question: ... Answer:") placed after a double newline at the end of a passage. It is a transition from arbitrary or often incoherent text into a reading-comprehension question about that text. Weak, scattered activations also occur on a few unrelated tokens.

35645.name: Go channel type keyword "chan", especially in "make(chan" when channels are created. It also fires more weakly on related concurrency and communication types such as channel, Queue, Receiver and CountDownLatch. Activation elsewhere is weak and scattered.

3565.name: Weak, diffuse activations on nouns and short phrases that name ready-made, reusable things provided for others to adopt or build on: templates, libraries, building blocks, predefined sets, reference implementations or architectures, guidelines, protocols, and product solutions or offerings. Nearby enabling phrases like "helps you to", "enable you to", "to choose from" and "to use" also activate, with the strongest responses in software and technical descriptions.

Weak, diffuse feature in technical/assistant-style text (mostly programming and instructions). It fires on nouns and phrases for generic tools, templates, examples or artifacts being offered or used, such as code, sample, example, prompt, framework, template, placeholder, dataset and Material UI/Tailwind CSS. It also catches nearby helper verbs like provide, craft, use and help. It is strongest on terms for sample or ready-made code and resources.

35662.name: Mid-word subword tokens inside scientific names of pathogens and organisms, strongest on the malaria parasite genus 'Plasmodium' ('mod'/'ium'). It also fires on 'falciparum', the 'imal' in 'antimalarial' and 'alar' in 'malar', and other Latin genus names such as Borrelia, Babesia, Cordyceps, Oryza and Flaviviridae. Occasional weak activations on unrelated punctuation and line breaks.

35664.name: The word "PRIMARY"/"primary" immediately preceding "KEY" in SQL table definitions (column constraints or CONSTRAINT clauses), strongest for uppercase in CREATE TABLE code; weaker for other key constraints (FOREIGN, UNIQUE) and prose mentions of a primary key.

35668.name: The tag name inside a closing HTML/XML markup tag, i.e. the token right after "</" (div, li, span, button, label, etc.). Activation is strongest for common HTML elements like div, li and button. Elsewhere it fires only weakly and sporadically on prose tokens.

3567.name: A diffuse, context-general feature with no single semantic theme. It fires on tokens that open a slot whose filler comes right after. Examples include prepositions, determiners and modifiers before a noun ("use of", "need for", "of this", "pace of new"), a decimal point before digits, the year prefix "201" in citations, "<td" opening a table cell, and a LaTeX backslash before a command. It is most active in structured or formulaic text such as HTML tables, math, URLs and citations.

35674.name: A mid-word subword token, usually starting with 'e' or another vowel, that follows a token ending in a vowel, so a vowel pair (oe, ae, ue, ee, ie, au) is split across the token boundary. It appears mostly in rare proper names and foreign or German/Dutch-style words (Roebuck, Glaessgen, Oestermann, Shoenfeld, Aesop). It fires most strongly on oe/ae combinations in surnames.

35682.name: Highly predictable, formulaic next tokens in boilerplate or structured text, such as "void" after "public static" in C# Main declarations, the YAML block indicator "|" after "title:", HTML closing-tag "</", and commas in repeated function calls. It also fires on stock-phrase continuations like "measured by". The YAML title block marker activates most strongly.

35694.name: Structural markup symbols at the start of a new line, most often the pipe "|" opening a Markdown table row, and also blockquote ">", "#", bullets, or indentation. Strongest in long repetitive runs of bare line-leading pipes.

35705.name: Words expressing ending, leaving, exiting, or going back, such as close, quit, exit, finish, halt, terminate, return/back, done, and bye. They often appear as UI or menu commands (Close, Back, Done, OK), program control (KeyboardInterrupt, break, Disconnect) or step-by-step instructions.

35734.name: Separators and values in metadata key–value fields, mostly ones naming a document's type, category or version (e.g. "Type:", "Document Version⏎", "Contribution to journal Article", "niveau recherche", "layout:"). It fires on the colon or newline right after the field label, or on the type value itself (e.g. "Article", "-review", "Paper"). These appear in repository records, catalog listings and front-matter headers.

358.name: A weak, diffuse feature with no single clear meaning. It fires mostly on the opening piece of multi-token names or unusual terms (e.g. the first fragment of a rare word, place name or software name) and on label-like tokens in structured or boilerplate text, such as citations ("et al.", "eds", PMCID), affiliations, photo credits, numbered list entries, and code or notebook markers.

3581.name: The word "Judges" (plural, capitalized), firing most strongly on "Circuit Judges" in the bench listing at the start of US court opinions ("Before X, Y and Z, Circuit Judges."). It fires weakly on other uses such as the biblical Book of Judges or Act titles.

3583.name: Quantitative statistics and tallies, especially numbers paired with units or counted items (yards, runs, passes, homers, calories, percent, deaths), and the connectives that chain several such figures into a list ("and", commas, "for", "in", "with"). Activation peaks on sports stat lines like "38 passes for 441 yards and three touchdowns" or "92 runs in 92 balls".

35842.name: A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires on mid-phrase tokens, often function words or predictable continuations, in boilerplate, SEO or promotional web text. It peaks inside title- or heading-like phrases such as “1Win Casino INDIA Offers free spin”, “21 Days Challenge to Shifting from Anxious to Calm” and “How to set up…”, and in garbled or broken sentences.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on many ordinary tokens (function words, punctuation, nouns) across running text. It is strongest in promotional or commercial copy, such as product listings, ads, hotel and real-estate blurbs, and calls to action like "contact us for your T shirts" or "Check out our other bundles".

35858.name: The word "Attorney" (or abbreviations like "Atty"/"Attys") in prosecutor titles, especially right after "U.S.", "United States" or "District" (e.g., "U.S. Attorney"). It fires most strongly on the "ty" ending of the legal-citation abbreviation "U.S. Atty.". Weak, scattered activations on other words in government-agency names and unrelated tokens.

35862.name: Fires weakly in scientific and technical prose, chiefly materials science and chemistry, at points where a specific material, compound, sample or system has just been named. Activation lands on the function words, commas, closing parentheses and final subword pieces that end or follow that noun phrase, just before its predicate or description ("has", "have", "was", "of", "for", "as a", "which"). Peaks occur on complex compound names and their trailing punctuation. There are scattered low-level hits elsewhere.

35872.name: Words for blood cancers, mostly the 'leukemia/leukaemia' token or its suffix pieces (strongest), plus their abbreviations (AML, CML, CLL, DLBCL) and the '-oma'/'-coma' endings of lymphoma, myeloma, sarcoma, glioma and similar tumor names.

Names of blood and lymphatic cancers, strongest on "leukemia" (including the "emia" piece of "Leuk-emia") and weaker on the "oma" ending of lymphoma, myeloma and hepatoma. It fires most when the disease is named as an example after "such as" or "has". Low-level activations on unrelated tokens are noise.

35896.name: Punctuation and separators (colons, dashes, line breaks) that end a role or field label in document front matter or metadata, such as "Supervisor:", "Primary Examiner —", "Contact:" or "Author(s):". They fire right before a person's or organization's name is given.

35909.name: Line breaks (mostly double newlines, sometimes fused with ')', '/', or '>' as in '<thead>⏎') that separate fields in boilerplate metadata of repository records and paper cover pages, e.g. after a URL, DOI, handle, or 'Link back to DTU Orbit' and just before the next label such as 'Citation (APA):', 'Final published version:' or 'Rights / License:'. Weaker hits fall on similar label words like 'Full'.

3591.name: Mainly the word 'deliver' and its forms (deliver, delivering, delivery), along with related ideas of conveying or transferring something: ship, shipping, arrival, arrive, hand, receive, present, distribution. Weaker activations come from tokens that share its opening letters, such as 'del' word-starts and the names Daniel, Dan, Del and Danny.

35912.name: The word "Unless" that opens the "Unless required by applicable law or agreed to in writing" clause of Apache License 2.0 boilerplate in code comment headers, right after the license URL line. Activation is near-zero elsewhere (weakly on an unrelated noun like "air").

35918.name: Fires mainly in contexts about supplying, sending or delivering documents and materials. The strongest hits are "of" after "service" or "copies" ("proper service of submissions", "copies of the audit"), plus "copy", "copies" and "delivery". Weak activations also appear on scattered function words and punctuation that follow a noun inside a list or a clause about provision.

35921.name: Boundary tokens that close a self-contained block of boilerplate or header text, such as a license/copyright notice, file header comment, promo/signup blurb or disclaimer, just before new content begins. These are typically end punctuation fused with newlines ('.⏎⏎', ')⏎⏎', '⏎⏎') or comment-closing markers ('#⏎', '**⏎', "'''"). A few weaker hits fall on ordinary mid-sentence words.

35933.name: Misspelled, garbled or corrupted word fragments, typically subword tokens inside a word that come from typos, OCR errors, phonetic or joke spellings, or spun/nonsense text (e.g. 'te-ii', 'volt-ge', 'p-prn', 'combin-atioti'). The token is the point where the spelling departs from the real word.

Word-final subword fragments that complete a word in a garbled, misspelled, or nonsensical way, so the result is not a real word (e.g. "fin-uhs-ed", "stat-etriet-ions", "fol-re"). These mostly occur in noisy, corrupted, or machine-generated gibberish text.

35939.name: Mainly the first digit chunk of a long number or code that is split across several tokens, inside identifiers such as DOIs, ISBN/ISMN numbers, URLs, file names, course codes, variable names and figure numbers. Weaker activations fall on boundary tokens in templated or boilerplate text, such as the newline after SEO-style service headings, "essay sample", HTML table tags and commas in addresses.

35940.name: In dates, the separator token (a space, slash, or hyphen) that comes right before the day number. It usually follows a month name or number, or a word like 'Accepted:', 'Published:', or 'on'. It is most frequent in publication, received, and accepted dates.

35941.name: Fires on the opening token of a document or structured block, such as the very first word or symbol of a text (namespace, using, #define, #ifndef, ![, <!--, titles), and especially the <thead token that starts the header right after a <table> tag.

The first token of a document (almost always) when that token is code-, command-line-, or markup-like: shell commands (python, pip, sudo), programming identifiers, preprocessor directives, HTML tags, and separator lines (=====, ####, ****). It fires most strongly on "python" at the start of "python manage.py ..." commands.

35946.name: Weak, diffuse feature in technical, code and structured text. It fires most on positional or index information: numbers after "line", "column", "position" or "index", along with their separators (colons, commas, brackets, spaces). It also fires weakly on code-block boundaries, indentation and other filler tokens.

35991.name: Mainly fires on the space token that falls between the reporter abbreviation and the page number in legal case citations (e.g., the gap in "F. Supp. 2d 677"). Weaker activations land on scattered function words that begin a following clause or complement, such as "that", "including", "When", and "you".

35995.name: The " com" token that begins a reverse-domain Java package name right after the "package" or "import" keyword (e.g. package com.example..., import com.google...). It fires more strongly after "import", especially when it follows a block of android/org/javax imports, than after "package". Weak, scattered activations on other word-initial tokens are noise.

36000.name: A diffuse, non-semantic feature with no clear topical theme. It fires on single tokens across many languages and formats, usually inside a predictable multi-token unit: split word fragments (C|REDITS, DEAD|LOCK, b|readcr|umb), digits within DOIs, ISBNs and URLs, set phrases ("risk of", "next on the", "注意ください"), and code or math syntax. The token is typically one whose continuation is strongly determined by context.

36004.name: Words for blockchain transaction costs, chiefly "fees" and "gas" (also "cost", "fee", "rate per"), mostly after "transaction". A weaker secondary trigger is the "#" before freelance project ID numbers, with "Gas"/"sey" also firing as name or code fragments.

36028.name: The verb "use" right after "you may not" in the Apache License 2.0 boilerplate ("you may not use this file except in compliance with the License"). Other restrictive "not allowed to use" notices activate weakly. Unrelated tokens show only faint, scattered activation.

36034.name: The noun completing a fixed legal/formal collocation, above all "fact"/"facts" in "material fact" (e.g. "genuine issue/dispute of material fact"). Weaker hits occur on similar set-phrase heads like "compelling state interest", "major bodily function" and "political opinion". Faint scattered activations on web boilerplate ("Related" posts) are noise.

36040.name: Page numbers in tables of contents, together with the dot leaders, spaces, or HTML table-cell tags (<td>, </tr>) just before them that separate section titles from their page references. The numbers themselves activate most strongly, especially when the same number repeats on consecutive entries. Line breaks after TOC entries activate weakly.

36062.name: Sentence-ending periods (sometimes with a closing parenthesis or newlines) in academic or technical abstract-style prose, typically closing a sentence that states a study's aim, scope, or topic, right before the next sentence begins. Activation stays on the punctuation, occasionally spilling onto the next sentence's opening word ("The", "It also").

36075.name: Fires very strongly on the "/env" token of the shebang line "#!/usr/bin/env" at the beginning of Python scripts. Elsewhere activation is negligible, with weak scattered hits on structural tokens such as <tbody>, list bullets, newlines and colons.

36078.name: The word "reply"/"replies" (often split into subword pieces like "ply"/"plies") in web forum, blog, and mailing-list boilerplate UI text. Activation is strongest by far for "ply" in Blogger "noreply@blogger.com" email addresses, and weak for similar interface labels (improve this answer, edit, talk, CrossRef).

3609.name: Words built on the root "activ-" (active, activity, activities, activate, actively, activists, inactive), plus weaker hits on related words for being lively, busy or in operation (alive, busy, restless, vibrant, running, fire up, back to life).

36126.name: Tokens immediately preceding a reference number, label index, or list item, mostly in academic/technical text: the space or bracket before a citation number ("[", "Ref. ", ", " in [2, 3, 4]), the letter prefix of labeled items (R27, R2, S4), and bullet or dash list markers. Weaker hits fall on the word before a listed name or example ("Part of the", "such as").

36127.name: Shell I/O redirection syntax, chiefly the '>' operator (also '<', '>>', '&>', '2>&1') and redirect targets such as '/dev/null'. The strongest activations are on '>' or '>/' directly before /dev/null. Weaker activations fall on related command-line tokens like dd's if=/of=, file descriptor numbers, and output-file arguments.

36128.name: Separators between consecutive items in lists of citations or names, chiefly the semicolon or comma that comes right after a year and before the next author in a multi-reference citation (e.g., "et al. 2002; Smith 2005"), along with the commas in LaTeX cite-key lists (sometimes merged with the next key's first letter). Weaker hits fall on other list delimiters such as opening brackets or parentheses before the next reference, table cells (<td>) preceding a name, and similar breaks before a new item.

36147.name: Mostly fires on tokens in the middle of identifiers, codes, or structured formatting, such as characters inside PDB IDs, PACS codes, catalog and URL numbers, and HTML table tag pieces. Some activations fall on word-fragment continuations inside names (e.g. "jack" in Blackjack, "one" in LoneRanger). The common thread seems to be near-deterministic continuation tokens within structured or reference-like text, though a few examples don't fit cleanly.

36184.name: Multi-character tokens that begin a recurring technical or web identifier: ":b" in the boilerplate "tag:blogger.com" ID, ".TimeUnit" in Java "java.util.concurrent" imports, and ".azure" inside URLs/domains. These fire strongly. Ordinary prose words and punctuation, often the word just after a noun, fire only weakly.

3620.name: Appositive or descriptive phrases that come right after a person's name and give their title, role, affiliation or other identifying detail (e.g. ", an analyst at", ", CEO of", "who is the adviser to", ", 66, of"). The comma right after the name and the role words are the strongest parts, typically in news-style quote attributions.

36222.name: The indefinite article "a"/"an" right after a preposition like "under", "by" or "to" in formal boilerplate. It peaks in license statements ("licensed/distributed/released under a … license", usually Creative Commons) and is weaker in phrases such as "operated by a", "served by a" or "subject to a".

36223.name: Tokens that come right before a specific name, value, identifier or list item is introduced. These include introducers like "called", "named", "namely", "is:" and "are:", plus colons and semicolons leading into lists. They also include code delimiters that open a literal or key, such as == ', =", (", [', <value>, `, a leading . before a file extension, and table pipes.

36227.name: Fires on tokens of words for medical specimen sampling and screening, peaking on the pieces of 'Pap smear' and 'cytologic'. Related tokens also activate: 'smear' and its parts ('sm-ear', 'smeared'), 'aspir' (aspirin, aspiration), 'mamm' in mammograms, swab, toothpick and wiping/fingertips. Activations elsewhere are weak and noisy.

36228.name: The tag name "body" inside an HTML closing tag (</body>), usually just before </html> at the end of a document. Other closing-tag names (main, div, container) fire weakly, and scattered unrelated tokens barely fire.

36249.name: Prepositions (mostly "for") and the words right after them that name the purpose, audience or use case in suitability or recommendation phrases, such as "not recommended for production", "less preferred for large numbers", or "not safe for all chars". Activation is strongest on "for" or the target noun ("general", "beginners") following words like recommended, preferred, suitable, safe or practical. It also fires weakly on similar prepositions in other languages ("для").

3625.name: Names of organizations and institutions, mostly government agencies, departments, and official bodies (e.g., USDA, NASA, Centers for Disease Control, Bureau of Land Management, police, ministry, commissioner), including acronym pieces and the final words of multi-word agency names. Activation is strongest on the head or last word of the agency name.

36261.name: Whitespace separator tokens, mostly tab characters and odd/extra spaces, that sit between fields or words rather than serving as normal word-leading spaces. Typical spots are tab-delimited columns, code indentation, headers and odd spacing in scraped web text. The strongest activations are tabs between fields in tabular data and code. There is weak firing on fragments in run-together boilerplate text (e.g., "PETITION", "Holidays").

36270.name: The first three digits of a year (e.g. "201", "202", "199") split off from the final digit, mostly in academic citations. Activation is strongest when the year is fused into a BibTeX-style citation key directly after an author name (e.g. "gowal2019scalable" inside \cite{}), and weaker in ordinary "Author et al., 2017" citations, dates and URLs.

36278.name: The method name "onCreate" in Android Java code, firing most strongly when it is declared as an overridden lifecycle method ("@Override protected void onCreate(Bundle savedInstanceState)") in Activity classes. Activation is somewhat weaker for public, Fragment, Dialog or ContentProvider variants and for prose mentions of the method. Weak activations on unrelated tokens in ordinary text are just noise.

36289.name: Closing delimiter tokens that end a bracketed or fenced block. The strongest activation is on '>' directly after ']]', as in the CDATA-style ']]>' ending. Weaker activation falls on the final backtick plus newline of a closing ``` code fence, and on closing tags like '', '' and ''. Other closing brackets such as ']', '}' and ']}' after nested structures also fire weakly.

3630.name: Fires on nouns tied to riding, mounting or wheeled transport, such as bicycle, horses, 'ride the bull', rider, wheelchair, wheel, brakes, sledges, Honda and electric vehicles, and is strongest on 'bicycle'. It also gives weak, scattered activations on other product, gear or device names and on word fragments.

Fires on words tied to motorcycles, riding and motor vehicles. The strongest hits are "motorcycle," "ride helmet(less)," "rode," "RIDE," "boda boda," "Hyosung" and "four wheeler." Weaker hits include motorhome, Motor racing, car model names, carts and rides. Activation is very weak (around 1) on assorted brand/name subword pieces and casual lifestyle or travel nouns.

36319.name: Small numbers, especially 3, 5 and 10 (also 4, 7), appearing as factors, divisors, primes or bases in number-theory contexts: prime lists (2, 3, 5, 7…), prime factorizations (2×3×…), divisibility checks (n % 3, "divisible by 5"), and base-10. Activation is usually on the second or third item of such a sequence, after 2 has already appeared.

36322.name: Tokens inside long runs of repeated filler or formatting characters, such as whitespace padding, dot leaders in tables of contents, dashes, ``` code fences, HTML/LaTeX fragments, &amp chains, and rows of symbols (†, ★, ♥). Activation is highest in the middle of the repetitive sequence. There are also weak, sporadic hits on ordinary words and punctuation.

36330.name: The word "born" (or "Born") in biographical statements giving a person's birth details, mostly in "[Name] was born" constructions just before a date, place or parents. Activation is strongest in formal biography or "Early Life" sections. Weak activation on other biographical fact fields such as "Height".

36359.name: Word-fragment tokens that begin a longer word split across tokens. Chiefly the Japanese hiragana "ま" (in ません, しまった, まで, まとめ, おまえ, etc.), and ".tom" as the start of ".toml" file extensions or domains like "tomcraft". Weak, sporadic hits fall on stray punctuation and variable tokens in code or math.

36384.name: Literature-review style attribution of prior work to its authors. The feature fires on author names, citation markers (closing ] or ), \cite{...}, et al.) and the reporting verb that follows (proposed, reported, showed, studied, designed), as in "X et al. [5] proposed...". It is strongest on the closing citation bracket and "al" right before the verb. Weaker activations appear on commas or periods introducing a subject, and on agents or actions in similar non-academic descriptions.

Tokens at the boundary between a cited source or named agent and the claim attributed to it, typical of academic-style (often fabricated) citations. Activation is strongest on closing citation brackets and parentheses, citation years, and 'et al'. It is also notable on the following attribution verbs such as 'proposed', 'tested' and 'claim'. Weaker activations fall on the ends of names or entities and on pronouns introducing what a person, paper or product did.

36388.name: Verbs, mostly present participles ending in -ing, that start a reduced relative clause right after a noun for a document, rule, or instrument (bill, law, order, decision, note, rule) and state what it does or requires, e.g. "a bill allowing", "laws banning", "an order requiring". Activation is strongest in legal or regulatory contexts.

36390.name: Clause and sentence boundaries, mostly sentence-final periods (plus some commas, closing brackets/parentheses, newlines and following connectives like 'but', 'and was', 'However,'). They typically close a background, historical or citation-style statement (origins, dates, 'pioneered by X (2003)', 'over 30 years ago') just before the text moves to new or contrasting information.

36405.name: The ".go" token appended to an identifier, firing hardest on Go source filenames (e.g. parser.go, app.go) and also on ".go" fragments inside URLs and domains (google, gov). Weaker activation on other file extensions like ".hs" and on stray dot or symbol tokens in code.

36449.name: The "ISHED" suffix completing the all-caps word "PUBLISHED" (and "FINISHED") in article or record metadata headers, typically followed by a colon and a date. Other tokens fire only weakly and show no clear pattern.

3647.name: The colon right after "Answer" in multiple-choice questions (A–D options), where the answer letter comes next. It also fires weakly on similar label-colon tokens such as "#:" and on the "->" before a return type, i.e. separators that come just before a value is given.

36478.name: Pieces of institutional affiliation and postal address lines, especially Japanese ones such as university and department names, city and ward names (Sendai, Nagoya, Chofu-shi) and hyphenated postal codes. The strongest activations fall on postal-code digits and hyphens (e.g. 980-8579, 814-0180) and on street-number blocks like 1-7-1. Similar address and affiliation tokens from other countries, plus URL pieces, get weak activations.

Pieces of proper-noun place names, institutions and addresses, mostly Japanese or other East Asian (romanized suffixes like -gun, -Do, City, University of Tokyo, Heavy Industries), plus postal codes, phone-number fragments and source tags like PhysOrg.com. Activation is strongest on administrative suffixes and the commas or separators that follow them in location and affiliation strings.

36488.name: The word "fact"/"facts" (in any case, and also as a subword in factor/factored, FACTS, superfacts), with weaker firing on related words like information, details, findings, trivia, nonfiction. Strongest for plural or noun uses meaning pieces of true information (math facts, interesting facts, empirical facts); weaker for the idiom "in fact" and for mere spelling matches.

365.name: A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires across stretches of fluent English prose rather than on any particular word. Activation spreads over whole multi-word clauses and phrases, usually after the opening word. It is strongest in continuous descriptive or personal sentences, such as definitions, reviews and narrated feelings or actions. It is weak and scattered on boilerplate, headings, code and metadata.

A diffuse feature firing on spans of generic, filler-like prose, typical of synthetic, SEO-spam, or subtly incoherent web text (e.g. fabricated facts, boilerplate explanations, marketing blurbs). It is not tied to specific words. It is strongest on fluent explanatory or opinion clauses such as "how much better blend tastes using these methods" or "I definitely have challenges with".

36534.name: Fires mainly inside code function bodies, especially on statement-boundary tokens like closing parens with newline, indentation, assignment '=', and control keywords (for/if/return), strongest in routines that manipulate or convert strings (splitting, replacing, counting, printing names). It also fires weakly and sporadically on function words in prose.

Tokens in source code (and code-adjacent explanations) that begin a new statement or line: indentation whitespace, comment markers (#, //) and the first comment words, control keywords (let, for, if, else, return), and assignment parts (variable name, '='). It peaks in messy or ill-formed code. Prose tokens get only weak activation.

36543.name: Nouns (and some nearby words) naming concrete amenities, fixtures, equipment, appliances, furnishings, or provided facilities, typically items within an enumerated list describing what a home, venue, or product has or offers. The strongest activations come from descriptions of property and amenities such as kitchen countertops, cabinetry, appliances, gyms, games rooms and retailers.

Concrete items listed as amenities, furnishings, supplies or provisions in descriptive or listing contexts. It fires most strongly on appliances and fixtures in hotel rooms, kitchens and homes (microwave, mini-fridge, stainless steel appliances, A/C, Nespresso machine), and more weakly on food items and other provided goods.

36547.name: Tokens in math/code/reasoning text that come just before a number, especially a minus sign or negative marker ("-", "负") and the spaces, parentheses or table separators preceding numeric values in calculations and comparisons. The strongest response is on a leading minus at the start of a line giving a negative result.

3657.name: A weak, diffuse feature whose strongest activations fall on phrases about inspecting, examining or verifying something: "do your research, visit the sites, double check", "click and look closely", "open", "checks the tag", "get a better look", "explore", "request documentation / conduct on-site reviews" and "further evaluation demonstrates". It also fires faintly on many scattered function words and nouns with no clear pattern.

36582.name: Weak, diffuse feature mostly firing on commas (and some following spaces) that separate an element from what comes next, e.g. between city and country/state in location lines, or after a verb in nonsense text. It fires most strongly in legal citations right after "cert. denied" or "affd", just before a reporter volume number.

36591.name: Expletive (dummy) subject constructions, chiefly "it" or "there" followed by a copula or auxiliary ("it is", "it's", "there will", "it was", "it can be"). The verb carries the strongest signal, especially in impersonal phrasing that introduces an evaluative or extraposed clause ("it is necessary/possible/important to…", "it is believed that…").

Expletive/dummy-subject constructions: the copula (is/was/’s) right after a non-referential "it" or "there" (and sometimes the pronoun itself), as in "it is necessary/possible to…", "it was found that…", "there is…". Activation is strongest on "is" in impersonal "it is + adjective/participle" frames.

36595.name: Weak, diffuse feature that peaks on words tied to outdoor adventure, climbing and rugged terrain: rock climbing, river trips, backpacking, slopes, vertical footage, alpine conditions, steep hills, scaffolds, footing, speleology, polar or Antarctic places. Weaker hits fall on related ideas of challenge, struggle and conquest, such as puzzles, platformers, bosses, assaults and defeats.

Words tied to physical challenges, adventure and outdoor exertion, chiefly climbing and mountaineering (mountain, climb, summit, ascent, expedition, hikes, trailhead). The concept extends to other demanding feats such as swimming, diving and difficult game content like platformers, raids, monsters and puzzles, plus extreme or superlative measures (tallest, fastest).

36600.name: Nouns, mostly mass or substance terms (lead, dust, paint, energy, text), that follow a quantity or partitive phrase such as "amount of", "piece of", "levels of" or "strip of". The noun names the material or stuff being measured.

Head nouns (mostly mass or plural) naming the substance or thing being quantified, typically right after a quantity or measure expression like "a lot of", "pair of", "100 grams of", "how much", "more" or a number.

3665.name: A weak, diffuse feature with no single trigger. It fires on continuation tokens inside multi-word titles, terms and set phrases, mostly the connecting words and word endings. The clearest cases are paper or article titles, including their URL-slug forms: "of", "for", "in", "-of", and suffixes like "ulsion", "ICS" and "ATION". It also fires on the final pieces of fixed compounds and collocations, such as Ku Klux "Klan", word "processing", risk "factors" and "frictionless". Occasional weak hits appear on code, math notation and non-English text.

36651.name: Function words and generic abstract nouns/verbs in the formulaic phrasing of academic abstracts and expository/promotional articles, especially purpose or scope statements ("investigate the effects of… on", "the role of… in", "explore its…", "this review will focus on"). Activation lands on the scaffolding words (the, of, in, on, effects, role, explore, investigate) that introduce the topic rather than on the topic terms themselves.

36658.name: Fires on the name "Davis" (strongest), whether it appears as a surname in person names and citations or in place names like UC Davis. Weaker activation on similar-sounding pieces ("avis", "Davies", "Dak", "Avery", "Travis") and on other name tokens, especially "Carlos".

36690.name: Technical and scientific terminology, mostly mathematical, physical, or computational, in academic writing. The feature fires on the head noun or final word-piece that completes a specialized term (e.g., "spaces", "function", "coefficient", "derivative", "matrices", "-ential"), especially in math-heavy contexts.

36734.name: Line-ending tokens that finish a structural opening line, most strongly the trailing underscore(s) plus newline closing an #ifndef header-guard macro name in C/C++ headers (just before the matching #define). Weaker activation appears on the '>\n' that closes an HTML <tbody> tag just before <tr>, plus scattered noise tokens.

36791.name: Digit chunks or separators in the middle of structured numeric strings (times, dates, years in citations, IDs, codes, section/equation numbers), usually a leading or intermediate part of a longer number that continues after the token.

36801.name: Positive/negative status markers attached right after a biomarker, gene, receptor or pathogen name, mostly in biomedical text.
