These include "+" or "−" after CD/cell-surface markers (CD8+, CD34+, CD11c−), "-positive"/"-negative" (HIV-positive, node-negative, ER+), and similar qualifiers such as "mutant", "-R" and "rich". The strongest activation is on "+" in immunology cell-marker notation.

36826.name: The word "collate", which fires most strongly on SQL COLLATE clauses setting a charset collation (utf8_unicode_ci and similar). Weaker activation appears on other forms like collation, collated and Java's Collator, and on related database/charset tokens such as the _ci suffix. The many other examples show only faint, scattered activity.

36827.name: The final tab character in a run of leading indentation, i.e. the last whitespace token just before a line's content, mostly in code and structured data (JSON, XML/HTML, LaTeX, scripts). It fires most strongly on deeper or continuation indentation. A weaker version fires on single spaces or table cells ("<td") that come right before a new item or value.

36832.name: Tokens in the middle of long, unpredictable alphanumeric strings such as URL hashes, tokens, DOIs, IDs and phone numbers. It peaks on random-looking base64/hash fragments and digit chunks deep inside identifiers. It fires weakly on odd filler such as aligned whitespace runs or out-of-place words in spammy text.

36840.name: Second part of compound honor or event names, chiefly "-Star" after "All" (e.g. All-Star Game). Activation is strongest for capitalized sports "All-Star" and weaker for lowercase "all-star" lineups and similar forms (All-American, All-Pro, All-State). It also fires weakly on other award or event name completions such as Hall of Fame, Pro Bowl and Ryder Cup.

Second part of sports honor/selection compounds, mainly the word after "All"/"all" or "Pro": "-star", " Star", "star", "-American", " Bowl" (All-Star, All-American, Pro Bowl). The strongest activations are on All-Star/allstar. Other weak activations are scattered and noisy.

36845.name: Points where a conditional or code block ends and an alternative branch or next statement begins. In code this is the indentation whitespace, closing braces and newlines after a block, and keywords like else, elif, else if, match and except, with else/elif firing strongest. In prose it is the matching connective that opens an alternative case, such as "or", "otherwise", "else it is", or the clause after an "if" condition.

36900.name: Fires most strongly on the word "log" as the name of the Go logging package in an import block (`"log"`). Weaker hits occur on other "log" tokens (" log", "=log", "/log"), often in garbled or code-like text. The faint scattered activations elsewhere, such as "If you're" phrasing, Chinese characters and code punctuation, appear to be noise.

36904.name: The word "authors"/"Authors" (plural), especially as a heading or label in publication metadata, author bylines, copyright lines, README sections, and submission guidelines; strongest when it introduces a list of names (e.g., "Authors:").

36905.name: Punctuation and abbreviation tokens inside academic citation and reference formatting, chiefly the "al" in "et al." in author-year citations, plus commas between citation numbers or author/year pairs, the period in "Fig." or section numbers, and line breaks after author/affiliation lines in scientific papers.

36938.name: Code tokens that refer to a parameter or variable by name, mainly C# "nameof" (strongest inside ArgumentNullException(nameof(x)) guard clauses). It also fires more weakly on exception constructors such as ArgumentNullException, on the opening (" of string parameter-name arguments, on <paramref>, and on C perror calls in error handling.

36940.name: Fires mainly on the syntax of visual-style specifications in code and markup, especially where a color or format value is about to be given. Typical spots are CSS property colons and '#' hex prefixes (color, font-size, font-weight, px), Python keyword arguments such as color=' and marker='o', enum lookups like PNG::blue, rgba( and ANSI escape codes like \033[34m. It also fires weakly on scattered punctuation and formatting tokens in prose, such as opening parentheses before 'e.g.', ** or * emphasis markers and quote/slash separators.

36989.name: Middle subword tokens inside corticosteroid drug names, strongest for "nis" in prednisone, prednisolone and methylprednisolone. Weaker on "exam" in dexamethasone and "ort"/"oster"/"one" in hydrocortisone, corticosteroids and cortisone. The few weak hits outside medical text appear to be noise.

36994.name: Category labels naming one component of a composition or demographic breakdown, usually right after a percentage, fraction or amount. These include chemical elements and compounds, macronutrients, gas mixtures, and above all race groups such as "white" and "White". Activation is strongest on racial labels in demographic lists.

37022.name: Timestamps and metadata in forum, Q&A and comment posts: dates, times, "X years ago" and username/byline fragments. Activation is highest on the day, year and hour/minute digits of StackExchange-style signatures (e.g. "Jul 9 '14 at 18:27"). Weaker activation falls on other boilerplate such as post numbers, "email" in comment forms and line breaks after these markers.

37045.name: Non-initial subword tokens (or later words) that complete multi-token proper names, mostly place names and institutions (rivers, towns, counties, universities), where the earlier fragments of the name strongly predict the completion, e.g. the ending of "Potomac", "Palisades" or "Appoquinimink".

37079.name: Tokens inside structured or list-like text such as code, config files, URLs/query strings, metadata fields, and numbered or bulleted lists. They usually begin a value or list item, coming right after a separator like ':', '=', '|', '-', or a comma. The strongest example is host/domain values in a config element (local.net|some.host.com).

37087.name: Words expressing control, power, authority, or dominance over something (e.g., "control over/of", "power", "authority", "ownership", "influence over", "governed", "ruled", "reins", "King/Queen"), often including the following preposition linking to what is controlled.

3710.name: Field-label or key tokens in structured or boilerplate web text (form fields, HTML attributes like name/alt/port, metadata labels like Name/DATE/TITLE/ID/doi, "Skip to main content", colons after labels). They mark the point right before a value or the main content follows.

Field labels and the separators that come right after them, where a name, title, value or identifier is about to follow. Examples include header and metadata fields ("Title:", "Company name", "Topic:", "Q"), words like "titled", "headline" and "addressed", key-value markers in code, JSON and HTML ("title\":", "id", "src", " ="), and URL query parameters ("?q", "?id", "?p").

37121.name: Tokens at boundaries between separate scraped text segments, where content is truncated or a new block starts. Strongest on "more" in "...read more" and "…show more content…" links, and on the space after the "–" that comes before a commenter's name and timestamp in StackExchange comments. Also fires on double newlines and other separators between unrelated chunks.

37154.name: Words naming one of several alternative variants or forms of the same underlying entity, mostly in scientific contexts. The strongest by far is "isoforms" (especially the "iso" token). Weaker matches include isotopes, isoenzymes, isomers, splice variants, subtypes, subsets, forms, members and paralogues.

37177.name: Type conversion and casting constructs in code: function-style casts like int(), str(), list(), Convert.ToInt32, C-style (int)/(float) casts, Rust 'as' casts, static_cast<int>(). It also fires on numeric rounding and math functions (round, Math.floor, np.uint8, sqrt) and on format precision digits (%.2f, {:.4f}) that coerce how values are represented.

37197.name: Pieces of math notation used as prefixes or modifiers in named mathematical objects, chiefly the "C*-" / "C^k" / "σ-" / "K-theory" type: the letter, the superscript (^, *, ast, ∞), and the trailing "$-" hyphen that joins the symbol to a noun such as algebra or diffeomorphism. Activation is strongest on the "*$-" / "ast$-" in "C*-algebra". Weak scattered hits fall on other symbol fragments, numbers in compounds ("1-form", "NG9-1-1") and punctuation.

37212.name: The word "division" as the arithmetic operation, firing strongly when it appears in Python's "from __future__ import division" statement and only weakly for other mentions of division (math or code contexts, "/" operator).

37226.name: Small integer digits (especially "2", also 10, 3, 4, 7) in math, code or scientific notation, chiefly when they act as a coefficient, base or multiplier attached to a variable, exponent or unit (e.g. 2k, 2m, 2π, 10^n, 2^n). The strongest cases are "2" as a coefficient inside subscripts or superscripts.

37247.name: The "<thead" opening tag that comes right after "<table>" at the start of an HTML table, typically one converted from a document (tables of contents, data tables). It fires weakly and only occasionally on other structural or boilerplate markers such as comment-banner symbols or footnote asterisks.

3727.name: The "/ajax" path segment in CDN script URLs (e.g., cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs, ajax.googleapis.com/ajax/libs) inside HTML script tags; other tokens activate only weakly.

37272.name: Nouns marking the arrival or beginning of something new, usually in "the ___ of" constructions ("with the advent of", "the emergence/introduction/rise/arrival/dawn of"). "advent" fires most strongly, and the "vent" piece in words like "adventure" also activates weakly.

37293.name: Tokens tied to rugged, off-road vehicles and rough-terrain toughness. The strongest matches are SUVs, pickups, off-roading, all-terrain and GMC. Weaker matches cover other vehicles and their parts (car, vehicle, lorries, seats, diff locks), outdoor adventure such as white-water rafting and skate shops, and durable or military-style gear (rugged, sturdy shoes, combat fatigues, MIL-STD, AK). The feature usually fires on the noun or on a subword fragment of the word.

37295.name: Punctuation, whitespace, newlines and separator tokens (commas, spaces, dashes, tags, line breaks) that act as delimiters between items, mostly in noisy, garbled, redacted, foreign-script or list-like text. Activation is strongest for commas separating repeated or masked items, such as runs of █ blocks or REDACTED.

3730.name: Fires weakly on short, predictable filler in templated or metadata text, mainly the digit after a decimal point in version numbers, ratings and measurements ("v1.0", "4.53 of 5", "pH 7.4"), and the last digit of years. It also hits boilerplate tokens such as bullet points, "times" in view counts, "Original language English" and separators in web page chrome.

Digits in version numbers and ratings, chiefly the part after a decimal point (the "0" in "1.0", "3.0", "v4.2.3") and scores like "4.8/5" or "3/5". Activation is strongest on version strings in URLs and licenses. It also fires weakly on values following a metadata field label (e.g. "Gender: Male", "GMT").

37307.name: Fires on the final token of a label, heading or compound name that introduces the content following it. It is strongest on "Forms"/"Form", as in dictionary-style "Different Forms" and "Word Forms" sections and "adj. form". It also fires on other headers that precede lists or blocks ("Badges:", "About the Lecture", "Rhymes for"). In code, it fires on the ends of class or annotation names that come right before parentheses or arguments (ModularForm, FusionCharts, SequenceGenerator, JoinTable).

37335.name: Words and phrases about safety, risk, and protective or regulatory considerations, such as safety concerns, hazards, danger, security, tamper-evidence, verification, legal or ethical considerations, health risks and adverse reactions. Weaker activations land on loosely related abstract nouns like trust, care, ethics, purity and regulation. Activation peaks on explicit safety, concern or hazard terms.

37352.name: Fires on the token immediately before, or at the start of, a named software package, tool, or product, typically in contexts like “using”, “such as”, “like” or “e.g.” and in tool lists. The token is often formatting markup that wraps the name (\textsc{, **, *, a comma between list items) or the first subword of the name (Power-, C-, E-). Other hits on tokens in spammy or unrelated text look like noise.

37365.name: Enumeration labels for list items, sub-questions, or multiple-choice options, such as letters (a, b, c, D, E), roman numerals, and numbers, along with their parentheses, periods, and preceding newlines. Activation is highest on later labels in a sequence (b, c, d) rather than the first one. Weaker activation appears on other structural formatting tokens, such as \text in \textsuperscript author affiliations, colons, and punctuation.

Labels and structural markers in quiz, exam, or problem formats. The strongest are the letters or numbers that mark multiple-choice options (A/B/C/D, a)/b)/c), (A)), especially later options and an "Options:" header. Weaker activation falls on related answer-format cues such as \boxed, "answer", "Hint", "Example", "Input", and the line breaks or spacing that separate listed items.

37399.name: The word "Astronomy" (or "astronomy"), firing most strongly in academic department names such as "Department of Physics and Astronomy" in author affiliations. It also fires on other uses like "National Radio Astronomy Observatory" and the journal "Astronomy and Astrophysics." Weak activations occur on the second discipline in other compound department names (e.g., "Biochemistry," "Statistics," "Aerospace").

The word "Astronomy" (capitalized), especially in academic department names like "Department of Physics & Astronomy". It responds weakly to related science-field names such as Aerospace or -ology words.

37405.name: A diffuse feature of news-style journalistic prose. It fires weakly on scattered content words and phrases in factual reporting and fires most strongly on longer spans that give the substance of a reported statement, claim, ruling or official directive. Typical examples are text following 'said', or clauses like 'ensure the implementation of Corona SOPs…' and 'the 16 cows that died is worth over N5m'.

A diffuse feature firing across formal news-report prose, especially politics, government, and public affairs. It is strongest on long spans of indirect reported speech or official statements, such as what officials said about problems, authorities, or government actions. These spans often come from South Asian or international news. Elsewhere it fires weakly on scattered content words and numbers like dates, durations, and counts.

37428.name: The first word or subword token of a new sentence or paragraph, typically right after a line break or heading, where the body text begins (e.g., the opening word of an abstract, article lead, or section).

37453.name: The second word of short website boilerplate and UI navigation phrases (e.g. "Skip to content", "Search form", "Menu Close", "bottom of page", "Connect with us", "Scroll To Top", "Forgot password"). These are fragments from scraped web page chrome such as menus, buttons and form labels. Activation is usually weak, with the strongest on "form" in "Search form".

Second word of web-page boilerplate UI labels scraped from site navigation, firing most strongly on "form" in "Search form" at the start of a page. It responds weakly to other interface element words such as contact form, submitting this form, menu, login, Log in, Footer, and Header.

37469.name: Fires on tokens inside formulaic or templated text where the next token is nearly fixed, such as the site header "Universe Guide", "#include <stdio" before ".h", "1." before "Introduction", "Disney" before "land", and list-introducing colons or bullet wording. Function words in stock phrases ("within the", "the time of") also activate it. The common thread is boilerplate structure rather than meaning.

37487.name: The ".lang" package segment in Java import statements (java.lang, org.aspectj.lang, commons.lang3, intellij.lang). It fires most strongly on java.lang followed by reflect, annotation or instrument. There is weak, sporadic activation on middle digit chunks of DOI numbers and on the second word of fixed phrases like "as a result" and "on the other hand".

37518.name: The opening parenthesis (or the words opening such a span, like "the", "hereinafter referred to as", "denoted herein as") placed right after a named entity or person, where an abbreviation, short name, or role label is about to be defined. It peaks on legal or document-style labels such as John Doe (plaintiff) and Employee ("Employee").

37525.name: The "d" in legal reporter citations such as "F.2d", "P.2d", "N.W.2d" (the second-series case-law reporter abbreviation after a volume number). Activation is strongest in federal-court citations. Other tokens fire only weakly and show no clear pattern.

37536.name: Exponents in math or code expressions, mostly the number right after a power operator (^, **, ^{), especially the "2" in x^2-style terms of polynomials. It also fires weakly on other subscripts, operands and trailing digits inside formulas.

3754.name: Control-flow jump keywords in code or pseudocode, chiefly "goto"/"GoTo" (strongest in batch scripts) and the "to" of "go to" in comments and step instructions, plus related jumps such as jmp, continue, Exit and LEAVE.

37555.name: Highly predictable continuation tokens that complete a fixed word, name or boilerplate phrase from its preceding fragment, e.g. the second half of a split word or brand name (Brain→Mass, Unab→ridged, ident→ificador), template syntax (\label→{) or set phrases (zur→Verfügung, Min→.Order). Activation is strongest on repeated web/LaTeX boilerplate where the token is almost certain.

37561.name: Blood-cell and hematology lab terms, most strongly the word "blood" in "red/white blood cells" and "complete blood count". It also fires on related words and word pieces such as cells, count, platelets, leukocyte, CBC and hemoglobin, and weakly on other lab-measurement terms.

37580.name: Highly predictable, formulaic tokens inside structured or boilerplate text. Typical cases are HTML table cells (<td>, <th>, src), LaTeX commands (align, ref, phantom arguments), URL and code fragments (/blob, .base, headerlink), and image placeholders. It also fires on template phrases such as "Timestamp Confirmation", "Special Emphasis Panel (", "et al" and "PMID". Activation is strongest where the next token is almost fully determined by the markup or template.

37589.name: Fires at junction points in noisy, boilerplate-heavy web text (spam, SEO pages, footers, contact info, URLs, CSS), such as newlines, punctuation, mid-number splits or words right before a predictable or formulaic continuation or an abrupt shift to a new segment or topic. It is positional and structural rather than tied to any particular meaning.

37611.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on hard-to-predict, information-bearing slot fillers: proper names (people, places, organizations), numbers in dates, versions and figures, and specific technical nouns. These usually appear right after a preposition, conjunction or label that sets up the slot. It often fires on the first subword of a rare name. No single semantic theme ties the examples together.

Weak, diffuse feature on the first token (or subword piece) of a content word that begins a new noun phrase, most often a proper noun such as a person, place, organization, product or month. It typically appears right after a preposition, article or verb, in the slot where the object or name is introduced. Numbers, titles (Ms, Mr) and some common nouns in the same position also activate it.

37616.name: Keywords that begin import/dependency statements at the top of source files (Java/Python 'import', 'from', Rust 'use', C# 'using' and 'namespace'), strongest on Java import lines. Weak activations also appear on boilerplate separators or labels before lists, such as 'Tags', colons and line breaks.

Keywords that begin import/dependency statements at the top of source files ("import", "from", "using", "package"), plus the newlines between successive import lines. The strongest activations are on Java "import" lines. There are weak, sporadic activations on unrelated punctuation or line breaks.

37629.name: Tokens inside formal or symbolic notation, mostly LaTeX math expressions (variables, subscripts, superscripts, fractions, sums, limits), plus code such as loop headers, assignments and function calls. Activation is strongest in the middle of long math formulas. There are weak sporadic hits on other text, such as boilerplate like 'Scroll to Top'.

Tokens inside mathematical notation, formulas and code, especially variable names, operators, numbers and LaTeX commands (e.g. \frac, \sin, ^\circ, \mathbb R, x^2). It is strongest in dense inline math expressions and weak on stray tokens in ordinary prose.

Mathematical and quantitative content: tokens inside math expressions, LaTeX formulas, variables, numbers and technical terms (integrals, functions, sets, units, chemistry names, code variables). Activation is strongest in dense formula or problem statements (e.g., integrands, function definitions) and weak on scattered numeric or technical words in ordinary prose.

37638.name: The keyword "defined" in C/C++ (and make) preprocessor conditionals such as "#if defined(...)" or "#if !defined", activating very strongly. Weak activations fall on scattered tokens in ordinary prose.

37642.name: Fires most strongly on navigation-related terms in web, UI or document markup, especially "navbar" in class names and filenames and "toc" (table of contents) anchors. It also responds more weakly to phrases like "return to list" or "return to the main menu". The many other weak activations on scattered function words and punctuation show no clear pattern.

37665.name: The "3" (and following "C"/".org"/"c") right after "W"/"w" in references to the W3C (World Wide Web Consortium): its name, w3.org URLs, XML schema namespaces and org.w3c Java packages. It is strongest in URLs and namespaces. A few unrelated tokens fire weakly.

37692.name: Speech-attribution verbs (mostly "said", also says/asked/added/explained/wrote) that come right after a closing quotation and introduce the speaker's name. The strongest activations follow emotional or personal quotes. It also fires weakly on "of" when it introduces the person or group something belongs to ("in the view of", "that of costar").

37696.name: The word "rewrite" in any form (rewrite, rewrote, rewritten, rewriting, re-write, ReWrite), including code, linguistic rewrite rules and revising history or text. Weaker on related words for reworking something (rephrase, paraphrase, reword, rebuild, remake, rewiring) and on look-alike tokens such as the name "Rew".

37706.name: The verb (mostly "is", also "was"/"has") following impersonal "It" in formal or technical prose, opening constructions like "It is known/important/difficult that…". It is strongest on the patent stock phrase "It is (accordingly/therefore) an object of the present invention", where "It" and "an" also fire.

37731.name: The placeholder attribute token ="#"> in HTML, mostly in href attributes of nav links (e.g. Home), strongest on the first link in a list. Much weaker activation on other markup/formatting tokens such as opening bold ** markers or list punctuation.

37750.name: Tokens that open a new entry in a repeated, parallel structure, such as list markers (bullets, asterisks, the period after a list number), declaration keywords that begin consecutive code lines (var, let, def, void, String, int), separators before the next quoted key or array item, and newlines or indentation preceding the next line. Activation tends to be higher when the pattern has already repeated earlier in the text.

37766.name: Separators (newlines, indentation, colons, pipes, closing tags, bold markers) that come right after a term, parameter name or section heading in structured documentation such as API docs, parameter lists, tables, man pages and safety data sheets, just before its description or definition text starts. Activation is strongest at the gap between a label like 'issortbool' or 'xk : ndarray' and its explanation.

37770.name: Words that express generality, breadth or non-specificity, most often "general" and what follows it ("general terms", "in general", "general sense/information/knowledge", "general-purpose", "generic terms"). Weaker hits are broad or diffuse qualifiers such as "global", "overall", "uniformly", "widely", "high level", "neutral" and "dull ache".

Words marking generality or broad, non-specific scope, most strongly "general" (also universal, abstract, broad, plain, basic, all, public), typically modifying nouns like questions, area or health and often set against something specific. Weak, scattered activations also occur on unrelated words and punctuation.

37805.name: Line-break tokens (often fused with trailing punctuation, spaces, pipes, slashes or brackets) in garbled, mixed-language, or ASCII-art/table-like text. Activation is strongest where the line ending is part of a repeated visual structure, such as diagram edges, table borders, or padded columns.

37819.name: The word "scope" and its variants (scoped, Scope, SCOPE), firing most strongly on the HTML attribute `scope="` in table header tags. Weak, scattered activations appear on unrelated punctuation and tokens.

37847.name: The opening parenthesis fused with the first named parameter ("(name", "(value", "(feature") in code annotations, attributes and decorators such as Java @Column/@RequestMapping, C# [Display] and Rust #[cfg]. Activation is highest for @Column(name, which typically names a database column or table. Non-code tokens activate only weakly.

3785.name: Marks the output or return type of a function or operation. The strongest cases are the type written right after "->" in Rust and Python signatures (u32, Self, String, int, RustIdent). It fires more weakly on nouns that name what something returns, yields or produces ("returns the column... permutation vector", "yields the indices of", "resultant percent value", "status codes").

37870.name: Fires weakly and diffusely on tokens at the start of a span that repeats or completes something predictable from earlier context, i.e. copying/induction-like positions. This is clearest in code, where it marks the first piece of a previously used identifier or argument (e.g., "(folder"Path, "sent"ryTraceHeader, "#n"FileNum, "${var.aws"). In prose it falls on function words just before a repeated name or phrase ("to" Thornaby, "the" curve) and on separators like ":" or "://" in structured fields.

The first token of an argument or complement right after a verb, preposition or function name, where the object is about to follow. It is strongest in recipe instructions ("melt the", "warm the", "bake at", "into the prepared") and on the opening parenthesis plus first argument of code calls ("setuid (pw", "(temp", "(kernel"). It also fires weakly on similar continuation points in ordinary prose.

37918.name: The ".version" attribute token in code, especially in "sys.version_info" Python version checks (also np.version, process.version). Other weak activations are noise.

37939.name: Fires in degenerate, repetitive or garbled text (repeated lines, symbol and character runs, broken code or mixed-script noise), typically on whitespace, newline, punctuation or markup tokens that act as boundaries just before a repeated segment starts again.

37967.name: The "://" (and following "www") of URLs in boilerplate license text, strongest for the Apache License URL in code comment headers (http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0) and weaker for Creative Commons license links; sparse weak activations elsewhere.

38026.name: Words for damaging someone's reputation with false or hostile statements. Activation is strongest on defamation, libel, slander and defamatory, and weaker on smear, malign, insult, disparagement, character assassination and reputation. It also fires weakly on related legal-offense terms such as battery, trespass, treason and maliciously.

38027.name: Words for retaliation and punitive responses, mainly forms of "retaliate/retaliation/retaliatory" (strongest in workplace and whistleblower complaint contexts). Weaker activations come from related ideas of payback or consequences, such as retribution, reprisals, revenge, backlash, repercussions, "strike back", punish, and "in return for".

38042.name: Nouns that name a particular item or position within an ordered mathematical structure, chiefly "term" (also element, entry, series, numbers, side). It fires most strongly after ordinal or index phrases like "nth", "12th", "3rd" or "the 5th", as in "nth term of a sequence" or "5th entry in row 12". It also fires weakly on unrelated tokens in math or technical text.

38055.name: Deictic words that point back (or ahead) to a nearby passage of the document, most often "above" (sometimes "below", "this", or Chinese 上述 + 代码/内容) right after a noun like "code", "text", "line" or "article". Activation is strongest in phrases such as "the code above" referring to a preceding code snippet.

38064.name: The word "cardiovascular" (strongest), plus related tokens naming body systems such as the circulatory, vascular, cardiopulmonary, respiratory and musculoskeletal systems. It fires most on the token that completes the system name, usually in health, disease or fitness contexts.

38069.name: Java persistence/ORM identifiers in code, most strongly the ".jpa" package segment in Spring Data imports (org.springframework.data.jpa), plus EntityManager, Hibernate ".Session", Doctrine "\ORM", and similar framework names like FLAG_ACTIVITY. Activations on ordinary prose tokens are weak and scattered.

38082.name: Nobility and aristocratic titles (Baron, Earl, Duke, Count, Marquis, Baronet, Viscount, Duchess, Lord), including the "of" that follows them in titles. Also fires on "Baron" as a surname (Sacha Baron Cohen, author citations) and on fragments like "bar-on" and "-onet".

38085.name: Commas that separate items in a short list of trait or attribute names, overwhelmingly inside Rust #[derive(...)] attributes (e.g. Debug, Clone, PartialEq). The strongest activations are on earlier commas in the list. Weaker firing occurs on commas in other compact attribute or tag lists, such as "(Score:3, Informative)", product feature lists, and LaTeX options.

38110.name: The backslash opening a LaTeX command (here \epsilon) inside a math expression, particularly right after a minus sign when writing a small-epsilon interval bound.

38129.name: Infinitive "to" (or another verb-phrase starter like auxiliary "have"/"can", or a preposition) opening a second, parallel clause after a coordinator such as "and", "or", "but" or a comma, as in "to X and to Y". The strongest cases repeat "to" after "and".

38135.name: Words that express an increase, intensification or onset of something: growth verbs and nouns (increased, rise, uptick, amplified, intensifies, mount, grown), comparatives and intensifiers (more, increasingly, closer, more seriously), and phrases for starting or heightening activity (began, ramped, emerged as, warming up to, shifting gears, focus on, rededicate).

38143.name: Separator and delimiter tokens (slashes, hyphens, dashes, pipes, commas, "vs", "x", semicolons, quote-comma sequences) placed between items in a list, compound, range or sequence. Often the separator is fused with the start of the next item (e.g. "/com", "-K", "-sh"). The feature fires at the junction between successive parallel elements: product names, file extensions, dimensions, initials, menu links, chained terms.

38182.name: Whitespace, indentation, and closing-brace/newline tokens in source code at boundaries between top-level members. They mark where one method, property, or block ends and the next definition starts, such as before a new "def", "sub", object key, or "this." assignment.

38187.name: Concrete values filling a slot after a key, label, operator or assignment, mostly numeric literals in code, config, tables or specs (e.g. width: 640, age = 15, Default is 1, < 25), along with units and value words that follow numbers (minutes, nm, seconds, six). Activation is strongest on short numbers assigned to parameters.

38235.name: Literal escaped line-break markup within text, chiefly the "\n" escape sequence (or the "n" after a backslash) inside code string literals, printf/print statements, and serialized text. It also fires more weakly on other break or separator markers, such as "<br" tags, "\t", "<td", and trailing double spaces before newlines.

Literal line-break markup written out as text instead of an actual line break: the backslash-n escape sequence (\n, or its 'n' after a backslash), plus related tab escapes (\t), HTML
/

tags, and trailing-space newlines. It is strongest on a full '\n' token, especially in runs or repeated sequences inside strings, code, or garbled text, and weaker on a lone 'n' following a backslash.

38246.name: The token right before a number or identifier code begins, usually a standalone space (also "-", "{", "(", "/", "§" or a letter prefix) that separates a label, model name, section or equation reference, or "=" from the digits that follow, as in "section 2", "Apex 90", "Eq. (1)" or "\cite{7}".

38252.name: Attribution of responsibility to a named organization or person: words like "by", "of", "from", "in" that introduce a producer, sponsor, curator, editor or affiliated institution, along with the parts of the organization names themselves (agencies, offices, departments, universities, companies). Activation is strongest on attribution phrases such as "produced by", "supported in part by", "presented by" and "a study by".

38261.name: Paragraph breaks (double newlines, often joined with a period, colon, question mark or closing bold **) that end a heading or intro sentence and come just before a new section's body. Activation is strongest at transitions into medical case-report narratives, such as after 'Case presentation', '**Case Report**', or 'we describe a case…', right before text like 'A 54-year-old female…'.

38297.name: Verbs or prepositions expressing that one thing comes along with or is attached to another, chiefly "accompanied/accompanying" and "with" in phrases like "distributed with" or "came with". Activation peaks on "with" in license and documentation boilerplate. A few weak hits fall on spaces after "=" and other filler tokens.

3834.name: Boundaries between clauses, sentences or code blocks: sentence-ending periods, closing brackets/semicolons, newlines and markdown fences, plus the first word or two of the next sentence or clause (The, This, If you, When you, For). Activation is highest where a statement or code block ends and a new one begins.

38344.name: The empty angle-bracket token "<>" (often with a leading space), as used in code for empty generics/template specializations, not-equal operators, or Perl's diamond operator. It also fires on similar symbols like arrows and slashes, strongest on template<>.

38370.name: Marks the second operand or item in a paired or binary construction, i.e. the right-hand term after an operator or connector that pairs it with an earlier counterpart (x - y, a * c, num1 > num2, P * Q, s_1 ∩ s_2, MgO in Al2O3 vs MgO, boys than girls, electron-positron, corners 0 and 1). It fires on the second variable, index, or subscript, most strongly in code and math expressions.

38388.name: Tokens inside formal mathematical/technical statements, strongest in definitional or hypothesis clauses that impose conditions on objects (e.g. "be a holomorphic function… Suppose |f(z)| ≤ 1", "satisfies f(t)≥0", "satisfy y(0)=y(h)=0", "assumed to be countable and connected"). Activation falls on connective words and inline LaTeX delimiters/symbols in these constraint-setting phrases. Weak scattered activations appear elsewhere on technical text, year digits, and code.

38394.name: Tokens that start the next item in a list of conditions or requirements, mostly in boilerplate legal, copyright, licensing and disclaimer text ("provided that X and that Y…"). The strongest activations fall on clause-linking words such as "that", "and", "and the" and commas, and on list bullets or dashes that begin a further stipulation.

38424.name: Fires mid-sequence where an arbitrary, hard-to-predict continuation follows. It is strongest on digit chunks inside long numeric identifiers in URLs, DOIs and article IDs. It also fires on decimal points before long fractional numbers (unit conversions) and weakly on spaces or punctuation just before a list item, number or parenthetical.

38451.name: Tokens of repeated characters within elongated or repetitive strings, such as stretched words and exclamations ("yeeeeah", "Aaaaah", "maaaaybe"), repeated punctuation, laughter, block glyphs, and placeholder runs like "xxxxxxxx" or "AAAAAAAA". Activation is mostly on the middle/later chunks of the run and grows as the repetition continues.

Long runs of the same character or token repeated many times (e.g. RRRR, OOOO, uuuu, ;;;;, xxx, soft hyphens, tildes). The feature turns on after the repetition has started and stays active through the rest of the run, with activation usually growing as the run gets longer. It is strongest for repeated uppercase letters in degenerate or glitch-like text.

38452.name: Fires strongly on the subword "aring" that completes "Rehearing" in legal case headers ("Rehearing Denied"). Elsewhere it gives only weak, diffuse activation on highly predictable continuation tokens in fixed phrases or boilerplate, such as "/App" in gmatclub.com/AppTrack, "going" in "are going to", and code or LaTeX brackets.

38456.name: A token that starts a new word glued directly onto the word before it with no space, as in compound identifiers, usernames, emails, URLs, code variable names, acronym chains and chemical names (e.g. noInitialize, newlab, acsmeetings, condgrad). Activation is moderate and fires on the second or later word part. Rare weak hits occur on ordinary function words.

38457.name: Tokens inside direct quotations of spoken remarks, typically an expert or source quoted in news/science journalism explaining something. Activation spans the running content of the quote (verbs, prepositions, nouns mid-sentence), strongest in the middle of explanatory clauses (e.g., 'what we want to do is use...', 'it may be that they are experiencing...'). It is weak or sporadic in non-quoted narrative text.

38462.name: Words about size, fit and suitability: sizes, dimensions, measurements and capacity, plus things made or chosen to suit a person or need (fit properly, custom-made, left-handed, levels, different options). It peaks on "size"/"sizes" and fit-related words.

Words about size, fit and measurement, especially for clothing and products: "size/sizes/sizing", size labels (S, M, L, XL, cup letters, shoe numbers), "fit/fitted/fitting", measures, inches, mm. Strongest on explicit size terms in shopping/product listings; weaker on loosely related product-spec and adjustment words.

38469.name: The verb "divide(s)" in the number-theory sense of divisibility ("a divides b"), strongest when it sits between two quantities in a math statement. Weak activation on related phrasing like "divisible by" and on scattered separators such as table pipes.

38476.name: Tokens at the start of a contrasting or alternative clause, typically its connective (but, while, yet, if, and), its subject (the unhappy ones, small companies, others, some, the Italian population), or the negation it introduces (does not, didn't). The activated tokens set up a counterpoint or second case opposed to the preceding statement. Activation peaks on a subject followed by a negated verb (e.g., "nominal variables do not").

A diffuse, weak feature with no single trigger word. It fires on tokens that open or pivot a clause in explanatory or logical text, especially code and code comments. These include conditional and causal connectives (if, when, so, but, or, Actually) and comment markers (#, //). It also fires on subject nouns or pronouns followed by "is" or "does" that set up a condition, as in "current is NULL" or "process is not". Some activations fall on structural boundaries such as colons, newlines, indentation and code fences.

38509.name: Weak, diffuse activation on content in scientific and technical text, mostly molecular biology and genetics (gene regulation, transcription, DNA, binding, cells). It fires mainly on the object or verb that completes a statement about a biological process or mechanism. The strongest response is on gene-regulation terms such as "post-transcriptional gene regulation".

38516.name: Leading keyword (modifier or type) that begins a declaration in source code with no access modifier in front of it, e.g. static, const, void, class, mod, internal. Activation is strongest for 'static' in static constructors and static nested classes or Main methods, as in C# and Java.

38532.name: Tokens inside academic citations and bibliographic metadata, such as journal names, volume/issue numbers, page ranges, years, author-name separators, DOIs, and table-of-contents page numbers. Activation is strongest on the spaces, punctuation and numbers that sit between citation fields, for example the space before a volume or year.

38538.name: The determiner "this" right after "use" in licensing or permission language, overwhelmingly the Apache License boilerplate "you may not use this file except in compliance". It is strongest when the use is restricted and weaker in permissive "free to use this" or other usage-terms contexts.

38552.name: The pointer asterisk in Go function parameter types, right after the parameter name and before the type (e.g. "t *testing.T", "r *http.Request"). Activation is strongest for "t *testing.T" in Go test function signatures. It is weaker for other pointer parameters and method receivers, and for the colon before a type in Rust parameters. Activations on other, non-code tokens are sparse and weak.

3856.name: Words that set up a comparison, resemblance or perceived impression, mainly perception and seeming verbs (sounds, looks, feels, seems, appears, comes across as) and comparison markers (like, as if, than, equivalent of, more X than Y). Activation is strongest on 'like' and the verb right after it, and covers the words that begin the description of what something resembles or seems to be.

Expressions of perceived appearance, resemblance or comparison, especially verbs like 'looks/sounds/feels/seems' followed by 'like', plus 'similar to', 'resemble', 'appears'. The strongest cases are descriptions of how something seems, often critical (e.g. 'looked cheap', 'sounding like homework'). Activations are weak and also scatter onto nearby function words.

38601.name: Comparison operators in code conditionals, especially " !=" in Go's "if err != nil" error-checking idiom (strongest). It also fires on " ==" checks against nil, 0 or status codes, and only weakly on structural tokens like "<thead>" newlines or switch cases.

38614.name: The subword piece "applic"/"aplic"/"lic", the stem of words like applicability, applicator, application/aplicación. It fires most strongly on " applic" when it is split from a following suffix, especially "-ability" in phrases like "wider/practical applicability of", and weakly on related forms in other languages.

38617.name: The final token of a type or class name in code, usually a parameter or variable type in a function signature or declaration (e.g. struct worker_t *, t_vars *, PdoDatabase $database, UserEntity) that is immediately followed by the variable name. Struct/typedef suffixes in C are strongest. Prose activations on nouns are rare and weak.

38670.name: Structural tokens that open a code block or body, especially the opening brace (often with a newline) right after a class, struct, or template declaration in C++-like code. Also fires on access-specifier colons (public:), the indentation that starts the first line of a body, Python def/docstring boundaries, and weakly on list-item dashes and other line-start punctuation.

38679.name: Sentence- or paragraph-ending punctuation (especially a period followed by a blank line) at points where the text suddenly switches to an unrelated topic, as in spammy or stitched-together web text. Activation is strongest when the next passage is incoherent with what came before.

38683.name: Structural tokens in HTML/XML markup, chiefly the ">\n" that closes a <thead> tag right before <tr>, plus the opening "<" of repeated XML elements (<color>, <property>, <item>). Weaker, sporadic hits fall on predictable tokens in boilerplate or list text, such as ID numbers after "#", "Leave a Reply" and list numbering.

38688.name: Words in purpose/result constructions that describe a cause producing an effect, usually a beneficial or enabling one. They typically come right after causative verbs (make it, helps, gives, boost, ensure) or open infinitive or purpose phrases (to achieve, to attract, to improve, for interest), as in 'make it easy', 'makes the music more potent' and 'ensuring that'. Activation peaks on explicit improvement or goal phrases such as 'to attract students and maintain their interest', 'even better' and 'more of a push'.

38689.name: A diffuse, weak feature that fires at syntactic boundaries where one clause or phrase ends and the next begins. It peaks on sentence-final punctuation (often followed by newlines), on commas, and on the final noun of a phrase just before a new clause or a connective such as 'or that', 'as', 'if', 'when' or 'that'.

Diffuse, weak activation at clause and sentence boundaries: the last word of a clause, the punctuation that ends it (commas, periods, colons, paragraph breaks), and the connectors or first words that open the next clause (because, if, that, but, The). The feature tracks points where one syntactic unit closes and another begins.

38710.name: The word right after an imperative verb or setup word in boilerplate web text, chiefly the object of "See" or "Read" ("See full list", "See content relevant to you", "Read jokes about"). The feature fires on the predictable next token of these templates, with weaker, scattered hits on similar slots in other text.

38716.name: Names of hostile regimes, militant groups and dictators that were adversaries of the US/West, chiefly "Taliban" (strongest) and "Saddam" (Hussein), with weaker hits on Khmer Rouge, Noriega and Vietcong. Activation is highest in conflict contexts such as wars, attacks and invasions.

38752.name: Verbs of directed movement, mainly "head" in the sense of going toward a destination ("headed for/to/out", "heading over"), which activate most strongly. Weaker activations come from other senses of "head" (heading as a title, headed by), from "handed/handing" (transfer to someone), and from "make their way".

38763.name: Tokens spelling the letter sequence "map" (map, Map, MAP, mapping, maple, /map, imap), strongest for the acronym MAP (MAP kinase, mean arterial pressure, MAPT). Also fires on "protein" in "mitogen-activated protein" (the P of MAPK) and weakly on look-alike acronym pieces such as "AP" or ".p".

38766.name: Geographic place names, mostly cities and towns, along with the words that set them up in location contexts: prepositions like "in"/"at", "including", "comprises of", and the commas and list separators in addresses and lists of places. The first subword of a multi-token place name (e.g. Kh-arkiv, Delf-t, Kiel) often fires as the model anticipates the location.

38813.name: The "www" subdomain token right after "http://" in URLs, firing most strongly in XML namespace URLs like xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" in SVG/HTML code. It fires more weakly on other URL hosts (googleapis, jquery's "code") and faintly on random tokens in code comments.

38814.name: Mostly numeric literals (multi-digit numbers, trailing digit chunks) inside math problems, equations, and code, especially specific values given as quantities or operands in a problem setup. It also fires weakly on scattered function words and punctuation in the same math/technical contexts.

38833.name: Number tokens (often fragments of longer numbers) containing the digits "78" or close variants such as 79, 178, 788, 798 or 978. They appear in any numeric context: prices, percentages, years, IDs, ISBNs, hashes and patent numbers. The bare token "78" activates most strongly.

3885.name: The ".view" package segment in Java import statements, strongest right after "android" (android.view.View, LayoutInflater, Menu, etc.). It is weaker in other package paths like android.support.v4.view or custom com.*.view packages. Scattered unrelated prose tokens show only faint activation.

38850.name: Punctuation (mostly commas, occasionally "and", a dash, or "in") that comes right after a complete clause or statement and marks the boundary before a continuation. The continuation usually adds a contrast ("but"), a consequence ("so", "and"), an elaboration or a qualification to the same sentence.

Commas (and occasionally other mid-sentence punctuation like semicolons or ellipses) that end a complete clause or phrase and introduce a continuation, often a contrast, qualification, or follow-up clause ("..., but", "..., not just", "..., so").

38857.name: A diffuse feature with no single meaning, mostly in technical, code or step-by-step reasoning text. It fires on tokens inside formulaic, highly predictable sequences where the next token is nearly determined. Examples include boilerplate code such as the logging format's 'asctime', 'from selenium import webdriver', 'utf-8' and 'else:', abbreviations like 'e.g.,', and line ends in numbered logic-puzzle clue lists. It also fires on common connective or function words in stock phrases, such as 'options are', 'looks like' and 'a memorable way'.

38859.name: Words that introduce or refer to questions, prompts, tasks, or items given to respondents (e.g., "questions", "asked to", "assignment", "surveys", "this question"). The strongest activations come in survey, questionnaire, and test contexts, especially where participants or students are being asked something.

Words about asking questions, mainly the nouns "question(s)" and the verb "ask/asked", in contexts like surveys, interviews, polls, quizzes and exams. The strongest cases are questions put to respondents ("questions asked the subjects to", "ask complicated questions"). Weaker activations fall on related words such as answers, polls, surveys, variables and assignments.

38910.name: The word "way" in the phrases "in any way" / "in no way", especially in legal disclaimers and liability or conflict-of-interest boilerplate (e.g., "arising in any way", "related in any way"). Other scattered tokens activate only weakly.

38917.name: A weak, diffuse feature firing on scattered tokens (often function words, verbs and connectors following an organization name) in formal institutional prose about organizations, associations, committees and teams and their activities, missions, members or initiatives. It is strongest in newsletter, press-release and 'about us' style passages, e.g. 'Membership Team / Welcome to issue…', 'we have been privileged to welcome…' and 'manages the … Trust's website'.

38924.name: Separator or assignment tokens that come between a key, name or label and the value that follows it. These are mostly code and structured data: "=", ":", "=>", "":", "<-", "):" plus newline and "," in lists. The feature fires at the point where the name has ended and its value or definition is about to begin.

38938.name: Closing parentheses (especially doubled "))" or fused with punctuation like ")." and ")$") that end a function call or argument, most strongly in nested math or code expressions such as f(g(x)) and print(int(z)); weak scattered activations on other tokens in math/code contexts.

38950.name: Closing delimiters (mostly ")", also "]", "}", "$") that end a numeric value, uncertainty, or range and sit right before a unit of measurement. It is strongest on parenthesized standard-uncertainty digits in crystallographic lattice parameters, such as the "2)" in 11.077(2) Å.

38963.name: Fires on a token that is a near-certain continuation of a fixed or formulaic sequence. The dominant case is "Fax" starting the next bullet after the e-mail line in the repeated NASA STI Help Desk contact boilerplate. Weaker cases complete set phrases or code idioms, such as "i.e.", "in conjunction with" and "socket.recv".

38976.name: Words in biographical or descriptive phrases that state a person's (or thing's) role, affiliation, background or credentials, especially the prepositions and verbs linking someone to a position, organization or place (e.g. 'served on', 'used to work for', 'worked in', 'senior', 'formerly', 'one of').

38978.name: A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires mostly in structured, repetitive or technical text such as code, numeric tables, timestamps, dates, lists and file names. It favours separator and boundary tokens: commas between list items, plus signs between odds, colons in times, periods after list numbers, spaces and units in data rows, and closing braces. It also catches partial-word or number fragments inside such patterns. It rarely responds to semantic content in ordinary prose.

Tokens inside repetitive, degenerate or garbled text such as code, markup, logs and symbol sequences. It fires on elements that repeat or nearly repeat earlier content (repeated lines, backtick fences, pipes, identifiers, number patterns), so it looks like a detector of copying or looping in low-coherence structured text.

38982.name: Delimiter and separator tokens, such as spaces, commas, pipes, ampersands, dashes, newlines, and quote-comma pairs, that sit between items in long repetitive sequences like number runs, page lists, table specs, and data arrays. Activation grows as the repeated pattern continues and becomes more predictable.

Separator or delimiter tokens (commas, spaces, pipes, plus/minus signs, backslashes, repeated connecting words) inside long, highly repetitive or sequential patterns such as number lists, counting sequences, and repeated strings. The feature fires on the predictable separator between repeated items, getting stronger as the repetition continues.

39000.name: Numeric operands that come right after an arithmetic operator (especially ×/* multiplication, also +, -, /) in equations and expressions, i.e. the second or later factor or term. It fires most strongly in chained multiplications. There are weak, sporadic activations on unrelated tokens.

39027.name: The token "width", most strongly as an attribute or property name in HTML/CSS/code (width="…", width: …px), and more weakly in prose about dimensions. Rare weak hits on lookalikes such as "with" and "setw".

39031.name: The separator token (space, end of dot leader, table cell tag, or opening parenthesis) that comes right before a page number or timestamp in tables of contents, indexes, and track or timestamp listings, i.e., the gap between an entry title and its number.

39037.name: Fires on structural boundary and function tokens within technical text such as programming or puzzle problem statements, code, and output-format instructions. Typical spots are sentence-ending punctuation followed by newlines just before new sections (Input:, Output:, Example:), opening parentheses that begin a parenthetical note (e.g., "(do NOT include quotes…"), spaces between numbers, and connectives like "not", "who", "since" and "the" mid-specification. It reflects a general transition-point signal in instructional or technical prose rather than any specific meaning.

39038.name: Fires strongly only on the ".A" in the legal citation abbreviation "U.S.C.A" (United States Code Annotated). Every other activation is weak and scattered over unrelated tokens such as conjunctions, commas and newlines.

39045.name: Authoritative bodies (judges, courts, councils, committees, agencies) and the verbs for their official actions, such as decided, announced, denied, granted, published, determined, ruled. It peaks on subject-plus-verb pairs like "judge denied" or "Committee decided".

39048.name: Place names and institutions tied to Maryland. The strongest are Baltimore, Maryland and Johns Hopkins, with weaker activation on other Maryland towns (Bethesda, Rockville, Silver Spring, Greenbelt, Hagerstown, Annapolis) and the state code "MD". It also fires faintly on related surnames and places (Hopkins, Montgomery, Cumberland, Calvert).

3907.name: Mentions of official positions, titles, and institutional bodies. It fires most strongly on government or organizational role words (Minister, Secretary, President, director, Coordinator, Ministry, Council) and the surrounding appositive or role phrases that introduce named officials or authorities. Activation is weaker for generic group or organization nouns.

Words tied to official positions, ranks and institutional hierarchies: government bodies, ministries, agencies, cabinets, secretaries, directors, officials, roles and promotions. Activation is strongest on political office terms like cabinet or Secretary of Defense.

39078.name: A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires on function words, punctuation and comment markers at pivot points in explanatory or code-like text. These include the start of inline code comments (#, //), the comma after discourse openers such as "However" or "To solve this problem", and words that begin a new clause or aside. It appears mostly in assistant-style reasoning or annotated code, marking where an explanation or qualification starts.

39082.name: Tokens in the middle of long sequences of meaningless, non-word letter codes. Activation is strongest for DNA/RNA nucleotide strings (A/C/G/T/U) and amino-acid peptide sequences. Weaker activation appears on other repetitive, low-meaning filler, especially the dot leaders in tables of contents, and on similar letter strings such as H/T coin-flip lists or codon tables.

39085.name: Fires on the token right before a key value is stated: the "Answer" label after multiple-choice options (just before the answer letter), and the standalone space token that comes before a number in math/word-problem text (e.g., "has 100", "group of 21").

The space token just before the first number in a quantity description, most often in math/probability word problems (e.g. "a bag contains 5…", "In a population, 10%…"). It marks the spot where a numeric count or percentage is about to be given.

39093.name: The "fmt" package name inside Go import blocks, i.e. the quoted token "fmt on its own line after import (. Weak, scattered activations on ordinary prose words are noise.

39116.name: Descriptions of particle or nuclear decay processes, firing most strongly on the parent particle and arrow in LaTeX decay notation (e.g. B_c \to, B^+ \to) and also on words like decays, beta-decay and decay products. Weak, diffuse activation appears across other physics and math text.

Fires mostly in scientific or technical text, on determiners, modifiers or prefix tokens that open a technical noun phrase (e.g. solar, lunar, proton, muonic, or 'the' before a term), so it anticipates a specialized term. Some activations are on generic words in non-technical prose, so the pattern is noisy.

39135.name: A diffuse feature of formal, academic or scientific prose, especially research abstracts. It fires weakly on structural and connective tokens: sentence-ending periods and commas, section or list numbers ("1. Introduction"), discourse transitions ("In addition", "In conclusion", "Despite the", "To"), and research-methodology words (study, evaluation of, tested for, quantify, results, characterized, studied).

39168.name: Standalone space token following a plus/minus operator in a polynomial or algebraic expression, just before the next coefficient/term (e.g. "x^2 - 5x"). Strongest in multi-term polynomials. Weak activations occur on tokens after a space or on " **" starting bold text.

39197.name: A diffuse, mostly weak feature. Its clearest pattern is hypothetical, speculative, counterfactual or predicted statements. It fires on modal constructions such as would be, would have been, might, could work, will affect, may have been and maybe, along with the predicate that follows them. The strongest case is the counterfactual 'would have been celebrating her 39th birthday today'. Elsewhere it gives scattered low activations on function words and punctuation in expository text, without a clear pattern.

392.name: Spans of promotional, engaging, marketing- or PR-style prose (blog intros, listicle hooks, mission statements, event and product pitches) that address or excite the reader. Activation is spread across whole phrases rather than single words, and is strongest on calls to action and enthusiastic hooks like "get ready to unwind" or "you've come to the right place". Dry technical or tabular text barely activates.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on generic, formulaic phrasing typical of synthetic or LLM-generated text, such as task directives ("compute", "calculate", "explore and provide"), upbeat or motivational slogans ("Team up for success", "help you find information"), and dramatic concluding narrative lines. It often appears in noisy or garbled text and peaks on catchy, cliché-like phrases.

39220.name: Tokens spelling "hang"/"hung" (and "-hung-" fragments like in power-hungry, hungrier, Hangzhou, Hangover), most strongly on the verb "hang" in all forms (hang out, hang up, hanging around, get the hang of) and capitalized name pieces containing "Hang".

3923.name: Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences, where the next token is predictable from earlier repetition: repeated phrases ("Loading...", "Final Four", "Sacred Valley"), number runs, list separators, whitespace or newline padding, HTML table tags, and repeated characters or symbols. Activations are generally weak and scattered, strongest on spaces and numbers in counting sequences.

Tokens inside highly repetitive, looping sequences where the same token or short pattern (words, symbols, newlines, quotes, table dividers, numbered markup) repeats many times. Activation is strongest for long runs of a single repeated token and weaker for loosely repeating or noisy patterns.

39244.name: The slash separating the DOI prefix (10.xxxx) from the suffix, often including the suffix's first letters ("/s", "/S"), in DOIs and journal URLs. Weak, scattered activations also appear on connective words in academic or affiliation text, such as "of" and "the".

39251.name: A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires mostly in boilerplate, templated, code or citation text. It tends to land on tokens whose next token is highly predictable: the last item before a closing bracket, parenthesis or brace (e.g. indentation before "}"), separators inside DOIs and URL paths, template keys, and fixed sentence-final endings like Korean "합니다". It also fires on scattered words in spammy or incoherent prose.

39252.name: Tokens immediately following the number three ("3", "three", "third", "3rd"). These are usually the unit or noun being counted (years, days, minutes, stars, features), or the continuation of a number or expression (",558", "%", "/4", "b", "-year", "hundred"). Weaker activations occur after other numbers or in numeric and date contexts.

39257.name: Affiliation markers in academic author lists: footnote symbols, numbers, letters or superscripts (and the separators/newlines/parentheses) that come right before an institution or department name, marking where one affiliation begins. Activation is highest on the index marker itself (1, ², †, *, a, closing brace of \textsuperscript), and weaker on following words like 'Department of' or punctuation.

39264.name: Backslash characters (\\ tokens), especially in code strings, regex escapes, Windows file paths (C:\\), and LaTeX line breaks or comments. Activation is strongest in code and path contexts.

39267.name: The tag name right after an opening angle bracket in HTML markup, chiefly the "a" of an anchor tag ("<a href=…" or "<a name=…"), especially inside table cells. Other tag names (img, table, font) fire more weakly. Scattered weak hits on ordinary prose tokens are noise.

39279.name: Mass nouns for transferable or stored content, chiefly "data" and also "information", "text", "files", "content", "code" and "ideas". They usually appear as objects of verbs of transfer, storage, processing or protection (send, transmit, exchange, store, encode, transform). Activation is strongest when the context describes data moving between systems.

Nouns for stored or transmitted digital content, chiefly "data" and also "information", "files", "content", "text" and "images". They usually appear as the object of verbs like store, access, transmit, restore or copy. Activation is strongest for "data" in technical computing and storage contexts, with weak firing on other abstract quantities such as payments and earnings.

39304.name: A diffuse feature firing on highly predictable tokens inside formulaic or boilerplate text. Most hits are the second word of fixed page labels or headings, such as "RSS Icon", "Rights Managed", "TLD Registrar", "Software introduction", "Detailed Solution", "Brain Mass" and "Por um escritor". It also fires on the bracket or space just before a citation or reference number, as in "[6]" and "(ref. 2)".

39340.name: Mainly the " =" sign in math or code equations, firing hardest when the left side is just "0" ("0 = ...") and also on similar relation symbols such as "\le". Weak, scattered activations also appear on boilerplate tokens like "Leave A Reply", "Sponsored:", "Citation for published version", and code indentation.

39346.name: Commas (sometimes fused with a closing quote or parenthesis) that come right after a noun phrase or the end of a complete clause and before more material, such as a conjunction, participial phrase, appositive, relative clause or list item. The feature marks the boundary where the sentence goes on with added or elaborating content rather than ending.

39375.name: The opening parenthesis (sometimes with a quote mark, "the", or "or") that comes right after a full multi-word name or term and introduces its abbreviation or short-form definition, e.g. "Social Security Administration (SSA)".

39386.name: Separator tokens such as commas, spaces, ampersands, and HTML <td> tags inside long, repetitive sequences like number lists, table rows, and coin-flip strings. Activation is strongest in the middle of a long run of repeated delimiters. Weaker activations fall on function words (and, with, that, the) in formulaic, promotional-style prose.

3942.name: Weak, diffuse activation on structural boundary tokens in formatted or code-like text: line breaks, closing brackets/braces followed by newlines, indentation whitespace, list numbering periods, table row tags, and the first token starting a new line, field, or list item. It marks the point where one structural unit ends and the next begins.

39431.name: The class-name token right after a package path in Java import statements, most often annotation names like .NonNull/.NotNull following "annotation", plus Lombok/Spring names such as .Component, .Data, .Param. It peaks on null-check annotations (.NonNull). Weak, scattered activations also appear on odd filler words like "typically" in spammy prose.

39434.name: Tokens in passages about scheduled or upcoming events. It fires on the words that describe what will happen and when, such as a game, session, meeting, trial, election or launch, plus their surrounding predicate words ("will take on", "when it convenes", "next stage", "starts in January"). Activation is strongest on forward-looking descriptions of a planned occurrence, like sports matchups and legislative or calendar events.

39442.name: A diffuse, weakly activating feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires sparsely across prose, code and data, most often on the last token of a noun phrase or clause just before a comma, period or continuation, such as a head noun, a verb, or an assignment '='.

39449.name: Mostly the token immediately before a number, strongest on the standalone space before a digit that gives a division remainder or leftover amount (e.g. "remainder of 3", "and 5 days", "5 modulo 4 = 1"). Weaker hits include newlines or dashes before numbers and scattered sentence-initial words.

39454.name: Final words of web UI link/button text that end a truncated snippet or point to further content, mainly "more" in "Read more", "(More)", "Show more", plus similar labels like "Read Next", "Click for Answer", "Apply Here", "full list", "Impact Factor", and ellipsis or back-link (↩) markers.

Words in link text placed after a truncated excerpt or teaser that lead to the full content, especially the "More" in "Read More", plus "reading" in "Continue reading", "Review", "Profile", ellipsis markers like "[…]", and "here"/"enlarge" in "click here".

39459.name: Weak, diffuse feature that most consistently fires on "who" (and sometimes the following verb such as "loves" or "uses") right after "directly left of the person" in zebra/Einstein-style logic-puzzle clues. It marks where the second referent of a positional relation begins to be specified. It also fires on code tokens that open an argument or value, such as getElementById(' or ="@ in XML attributes, which is the strongest case.

39461.name: Delimiters that separate entries in a list of names or similar items: commas, semicolons, newlines, ");", "),", "],", "&" and "and". They fire at the boundary right after one item and before the next, most often in author, credit, contributor or recipient lists, and also in lists of patent classification codes.

39464.name: Line-ending and indentation tokens at structural boundaries in code and markup. The strongest cases are the newline and indentation after the last line of a doc comment (e.g. after "@var array" or "@return"), just before the closing "*/". Weaker cases are the ">⏎" that closes a table cell or header ("" / "") before the next cell in HTML tables. The feature also fires weakly on stray prose tokens at clause ends.

39477.name: The "import" keyword at the start of Java import statements, mainly in the later lines of an existing import block, where it follows earlier imports, often ones that share the same package prefix. One weak exception is "to" in English prose.

Function words (prepositions or pronouns) that begin a qualifying phrase right after an otherwise complete clause, adding the method, source, or condition, e.g. "computed using…", "tumor from…", "and you meant…".

39499.name: Highly predictable tokens inside repeated or templated text: words that copy an earlier pattern in the context, such as "Lorem ipsum", "TEXT TO BE EDITED", item_five, test3, ncis~, "Life! death!" or 제목/내용 table cells, and stock web boilerplate like "Your email address will not be published", "Tu dirección de correo" or "forgot password". Placeholder and dummy text activates most strongly.

39504.name: The conjunction "or" in the legal boilerplate phrase "express(ed) or implied", firing most strongly in Apache License headers ("WITHOUT WARRANTIES OR CONDITIONS OF ANY KIND, either express or implied"). It fires more weakly in other warranty or endorsement disclaimers, and faintly on similar paired-adjective conjunctions ("verbal and written").

39525.name: Words that point back to earlier work or past events, typically in scientific or reporting prose. The strongest cases are phrases citing the authors' own or others' prior research ("our previous study", "we have reported", "recent paper [5] we introduced", "et al. [2017]"). Weaker cases are temporal markers ("recent", "previously", "earlier", "ago") and reporting verbs ("reported", "proposed", "introduced", "showed").

39558.name: The word "treatment" and its forms (treat, treating, treatments), plus related words like management, diagnosis, cure, therapeutic, medication and solution. These mostly appear in medical contexts as the action applied to a disease or condition, often in the phrase "the treatment of [disease]". Activation is highest for "treatment" right after "the" or "for" when a named disease or condition follows.

Words for treating or remedying a condition, mostly "treatment"/"treat"/"treating" and near-synonyms (management, cure, remedies, solution, controlling), plus purpose phrases like "used to treat". Activation peaks in medical contexts such as "the treatment of [disease]" or "used to treat [condition]". Weak scattered hits appear on unrelated function words.

39607.name: Language describing transitions, contrasts or changes between two states, phases, categories or forms (e.g. "from liquid to plasma", "transition from first form to the second", "wet-to-dry", "chaotic or non-chaotic", "transformed into"), mostly in scientific or technical text. It fires most strongly on the connecting words (from, to, into, between, and/or, non-) and on the names of the contrasted states.

39686.name: Words forming the content of direct or reported speech, i.e. utterances introduced by speech verbs (said, replied, asked, answered, proclaims, saying). The strongest cases are rhetorical questions and emphatic declarations, often in biblical or archaic register (e.g. 'Do we not very well know that…', 'I am not ashamed of…'). Scattered weak activations also occur on generic statement text, including boilerplate.

39704.name: The verb "grant(ed/s)" in formal licensing and permission boilerplate (e.g., "Permission is hereby granted", "the author hereby grants", "use is granted without fee"). It fires most strongly after "is hereby" in software-license headers, and weakly on other performative legal verbs like "notified", "acknowledged" and "declare".

39715.name: Separators and items inside repetitive, enumerated sequences: page-number lists (1 2 3 4 5), table header/cell tags, column indices, and delimiters (spaces, pipes, commas, dashes, &) between successive list or table entries. It is strongest on the middle elements of consecutively numbered runs and repeated HTML th/td cells.

39740.name: The noun that follows "Supplementary/Supplemental/Supporting/Additional" in scientific-paper boilerplate, e.g. "information", "material", "data" or "file". It is strongest in "Supplementary data are available at…" notices and weak on scattered unrelated tokens.

39773.name: Control-flow and branching keywords in code or code-like text, strongest for "case" in switch statements and also firing on "switch", "match", "when", "if" and "for", typically at the start of an indented line.

39777.name: Acronyms (or their final subword pieces) naming a classification or identifier scheme that introduces a list of codes or numbers in paper and product metadata, e.g. PACS, AMS, JEL, OCIS, CAS, MSC, CCS. It is strongest on "ACS" in "PACS numbers" in physics abstracts and weak on other short acronyms and on stray punctuation or whitespace.

39781.name: Words for ulcers, plus weaker hits on other lesions and surface damage. The strongest activations are on "ulcer" and its pieces ("ulcer", "ul-cers", "ulceration", "ulcerative"). Weaker hits cover related sores and pits: sore, canker, blister, crater, pitting, cracked skin, abrasions, nodules and scabs.

39790.name: Tokens inside formulaic boilerplate such as licensing statements, citations, site headers/footers and timestamps. The strongest are "License" and the comma after it, plus "terms of", in Creative Commons open-access notices. Weaker hits are the punctuation or newlines that close a fixed name or tagline (e.g. after "IUCN Red List of Threatened Species", a site slogan or a publisher name).

39793.name: Highly predictable continuation tokens inside fixed formulaic or structured text, especially "al" after "et" in academic citations, and also URL extensions like ".html", address and DOI punctuation, and stock boilerplate phrases.

39815.name: The final digit(s) of a phone number (also weaker on endings of ISBN/ISSN or other long ID codes), plus sometimes the punctuation or space right after it. Activation is strongest on the last digit of a hyphenated contact phone number.

39827.name: News-report prose, especially wire-style coverage of violent or conflict events such as attacks, bombings, killings and security incidents. It fires most strongly on the narrative connective tissue of the reporting: casualty phrases like "At least 13 soldiers killed", "which killed two", "bombing by the Taliban targeting", attribution words like "reported", "according to" and "announced", and sentence or paragraph boundaries and transitions like "Earlier,", "But" and "Adding to this".

39831.name: Tokens in metadata/attribution fields naming who produced, assessed or reviewed something (author, assessor, examiner, user avatar, AUTHOR constants), strongest on 'LEAD_AUTHOR'; weak, noisy activations also appear on citation numbers and other boilerplate tokens.

39833.name: Type-checking operators/functions in code: JavaScript "typeof" and Python "type(...)" used to inspect a value's type, especially right after if/return/print/( in conditional comparisons. Fires most strongly on typeof in JS type checks, and also on typeof showing up in garbled or random text.

39839.name: The leading keyword or command that begins a line or statement in code, config files, or structured lists, especially when it repeats the same opening word as previous lines (e.g., print, puts, Define, const, set, view, Added, Sprite, REMARK). It marks the start of a repetitive, templated line.

39860.name: Weak, diffuse feature on structural or syntactic tokens in code-like or highly repetitive, templated text, such as assignment operators, return keywords, opening quotes or parentheses, arrows, commas and spacing in lists. It typically fires at the point just before a value or literal is supplied, especially in toy or garbled programming snippets that repeat the same line pattern.

39861.name: Terms for gastric acid reflux and backward flow, mostly medical and often word-final subword pieces: strongest on "reflux" (acid reflux, GERD), weaker on related ones such as "-lux" in efflux/subluxation, "urg" in regurgitation, heartburn, antacids, back-up and stomach acidity. Some spillover onto unrelated word fragments.

39863.name: The conditional keyword "if" in code, firing most strongly when it begins a condition inside a loop body (for/while). It also fires more weakly on other tokens that open a filtering condition, such as filter closures, lambda arrows, comprehension ifs, and logical operators.

39876.name: The token "dop"/"Dop" opening a word such as Doppler, dopamine, doppelganger or doping, strongest in noisy, garbled text. Weaker activation on the Cyrillic "оп" after "д" (as in дополнительно, допустим) and occasionally on " code".

39937.name: Words in instructions specifying the format or precision of an answer or output, most strongly "to (the nearest)" after "round/rounded". Weaker on phrases like "express your answer as/in", "print as a", "finish your response with", and "use the markdown".
