39940.name: Tokens inside names and acronyms of formal frameworks, guidelines, and research-methodology terms, especially the later word-pieces of an acronym or its expansion. Activation is by far strongest for the PRISMA systematic-review reporting guideline (“Reporting”, “MA”). It is moderate for related scientific-reporting vocabulary such as RE-AIM, NNT, intent-to-treat, trial registration, preregistration, flowchart, checklist and bias. It fires weakly on other acronyms (DASH, GMP, DOAJ) and on list bullets in structured documents.

39947.name: Prepositions, chiefly "of" and occasionally "for" or "from", that link a head noun such as version, episode, launch, title or members to the specific entity it belongs to or describes ("version of iOS 8", "episode of the program"). Activation is strongest when the head noun names a part, instance or edition of a named work, product or organization.

40006.name: Mostly the word "Destination" in the boilerplate "Send to / Choose Destination" header of PubMed-style abstract pages. It also fires weakly on tokens that finish a fixed or predictable phrase or formatting unit, such as the end of a name (San Francisco), a word suffix, citation punctuation, hashtags and HTML tags.

40027.name: The assignment/binding operator right after the loop variable(s) in a for-loop header, strongest for Go's " :=" in "for _, v := range ..." statements. It is weaker for C-style "for i :=" or "=" and for Python's " in" before enumerate. Unrelated tokens get faint activations.

40028.name: The " (at" opening the parenthetical "(at your option)" in GPL license boilerplate ("or (at your option) any later version"). Activation is weak for other punctuation that begins a parenthetical aside after "or", such as a dash or "=".

40052.name: Inner subword pieces of pharmaceutical drug names, mainly antibiotics and chemotherapy agents. The strongest response is to "xor" in doxorubicin; weaker responses fall on "acy" in tetracycline-family names and "yc" in doxycycline. Weak firing also occurs on similar-looking fragments outside drug names (e.g., the bitwise term "xor", "sync").

40054.name: The final "UM" token completing the all-caps word "MEMORANDUM" at the head of formal documents (memos, memoranda of understanding, court opinions). Weak, sporadic activation on unrelated function tokens.

40080.name: Fires on a junction token, such as punctuation, a space, a newline, a preposition or conjunction, or a word fragment, that sits mid-phrase right before a predictable continuation. It is especially common in templated web boilerplate: dictionary-site headers ('słowo, na przykład'), 'Local time in X: [time]', citation separators (doi., page-range dashes), and freelance-bid listings.

40096.name: Head words that complete a noun phrase or technical term, typically the last word of a compound (e.g., 'Reynolds stresses', 'smart farming', 'medicinal uses', 'water treatment'), often items in lists or titles right before a comma, 'and', or period. Mostly found in scientific, technical, or descriptive prose, with weaker firing on sentence-final punctuation and newlines ending such clauses.

40106.name: Separator characters (mostly hyphens, also underscores or slashes) inside identifiers, URLs, filenames and reference codes, typically sitting between an alphabetic prefix and a following number or ID (e.g. LETT-5789, section-1, img_01, ISBN 978-). Occasional weak hits on ordinary words in garbled text.

4013.name: Diffuse, weak activation on boilerplate and metadata text such as site disclaimers, license and copyright notices, "X is a question and answer site" blurbs, citation and legal references, and web page navigation or help notes. It fires on scattered function words, numbers and punctuation within these formulaic passages rather than on any single token type.

40138.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires in technical text (code, math, and problem statements), most often on function words in code comments about placeholder or simulated logic, e.g. the "with" in "replace with your actual…" or the "to" in "save to a file (simulated)".

40142.name: Weak, diffuse feature centered on word pieces and words tied to promises and binding commitments: strongest on the "issory" in "promissory", and also firing on "promise"/"promised", "covenants", "note" in the debt sense, "obligor", and "Projected". It also fires on the fragments "ord" in "primordium" and "ory" in "Promontory", apparently because they resemble the spelling of "prom-" words. Scattered low activations elsewhere, on newlines after boilerplate, parentheses and similar tokens, look like noise.

40150.name: Fires most strongly on abbreviated words inside legal and academic citations, such as court and reporter names ('Cir.', 'App. Div.', 'Civ. Prac.', 'Gen. Laws', 'C.C.', 'CRIM.'). These are mid-citation tokens where a fixed continuation is expected. Weaker activations land on assorted tokens partway through a phrase, mostly function words and verbs ('provides', 'can', 'has', 'for', 'that'), right before the main complement follows.

40159.name: A largely position-agnostic feature that fires on single function-like or connective tokens in the middle of running text or code: prepositions, conjunctions, determiners, commas, auxiliaries and whitespace or indentation. These are tokens where the following content word or argument (a noun phrase, parameter or clause) has to be predicted. Language and domain don't matter; examples include lists, code, scientific prose and French.

40167.name: The word "INCLUDING" in all-caps legal disclaimer/license boilerplate (after "EXPRESS OR IMPLIED,"), introducing a list of warranties. Weak, incidental activations appear on other qualifying or continuation tokens.

40189.name: Tokens completing the names of semiconductor, electronics and component companies (Micron, Microchip, Analog Devices, Texas Instruments, STMicroelectronics, Freescale, Infineon, Renesas, Atmel, Nordic Semiconductor). It fires on the later subword or second word of the name, usually in technical, datasheet or industry-news contexts. It weakly fires on related electronics jargon such as "datasheet" and "semiconductor".

4019.name: Mentions of the Python programming language ("python"/"Python", including shebang paths like /usr/bin/python, "python manage.py", python.org, .py, pip, sys.path). It fires more weakly on other programming language names (Ruby, Haskell, Basic) and on technical or path-like code tokens.

40198.name: Function words and punctuation (articles like "the"/"a", commas) in the middle of expository, informational text such as guides, lists and explainers. They tend to sit right before a descriptive or explanatory continuation, for example "is a well-moderated…", "at the bottom…" and ", because…". The examples are sparse, so this pattern is tentative.

40208.name: Structural opening tokens at the start of a line or element in code or markup, chiefly the "<" that opens an XML/HTML tag after indentation. It also fires on other line-leading delimiters in indented or structured text: tabs, "def", ":", "-", tree-drawing characters, "**", and "((".

40210.name: Average statistics, strongest on sports stat lines like "averaged 17 points, four rebounds and four assists per game": fires on "averaged", "an average of", the numbers and "per game". Weak activation on other numeric figures and on "main" in the boilerplate "Skip to main content".

40250.name: Punctuation, mostly an opening parenthesis (sometimes a bracket, dash or space), that comes right after a title, name or heading, especially near the start of a document, and opens a parenthetical or subtitle-like addition such as an acronym, year, credit, version or clarification.

4026.name: Weak, diffuse activations in formal academic, institutional, or project-description text, such as paper titles, abstracts, theses, affiliations, and initiative announcements. It fires mostly on structural or transitional tokens: sentence breaks, paragraph newlines, discourse openers like 'However' or 'Moreover', and phrases framing the research or project ('This research originates from', 'within the Top Institute', 'Project Director', 'Doctoral thesis').

40263.name: The "/**" token that opens Javadoc/doc-block comments in code, firing most strongly when it begins a documentation comment right before a class member, field, constructor or method. It is weaker for "/**" used as a path wildcard (e.g. "/css/**") or in URLs, and there is only faint, scattered activation on unrelated punctuation or formatting tokens.

40310.name: Separator tokens (spaces, newlines, double newlines, ">\n" in HTML tables, pipes, dashes) placed between items of a repetitive, predictable sequence, such as numbered pagination (1 2 3 4), number or year runs, alphabet indexes, figure labels, answer options, list entries, and table rows/cells. Activation is strongest deep inside long runs of structured, enumerated content.

40320.name: Later sub-segments of dotted package or namespace names in code declarations (Java package, C# namespace/using, Python import, include paths), especially the final descriptive module name such as .models, .service, .adapters or .view. Activation grows toward the end of the qualified name and fades after it. Only weak, scattered activation appears outside code.

Tokens that continue or extend a hierarchical name or path in code/technical text, most strongly submodule components after a package name in Python import statements (e.g. '.utils', '._utilities.enums'), path separators, and suffixes in package/module listings. Weaker activations occur on function words ('a', 'for') in technical prose.

40321.name: The word "Court" (and related judicial/institutional terms like "court of", "App. Div", "Judicial") directly after a jurisdiction or place name (U.S., Texas, California, New Jersey), mostly in appellate-court titles such as "Court of Appeals".

40343.name: Function words and clause-opening phrases in instructional, tech-support or how-to prose aimed at the reader, especially conditional or advisory framing such as "If you…", "Please make sure…", "You will/may…" and "For instructions on…".

Diffuse, low-level activation on function words and verb phrases in instructional, conditional or advisory text (tech help, how-to guides, terms/notices). Strongest on hedged or conditional clauses addressed to the reader, such as 'if you do not have', 'you don't need to', 'this method requires you to' and 'a problem which may be cleared', with modals, 'to' and clause boundaries.

40355.name: Separators between author names in academic author lists and citations. These are usually commas, but also semicolons, "and", "et" (as in "et al."), and punctuation fused with a closing bracket or period ("},", ".;", "),", ".,"). Activation is strongest for commas that follow an affiliation superscript in paper bylines.

40358.name: Weak, diffuse activations on words that express evidence, attestation or documentation, i.e. how something is known, recorded or dated. These include source and attribution phrases ("records say that", "data from", "tells us", "as evidenced", "reported", "report of", "observations", "known", "extant written texts"). They also include earliest-occurrence and dating phrases such as "as early as", "since at least 2017", "circa", "oldest form" and "first mentions". Activation often falls on the preposition, "as", or the date or citation token linking a claim to its supporting evidence or time point.

40412.name: The token immediately following "the" (or a similar slot expecting a noun) when it is surprising or ungrammatical there, such as a preposition like "in"/"of", or an odd capitalized word fragment (Is, W, V, All, There). The strongest cases are "the in".

40419.name: Narrative prose in scriptural or archaic register, especially Bible verses. It fires most strongly on clauses that advance the story, typically 'And/Then + subject + past-tense verb' such as 'And it was so', 'he said', 'began to speak boldly' and 'approached and say to him'. Weaker activations appear on verbs and connectives in other storytelling text.

40422.name: Word pieces that complete technical terms about heat or material behavior, mostly the part after a "therm" prefix ("oplastic", "oe"lectric, "oc"ouple, "ore"gulation, "ally"). It also fires on related material-property words such as plastic(izer), elastomeric, ductile, melt and heat-sealing. Activation is strongest on "thermoplastic".

40459.name: The subject of a reading-comprehension question, the word right after "What is/was" or "of". It is usually "the" or the noun it introduces, such as author, user, speaker, text or number, and is strongest for the person whose views are asked about ("the author's…", "the user's…").

40467.name: Indentation whitespace and the opening " <" of the first child tag right after <head> in HTML documents (typically before meta or title), with weaker activation on <html>/<head> tags and similar boilerplate HTML openings.

40477.name: Institutional affiliation text, typically in author bylines of academic papers. It fires on words like University, Department of, Institute, School and College, on the commas and parentheses that separate parts of the affiliation, and on the address details that follow (city, state, postal code, P.O. Box). This holds across English, Spanish, Portuguese and French forms (Universidad/Université, Instituto, Laboratoire).

40508.name: Word-internal subword pieces of biochemical terms, chiefly the fragment just before the "-ase" suffix of enzyme names (dehydro|gen|ase, re|duct|ase, oxid|ase, ester|ase, -id|ase). The strongest activation is on "gen" in "dehydrogenase". Weaker activations fall on similar mid-word chunks of other biochemical words (heter|ot|rophic, decar|box|ylation, trans|amination).

4053.name: Mostly weak, diffuse activation on technical and code text. It is strongest on CPU/assembly instruction mnemonics such as LD BC, ADD and NOP. Weaker activations hit command names, keywords and identifier fragments in code, shell commands and technical docs (e.g. rm, ssh, let, Dim, GET).

40530.name: Android/Java code identifiers built around the "-able" type and resource names. Activation is strongest on Android resource directories like "R.drawable", "R.mipmap" and "graphics.drawable", and moderate on "Drawable" class names and the Java "Throwable" type in throws clauses, catch blocks and parameters. Other text (e.g. "Synonyms" in dictionary headers) gets only weak, scattered activation.

40546.name: The token "McC" opening a Scottish/Irish surname (McCarthy, McCain, McCloy, McCullough), activating most when it follows a first name or initial in a person's name. All-caps "MCC", lowercase "mcc", and longer pieces like "McCorm" activate weakly.

40551.name: Spam/SEO keyword phrases dropped into otherwise unrelated or machine-spun text, such as product or search-query strings (gummies, male enhancement, drug prices, loans, court records, thesis titles) that break the sentence's flow. Activation is highest on the inserted commercial keywords, especially pharmaceutical, cannabis and enhancement terms.

40561.name: Words naming collections or container data structures, i.e. a group of multiple elements. These include programming types like list, array, vector, tuple, set, map, Vec, HashSet, Container and seq, and general or mathematical terms like collection, set, sequence, series, mixture and samples. Activation is strongest on list, set, collection and Vec.

40632.name: Abbreviated suffix words that close a proper name or list, typically followed by a period: corporate designators (Inc, Corp, LLC, Co, Bros), generational suffixes (Jr, III), and other abbreviations such as Rd, Vol, Univ, ft, and list-ending 'etc'. Activation is strongest for Inc, Jr, and Corp.

40635.name: Words tied to theatre, musicals and show business, peaking on "Broadway" (also "musical", cabaret, Bollywood, Sondheim, Cirque du Soleil, theatre, belting a song). Weaker hits fall on entertainment-district places (Harlem, Vegas, 42nd Street) and on arcade or pinball games.

40637.name: Fires strongly on legal-profession terms, especially "counsel" in the phrase "of counsel" in court-opinion attorney listings (weakly on "law firm"). Other activations are faint and scattered across function words like "of" and "the" in ordinary prose.

40641.name: Punctuation and separators that come right after a source title in citation or publication metadata, mostly a journal name. They mark the shift to the year, volume, issue or pages, as in "J Med Res;", "Eng." or "Theory,". Activation is strongest on the first delimiter after an abbreviated or full journal name, and weaker on later year, volume and page pieces and on labels like "Chapter", "Published" or "Report".

Punctuation and tokens immediately following the name of a publication (journal, newspaper, news agency, book source) in citations or datelines, i.e. the separator (comma, period, colon, dash, parenthesis, newline) or volume/year/date info that comes next. Strongest on the period after abbreviated medical journal names (e.g. 'N Engl J Med.', 'Arthritis Rheum.') before the year.

40670.name: The word "derivative" (especially after "the", "first" or "second") in calculus and math problem text. Weaker activations fall on related math operation nouns such as sum, limit, gradient, rate and acceleration that follow "find/compute the".

40672.name: Sentence and paragraph boundaries, mostly periods or closing punctuation fused with newlines (".⏎⏎", ").", "?⏎⏎") at the end of a sentence, along with the first token after a line break. It mainly appears in incoherent, spun or SEO-spam text where a topic shift follows. Activation is strongest on a period plus double newline closing a paragraph.

40686.name: Flags and options in shell/command-line commands, especially those after a dash, strongest by far on "rf" in "rm -rf", also high on "mkdir -p" and "rm -f". Weaker on other destructive or deletion operations (delete[] in C++, removedirs, DROP IF EXISTS, -y confirmations).

40720.name: Fires on tokens immediately before an expected digit or number, such as year prefixes (201, 202, 194) awaiting their final digit, separators (spaces, commas, hyphens, brackets, '.[') ahead of numeric values, and issue/volume numbers in dates, citations, lists and code. A few activations on ordinary words are weak and fall outside this pattern.

40738.name: Line breaks (often double newlines) that end a document's header or metadata line, most often a date or byline, right before the title or body text starts. Weaker activations land on other header-boundary tokens like separators, closing brackets, or 'by'.

40769.name: Generic, formulaic phrasing in promotional, SEO-style or marketing web copy. It fires mostly at sentence boundaries (periods, commas) and on stock sentence openers and connectors such as "These", "This", "With", "We are", "You can", "It helps to" and "make sure that". Activation is strongest on boilerplate self-promotional claims like "We are a technical team having immense years of experience".

A diffuse, generic feature that fires at clause and sentence boundaries in expository or descriptive text, often LLM-generated or synthetic. It shows up on periods, commas, newlines, and the first words of the next sentence (e.g., The, It, We have, Through, specializes) at the point where the text moves on to elaborate on an entity or topic it has just introduced. It also fires on repeated templated tokens, such as the T in 1 ≤ T.

40805.name: Modifier words, mostly nouns used attributively or relational adjectives, that name a domain, field or aspect (safety, security, health, design, ethical, technical, measurement, logistic). They typically come right before a head noun such as concerns, issues, challenges, standards, applications or standpoint, or after 'due to' or 'a matter of', and specify the dimension in which a problem or quality applies.

40809.name: Verbs of acquiring information or knowledge ("find out", "learn", "know", "determine", "discover"), usually the verb itself or the particle after it. Activation is strongest on "out" in "find out" and weaker on the others, especially in "to learn/know more" constructions.

Verbs and verb completions expressing acquiring or seeking information, most strongly "out" in "find out" and "know" after "want/need to". Weaker hits include learn, figure out, determine, uncover, the Chinese 知道, and the recipient in "tell you/us".

40833.name: Names of organizations and their locations, especially companies, manufacturers, suppliers, and universities given as affiliations or sources (e.g., in scientific methods parentheticals like 'Alfa Aesar, Ward Hill, MA'). It fires on the name pieces, corporate suffixes (Inc, LLP, AG), and city/state parts, strongest for supplier attributions.

40836.name: A diffuse, low-intensity discourse-structure feature in expository or argumentative prose. It fires mostly at transition points between ideas: sentence-final periods, paragraph breaks, and list or section boundaries. It also fires on the openers or connectives that begin the next point, such as However, Recently, That is, Please, and This is how he summarized. It is strongest where an argument pivots or a new claim or summary is introduced.

40838.name: Tokens that complete a highly predictable, often formulaic multi-word term or template: boilerplate phrases (Open Access Publications, Open Content Licence, maxPaginationLinks), set phrases (without replacement, length decreasing), terms repeated from earlier context (Nota do Pedido), and function words or punctuation that continue a standard construction.

4085.name: The first token of a modifier that comes before a noun, usually right after a determiner like "a", "an", "the" or a possessive. Most often this is a number or number word forming a compound modifier, such as "a six-hour", "a 20% discount", "a one-day" or "a 5 week". Other prefix-like modifiers such as all-, mid-, no-, double- and large- also appear. Activation is strongest on numbers and "one", and on the space token before digits.

Numbers (digits or number words) and similar quantity modifiers that come right after a determiner like "a", "an", "the", "this" or "his" and begin a modifier, usually a hyphenated compound such as "two-month-old", "four-door" or "eight-hour", or an ordinal or measurement. Activation is highest on spelled-out numbers before a hyphen.

40890.name: Fires most strongly on the Thai combining vowel mark 'ั' (mai han-akat) inside Thai words. Elsewhere activation is only weak and scattered: word fragments/suffixes, Slashdot user-ID digits and spaces before emoji. Other non-Latin scripts (Korean, Chinese, Arabic, Armenian, Kannada) get no activation.

409.name: A weak, diffuse latent that peaks on play-by-play descriptions of physical action in sports and fights, such as wrestling moves (lockup, knee, forearm, chop), a runner tagged at home plate, or a player fouled. Weaker activations scatter across event narration, like a currency vacillating, a swing that misses, a car going too fast, or players walking onto the pitch.

Descriptions of sports and competitive gameplay, such as scoring plays, tackles, ball distribution, race strategy, deficits to overturn, and course mistakes. Activation is strongest in play-by-play or game-recap narration (e.g., "3-point play", "attempted to tackle"). Weaker activations fall on physical actions, maneuvers or tactical phrasing in non-sports text.

40930.name: Highly predictable continuation tokens that complete a word or phrase from context: mostly mid-word subword fragments inside URLs and domain names (e.g., the rest of 'measurement' or 'software'), plus fixed collocations such as a unit after a number, a Chinese classifier after a demonstrative, and a repeated breadcrumb word.

40944.name: Tokens containing the letter sequence "ip"/"pip", especially the standalone word-start "pip" (Python's pip install, pipette, pipeline, Pippen, Piper). It fires most strongly on the Python package manager and on pipettes. Weaker activations appear for "pipe"/"piping" and for mid-word fragments like "ipp" (Kippur), "iper" (piperidine, Piper) and "IP".

40962.name: A diffuse, low-level feature for low-quality web text: SEO spam, casino and pharmacy spam, spun or machine-generated prose, and repository/metadata boilerplate. It fires most strongly inside incoherent, word-salad or mixed-language spam passages, such as pharma spam with stray Portuguese words or nonsensical essay-mill text. It fires weakly on scattered tokens in ordinary boilerplate like page view counts and archive notices.

40974.name: Words for spread, movement or encroachment, especially "invasive"/"invasion" (invasive species, invasive cancer) and cell migration/motility/metastasis. Activation is strongest in biomedical contexts describing cells moving or spreading. Related biological process nouns (formation, transformation, angiogenesis, phagocytosis) fire weakly.

41000.name: The final "0" of the Apache License URL "LICENSE-2.0" in code license header boilerplate. Activation is strongest when the URL is followed by a newline and the comment continues with "Unless required by applicable law", and weaker when other text follows it on the same line. There are faint, sporadic activations on unrelated boilerplate boundaries, such as a sentence-ending period plus blank line, a byline fragment ("escrit"), or spacing before bid counts.

41010.name: The " javax" package token in Java import statements (and qualified names like new javax.swing...), strongest when it repeats after earlier javax imports in a block; weak scattered activations on numeric fragments such as decimal points and timestamp digits.

41027.name: Class and type names for programming objects, mainly UI menu items and views. Activation peaks on "(MenuItem" inside Android's onOptionsItemSelected(MenuItem item) signature and is strong on "android.view.MenuItem" imports and getItemId. It is weaker on related types such as AdapterView, ItemStack, JMenuItem, ToolStripMenuItem and (Message, which usually appear in import lines or method parameters.

Mostly fires on tokens inside mathematical or LaTeX-formatted text, especially the command name in \text{...}. It also fires on plain words such as "the" embedded in math explanations, and occasionally on a noun in garbled, incoherent prose.

41028.name: Tokens inside a repeated identifier that the model can predict by copying earlier context, most strongly the first subword pieces of custom package or namespace names in Java/C#/PHP import statements (e.g. com.<<.g>>em, se.<<.f>>idde, org.<<.d>>avidlin). Weaker activations fall on other repeated code identifiers, indentation, and recurring boilerplate or list patterns.

41029.name: Backslash characters (\, \\, '\\') across contexts: LaTeX commands (\textsubscript, \begin, \cite), escape sequences (\n, \t), file paths, stray escaped text, and the word "slash" in "backslash"; occasionally other odd separator/escape-like tokens.

Backslash tokens (\, \\, \ followed by newline) in any role: escape sequences like \n, LaTeX commands like \boxed, and diagonal strokes in ASCII art/diagrams. Weaker activation on vertical bars and line-drawing characters in text diagrams and tables. Strongest when the backslash forms a diagonal line in ASCII drawings.

41038.name: Mentions of characters in narratives, plot summaries or historical accounts, often antagonistic or authority figures (kings, nobles, villains, a cruel lion, Polonius). It fires on their names, the pronouns referring to them, and the verbs or clauses describing what they do to others, with nearby punctuation sometimes included.

41070.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires on tokens that are surprising or out of place in context, especially in disfluent, ungrammatical, garbled or spun/machine-generated text. Typical cases are wrong word choices or broken syntax ("protected to therapeutic massage", "in order the design to work", "to initial aerosol formation"), odd fragments of names or URLs, and unexpected list items. It reflects local unpredictability rather than any specific meaning.

41071.name: The "/bootstrap" path segment in URLs or file paths for Bootstrap CSS/JS assets in HTML link tags, especially just before ".min.css". Other slash- or dash-prefixed path and option tokens activate only weakly.

41096.name: Fires on words for persecution and oppression: the persecution/persecuted/persec- stem fires most strongly, especially after 'fear of' or in refugee and religious contexts. Related terms like oppression, repression, exile, censorship, burning at the stake, witch hunt and hounded fire more weakly.

41101.name: The separator (space, hyphen, en dash, slash) or prefix token that sits between a citation or database identifier and its long numeric ID, e.g. "FR 50724", "PMC 3152826", "WL 5703944", "FR Doc. E7–17502", "rs.3.rs-477842". It fires just before the number begins. Activation is strongest for the space in Westlaw (WL) cites and Federal Register cites.

41120.name: Formal regulatory and research-compliance language, peaking on ethics approval statements in scientific papers ("experiments were approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee"). It also fires on funding acknowledgments ("research was supported by"), conducting work under guidelines or licences, and compliance with rules and regulations, with weak activation on generic procedural wording.

41130.name: Punctuation that closes a case label in switch/case statements. It fires most strongly on the closing parenthesis of shell case patterns (e.g. "*)", "g)", "")"), together with any newline and indentation after it. Colons ending C/JS/PHP case labels activate more weakly.

41143.name: Technical/physiological measurement terms, strongest for pulmonary function test terminology (vital capacity, FVC, FEV₁, forced expiratory volume/flow, airflow, airways). Weaker activation on other scientific quantities, variables and abbreviations (torque, Vmax, kcat, conduction velocity, perfusion).

41147.name: The word "neck", most strongly when it refers to the literal body part (human or animal anatomy) or the neck of an object such as a guitar or jar. Weaker activation for idiomatic or compound uses like "breakneck", "neck of the woods" or "neck-and-neck", for "necklace", and for nearby body words like "head".

41154.name: Words for hard or solid lumps and masses, especially ones that form inside the body or have to be removed: stones (kidney stones, hailstones), blood clots and thrombi, cataracts, polyps, crystals, microliths, floaters, ice. Strongest on 'stones' in a medical context. Weaker, scattered firings land on unrelated tokens such as paragraph breaks and 'Presentation'.

41180.name: Positional/coordinate property names in code, such as x, y, cx, cy, row, col, and the CSS offsets top, left, and bottom. These usually appear as a key or argument right before a value is assigned. The strongest cases are x/y attributes in SVG, JSON, or function calls and "top" in CSS absolute positioning.

41196.name: Words that set the scope or domain of a topic, typically temporal spans (history, period, over time, twentieth century, a hundred years), geographic or national ranges (world, global, American, British, Africa), or academic subject areas (science, programming, literature, politics). Activation is strongest on phrases spelling out wide breadth, such as 'from all over the world' or 'the whole history of the universe'.

41230.name: The final word or suffix that finishes the name of a biological signaling molecule, typically "factor(s)" after a descriptor (strongest in "growth factor", "tumor necrosis factor", "Transforming Growth Factor"; weaker after "transcription"), plus head nouns and endings like "protein", "hormone", "peptide", "-ase" and "-in" in protein, hormone and cytokine names.

41271.name: The " org" package prefix in Java import statements (e.g., import org.springframework / org.junit), strongest when it follows a preceding org import line (repeated org imports, especially junit test imports). Weak scattered activations on unrelated prose tokens and paragraph breaks.

41307.name: Fires mostly on the space token right after "F. Supp." in legal case citations, just before the page or series number (e.g. "F. Supp. 1081", "F. Supp. 2d"). It also responds weakly to other separators or function words that come right before a reference, number or math expression, such as commas in author lists, " $", " \(" and "vs.".

41309.name: Fires on function words and verbs inside stock, formulaic phrasing typical of news writing, especially sports journalism. Examples include "held on to the one-goal lead to seal", "has been hard hit by a", "rules out knee-jerk", "coming into this fixture with some happy memories of" and "continue to dominate". These are predictable collocations and connective words (prepositions, articles, auxiliaries) within clichéd narrative expressions, rather than any specific content word.

41318.name: The word-start token " photoc" (or "oc" following "Phot") that begins words like photocopy, photocatalysis, photocell, photocurrent, photocycle. It fires most strongly in scientific photocatalysis contexts and more weakly for photocopies.

41325.name: Descriptions of how a product, app, service or system works or is used, especially features and user actions (you can click/choose/contact via email, will automatically…, play games on apps, prizes awarded). The weak activations are spread over the functional and procedural wording in these explanations of capabilities, interfaces and mechanisms.

41335.name: The name "Wilson" in any context: surnames of people, citations, places, institutions, and named concepts. Similar names such as "Watson" and the "son" ending of names activate only weakly.

41341.name: Final token of a username or person's name in forum, comment and email bylines (e.g., 'Jeff Newmiller wrote', 'posted by'), usually a word-piece completing a surname or handle just before post metadata. It also fires weakly on the leading space of bulleted list items after a colon and on line breaks following a byline.

41344.name: The word "nearest" in rounding phrases ("round to the nearest integer/whole number/hundredth"), in math problems, code comments and docs.

41356.name: Tokens partway through long repetitive, highly predictable sequences, such as runs of dots, dashes, symbols or separators (table-of-contents leaders, ASCII rules), table cells (LaTeX &, HTML <td>), numeric lists and grids, and IP-address segments. The latent fires on later repeats in the pattern, where the next token can be predicted from what came before. It fires weakly on occasional ordinary words in spammy or garbled text.

Tokens inside long runs of repeated, degenerate, or filler-like content (repeated whitespace/newlines, bullets, backticks, brackets, symbols, characters, or short words). It activates mid-sequence once the repetition is well established, often in garbled or ASCII-art-like text, with weak activation elsewhere.

41367.name: The word "vein" and the related root "ven-" (venous, intravenous, venepuncture). Activation is strongest for anatomical blood vessels, especially "venous", and weaker for figurative uses like "in this vein" or "in your veins". It also fires weakly on other vascular and lymphatic terms (lymphatic, capillary, portal, phlebo-).

41374.name: Words marking something as optional or not required, peaking on "optional"/"Optional"/"Option<T>" and especially "nullable"/"@Nullable" (strongest in JPA column definitions and schema tables). Appears in code type annotations, API docs, config/schema fields, RFC 2119 boilerplate ("OPTIONAL") and prose (optional protocol, optional dependencies); occasionally fires weakly on related notions such as "None" in type unions and "non-required".

41401.name: Separators (spaces, commas, semicolons, parentheses, letter prefixes) placed just before the codes in lists of classification codes, such as MSC, PACS, JEL, ACM descriptors, patent classes, OEIS cross-references and 'Part of the ... Commons' disciplines. Activation is strongest on the space right before a numeric code, especially later items in a list.

41408.name: Action verbs or gerunds/nominalizations naming the purpose or function of a method, device, approach, or system, typically right after "method for", "approach to", "a way to", "used to" in technical or scientific abstracts and patents (e.g. measuring, detecting, reducing, managing). The following "of" is sometimes marked too.

4143.name: Punctuation, whitespace or newline tokens (colons, commas, line breaks, spaces, opening quotes/brackets) that come right after an unfinished phrase, often a preposition or introducing word like "is", "by", "that" or "because". They mark a break just before the expected continuation, such as a list, formula, quote, URL or name.

41449.name: The negation operator "!" right after an if condition opener (shell "if [ !", "if (!", "if !"). It also fires more weakly on conditional keywords themselves, especially preprocessor directives like #if, #ifdef and #ifndef, and faintly on stray spaces in byline or date text.

41478.name: Boundary tokens that come right before a new segment or response begins, such as colons after "Answer"/"Output"/"A", newlines after a question or a code block, and option dashes. Activation is strongest at answer/response prompts in Q&A or instruction-style text.

41485.name: The second (or final) item in a coordinated pair or list, typically the noun or name right after a conjunction such as "and", "or", "&", a comma or a slash. Examples include "England and Wales", "US and Canada" and "TCU/Baylor". Place names (countries, states, cities) activate most strongly.

41494.name: JavaScript global object names, chiefly "document" (also window, body, function), used as the argument or receiver in DOM/jQuery code. Activation is strongest inside jQuery wrappers like $(document).ready and weaker at the start of statements like document.getElementById. There is also weak, noisy firing on stray spaces or newlines in non-code text.

41496.name: Fires on the first token of a condition, right after a conditional or logical keyword (if, elif, else if, match, or, ||, &&). This is usually an opening parenthesis, a variable name, or 'the' or '$' in prose and math 'if' clauses. It marks the start of a boolean condition or clause.

41517.name: Names of historical dynasties, empires, eras, peoples and ruling powers (e.g., Qing, Tang, Mongol, Tudors, Habsburg, Edo, Persia), often the token after "the" or a name fragment, strongest for Chinese/Asian dynasties and periods.

Proper-name tokens (often word fragments) for historical dynasties, empires, rulers, peoples and ancient or fictional realms (e.g., Qing, Habsburg, Hohenstaufen, Ottoman, Aztec, Goguryeo, Sith). Activation is strongest on dynasty and royal-house names and weaker on other historical or exotic place and person names.

41519.name: Epigenetic and post-translational modification terms from molecular biology, especially histone/DNA chemical marks. Activation is strongest on "modifications" after "histone" and on the parts of "acetylation" and "methylation". It also fires on histone residue labels like the 3 and 4 in H3 and H4 and K4. Weaker activations appear on related chromatin and enzyme terms such as deubiquitination, corepressor, ChIP-seq, remodeling and neddylation.

4152.name: A weak, diffuse pattern that fires on tokens inside repetitive or parallel structures, such as list items and their separators, array indices, numbered sequences, table cells, and repeated math or code expressions. It responds most to separators (commas, brackets, operators) and to successive elements once the pattern has been established. Prose examples are rare and weak.

41529.name: Tokens at the start of JavaScript DOM/jQuery statements, mainly the jQuery selector call "$(" (also "$('#", "$.", "jQuery"), plus global browser objects like "document"/"window" and methods such as ".getElementById"/".querySelector". Activation is strongest on "$(" at the beginning of a line, as in $(document).ready or $(function).

41555.name: A diffuse feature for code, math, and technical problem text. It fires on tokens that start a new statement, expression, argument, or clause: line-initial keywords (create, class, var, from, for), indentation, prompts, opening brackets or parentheses, assignment operators, separating commas, and instruction verbs (Apply, Suppose, Provide). The common thread is structural boundary positions where a new syntactic unit begins.

41556.name: Mostly fires on the ">⏎" token closing an HTML table tag, above all "<thead>" right after "<table>" and before the first "<tr>" header row. Weaker scattered activations land on mid-sentence function words or structural tokens that precede upcoming structured or listed content (e.g., list dashes, dot leaders, line breaks).

41563.name: The word "figures" (and "Figures", "FIGURES", "Fig") meaning illustrations in documents, papers and books, strongest in "List of Figures", "high resolution figures" and "Some figures may appear in colour". Weaker on related visual or supplementary content nouns: tables, charts, graphs, slides, maps, photos, references.

41584.name: Verbs and prepositions that link a speaker or source to the audience or outlet receiving the communication, especially "told" right after a closing quote and speaker name in news attribution ("she told the jury", "he told AFP"). Weaker activations come from similar "to"/"with"/"for" and tells/gave in reporting contexts ("speaking to", "interview with", "shared with me").

41632.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires sparsely on scattered tokens, most often in text about reality, existence and the limits of knowledge: whether something is "really there" or "actually" happened, nobody really knowing, observation and measurement, causality, conditional independence, existence versus essence, Occam's razor, the universe/World. Many hits are on function words or name fragments with no clear shared meaning.

41647.name: The "/null" token completing the Unix null device path "/dev/null", mostly in shell output-discarding redirections (> /dev/null, 2>/dev/null, &>/dev/null). It also fires weakly on "/null" elsewhere (e.g. "blank/unknown/null") and very faintly on unrelated tokens.

41649.name:
Sentence-final punctuation fused with newline(s) (e.g. ".

", "].

") marking the end of a paragraph, mostly in academic/scientific abstracts or papers, right before a new paragraph, section, or metadata begins.

41661.name: Mainly the token "nav" (and similar UI names like "menu") at the start of HTML class or id attribute values (e.g. class="nav", id="nav-item"). It also fires weakly on other website boilerplate and navigation text, such as "Leave a comment" sections in several languages, "doi" in URLs, and transitions between spammy or boilerplate segments.

41689.name: Names of software frameworks and libraries, mostly JavaScript and web frameworks (Ext, Backbone, Ember, Alpine, Cake, Polymer, MooTools, Dojo). Activation sits on the name token or a word-piece inside it, and is strongest where the name appears in code or a list of tech stacks. Similar-looking ordinary words (e.g. "Extremely") fire weakly.

41707.name: Whitespace tokens (runs of spaces, space+newline combinations, and indentation at line starts), mostly in repetitive, degenerate or code-like text. Activation is strongest in long repeated blank-line sequences and on leading indentation after a newline. It also fires weakly on other repeated filler tokens such as repeated "the" or "**".

4173.name: Words or word pieces that name a field, sector, industry, or domain of activity, such as healthcare, retail, biotechnology, life sciences, energy, or defence. They often appear as modifiers before 'sector'/'industry' or in department and organization names. Activation is strongest on the domain noun itself, e.g. 'sciences', 'biotechnology', 'healthcare'.

41735.name: Tokens in the concluding step of a calculation or logical argument, where a result is derived or stated (e.g., "so the least amount is 301", "therefore ΔG < 0", "we get that P is also…", "= 1900", "Nm=3000 rpm"). The strongest activations fall on inference words (therefore, so, thus, hence, we get that, implies, means) and on the final value or statement that follows them, mostly in math, physics and code contexts.

Final steps of mathematical or logical derivations: concluding equations and results ("= 820", "x =") and wrap-up phrases like "Therefore," "Thus, the ... is", "yields", "So the sum ... is" that state the answer or the conclusion of a proof or calculation.

41738.name: Imperative or advisory phrasing that tells the reader what to do next, usually as a suggested remedy or alternative after a problem or unavailability: "try another", "check back later", "try clearing", "you may need to explore other alternatives", "please select". Activation is strongest on the action verbs (try, check, find) and the start of the instruction, including the preceding punctuation.

41767.name: Fires strongly on the closing word of standard MIT-style license boilerplate ("...OTHER DEALINGS IN THE SOFTWARE"). Elsewhere it gives only weak, diffuse activation on highly predictable continuations of fixed phrases or structures, such as "et al", "such as", "known as", and repeated HTML table cell tags.

41817.name:
Structural boundary tokens in AI-assistant style responses, mostly in markdown and code-heavy answers. They fire where one segment ends and the next begins: closing code-fence backticks, newline-bearing sentence ends (".
", ":

", "**

"), list numbers, table pipes, and transitions like "Let's", "Alternatively" or "These".

4182.name: A diffuse, weak feature with no clear semantic focus. It fires sparsely on scattered tokens: verbs, nouns and punctuation in prose, and identifiers or operators in code. It is somewhat more frequent in procedural or sequential text such as instructions, steps, "then do X", lists and code. The strongest activations fall on code annotations and formula operators.

41839.name: Words and phrases about naming, labeling, or terminology, i.e. how something is called, termed, described, or referred to (name, call, term, known as, named after, refer to, describe, so-called), plus the nearby words that introduce the label.

41874.name: Action/function names being invoked, mostly method or command names right after an accessor (., ->, ::) or a CLI program (connect, read, findClosest, textSearch, runString, step, flags). It also fires more weakly on action verbs after "to" or "can" in prose (ensure, convert, find, assist).

The action or operation word that directly follows an agent or object: verbs after a subject or modal ("does not endorse", "will produce", "module determines", "might block") and method or function names after an object accessor in code (".build", ".Print", "->QuerySongs", ".getPropertyValue"). It also fires on similar action or resource segments in URLs and commands ("submit", "?q", "/projects", "wpt run").

41875.name: Fires in mathematical/formal text on the listed generators, variables or elements that define a structure: entries inside group presentations (\langle x_1, x_2, … \rangle), set braces {a, b, c}, polynomial-ring variables (F_q[t]) and function arguments (x). It also fires on the words introducing such generating data ("generated by", "span", alphabets, predicates). The strongest activations are on presentation generators, the separating commas and ring indeterminates.

41878.name: The word "stress"/"stresses" (and close relatives like shock, damage) across senses. It fires most strongly in biological/environmental contexts, such as plant abiotic/biotic stress, heat stress, oxidative stress and stress responses. Psychological, mechanical and testing senses activate it more weakly.

41887.name: Additive discourse words that mark adding more information to what came before, chiefly "further" used as an adverb directly after a subject or modal (e.g. "X further acknowledged/relates"), which fires most strongly. It also responds, more weakly, to "also", "additional(ly)", "furthermore", "equally", "another" and "next", and to the Chinese 又/再 ("again/also").

Additive discourse adverbs marking continuation or elaboration of a prior point, chiefly "further" (strongest when used mid-sentence between subject and verb, e.g. "He further stated", "hereby further certified"). Also fires on synonyms such as furthermore, moreover, additionally, in addition, also, likewise, equally and even more, plus occasional sequence words like first and next.

41899.name: The pointer asterisk directly after "void" in C/C++ code (void*, void *, (void *)), marking a generic void pointer type; other tokens are only weakly active.

41906.name: Highly predictable continuation tokens in repetitive code structures. It is strongest on the indentation whitespace and opening tokens of a new line that repeats a previous statement pattern, e.g. print, sb.Append, transformation.append, dataGridView1.Rows[n].Cells, or HTML tags like <li>. It also fires on line-ending punctuation such as ]);⏎ and on break statements. Activation in prose is weak and diffuse, falling on ordinary function words, paragraph breaks and predictable nouns.

41932.name: Place names (cities, states, venues), especially ones that stand in for sports teams or organizations (e.g., Baltimore, Pittsburgh, Atlanta, Washington). Activation is strongest in sports contexts where the location acts as a team or as the site of a game.

Place names (cities, states, regions), especially when they stand for sports teams, institutions or governments (e.g. "Chicago", "Cleveland", "New York", "Washington"). Activation is strongest on the final token of the name and in sports contexts. It also fires weakly on other team or organization references ("OU", "Imperial", "team").

41944.name: The separator and second number in a score, tally, or ratio comparing two opposing counts (vote splits like 7-2 or five to four, game scores, win-loss records, poll results, X-to-one margins). It fires most strongly on the hyphen or "to" and the following number, especially in court and legislative vote counts. It also fires weakly on words like "unanimously" and on the space before the second count.

41958.name: The word "newspaper(s)" and synonyms such as "paper(s)", strongest for "newspaper" itself. Weaker activation goes to related news/print media terms (tabloids, publications, magazine, media, broadcaster, gazette) and to word fragments like "new|sgroups" and "new|scast".
Words referring to newspapers and print news outlets, strongest on "newspaper(s)" and also "paper", "daily", "tabloids", "gazette", "Zeitung", "periodicals", and related press or news-media terms.

41976.name: The operand that immediately follows an arithmetic operator or sign, especially a minus, negation or plus (e.g. "-1", "+=0.5", "±5", "~bn"). It is usually a number, strongest when it is a negated value in parentheses like "(-1)" or a decimal after "-=".

41987.name: The word "damages" in its legal or financial sense, meaning monetary compensation claimed, sought or awarded for harm or loss (lawsuits, liability clauses, insurance). It fires most strongly after verbs like "seek", "claim", "sued for" or "in damages". There is weaker activation on related words such as "compensation", "award" and "reparations".

4199.name: A diffuse, weak feature, densest in code. It fires on highly predictable tokens: second halves of split words (Hou-this, l-umin-osity, Countergl-omp), and identifiers, variables and arguments copied from earlier context (user.password_hash, message, average, InstallMode). It also fires on boilerplate continuations such as 'top of page' and 'Date of Birth:'.

42016.name: Terms for dimensionality and low-dimensional or layered geometry, mainly in physics and materials science: "-dimensional" after one, two or three, "2D" and "0D", layered, thin film, platelets, laminates, surfaces, planes and van der Waals materials. Activation is strongest for "two-dimensional crystals", "one dimensional" and "layered".

42034.name: A diffuse feature with no clear semantic content. It fires mostly on structural and formatting tokens, such as newlines, spaces, brackets, slashes, backslashes and punctuation. These usually sit inside markup, LaTeX, code, tables or garbled multilingual and symbol-heavy text, often at boundaries between segments. It also fires occasionally on ordinary function words like "of" or "in" in prose.

42044.name: The C/C++ preprocessor directive "#ifdef" (or "ifdef"), especially when it starts a line after includes or comments and introduces a conditional block such as __APPLE__, WINDOWS or __cplusplus. Other tokens show only weak, incidental activation.

42062.name: Predictable tokens inside recurring boilerplate and list structure. These include list item numbers at the start of a line (most often "3"), "Reply" after "Leave a" in blog comment footers, the "- You may freely distribute" line in repository license text, "and" in "distribution, and reproduction" from Creative Commons notices, and similar formulaic web or template text.

42068.name: Words in narratives about people relocating or traveling between places, such as migration, immigration, arrival, departure, refugees and settling somewhere. The strongest activations fall on movement verbs (came, moved, arrived, leave) and on the prepositions and time phrases attached to them (to, in, from, a year, ago).

42091.name: Highly predictable tokens inside formulaic, templated or boilerplate text, mostly the next expected element of a conventional sequence. Typical cases are the "PATCH" tag in bracketed mailing-list subject lines, field names in CSV headers or allowed-HTML tag lists, RIS citation tags (TI), and fdisk output such as "minimum/optimal". Weaker activations fall on list and enumeration punctuation and on set phrases.

42093.name: The subject of a new sentence or paragraph, usually just after a line break, and above all the main verb that follows it (is/are/has/had/would be/was established). Activation peaks at the transition from the subject noun phrase (often the final subword of a name or the head noun) to its verb or auxiliary.

42095.name: Word-piece tokens inside anatomical terms for joint and tissue linings, by far most strongly the "ov" (and "ial") in "synovial", "synovium" and "synovitis". Weaker hits fall on similar anatomical fragments such as "articular", "periosteum", "pleura", "intima" and "joint capsule". Scattered faint activations on function words and punctuation appear to be noise.

42128.name: Text about people being hired, cast, attached, or brought onto projects (especially films, art and entertainment), with the feature firing on the predicate and function words around who joined, was chosen for a role, or collaborated (e.g. "attached … to", "was given", "who would be best for the role", "teamed up with"). There is weaker activation on scattered punctuation and connectives in similar narrative contexts.

A diffuse feature firing in AI-assistant-style, markdown-formatted responses (code, problem statements, lists). It tends to fire on words about prerequisites, requirements or assignments, such as what is needed or installed, what applies to each case, or who is slated or gets to do something. It also fires on some structural tokens like headers.

42133.name: Arguments inside parentheses that follow a function, operator or space name in math notation, especially the domain or underlying set of a function space or measure (e.g. the X in L^2(X), the R^d in W^{2,2}(R^d), the G in π(G), the S in P(S)). The opening parenthesis together with the argument is marked. Activation is strongest for spaces such as L^p(...) and Sobolev spaces. It fires weakly on similar argument tokens in code and in ordinary prose.

42135.name: Fires most strongly on "BASIS" in the Apache License boilerplate phrase 'distributed on an "AS IS" BASIS'. Other activations are weak and scattered over function words, punctuation and filler tokens with no clear shared meaning.

42151.name: Word fragments in noisy or corrupted text, such as truncated, misspelled, hyphen-broken, or OCR-garbled words, and words split oddly across line breaks (e.g. 'n'+'ose', 'f'+'amiliar', 'devel-'/'op'). The feature fires on the subword piece where the normal word boundary is disrupted, often at the start of a line or a lost first letter.

4217.name: Diffuse, low-level activation with no clear semantic theme. It fires mostly mid-way through arbitrary character strings such as numbers in phone numbers, IDs, URLs, prices and codes, subword fragments of names and foreign words, and occasionally on function words or paragraph breaks. The strongest hits are numeric chunks inside codes or prices (e.g. "SM 1417", "$187."). Overall it reads as a generic token-continuation feature for unpredictable sequences.

Tokens in the middle of alphanumeric identifiers and codes such as model/part numbers, phone numbers, IDs, hashes, URLs, dates and timestamps, mostly digit chunks and letter fragments inside longer strings. There is also weak, scattered firing on ordinary words.

42185.name: Fires on the second word of stock multiword prepositional/adverbial phrases, i.e. the slot just after the preposition that predicts the fixed ending. Strongest on 'this' in 'in this case'; also 'that' in 'at that time', 'other' in 'in other words', 'case' in 'in the case of', 'recent' in 'in recent years', 'for' in 'for example', 'to' in 'according to'. Activations elsewhere are weak and scattered.

42198.name: Tokens right before a proper name (usually a person's surname), mostly the connector " and" between two surnames ("Simon and Doctorow", "Millican and Alexander"). Also commas, closing quotes, "says", "by", "under", and line breaks that come just before a name.

42203.name: Words in boilerplate calls to action and alternative-option phrasing ("you can also…", "alternatively", "or visit", "share with your friends", "submit … using", "click here to find out how to"). The activating tokens are mostly prepositions or determiners that introduce the means or channel (using, via, by, under, in accordance with). They also fire on the nouns or punctuation that end such instructional or site-navigation phrases.

42210.name: Mostly fires on "-items" completing the CSS property "align-items" in flexbox code. The other hits are weak and scattered, mid-word or mid-phrase continuations in garbled or unusual text.

42211.name: Speech attribution in journalistic or quoted text. It fires on speaker names, pronouns (he, she) and verbs like said, says, adds, told or noting that sit next to quotes. It also fires on the punctuation and sentence or paragraph boundaries around attributed statements, with the strongest response to the speaker name and the attribution verb.

42236.name: Mostly fires on fixed words inside website boilerplate and navigation, not in the article body. The strongest case is "doc" in PerlMonks' "Comment on ( #3333=superdoc: print w/ replies, xml ) Need Help" footer. Next is " comments" in DEV Community's "Top comments (N)" heading. It also hits other site chrome such as the "DEV Community" header, "Flag as Inappropriate", "Editor", "Ends:" and "Trefflista". Weaker activations land on scattered ordinary words in prose.

42269.name: The word "manifest" (including its split pieces like "man"+"ifest", capitalized "Manifest", and "Manifesto"/"Manifestation"). It fires most strongly on software and config senses such as manifest files, manifest.json and the Android Manifest, and more weakly on manifesto uses.

42272.name: The "async" keyword in code, especially as a method modifier in C# function declarations (after public/private/static/override, before Task), also in Python/Rust async defs and related coroutine markers; weak, scattered activations on unrelated tokens.

42303.name: Person names in scholarly contexts, mainly author bylines and citations in scientific papers. It fires on first names, surname fragments, initials and the separators between authors (commas, semicolons, "and", "et al.", affiliation superscripts, years). It is strongest at the start of author lists that follow a paper title.

42344.name: Predictable continuation tokens in formulaic text, strongest on "App" beginning "Appellee/Appellant" after a party name and comma in legal case captions (also "App. No."). Weaker on other fixed sequences like "consectetur" in Lorem ipsum, names in lists, and sentence breaks.

4236.name: A diffuse, weakly-activating feature with no clear semantic theme. It mostly fires on function words such as articles, prepositions and conjunctions ('a', 'the', 'of', 'and', 'for'), and on punctuation at phrase or line boundaries, where a new noun phrase or content segment is about to begin. It occasionally fires on word fragments too. The strongest isolated hit is 'buy' in 'where to buy'.

A diffuse, weakly activating pattern with no clear semantic theme. It mostly fires on function words such as prepositions ('for', 'as', 'of', 'with', 'in'), articles ('a', 'the'), conjunctions and punctuation (commas, periods, brackets). These usually sit just before the start of a new noun phrase or named entity, at phrase boundaries in ordinary web text. The strongest activations come at such transitions, for example 'for' before an object, ', a', ' (www', and 'and' in lists.

42378.name: Temporal or conditional subordinate clauses that describe a triggering experience or event (e.g. "when I heard", "the minute I left the theater", "after realizing", "once you think about it"). They set up the moment of perception, discovery or action that leads to a reaction or realization in the main clause. Activation is highest on the subject and the experiential verb (heard, seen, found, left, encountered).

42390.name: Separator punctuation inside citation identifiers such as DOIs, arXiv IDs, bibcodes and URLs, typically the dot, dash, slash, space or underscore between a volume or number and a following page or article number. It fires most strongly on the padding dots in ADS bibcodes (e.g. 'ApJ...499..810C'). Activation on ordinary words is weak.

42394.name: Transition points in web-scraped text, chiefly sentence-ending periods and double newlines that close website boilerplate (privacy-policy notices, keyboard-navigation hints, comment forms, "Related Posts") just before another boilerplate or foreign-language block begins. A few hits are other predictable fragments: "www" in a URL, a name suffix ("-bootstrap"), and the token right after "called".

42402.name: A diffuse, weakly activating feature that mostly fires on tokens inside or next to numeric and quantity expressions: number words and fractions (one, half, quarter, two, six, twenty), ordinal suffixes and words (nd, th, second), dates and weekdays (Friday, Wednesday, September of), units (pages) and comparisons (or lower, × the). It also fires on list or enumeration connectors (1, 2 or 4; x, y and z). The remaining activations are scattered punctuation and function words with no clear pattern.

Weak, diffuse feature on mostly low-content connector tokens (of, per, by, an, and, the, th) inside formulaic constructions, especially right after numbers or names in dates (“March of”, “27th of”), rates and prices (“$10 Per”, “$7.25 an hour”), measurements (“43 inches by”, “6-foot”) and lists. The token links one element to the next in a fairly predictable pattern.

42411.name: The ".exports" token in JavaScript "module.exports" statements, typically at the end of a file, with weaker activation on "export" in "export default" lines.

42422.name: Keywords that begin a new statement in code, mostly control-flow words like "if" (strongest, especially "if ("), plus "match", "for", "while" and "try", usually at the start of an indented line that follows an assignment. It fires weakly on other statement-initial tokens (print, log, #) and on sentence-initial words like "If" or "The" in prose.

42429.name: Mathematical property adjectives describing size or cardinality, especially "finite" and related terms (countably, finitely generated, finite-dimensional, compact, bounded, infinite, integer), used as qualifiers of sets, groups, spaces or numbers in technical writing.

Mathematical property adjectives describing size or boundedness, chiefly "finite"/"finitely" (strongest in "finitely generated"), plus "countable", "compact", "infinitely", "constant" and "linear", typically as predicates or modifiers of sets, groups, numbers and functions.

42433.name: The final segment of alphanumeric classification codes, mainly in academic and patent front matter (PACS, MSC/AMS, JEL, Int. Cl., OCIS). It marks the trailing digits or letters after the code's prefix, such as the 'b' in 85.60.Jb or the '10' in 47H10. Activation is strongest on PACS letter suffixes and MSC digit endings. It is weak on stray text tokens.

42441.name: The word "bargain" in all its forms (bargain, bargains, bargained, bargaining, including split tokens like "barg"/"arg"+"aining"), firing most strongly on "bargaining" in labor or negotiation contexts such as "collective bargaining". It also fires weakly on related trade terms like "barter" and on look-alike pieces ("barge", "Bhargava"), plus faint activations on paragraph breaks in website boilerplate such as "Leave a Reply".

42449.name: Words that name the ordinary, mortal or earthly realm, usually set against something higher, alien, supernatural or beyond. Typical hits are Earth/earthly, human (beings), our bodies, mundane, ordinary, reality and the present. Activation is strongest when humans or Earth are contrasted with aliens, the divine or paradise (e.g., "to human beings", "people of Earth", "earthly paradise", "this body is named").

Words that denote the mundane, mortal, earthly realm of human existence, often in implicit contrast to the divine, spiritual, supernatural or nonhuman: "humans", "mortal", "this life", "here", "our world", "our plane", "Earth", "material brain", "human construct". Activation is strongest where the word marks this-worldly human existence as opposed to something beyond it.

42451.name: Sentence boundaries inside memorized boilerplate legal and license text, peaking on the period and following space after "contributor license agreements" in the Apache license header (just before "See the NOTICE file"). Weaker activations appear at similar points in other stock phrases, such as the journal "page charges." disclaimer and other license wording.

42494.name: Tokens that complete a highly predictable, formulaic unit, such as the final word of boilerplate phrases ("Best regards", "properly cited", "Getty Images", "In conclusion", "standard output"), measurement units after numbers (lb, MB), and closing code, LaTeX or HTML elements. These often fall right before a line break or punctuation that ends the segment.

42517.name: First-person pronouns (mostly "we" and "our", also "I", "my", "us") that refer to the author or speaker's organization, research group, institution or court (for example, "we found" or "our lab"), especially after a clause boundary or a preposition. A few weaker hits are other self-referential tokens, such as "it" or "its" for a court or committee, or "have" after "We".

42542.name: Tokens in descriptive or biographical definitions that state an entity's role, occupation, or category, such as the head noun of a profession or role (player, footballer, actor, engineer, team, driver) and the words that follow it (played, for, known for, plays in). Activation is strongest for sports roles, especially "football-er" and "player".

42544.name: Footnote and citation markers, usually the number (most often "1") right after a sentence, word, or author name, written as superscripts, bracketed [1], parenthesized (1), or LaTeX ^{1}/\textsuperscript. Bracket and superscript wrappers and the space before an inline reference fire more weakly.

42547.name: The leading-zero hour digits of a UTC timezone offset that follows a timestamp's + or - sign (e.g. "-0400", "+08:00"). Activation is strongest for the four-digit RFC 2822 email-header style ("-0700", "-0500") and weaker for ISO 8601 "+08:00" forms. It fires faintly on other zero-leading digit chunks such as phone numbers and DOIs.

42553.name: Verbs and objects in calls to action naming the things users can do on a site or platform, especially community participation and contribution (share, comment, post, ask/answer, connect/interact with others, submit, add). They often appear as lists of options in website boilerplate, with the strongest activation on sharing and interacting phrases.

42576.name: Language about serving a period of confinement or punishment, chiefly prison or jail terms. The strongest signal is the verb "serving" plus the duration or "sentence" that follows it. Prison/jail nouns, release or discharge "from prison", and words for the length of a term or service period also fire. There is weak, scattered activation on unrelated function words.

42578.name: Names of parent/base classes or interfaces in class inheritance declarations (after "extends", ":", or inside Python class parentheses), strongest on "Base"-prefixed superclasses like BaseFragment, BaseValidator, ApiClientBase; weaker on related superclass calls and other type names in code.

42625.name: Head nouns naming a measured quantity (mostly income/salary, plus price, revenue, ratio, temperature), usually after a qualifier like per capita, average, base or yearly and directly before the reported value. Strongest on "per capita income".

42626.name: The dash that begins a command-line option or test operator in shell code (e.g. -f, -z, -e, -ne, -rf), firing most strongly on file/string test flags right after "if [" and on "!" negation. It also responds weakly to other conditional-check prefixes in code such as os.path, .is/is_, IsObject and empty() inside if statements.

42643.name: Vertical bar / pipe characters ("|", and similar box-drawing verticals like ⎢ or ║) used as separators or borders in tables, ASCII diagrams, comment boxes, matrices, and website navigation/metadata strips. Activation is strongest inside ASCII-art diagrams and grids with many aligned bars, and weaker for single inline separators.

42659.name: Separator tokens (usually newlines, spaces, or periods) at the boundary between consecutive items in a structured, enumerated sequence such as tables of contents, numbered lists, chapter and section numbers, catalog entries, and number runs. The token fires right after one item ends, often after a trailing number, and just before the next index or title begins. There are a few scattered prose activations that don't fit.

42660.name: The space token right after a reporter or journal abbreviation in a legal or academic citation (e.g. "N.Y.", "Colo.", "vol."), just before the volume or page number. Activation peaks inside court case citations.

42674.name: Words for rotating or sequential image displays, especially "carousel" (strongest in web/UI contexts like Owl Carousel), plus slider, slideshow, and gallery. Weaker activation on related senses such as merry-go-round, baggage carousels, and the coaching carousel, and faint unrelated hits elsewhere.

42678.name: The word "FLAGS"/"flags" for compiler or build options, strongest as an uppercase suffix in build variables like CFLAGS or CXXFLAGS. It fires weakly on similar argument or modifier suffixes such as "_args".

42680.name: Method or property names that come right after a dot or arrow in code, especially jQuery/DOM calls on selector results such as $('...').attr, .css, .each, .remove. A few weaker hits fall on numbers inside brackets and on spaces between price and duration in freelancer listings.

42723.name: The preposition "of" (sometimes "for") right after an institutional head noun such as Department, Ministry, Bureau, Institute, School or Secretary, in the formal name of an organization or office. Activation is strongest for US federal government departments (Department of Agriculture, Defense, Energy, Transportation). It is weakest in academic affiliation lines such as university departments.

The word "of" inside names of government bodies and institutions, especially right after "Department" or "Ministry" (also "Bureau", "Institute", "Society"), where activation is strongest for "Department of". Weaker hits fall on other function words that come just before a noun or name: "of" in ordinary phrases, "a", "an", "each", Python "import" and opening quote marks.

42725.name: Command letters inside SVG path data strings, especially the cubic Bézier curve command "C" that comes right after a coordinate. Other curve and line commands (Q, l) activate more weakly, as does a stray "C" outside a path.

Tokens that begin a new entry or type label in structured, list-like text. The strongest case is a ranked list restarting at "1" after item "5.". Other cases are NMR peak multiplicity codes (dd, dt), DNS record types (SOA), format codes (c3B), and boundary tokens before a new section or field.

42728.name: Tokens that come right after a person's name, mostly a surname, especially in citations and author bylines. Typical cases are "et" in "et al.", the commas and initials in author lists, and the year digits or reference brackets that follow. It also fires on whatever follows a name in prose or headers, such as appositive commas, titles (Jr., PhD, professor), separators (|, -, —), and verbs like "said" or "explains".

42729.name: Mostly fires on whitespace and indentation tokens at the start of lines, especially the spaces before bullets or numbered items in lists and the indent before code braces. It also fires on other structural tokens such as list and section numbers, HTML table tags and colons in key: value lines. There are scattered weak hits on mid-word subword pieces and ordinary words, so the pattern is diffuse rather than tied to meaning.

A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires on highly predictable structural or continuation tokens. The clearest case is leading whitespace or indentation before numbered or bulleted list items and in code. It also fires on code and URL boilerplate such as a language tag after ```, "https" and ".g" in e.g. Other triggers are mid-word fragments of names or terms that repeat earlier in the text, such as W in WBC and Leseda. Activations elsewhere on ordinary words are weak.

42742.name: Words inside quotations, famous sayings, aphorisms, poetry or literary prose, with the strongest activations on memorable, stylized or rhetorical phrasing (e.g. "the true scientific method is this", "Every heart has its secret sorrows"). Weak, scattered activations also appear on ordinary narrative or first-person text.

42754.name: Sentence- and segment-ending punctuation (mostly periods, also ?, commas, newlines) at clause/sentence boundaries, especially where web boilerplate, disclaimers, or promotional text finishes a statement and a new sentence or section begins.

42760.name: Mentions of messenger RNA, overwhelmingly the token " mRNA" (also "RNA"/"RN" after a split "m", and "messenger RNA"), mostly in molecular biology contexts about gene expression and transcript levels. Related nucleic-acid terms such as cDNA, DNA and transcript(s) fire weakly.

42767.name: The main verb or predicate, plus the words right after it, in titles, headings and questions, especially after "How to", "What is" or "Is it possible". It fires most strongly on action verbs that state the task or topic (filter, evaluate, replace, use, represent, administer).

42793.name: The words right after "even" (or a similar concessive or inclusive word like "though" or "including") that introduce the surprising or extreme case being emphasized. These are mostly prepositions, determiners and noun-phrase starts such as "even in the", "even amongst those" and "even the". Sometimes "even" itself is marked.

428.name: Tokens that begin with or contain the letter sequence "ab"/"AB" (e.g. abstract, abuse, ability, above, abounds, Abraham, Abass, sabre), strongest when "ab" starts the word. It also fires weakly on nearby a-initial words such as about, available, adoption and Africa.

42804.name: A diffuse feature that is strongest on smooth, formulaic, generic expository prose of the boilerplate, SEO or LLM-sounding kind. Typical sources are job ads ('strong understanding of…', 'track record of working'), tech marketing ('scalable and can quickly defend'), and bland biographies ('a force for good'). It fires across whole clichéd phrases and on the sentence-ending periods and line breaks within them. Elsewhere it gives only weak, scattered activations on punctuation, formatting and random tokens.

A diffuse, weakly-firing feature with no clear lexical trigger. It spreads across runs of ordinary function words, punctuation and repetitive tokens, often in garbled, synthetic-looking or repetitive text. It is strongest at sentence and clause boundaries: periods, paragraph breaks, and the transition words that start the next clause ("However", "Similarly", "but", "and").

42814.name: Scientific and academic research prose, especially framing language that motivates or summarizes a study: statements of knowledge gaps ("little is known", "not well understood", "we still lack an understanding of", "we do not currently know"), research aims ("to better constrain", "to provide a basis for assessing"), and findings or implications ("the findings provide", "this helps us better understand"). Activations peak on these phrases and on sentence boundaries (periods, newlines) where such framing begins.

42815.name: Immunology terms for antigen presentation, especially MHC / major histocompatibility complex ("HC" in MHC, "patibility", class I/II, molecules/complexes, HLA, CD1d) and "-presenting" in antigen-presenting cell. The verb "present" for peptides also counts. Activations elsewhere are weak noise.

42836.name: The merged punctuation token ";<" (a semicolon directly followed by an opening angle bracket), often arising from HTML entities such as "><" or " <" in garbled code or markup text. Weaker activation occurs on other symbol tokens nearby, such as a lone "<", " +", "+[" and ";"".

42873.name: Numeric tokens used as operands in arithmetic expressions, especially the second factor in a multiplication (conversion factors, multipliers, decimal digits after "0.") just before an equals sign or result; strongest on multiplier and conversion-factor digits in worked calculations.

42893.name: The "CURLOPT" constant prefix in PHP curl_setopt calls (e.g., CURLOPT_URL, CURLOPT_RETURNTRANSFER), which activates strongly. Elsewhere it gives only faint, scattered activation on unrelated tokens, mostly API constant fragments in code (e.g., Intent.EXTRA, SO_SNDTIMEO).

42913.name: Tokens in software testing contexts, firing most on test-runner machinery such as JUnit/PowerMock RunWith(PowerMockRunner.class), unittest.main(), 'test runner', 'Run Selected Tests' and mvn -Dtest. Elsewhere activation is weak and scattered over code, URL, path and document-formatting tokens.

42934.name: Numbers (sometimes letters) that serve as locators in citations and references, such as page, line, section, figure, equation or footnote numbers, usually inside parentheses after a quotation or after labels like "p.", "Line", "Fig." or "at". Activation is strongest for page numbers in parenthetical citations after quotes.
