Numbers used as page or reference locators in citations, mostly after "p.", "pp.", "page", inside parentheses after an author or year, or in index entries and number ranges. Occasional weaker hits land on other numeric values or on sentence-initial "However".

42950.name: An opening quotation mark or backtick (often with a leading space) that introduces a quoted name, term, title, UI label, command, or code identifier, usually right after a word like "the", "a", "click", or "called". Activation is highest when the quote encloses a technical or interface element such as a button, menu, tag, or keyword.

42955.name: Fires most strongly on ":image" in data URIs ("data:image/..."), and also on ";base" (as in base64) and on "-dialog" in HTML class names like "modal-dialog". These are web markup/embedded-resource tokens. Everything else is a faint, generic response to code fences, line breaks and function words.

42960.name: The subword token "Dul"/"dul" (and "ul" after D) beginning words like Dulbecco, Duluth, Dulles, dulcet, dulled, and Dulce. Activation is strongest on "Dulbecco" (including its "cco" piece) in cell-culture medium names. Scattered unrelated tokens fire only weakly.

42969.name: Separator or delimiter tokens (commas, colons, semicolons, opening quotes, slashes, pipes, and occasional function words) that sit at a boundary in formulaic, templated, or list-like text, right before the next item or field begins. Typical contexts are repeated unit-conversion phrases, metadata headers (Version:, Published:), URLs and itemized lists.

4299.name: The day-of-month number in a date, plus any ordinal suffix (th, nd) or a month name that follows it. Common formats include 'May 18, 2015', '28 Feb 2024' and numeric forms like 02/26/2019 or 26.01.2018. Activation is strongest when the day follows a written month name, especially one preceded by a weekday (e.g. 'Saturday, May 11'). It is weak for purely numeric dates, timestamps and non-date numbers.

43028.name: Tokens that end the fixed boilerplate or UI text of scraped web pages, such as "Jump to navigation, search", review/bid counts on freelance sites, "Need Help", "accept rate: %", "Google Scholar", timestamps, HAL IDs and ".com" in emails. They typically come right before a line break and the start of the page's actual content.

43030.name: Structural formatting tokens at line boundaries, mostly leading whitespace/indentation at the start of a line (often a dedent before a closing tag, bracket, brace or "End"), bullet or list markers (•, ·, numbered items) and line-ending tokens like ">⏎", ".⏎⏎" and ":⏎⏎" that come right before such lines. Activation is strongest on indentation preceding closing XML/code elements.

43037.name: Mostly fires on the "Answer" label right after the lettered options of a multiple-choice question, where the answer is about to be given. It fires more weakly at other transition points just before a key item is introduced: the break before a new question, a space or "$" before a math expression, and connectives like "However" or "This".

43064.name: The token right after a copula or assignment verb ("is", "are", "be", "=", "added", "kept") that begins a value, usually a lone space token placed just before a number. It appears mostly in math word problems and code where a variable or quantity is being given a specific value.

43070.name: Mostly fires on "Judge" in the author line of court opinions (e.g., "NAME, District Judge."), which opens the opinion text. Elsewhere it gives weak, scattered activations on commas that introduce participial clauses and other miscellaneous tokens.

43077.name: Demonstrative or referring pronouns (mostly "This", also "It", "These", "this") that open a descriptive sentence right after a heading, title, label, colon, or docstring start. They point back to the just-introduced item (file, method, section, article, term) in order to explain what it is or does. Activation is strongest in code comments and docstrings.

43090.name: Three-digit number tokens inside long digit strings that repeat the same chunk over and over. Activation is strongest for long runs of zeros ('000…'), moderate for other repeated digits (111, 333, 444), and weak for chunks recurring in periodic sequences (e.g., 678 in 1234567890 cycles) or repeated words.

43105.name: No clear semantic theme. It fires on single, mostly generic tokens in the middle of a phrase, often just after a word that opens a parenthetical, subordinate or purpose construction (e.g. "(as cast", "(due to a", "in order for the", "it may"). Some hits fall inside bracketed glosses, such as Japanese furigana readings, or in noisy, spam-like text.

43123.name: Punctuation, often followed by newlines, that ends a heading, salutation, or speaker label and comes right before the main body text begins. Typical cases are the colon/period after "Abstract", the comma/colon after "Dear Editor/Mr. X", and the colon after a speaker byline or judge's name. A few weak activations fall on scattered mid-sentence words.

43134.name: Fires on the subword "amin", most strongly as the word-initial piece " lamin" (laminate, laminated, laminar, laminations) in technical or materials contexts. It fires more weakly on "amin" inside other words, such as chemical names (acetaminophen, amino-, deaminase), foraminifera, and names like Jamin.

43159.name: The tag name "title" inside a closing </title> tag, mostly in HTML document heads. It fires most strongly when a normal <title>…</title> page title is being closed. It is weaker for XML book records or malformed markup, and only faint on unrelated punctuation and words.

43189.name: Attribution context for named people (often researchers or experts) in news and science writing. It fires on the words just after or around a name that describe the person's role, title, or affiliation: appositive commas, “who…”, “lead author/co-author of”, “professor”, “said/says”, “and his colleagues”, “at/of [institution]”. Activation peaks on the comma right after a name and on role words like “author” or “who” that start a description of the person's part in a study.

43257.name: Content words and connecting function words (prepositions, articles, of/in/on) inside dense technical or scientific prose, especially abstract-style descriptions of mechanisms, measurements, and processes (e.g., adsorption kinetics, electrical conduction, gene regulation). Activation is diffuse and spreads over noun phrases and the prepositional links between them, not over one particular word.

4326.name: Code import/include directives, especially tokens fused with or following a '#' (e.g. "#import", "#include", "#from", "#print"), as in C/Objective-C preprocessor lines or commented-out Python imports. Activation is strongest for "#import" at line starts. There are weak, scattered activations on ordinary prose words.

43277.name: Words about periodic or cyclical timing, strongest for biological clocks and circadian rhythms (e.g. 'circadian', 'body clock', 'sleep-wake cycle'). Weaker activations cover oscillations, seasonal and annual cycles, diurnal or pulsatile variation, migration and chronobiology, often on word fragments such as 'adian', 'al' or 'oscill'.

43281.name: Mainly the word "greater" in comparison questions ("which is greater", "is greater than"), plus related comparatives like "heavier"; also recurring boilerplate fragments such as "Satisfaction guar(anteed)", "EDITORIAL BOARD", and Korean "확인" (check/verify).

43310.name: Fires weakly and diffusely on tokens inside repetitive, formulaic, or low-information text. The strongest cases are HTML table cell tags (td/th and their closing brackets and newlines) and suffixes in spam-like gibberish prose (-ized, -ability, -atively). It also responds to repeated song-lyric phrases, dot leaders, LaTeX spacing runs, and lists of numbers or prices. In ordinary prose it picks up sentence-final periods and paragraph breaks where one section or topic ends and another begins.

43324.name: The word "input" (and variants like Input, _INPUT, inputs, <input) in code and prose, especially as a programming identifier or as the HTML input element. Weaker activation on related user-entry and form-control terms such as field, textbox, checkbox, radio buttons, LineEdit, edit/insert mode and Button.

43325.name: Names of software libraries, modules, packages, and their types or classes, mostly inside import/use/crate statements in code (e.g. pandas, pd, PIL, pathlib, serde_json, regex). It often fires on the later sub-token of a compound library name (bitarray, pybedtools, openpyxl) and sometimes on product or tool names mentioned in prose.

43335.name: The HTML "<meta" tag token, typically the first meta tag inside <head> (e.g. "<meta charset=..."). It fires most strongly right after <head> and more weakly on later meta tags. Activations on scattered punctuation in prose or math are negligible.

The HTML "<meta" tag opening token, especially the first meta tag in a document head right after <!DOCTYPE html>/<html>/<head> (e.g., <meta charset=...>). Other activations are weak and scattered (prepositions, list dashes, other tags).

43360.name: CSS references in HTML, firing most strongly on "/css" in the MIME type type="text/css" and on "stylesheet" in rel="stylesheet" link tags. Weak activations also occur on code boilerplate such as blank lines after Python imports.

43385.name: Later digit chunks inside long multi-token numbers (after a comma, decimal point, or a prior digit group), such as trailing digits, decimal places, "000" groups and continued Roman numerals, with occasional unit words or name suffixes that directly follow a number.

Trailing digit chunks (and separators) inside long multi-token numbers: the later/final tokens of large integers or precise decimals, typically in computed results, conversions, prices, and measurements, not the leading digits.

Trailing digit chunks inside long multi-digit numbers. These are the later tokens after the first chunk, as in computed results, conversions, sequences and IDs. Activation is strongest deep in very long numbers.

43388.name: Nouns that name a quantity or numeric value, mostly monetary: amount, sum, cost, price, total, figure, value, number (also Italian/Portuguese equivalents like Subtotale and Valor). They fire most strongly on "sum"/"amount" in financial contexts such as "a sum of money" or "principal amount", and weakly on physical quantities like weight, distance and force.

Nouns that stand for a quantity or numeric value, especially monetary ones: "amount"/"amounts" (strongest, e.g. "amount due", "total amount"), plus "sum", "total", "number", "balance", "cost", "principal", "funds", "distance" and "how much". They usually appear in math word problems, financial text or code, and are often preceded by modifiers such as "total", "loan" or "maximum".

43389.name: The token "loc" starting "loci"/"locus" in genetics contexts (strongest after "genomic", "trait", "polymorphic"), plus related genomic location nouns (regions, sites, genes, variants); weak firing on other "loc" words (locates, locusts) and stray tokens.

43395.name: Methods-section language in scientific papers and abstracts. It fires on the transition into describing study design, participants, materials and procedures, such as "Methods", "Patients were investigated by", "N = 121", "was assessed via", "were available", and "is obtained by". It also catches sentence boundaries and section headers (INTRODUCTION, METHODS, Materials and Methods) that lead into these descriptions. Activation is strongest at the start of methodological statements about subjects, data sources and procedures.

4340.name: The word "In" (sometimes with a following "the"/"a") at the start of a sentence or paragraph, opening an introductory prepositional or transitional phrase such as "In fact", "In this case", "In a paper". It activates most strongly right after a period or line break. Lowercase mid-sentence "in" and other sentence openers like "After" activate only weakly.

43402.name: Comment and annotation markers that open an explanatory note, chiefly code-comment delimiters (#, //, ###, /*) at the start of a comment line, especially one that continues a multi-line comment. It also fires weakly on analogous line-leading markers in prose and markdown such as bullets (-, *, •) and bold headers (**).

43405.name: The ".http" package segment in code paths, especially Java imports of javax.servlet.http (strongest), plus org.springframework.http, django.http and req.http in VCL. Other package segments (.entity, .core) and miscellaneous tokens like list-bullet spaces fire only weakly.

43406.name: Tokens within formulaic, auto-generated web-page boilerplate such as metadata labels, listing and catalog fields, unit-converter phrasing, tutor-site templates, citation codes and URL paths. The marked token usually sits at a fixed template slot, often just before a variable value like a number, date, name or category.

43413.name: Personal names, chiefly the first names or first name/surname fragments of people (especially female names like Lisa, Emily, -isa), often in bylines, author lists, or credits; also occasionally proper-noun or taxonomic name fragments (Pis-, Mayo).

43423.name: Sports narrative about player and game performance, strongest in baseball and cricket recaps and stat descriptions (e.g., 'went 2-for-4', 'reaches base on a hit, walk', 'one batter after another'). It fires on the connective and function words, player names and verbs describing the action. Weak scattered activations appear on similar play-by-play text in other domains such as poker, casino games and card rules.

Sports play-by-play and game-recap narration, strongest in baseball. It fires on the function words and connective tokens that carry the action forward: prepositions, articles, commas, periods and phrases like "started with a", "after a single by", "hits a … to center field". It also lights up on numbers in stat lines such as "with 35 walks and 10 … in 61 games". Activation is highest in dense sequences of plays, and weak on isolated tokens in general sports text.

43442.name: The verb or auxiliary that comes right after a subject noun phrase, most often 'is' or 'are' and also 'has', 'have', 'will', 'can' or 'be'. The subject is usually an abstract information noun such as data, information, content, text, values or steps, and the verb often begins a passive or status statement (e.g. 'data is obtained', 'information is intended').

43444.name: Double newline that comes right after a blog or article header line, such as a date (strongest for full weekday-plus-date lines like "Monday, 21 November 2016"), an author name, or a read time, just before the post title or body begins.

The double newline right after a date line heading a blog post (e.g., "Monday, 29 June 2009"), marking where the post title or body begins. It fires most strongly on day-month-year (British-style) dates and dates at the very start of the text, and less on US-style dates following "Pages".

43447.name: A diffuse, low-specificity feature with no clear single theme. Its strongest and most consistent trigger is file-extension tokens (.html, .txt) that complete URLs or filenames. It also fires on closing punctuation such as ')' and '>' that ends a bracket or HTML tag. Beyond that, it picks up scattered function words and verbs ('find', 'play', 'avoid', 'between', 'while', 'containing'), often in web, technical or promotional text.

43452.name: Version numbers and hyphenated variant parts that follow a license or standard name, especially in Creative Commons (CC BY-…-SA 2.0/3.0/4.0) and BSD license strings. The strongest response is to the clause or version part right after "BSD" ("3-Clause", "-3"). Weaker responses go to the hyphens and "-B" in CC-BY and to version digits after names like HTML or RSS.

43462.name: Separators (spaces, commas, minus signs) between numeric coordinates in SVG path data and similar number sequences (bezier curves, cubic-bezier args). Strongest on the space between two numbers in path strings, and weak on unrelated filler tokens.

43463.name: Punctuation and delimiters that close a label or prompt and come just before a value is inserted, mostly in code: colons, equals signs and closing quotes at the end of strings passed to print/cout/log calls (e.g. "Name: " + x, "answer = "), plus label-ending tags, newlines and similar marks in prose and markup.

43474.name: Mostly fires on a short variable or register prefix letter (r, R, v, x, p, d, s, a, $) that comes right before an index number, as in R1, v3, r2, x4 or $v. It is strongest on register names in assembly-like or code lists. Weaker, scattered activations appear on other tokens in code, math and structured text.

43477.name: The ".ui" token, mainly as a package segment in Java/Python import paths (e.g. org.springframework.ui, selenium.webdriver.support.ui, com.app.ui) and also inside URLs or emails such as .uiuc.edu, .uiowa.edu and are.ui.ac.ir. It fires most strongly on code imports. The occasional weak hits on ordinary prose tokens are noise.

43478.name: Punctuation and tokens that sit inside academic citations and references, typically right after an author name and before the year or title. Common cases are the opening parenthesis before a year ("et al (2010)", "Smith (1998)"), the comma after an author's name, "et al.", "pp"/"page" markers, and bracketed reference numbers. Weaker activations come from similar delimiters in math/LaTeX notation and other reference-like structures.

43501.name: Font specifications in web/CSS code, especially the family and weight parameters in Google Fonts URLs (e.g. "Roboto:wght@300;400;700"). Activation is strongest on numeric font-weight values (400, 500, 700) and their separators, and weaker on CSS font-weight values and font style names like "Regular".

43512.name: Opening tokens of code attributes, annotations and decorators, such as Rust #[ / #![, Java/TypeScript/Python @ and C# [. Activation is strongest when the annotation follows another annotation or a declaration and comes right before a struct, class or function. Commas inside derive lists show weak activation.

The "@" symbol starting a decorator or annotation line in code (Python decorators like @lru_cache and @dataclass, Java/Scala annotations, BibTeX entries). It fires most strongly at the start of a line just before a def or class. Other line-initial code punctuation activates it weakly.

43518.name: Separators and leading fragments inside structured identifiers and timestamps, especially dates, IDs and URL numbers that repeat or closely mirror a value seen just before. Typical hits are hyphens, slashes, spaces, month names and the first digit chunk right before the repeated part, as in updated dates, HAL IDs, NPR embed IDs and ISO datetimes.

43526.name: The "-align" token in CSS alignment properties, almost always "text-align" (occasionally "vertical-align"), in stylesheets and inline style attributes. It fires most strongly inside inline HTML style="..." strings. A few unrelated tokens show weak activations.

43538.name: The "<?" token that opens a PHP code block ("<?php"), firing most strongly at the start of a line after a code fence or heading. It fires weakly on "<?" in XML declarations and garbled text, and faintly on unrelated tokens like punctuation and indentation.

43544.name: A diffuse, low-semantic feature with no clear topic. It fires mostly on tokens at structural or segment boundaries: words opening a new sentence or clause ('Like', 'Since', 'the', 'and'), list bullets, indentation whitespace, line breaks, and the spaces before numbers. Its strongest activation is on arbitrary fragments inside IDs or URLs (e.g., '802', 'j').

43560.name: Markdown horizontal rule separators ("---" plus newlines) in assistant-style responses, placed after an introductory paragraph and right before a new section heading (## / ###). Weaker activation on other paragraph breaks or section-boundary tokens (".⏎⏎", LaTeX \section, blank lines) that likewise mark a transition into a new section.

43562.name: The leading-zero number chunk "021" (also "022", "001", "016", "018") at the start of a longer number. It fires most strongly when it begins a Boston/Cambridge, Massachusetts ZIP code after "MA" or "Massachusetts", peaking on the FSF license address (Boston, MA 02110/02111). It fires weakly in other IDs such as phone prefixes, DOIs, HAL IDs and patent numbers.

43576.name: Separators between items in a list, especially the semicolons, commas, "and" and closing parentheses right after a year in academic in-text citations (e.g., "Smith 1986; Jones 1990"). The final digit of the year just before the separator also fires. Weaker activation on delimiters in other enumerations such as numeric lists, classification codes and dates.

43580.name: Words about visual outlooks and scenery, strongest on "view(s)" (especially "view(s) of" for a vista from a place) and on scenic modifiers or verbs of looking out such as panoramic, spectacular, breathtaking, landscapes, backdrop, overlooking and looking over or down upon.

43617.name: Mostly Java/Spring-style code, especially dependency-injection and configuration such as @Bean(name="...") definitions, Factory/FactoryBean classes, org.springframework imports and annotations. The strongest firing is on the quoted bean name and the method signature that follows a @Bean annotation. Weak, scattered activations also appear on other config or code syntax and on random prose tokens.

43626.name: Words tied to monitoring, surveillance and data collection, such as dashboards, sensors, telemetry, checks, warnings, status tracking, control panels and data sources. It fires most strongly on nouns and verbs for observing or measuring a system's state and reporting it.

43640.name: Tokens that open a string literal in code, i.e. opening quote marks often fused with a call paren or prefix: (", (f, $", !(" in Rust macros, """ / ''' / backtick template openers. Strongest on interpolated/format strings and multiline string starts; weak on other opening delimiters like backticks or quotes in prose.

43667.name: The "par"/"epar" subword token inside the word heparin and related terms (heparan, heparanase, heparinized), especially following "he"/"H". It fires weakly on "par" in other words such as names (Caspari, Korpar).

43683.name: Tokens spelling "it" in any form. Mostly the pronoun "it"/"It" (subject, object, expletive/dummy uses like "it is", "it turns out", "what it means"), but also case and orthographic variants such as "IT", ".it", "its", and "itch".

The word "it" (and variants such as "It", "its", and misused "it's"), most strongly when it opens a sentence or paragraph as a subject, often a dummy or expletive subject ("It's...", "It is said"). It also fires weakly on "IT" in the sense of Information Technology.

43686.name: Citation and reference numbers in academic or technical text, most often the digit inside brackets or parentheses such as [3], (18) or \cite{7}, plus figure and reference labels and the final digit of citation years. It also fires weakly on scattered tokens unrelated to citations.

43710.name: Adjective-forming suffix tokens that complete drug-class or therapeutic words, mostly after an "anti-" prefix, especially "iral" in antiviral/antiretroviral (strongest, typically before words like therapy, drug or activity). Weaker cases include -ptic (antiepileptic), -arial, -mic, -acterial, -pressive and -ian. Occasional weak hits on HTML "<td" table tags.

43727.name: Words for kinds or subtypes within a group, mostly of plants, animals, or microbes: variety/varieties, breeds, strains, cultivars ('cv.', 'var.'), species, variants, hybrids, models, types, grades. It also fires on 'cultiv-' (cultivate, cultivation, cultivators) and other horticulture or breeding terms. Weak, scattered activations appear on list-like or category nouns and on paragraph breaks.

43736.name: Vocabulary of the American football pass rush and defensive pressure on the quarterback: sacks (strongest), blitz, pass rush, tackles for loss, defensive end, EDGE, linebacker, and names of pass rushers. It also fires weakly on 'sacked' in the sense of a city being plundered, with faint scattered activations on unrelated function words.

43764.name: Given names of real people, and the subword pieces that spell them, appearing in lists of names, signatures, contact or staff listings, and credits. It fires on the first-name tokens that come right before a surname. A few weaker hits land on unrelated tokens.

43777.name: Words tied to randomness and random generation, mostly "random" in its many forms (random, randomly, randomized, pseudo-random, Random) and especially in code (rand::Rng, random.random, tf.random_uniform, import random). Related concepts also fire weakly: uniform distributions, sampling "from" a distribution, generators, fair dice and passwords. The "np" in "import numpy as np" activates as well, apparently as part of random-number code contexts.

43817.name: The closing bracket plus newline right after the opening tag of a structured block, usually the ">\n" ending <table> or <thead> just before <tr>. Similar tokens fire after <ul> and after LaTeX \begin{itemize}/{table}/{tabular}. Weaker activations land on the whitespace before list items. The feature marks the start of a table or list body, where row or item content is expected next.

43826.name: Author bylines and biographical blurbs, typically at the end of an article. It fires most strongly on the words right after a person's name that introduce their role or credentials ("is a", "is the", "received his", "Senior Fellow", "contributing editor"). It also fires on the author names, contact or credit lines, and line breaks in these sections.

43835.name: The "for" keyword opening a loop in code, plus its opening tokens like "(" or "(int". It fires most strongly on a nested inner loop placed directly inside another loop. Weaker hits come from other iteration constructs: foreach, SelectMany, nested LaTeX sums and integrals, and "Loop over all" in prose.

43871.name: Weak, diffuse feature centered on formal name-and-title contexts such as academic signature blocks, author lists, approval pages and job descriptions. It fires on the punctuation and line breaks separating a person's name from credentials (", PhD", "Ph.D.⏎"), on affiliation markers, and on job titles or roles (professor, Director, Attorney, Editorial Board). Scattered activations elsewhere are faint.

43888.name: The word "pathogen(s)", usually split as "path" + "ogen"/"ogenic", with the noun "pathogens" firing strongest. It responds weakly to related harmful-agent words such as infectious agents, pests, allergens, carcinogens and mutagens, and to other "-ogen" endings like adaptogen. The few weak hits on table-of-contents dot leaders and stray numbers look like noise.

43904.name: The word "argument" and near-synonyms (parameter, operand, premise, object, arg), most strongly as the input value passed to a function or command in programming. Weaker activation on other senses, such as mathematical arguments, logical premises/assumptions and grammatical objects.

43911.name: Separators that follow a parameter, field or variable name and introduce its type or description, mostly in code docstrings and API docs. Typical forms are "name : type", "param:", "x -", "# comment", "// comment" and an opening parenthesis. The strongest activations are on the colon after argument names in docstring Parameters/Args sections; the argument name and type tokens around it activate more weakly. Weak activations also appear on punctuation that starts an explanatory clause in prose.

4394.name: Fires in news and article prose on markers of sourcing and discourse structure. The strongest hits are attribution phrases naming where information comes from: "Business Insider reports that", "Via BleepingComputer", "The Sun reported", "according to", "as per", "said", "news release", "NSA's guidance". It also fires on sentence-final punctuation followed by a paragraph break (".⏎⏎") at transitions between paragraphs or sections.

Discourse boundaries and source/attribution markers in news and blog text: paragraph breaks after headlines or sentence ends, closing punctuation of quotes, and phrases that cite or point to a source or the article itself (e.g. wire-service credits, 'reported', 'appeared at', 'Read more', 'Story continues below', 'read the rest of her post', publisher and edition info). Activations are generally weak and diffuse.

43952.name: Words inside fixed, formulaic multiword expressions and discourse connectives (e.g. 'as a result of', 'with regards to', 'similar to', 'in fact', 'in addition', 'despite the fact that', 'keep track of', 'pertaining to', 'ought to', 'Nonetheless/Moreover/However'), especially where the next token is a highly predictable preposition or function word ('of', 'to', 'from', ','). Common in boilerplate or spun web prose. Weak activations also appear on predictable formatting fragments (e.g. 'superscript', table tags).

Tokens that open a fixed, highly predictable multi-token expression, mostly transition words and set phrases. Common cases are sentence-initial "However" and the first character of 然后 ("then"). Others are the key word in phrases like "by means of", "with regard to", "in addition to", "along with", "taking into account", "allow you to", "which sort of" and "the free encyclopedia", plus mid-word pieces in Vietnamese (hoặc, lớn). These often appear in noisy, mixed-language or code-like text.

43955.name: The ".annotation" package segment in Java import statements (e.g. org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation, javax.servlet.annotation, androidx.annotation), and occasionally similar namespace segments like PHP "\Annotation". Activation is strongest in Spring and javax imports. Unrelated tokens such as table-of-contents dot leaders fire only very weakly.

43959.name: The Android method name "setContentView" (or its "ContentView" piece) in Java Activity code, typically called right after super.onCreate(savedInstanceState) to set the layout via R.layout. Other weak activations are scattered and uninformative.

4397.name: A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no clear single concept. It activates sporadically on many token types: numbers and items in comma-separated lists, math operators and LaTeX symbols, punctuation, and citation brackets. It fires most strongly on hard-to-predict or surprising content, such as citation markers like "[6", nonsensical word salad, and incongruous lists of unrelated nouns.

Weak, diffuse activations in incoherent, word-salad or garbled machine-generated text. It tends to fire at points where coherence breaks down, most often on sentence-ending periods and the tokens just after them, and on nonsensical noun phrases or numbers. It does not track any specific word meaning.

43997.name: Narrative prose summarizing fictional characters' backstories and plots, as in wiki or fandom character biographies (e.g., 'X was a lab assistant to...', 'Blaze decided to travel there'). Activation is spread across the running text, mostly function words, character names, verbs and clause boundaries, and is strongest at the start of a new biography section or sentence about a character.

440.name: Separators within lists, enumerations and sequences of parallel items: commas, "and", periods, newlines, bullet dashes and pipes that sit between consecutive list elements, clauses or entries. Activation is strongest in long repetitive enumerations such as number lists, bulleted instructions and constructor initializer lists.

44003.name: Indentation whitespace, line breaks, and closing comment/annotation tokens (e.g. "*/" plus newline) right before a class member declaration in code, chiefly access modifiers like private/protected/public on fields. Activation is strongest on a doc-comment close followed by the modifier. There are weak, sporadic hits on stray spaces or tokens in prose and HTML.

4402.name: Citation and reference markers: numeric tokens inside brackets/parentheses/superscripts referring to sources (e.g., [10], (29), [1]), plus final digits of years in author-year citations. Strongest on standalone bracketed reference numbers; weaker on other trailing numbers, IDs, and page markers.

44023.name: Identifier names right after a CSS class or selector dot (e.g. ".post", ".form-control", ".data-pdf"), most often in querySelector, jQuery, classList or stylesheet code. The first word of a hyphenated class name is especially marked. Weaker activations land on similar name components inside other code identifiers and occasional prose nouns.

44031.name: In scientific and experimental writing, the head noun of the biological or material subject being studied or acted on. Strongest on "cells" (including named cell lines like Vero cells, RAW 264.7, CAFs, DCs), and also fires on proteins, enzymes, polymers, organisms such as mice or chickens, extracts and films. It often marks the final token of the term, typically after modifiers like "cultured", "infected" or "blended".

44040.name: A diffuse, weak feature for structured informational, guide-like text such as travel itineraries, tour descriptions, event agendas and schedules, and step-by-step instructions. It fires most strongly inside day-by-day itinerary entries (e.g. "Day 1: New Delhi … Morning Visit: It will"). Weaker activations land on list or step markers ("1.", "First", "Then"), agenda or table cells ("Registration", "Panel Discussion"), and promotional travel or experience phrasing ("expedition visits", "options available for a journey").

44050.name: In code, the name of a configuration, options or argument container object (config, settings, params, args, kwargs, options, cfg, props) used just before a member access, key lookup or .get() call to pull out a specific field. The bracket or quote opening that lookup also fires (e.g. .get(', ["). Weak firing occurs on prose that refers to an option or parameter by name.

44053.name: Connective tokens ("that" in "is that", colons, commas, periods, bullets, "because") right after a phrase introducing a drawback, limitation or problem ("the downside is", "disadvantages:", "unfortunately,", "however,"), at the point where the specific negative point is about to be stated. Weaker on similar slots before lists of features or other explanations.

Function words and punctuation (mostly "that", "is", "because", commas, colons, periods) at the point right after a statement introducing a problem, drawback, flaw, limitation or concern, just before the clause explaining what it is (e.g. "the problem is that…", "one drawback is that…", "has a fatal flaw:").

4406.name: Weak, diffuse activation on the start of a noun phrase serving as the object or complement of a preceding preposition or verb. Typical governing words are 'to', 'with', 'by', 'from', 'of', 'through', 'beyond', 'around' and 'meet'. Activation covers determiners and demonstratives ('the', 'this', 'that', 'its'), pronouns and the head noun or name, as in 'to the show', 'beyond this world', 'of the Danube River' and 'by Kathleen'. It is strongest right after the governing word and fades across the rest of the phrase.

44064.name: Physics measurement terminology, especially particle and nuclear physics: measured quantities and kinematic variables (transverse momentum p_T, azimuthal modulation, muon yields, angular distributions, coincidence detection of electrons and ions, emitted particles, spectra). Activation is strongest on these experimental-physics phrases and weak or scattered on other technical nouns.

44066.name: The predicate or evaluative word that comments on a preceding subject or topic, typically right after it or after 'is/was'. It fires most strongly on passive participles saying a situation is complicated, hampered, fuelled or obscured, often followed by 'by'. It also fires on intensifying or additive transitions such as 'Adding to the drama', 'further' and 'even gloomier'. Most other hits are weak, on ordinary copulas and adjectives like 'is', 'consistent' and 'noteworthy'.

44070.name: Fires at the boundary right after a named term, variable, label, heading or function signature, on the token that introduces its definition, value or body (e.g. " =", ":", " {" + newline, "is equal", " if", a closing quote-period, or a line break after a header). It marks the transition from the thing being defined to its content, in both code and prose.

44074.name:
Line-ending punctuation and whitespace in source code, mostly the closing token of a statement or header (e.g. ">
" after #include <x.h>, ";

" after import lines, ")
" after calls) and the indentation that follows. It fires most strongly on preprocessor include and import lines. Weak activations also land on scattered separators in prose.

44098.name: Tokens on the right-hand side of an equation or assignment, after the '=' sign, especially binary operators (+, −, –, %, mod) and the first term or digit of the expression (leading digits of decimals, \frac, \sqrt, e^{, ln). A weak, sporadic version also fires on continuation words in non-math text (e.g. 'online' in spam, 'flight', 'fewer').

Tokens inside mathematical expressions, equations and word problems, especially binary operators (+, -, minus, times) right after an operand, along with numeric values after '=' or 'is' and closing parentheses. They mark the point where a formula or calculation continues with its next term.

44117.name: In academic paper author lists, the token right after an author's name that starts the affiliation marker: LaTeX superscript openers ("cript{", "(^{", "^"), opening parentheses, spaces, asterisks, or commas just before affiliation numbers/letters. Plain Unicode superscript digits and symbols (¹, †, ‡) get little or no activation.

44124.name: Mainly fires on the word "LICENSE" in file names and URL paths (e.g. /blob/master/LICENSE.txt, apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0, "file": "LICENSE"). Everything else gets only weak, scattered activation on common function words.

44125.name: Fires on "LICENSE" in the standard source-code license header phrase "found in the LICENSE file". Elsewhere it fires only weakly on words just after a preposition or determiner ("in", "with", "the") that start a noun phrase.

44128.name: Trailing or middle digit chunks inside long identifier strings such as IDs, URLs, hashes, DOIs and HAL/project numbers. It fires on the later sub-tokens of an ID once several digits have already appeared. Activation is strongest deep inside very long numeric IDs, like blogger IDs.

44137.name: Superlative or extremum words (smallest, largest, maximum, highest, least, greatest, first), usually right after "the" in math or programming tasks that ask to find an extreme value. Activation is strongest for "smallest" and "largest" in questions like "which is the smallest".

44156.name: Package‑name segments in code import paths, especially Java imports: strongest on Spring's ".stereotype" (preceding Service/Component/Controller/Repository), with weaker activation on other library namespaces such as lombok, butterknife, github.com/stretchr, ".RestController", and ".Spring". Rare, faint activations appear in unrelated prose.

44166.name: The backslash-u token that begins a Unicode escape sequence (\uXXXX), e.g. \u200b or \u00b7, in code, regexes, JSON or garbled text. It fires most strongly on the combined "\u" token and weakly when the "u" or "uf" is split off after a separate backslash.

44189.name: Words and word pieces denoting disability, impairment or incapacitation: physical or sensory disabilities (wheelchair, paraplegia, mute, blind, crippled, palsy, hobbling), debilitating illness or states (coma, vegetative state, polio) and helplessness. Mobility-related terms, especially "wheelchair", activate most strongly. Puns or other senses of the same words, such as handicap bets, also trigger it.

Words denoting physical disability, impairment, or incapacity (e.g., crippled, handicapped, paralyzed, disabled, impaired, lame, helpless, coma, wheelchair, crutch), including literal medical uses and figurative senses of being rendered powerless or immobile; strongest on 'cripple', 'paralyzed', 'handicapped', and 'wheelchair'.

44195.name: The words "See" and "the" in cross-reference phrases ("See the…") that send the reader to another file, page, link or document. The phrase often sits in boilerplate such as licenses, copyright notices and citation notes. It is by far strongest in the Apache license header "contributor license agreements. See the NOTICE file".

44201.name: The token "fff" (also "ffffff"/"FFF"), firing most strongly when it is a hex color code right after "#" in CSS or styling code, typically white (#fff) for color or background. It fires weakly on "fff" strings in non-color or garbled contexts.

44227.name: The "li" in HTML list-item tags (<li>), firing most strongly on the first item right after an opening <ul> or <ol>, and more weakly on later items. It also fires on similar list-item markers like LaTeX \item and escaped <li>, with faint activity on scattered unrelated tokens.

44229.name: Diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires on tokens in repeated or boilerplate text, where the continuation copies material seen earlier. Typical cases are image captions or filenames that restate a preceding title (e.g. 'runtime verification 3', 'led solar lantern 2'), URL and ID fragments that repeat earlier numbers or names, repeated headings, and stock phrases like 'Part of the ... Commons'. Hits also occur on scattered ordinary function words and punctuation.

44236.name: The token "doctype" (and variants like "CTYPE"), especially in the HTML declaration "<!doctype html>", with the strongest response there. Weaker activation appears on other code or markup keywords like "SET NAMES" and on scattered tokens in code, numbers or technical text.

44263.name: Words tied to sewing and needlework: sew/sewn/sewing (strongest), stitch, seam, embroidery, garment, tailor and patch. It also fires on figurative uses ('stitch up deals', 'sew up urban parts'), look-alikes such as sewer and Sears, and nearby crafts and fasteners like buttons, zippers and woodworking.

44276.name: Evaluative commentary on a person's or thing's qualities, especially reviews praising performers or creators (acting, performances, roles, skill), most active in praise like 'strong performances by its talented cast' or 'handled the vocal duties well', often on the verbs, appositive clauses ('who also starred') and punctuation that link a named person to the assessment.

44300.name: The leading segment (first digits or letter prefix) of formal classification or reference codes in academic, patent and grant metadata. Examples include MSC/AMS subject classes like 65M22, PACS numbers like 78.67.De, JEL codes like C100, patent Int. Cl. codes like G06F, EC numbers, and contract or grant numbers. Activation is strongest for the leading digits of math subject classification codes.

44306.name: Programming code, especially string-searching and slicing logic that locates substrings (find/indexOf/substring) and computes offsets with lengths. It peaks on statement endings like ');⏎' and ')⏎', the assignments that follow them, and the index variables. Elsewhere in code and prose it fires only weakly on punctuation, line ends and loop or operator tokens.

44312.name: Leading indentation (tab or spaces, sometimes with the opening quote) at the start of a line inside a Go import block, especially right after a third-party package path like "github.com/...". Activation is strongest when the next import is also a github.com path. Scattered weak activations on unrelated prose tokens are noise.

44327.name: Fires most strongly on long runs of repeated hex 'f'/'F' characters (e.g. 'ffffffff', 'FFFFFFFF', 0xFFFF… max-value constants). Elsewhere it gives only weak, scattered activations on common function tokens such as 'e.g.,', 'the' and punctuation.

44337.name: Command-line flags and setup directives at the top of shell/Perl scripts. It fires most strongly on the option letters in shell 'set -e' / 'set -x' / 'set -o' and somewhat less on shebang flags like 'perl -w' and 'sh -x'. Weaker activation appears on related script preamble boilerplate such as 'use strict', PHP 'declare(strict_types)', SQL SET @ variables and echo/exit lines.

44348.name: Numeric constants and conversion factors, mostly in code or math: magic numbers for units, time, and size such as 1024, 1000, 60, 24, 86400, 8 bits, and powers of ten. The final digits of these numbers fire most strongly, as do the operators (*, /) that combine them. The strongest example is a size product like 1024 * 1024.

Numeric literals and their trailing digit tokens in code and math, especially conventional constants such as powers of two (1024, 8192, 16), time and unit conversions (60, 365/366, 1000, 360), and zero-padding chunks of large numbers. The feature also fires on nearby arithmetic operators like *, / and == in numeric expressions, and is usually strongest on the last token that completes a familiar number.

44410.name: No single semantic theme. The marked tokens are mostly highly predictable continuations of a fixed phrase, template or formatting convention. Examples include "Apart from", "Answer in units", "thread::spawn(move", "</copyright>", a parenthesis after a speaker name and a newline after a dateline. Many fire on the second or later piece of a split word or name, such as "Doub"ledRelic, Codem"anship" and Han "Yi".

44418.name: Diffuse feature centered on operators and structural tokens in math and code, mostly binary operators (especially minus, also plus, equals, ==, /, times) that join operands within an expression, plus delimiters such as colons after 'question', docstring indentation and separators. It fires on the token that links two parts of a formula or statement.

44429.name: Denominators in fractions and divisions, meaning the tokens right after a slash, "over", or inside the second brace of \frac{}{} in math, code and formulas (e.g. "1/N", "/n", "\frac{1}{r^n}"). Single variables, powers and constants in that position fire most strongly. There are occasional weak hits on 'per'-type units after a slash.

4443.name: Names of news outlets and media sources, firing on the final or distinguishing token of the publication's name (Times, Post, Globe, Tribune, Weekly, Variety, Reuters, AP, AFP, Media, Eurogamer). It also responds to generic media words (newspapers, press, radio) and source attribution contexts such as photo credits and 'told X'. Weak activations occur on website domain pieces and dateline line breaks.

Names of news outlets and publications, especially the final word of a newspaper title (Post, Times, Herald, Independent, Advocate, Globe), plus words like "newspaper" and "press". Activation peaks when the token completes a paper's name and the outlet is cited as a source ("told the New York Times", "the Washington Post"). Other media brands such as radio stations, magazines, journals and websites fire weakly.

44432.name: Stray symbol and operator tokens, mostly " =" (also ==, :, -, /, ~, _), that show up in garbled, nonsensical text mixing code fragments, multiple languages and random characters. They often sit at a line start or between unrelated words like a pseudo-assignment. The strongest activations are on lone "=" tokens after a line break or heading marker.

44437.name: Opening tokens of markup or code syntax at the start of a new element or line, usually after indentation: HTML/XML tag openers ("<", "><" before strong, "<tr"), LaTeX backslashes before commands like item, hline, centering or toprule, Rust "#[" attributes, and bracketed list markers. These fire mostly on structural delimiters that begin nested items in structured documents.

44438.name: Fires on the subword "ember" (and close variants such as "umber", "ober", "amber", "bers", "bars") as a piece inside words or names, e.g. Ember, dismember, November/September, Pemberi, and surnames like Kemberly. It is strongest when "ember" sits mid-word in an unusual or foreign name.

44454.name: The phrase "under the" (strongest on "under") that closes the standard Apache License boilerplate in source-code headers: "governing permissions and limitations under the License." The other weak activations are scattered, unrelated tokens.

44475.name: Tokens inside dense, low-predictability symbolic or non-prose sequences: numbers in lists/tables/arrays, code arguments, math subscripts, hex/byte strings, random hashes, URL encodings, mojibake and emoji/unusual-character runs. It responds most strongly to individual elements of repetitive structured data (digits, commas, separators) and to garbled or rare-script characters. It is only weakly active on ordinary prose.

44500.name: The ".impl" segment in Java package and import paths (e.g. com.x.service.impl, org.apache.http.impl.client), marking implementation subpackages. Activation is strongest in import statements and package declarations. The few weak hits elsewhere are scattered ordinary prose words or commas.

Single tokens in noisy, garbled, or incoherent text (word salad, code fragments, broken formatting), typically right after odd punctuation, symbols, or a split word, where the token continues or completes a fragment (e.g. 'htm'→'l', 'e.g'→'.,'). The feature seems to track unpredictable or corrupted-context positions rather than any specific meaning.

44506.name: The " org" token right after "import" in Java import statements (start of org.* package paths like org.springframework, org.apache), strongest in runs of consecutive org imports, especially near the end of the import block.

44528.name: Literal string values or search patterns, mostly in code or technical instructions: the content inside quotes or string literals (tags, keywords, file names, path fragments, displayed messages) being matched, compared, searched for, or printed, especially just after an opening quote or as a grep/startswith/replace target.

4453.name: Temporal prepositions and conjunctions that anchor a time relative to a reference event (since, after, following, once, upon, from, post-, when), strongest when marking time elapsed after an event (e.g. 'shortly after its arrival', 'years after his ouster').

Temporal prepositions and conjunctions that place something relative to a reference event, chiefly "after" and also "since", "upon", "following" and "within minutes of", together with the determiner, pronoun or auxiliary that follows them. Activation peaks on "after" when it comes right after a time expression such as "shortly", "long", "a week", "40 days", "months" or "immediately". Weaker activations land on other spatial or relational prepositions like "above", "of" and "from".

44546.name: The final digit of a hyphenated numeric code, mostly the 4-digit suffix of a ZIP+4 or Japanese postal code in an address (also ISSNs, phone numbers, resolutions). It is strongest on the FSF Boston address "02110-1301".

44547.name: Stem cell and embryology terminology in biology text. Strongest on "stem" in "stem cells" (embryonic, pluripotent, induced) and on the "SC" in iPSC/hiPSC, with weaker activity on "cell(s)" and on the "onic" of "embryonic". Faint activity on related lab terms such as cultured cells, -blasts, callus, cloning and nuclear transfer.

44565.name: Fires in journalistic or expository prose, mainly where a sentence's subject (a named person, organization or report) is introduced and then described. Activation peaks on the clause structure that attaches information to that subject: relative pronouns and auxiliaries ('who is working on', 'which functions as'), appositive commas, attribution verbs ('said that', 'says') and time framings ('Six years ago'). Isolated weak hits on scattered word pieces elsewhere are mostly noise.

Fires most strongly on “verified” in the boilerplate “Short Answer ⏎ Expert verified” that precedes homework-style answers. More weakly and diffusely, it picks up words and punctuation in statements that lend authority or credibility. These include attributions and sources (“according to human rights groups”, “said in an analysis”, “the organization tracking…”), official names and institutions, confirmations (“That's correct”) and official recognition. It also catches scattered list numbers and commas in confident, often fabricated-sounding expository text.

44572.name: The identifier suffix "_err" in code, firing hardest on Rust's ".map_err" error-conversion method and more weakly on other error-handling names (format_err, is_err, ok_or, AddFailure, $ev_err); scattered unrelated tokens show only faint activation.

44574.name: The closing token of fixed multi-word titles or role phrases, often legal, Latin or official, that follow a noun as a postpositive modifier (ambassador-at-large, mayor pro tem, party in interest, attorney-in-fact, court-appointed, in loco parentis, aide-de-camp). It also fires on "Joined" after a member-rank label in forum profile headers.

44576.name: The noun right after a verb or modifier in short UI/share-button boilerplate and technical noun compounds, strongest on "article" in "Share article via email". It also fires weakly on "link" in "Copy link" and on compound heads like "security updates" and "module development".

44597.name: Fires overwhelmingly on "NSObject", the Objective-C/Cocoa root class and protocol name, in programming documentation. Other tokens show only negligible activation.

44599.name: Names of GUI widget classes in code import statements, mostly the class token after android.widget (TextView strongest, then Button, EditText, Toast, ListView, ImageView) and javax.swing (JLabel, JPanel, JButton), plus similar UI components in other frameworks (kivy Label, gtk Label, JavaFX). Activation sometimes extends weakly to the following semicolon/newline.

446.name: The last word of a clause or sentence, typically the head noun (or adverb/adjective/verb) that completes a phrase immediately before a period, comma, or conjunction. It fires most strongly on sentence-final nouns that close a prepositional or object phrase (e.g. "environment", "society", "horizon", "time").

Phrase-final words that complete a noun phrase, clause or idiomatic unit, typically the head noun or closing word right before punctuation, a preposition or a new clause (e.g. "memory usage.", "further assistance.", "after the fact.", "get there,"). The pattern holds across prose, code comments and several languages. Activations are weak on fragments in repetitive or garbled text.

4460.name: The "bin" directory component in file paths, firing hardest on "/bin" and "/env" in shebang lines like "#!/usr/bin/env python" at the start of scripts. It is weaker on other bin paths (GOPATH/bin, cgi-bin, /sbin) and faint on nearby script-header tokens like "coding" and "import".

44647.name: Words that refer back to a prominent person, usually a leader, politician or other public figure such as a president, monarch, general or coach. They are mostly possessive pronouns and possessive 's (his, her, their, Trump's), subject pronouns and relative "who". Activation is strongest in political or governing contexts, such as a person's administration, government, campaign, reign or office.

44655.name: Tokens inside the titles of academic papers, articles and reports, especially in citations and reference lists. Activation is strongest in the body of the title right after the citation year '(2005).' and on connecting words like 'of', 'in', 'and', subtitle colons and descriptive nouns ('Comparison of', 'Systematic Review', ': a randomised double-blind').

44664.name: The word "burden", and to a lesser extent "proof", in the legal/argumentative phrase "burden of proof" and its synonyms (onus, responsibility, task) for who must prove or show something, usually after "the"/"bears the".

44665.name: Section headings and front-matter labels that open a document's main content after title or author info, such as Abstract, Contents/Table of Contents, Acknowledgements, Introduction, Chapter, Summary and Keywords. Activation is strongest on "Contents" and "Abstract".

44692.name: Words naming the anatomical or physical site or body part where something occurs or is located. These are mostly organs, tissues and body regions (heart, nose, soft tissues, carotid vessels), typically following "of/in/on the" in medical text. Weaker activations land on similar location-like or category nouns in other domains (spectrum regions, organisations, transit).

44695.name: Tokens made of underscores (e.g. "_", "___", "._", " __", "|_|"), which serve as blanks, separators or identifier prefixes. They usually sit in garbled, mixed-language or code-like text and often come right before an identifier or word.

44711.name: The number right after a hyphen or dash that closes a numeric range, and it is often abbreviated. Typical cases are the end page of a citation (e.g. 531-9, 208-14) and the end year of a span (1954-55, 1918-19). Activation is strongest for shortened end page numbers in journal references.

44712.name: Weak, diffuse activations within clauses stating a condition or attribute of a person that bears on their eligibility, impartiality or qualification, such as being disqualified, having a relationship with someone, holding personal knowledge, or having a conflict of interest. These appear mostly in legal or procedural text about jurors, judges, witnesses and donors. The strongest examples involve a juror being caught in a relationship or being disqualified from service.

44715.name: Method-call tokens attached to an object in code, especially ".use" in Express-style "app.use(...)" middleware registration (strongest). Other method calls that attach or register something (.add, .connect, .pipe, .apply, .run), along with useEffect and middleware, activate weakly.

44767.name: Zero digits (and similar placeholder values) repeated within structured sequences such as matrices, arrays, tuples, tables, and numeric lists, firing most on zeros that follow other zeros or repeated filler cells (e.g., "", "*", ".").

44771.name: Separator or formatting tokens (colons, dashes, spaces, newlines, HTML tags like <td>/>, "by", "{") that immediately come before a list of author or person names in bibliographic metadata, such as after "Author(s)", "Contributors", "AU -", or "posted by".

44787.name: Qualifiers in legal, licensing and payment terms that restrict or define rights and obligations, mainly the non-/ir- prefixes and -able endings in words like non-exclusive, non-refundable, non-transferable, irrevocable and NonCommercial. Also scope words such as exclusive, worldwide, absolute, lifetime and first lien. Strongest on "nonexclusive rights".

44812.name: Short symbol-cluster tokens that open template or code directives, chiefly "<%" (and the "%" right after "<"), plus similar punctuation combos like "#@", "*@", "}@", "//@" and "%@". These usually appear at the start of a line or document, often inside garbled, mixed-language or code-like text. Activation is strongest for a leading "<%" tag.

44815.name: Words derived from the root "calcul-" (calculate, calculation, calculated, calculator, calculus, calc), plus a few weaker hits on synonyms such as computation. They appear across math, science, code and everyday contexts, and fire most strongly on verb and noun forms meaning to compute something.

44821.name: Fires on tokens inside garbled, low-predictability or foreign-script text: Lorem-ipsum Latin fragments (eu, incididunt, justo, -ibus), subword pieces of non-English words (Somali, Kyrgyz, Xhosa, Yoruba, Vietnamese, Pashto), rare CJK/Arabic glyphs, base64 strings, and nonsense code. A weaker recurring case is "Two" opening a quoted NLI premise.

44852.name: The closing ">" plus newline token ending an HTML table section opening tag (mostly "<tbody>", sometimes "<thead>"), right before the first "<tr>" row. It also fires weakly on a few unrelated prose tokens (a period ending a sentence, "up").

4489.name: Comparison and relational operators, strongest for symbolic inequality operators (>, <, >=, <=) in code conditionals and math, weaker for LaTeX forms (\leq, \geq, >), word equivalents (above, below, exceeds, between, within, at least), and breadcrumb '>' separators.

44891.name: The noun completing a 'supplementary/supplemental/supporting ___' phrase in academic papers, such as material, information, file or materials, often as a section heading. It peaks on 'Material' right after 'Supplemental/Supplementary', and occasionally fires weakly on similar appended-section headings like Appendices or Related Files.

44924.name: Version identifiers inside URLs, file paths and code: the minor/patch numbers after dots in version strings (e.g. 3.6.0, 1.13.1, Python3.11) and version-like path segments such as /latest, /stable, /dev, /current, @latest. Activation is strongest on the final patch digit of multi-part versions in CDN script/stylesheet links.

44925.name: Tokens that end or complete a phrase which is a repeat of an earlier one in the context. Typical cases are repeated lines, list items, boilerplate and refrains (e.g. "Invalid Input", "Show more", "Monthly Budget", "lived a method", repeated numbers or units). The feature is predicting the final word of a copy. Activation is strongest in highly repetitive text and grows with the number of repetitions.

Tokens inside highly repetitive, degenerate text: it fires on a token that repeats an earlier identical token or pattern (looping lists, repeated words, symbols, tags, code fragments, whitespace). Activation rises as the repetition goes on.

44939.name: Words about storing, saving, recording or writing data or other content (save, store, record, archive, copy, write, output, log, notes, file modes like "w"), usually verbs in technical or software contexts. "save" and "record" activate most strongly.

44946.name: Backslash tokens, mostly a backslash right before a newline (line-continuation or LaTeX \\ line breaks), firing most strongly in long runs of repeated backslash-newline lines in code, math, or garbled text. Weak activations also land on other stray formatting tokens such as " **" or extra spaces.

44947.name: Fires strongly on the capitalized fragment "EVENT" in the Swedish boilerplate "EVENTUELLT nedladdningsbar" ("possibly downloadable") found on thesis-listing sites. Elsewhere it shows only weak, scattered activation on assorted tokens, often word fragments or non-English text, with no clear shared meaning.

44958.name: Scientific and biological prose that describes where something is located, expressed or distributed. The strongest activations fall on predicate words such as "expressed", "is found", "distributed in", "localized to", "colocalizes with", "enriched at", "occurs" and "binding to", and on the nearby function words leading to a tissue, region or condition. There is also weak, diffuse activation on other tokens in technical text.

44963.name: A diffuse feature active across technical, software, and documentation-style text, such as programming, editors, config files, rules, and syntax. It mostly fires weakly on function words, sentence-ending punctuation, and newlines. It peaks on terms about code editing and programming languages, such as "highlighting", "snippets", "language name", and "React".

4497.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly inside standardized publishing and legal boilerplate: copyright and permission notices ("strictly personal, individual use", "open content license", "reprint/republish… creating new collective works"), open-archive disclaimers ("deposit and dissemination"), citation and research-portal templates (closing quote before "Together they form a unique fingerprint"), and trademark or official-use disclaimers. It especially activates on words about using, reproducing, distributing or documenting works, and sometimes on year digits and punctuation in this kind of metadata. Elsewhere it fires sporadically on word fragments and stray tokens.

44984.name: Proper names of places, peoples and regions (countries, states, cities, nationalities, demonyms), often split into word-piece tokens, frequently appearing in titles or headlines. Generic geographic or institutional words (national, region, University, Earth) also fire, but more weakly.

44997.name: Separators and markers that follow an author's name in a paper's author list, such as commas, "and", affiliation numbers, symbols like *, †, §, and the closing braces or $ of superscript markup. Activation is strongest on the comma or closing token right after the affiliation superscripts.

45006.name: Words tied to jobs and professional roles, especially teaching and academia: teachers, professor, faculty position, school administrator, teacher-facing practice, NCATE. Weaker activations land on general work and office terms (job, positions, public office, civil service, training contract, salaries) and on institutional affiliation text in author lists.

45014.name: Tokens that start or define iteration, mostly the loop keyword "for" (and foreach, while, .for, ng-repeat, for_each, For…To) plus loop-header pieces like the iterator variable, "in", "auto". It also fires on math iteration ranges such as the subscript after ∑/∏ ("_{") and Mathematica-style {n, 1, 4}. The strongest activations are explicit loop or repeat constructs, including prose that names "the for statement".

45017.name: The verb "point" and its inflections (point, points, pointed, pointing), especially "point out" and "point to" for drawing attention to something or indicating evidence, and also physically directing a finger or object. It also fires weakly on related words such as pinpoint, finger, direct, and translations like señala and 指.

45027.name: Fires most strongly on the closing quote of the C++ linkage specification extern "C" (especially when a newline or brace follows). Elsewhere it is weak and diffuse, mostly on stray spaces before numbers or names and on small function words in the middle of a phrase.

45041.name: Year and date numbers in metadata boilerplate, mainly copyright notices ("Copyright 2013", "© 2011"), along with "Published", "Updated" and "Created" timestamps. Activation falls on the space right after the label and on the final digit of the year. It also fires weakly on the space before the first item of a numbered list.

45046.name: The suffixes "-able", "-ability" and "-iable" attached to legal or procedural verbs to form legal-status terms (copyrightable, impeachable, justiciable, appealability, patentability, assignability, maintainability). Other scattered tokens such as articles, punctuation and newlines fire only weakly.

45082.name: Whitespace and indentation tokens (runs of spaces, tabs, or a mid-title line break) at the start of a new line that begin a heading, section label, or document element. These appear in scraped web pages, forums, and formal documents such as laws and theses. Occasionally the feature fires on a short heading or separator word instead (e.g., "OF", "NUMBER", "vs", "|").

45109.name: Subdomain name pieces in URLs of academic institutional repositories, strongest on "commons" in "digitalcommons" (e.g. after "Follow this and additional works at:"). Weaker on related repository names like scholarworks, escholarship, dspace, hdl.handle, eprints and repository, plus the word "works" in that boilerplate phrase.

45113.name: Statements describing what will happen as a promise, reassurance or expected consequence (e.g. "then we will display it", "assured that improved wages would", "all would be well", "an attempt will be remade"). Activation is strongest on future and modal constructions (will, 'll, would, be) and the clause they introduce, often after a condition or a verb of assurance; most other tokens fire only weakly.

Main-clause predicates describing a future or conditional outcome, especially "will" constructions announcing what will happen (e.g., "we will send", "a representative will contact you if", "will be updated"). It also fires on the subject and comma that open such a clause after an if/when condition, often in procedural, customer-service or shipping notices.

4513.name: The last token of an operand or left-hand side expression immediately before a relational or equation operator (=, ==, >, \geq, \rightarrow, "is equal to") in math, LaTeX and code. Weaker activations occur on prose words ending a phrase before a verb.

45177.name: The closing quote (often merged with a slash, brace or comma) that ends a URL or file-path string, most often inside an HTML href or src attribute just before the next attribute or '>'. Activation is strongest right after long URLs or file names (.html, .php, .jpg). Occasional weak hits on unrelated words and punctuation are noise.

45207.name: Word-internal subword pieces (often a vowel or accented/diacritic character) inside non-English or foreign words and names. These include non-ASCII letters in Latin-script names (í, é, ł, á), mid-word fragments in Greek, Cyrillic, Devanagari, Thai, Arabic and Korean script, and IPA symbols. Activation peaks on vowel or diacritic tokens in the middle of rare words.

45235.name: The ".ViewGroup" token in Java/Android import statements ("import android.view.ViewGroup;"), typically following android.view.View. Elsewhere only faint activations on scattered tokens, mostly sentence-ending periods followed by paragraph breaks in technical prose.

45239.name: Separators and items in enumerations of alternative values, chiefly "or", commas, "and", and slashes in phrases like "X or Y", "A, B, or C", or "either 1 or 8". It is strongest in chemical or math definitions that list allowed substituents or values, such as "represent hydrogen or methyl" or "K = ℂ or K = ℝ". It also fires weakly on the listed options themselves.

45265.name: Coordinate pairs and tuples, mostly in code: commas, spaces and numbers separating x/y values in calls like Point(0, 0), moveTo(x, y) or arrays such as [[0, 0], ...]. Also fires on the 'y' variable in coordinate contexts and on space-separated number pairs or dimensions (e.g. 6 6, 1179 x 2556). Weak, scattered activation on unrelated prose tokens.

45270.name: Tokens in code and math notation that begin an argument or operand: the first variable, operator or literal right after a keyword, function call, operator or delimiter (e.g. after print, if, while, return, =, +, a comma). It is strongest right after print statements.

45281.name: A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires on the first token of a new name, term or code identifier, usually the first piece of a multi-token word. Examples include "Calc" in Calcitriol, "Cust" in CustCNV, "Process" in ProcessedLine and "tf". It also fires on separators and structural tokens such as "::", "{", "-", the dot in section numbers and commas in lists, mostly in technical, code or list-like text.

45294.name: Tokens that close a condition or command in shell scripts, most strongly the closing bracket plus semicolon (" ];", " ]];") right before "then" or "do". Weaker activations go to other condition terminators such as "]" followed by a newline, "`;", ";", "))", and line breaks before do/then or a brace.

45331.name: Fires overwhelmingly on the ".LoggerFactory" token in Java imports of "org.slf4j.LoggerFactory", usually right after "import org.slf4j.Logger;". It responds much more weakly to other final class names in dotted Java import paths (.Logger, .RequestMethod, .ActionListener, .Paths) and very faintly to scattered predictable boilerplate tokens ("ABSTRACT", "Wikipedia β", "SET NAMES").

45337.name: Structural tokens inside code bodies: leading indentation whitespace, braces, closing parens with newlines, semicolons and control keywords (if/else/for/match), especially in nested conditional blocks that return or set boolean flags (return true/false, flag=false). Weak activations on punctuation and list numbering in prose.

45340.name: The word "Introduction" (often as INT+RODUCTION in capitals) used as a section heading, usually in academic papers right after the abstract or keywords, often numbered ("1.", "I.", \section{}). It fires most strongly when numbered and weaker in tables of contents. Other document section headings such as Abstract, Summary or Update activate it weakly.

45342.name: A single mid-sentence token, usually a function word or punctuation mark such as "the", "and", "because", ":", ")" or "e.g.,", that sits at a transition point just before a new noun phrase or clause. The tokens share no clear semantic theme, so the feature seems to track position or syntax rather than meaning (two examples happen to precede mentions of rising sea levels).

45350.name: Recipe-style listing of the ingredients in a solution, medium, or mixture. It fires on verbs that introduce components (containing, supplemented with, adding, final concentration of) and on the concentration numbers, decimal points, separating commas, and "and" that come before the next ingredient. It is strongest in lab protocols that list buffer or media composition.

45366.name: The first word of a new sentence or paragraph, usually the article "The"/"A"/"An", at sentence starts in formal academic or scientific prose (often right after a citation or period) that introduce a new topic noun phrase.

45369.name: Closing/boundary tokens that end a span, chiefly the "). Weaker activation on other span-ending punctuation, such as closing parentheses, periods/newlines ending docstrings or sentences, and commas or semicolons at clause breaks.

45389.name: Code handling web requests and responses, especially XMLHttpRequest, fetch and requests. It fires most on property accesses and checks of the request state: .onload, .open, .status, status_code, 'state change', and the 'if (' that checks the response. There is weak, diffuse activation on other attribute accesses (.length, .type) and on connective words in technical prose.

45399.name: Highly predictable tokens that complete a fixed construction, strongest for AM/PM markers after clock times (e.g. "4:00 PM", "9 am"). Units after numbers ("14 feet") and set phrases like "in addition (to)" or "for X to" also fire.

45432.name: Names of people or organizations serving as the source or speaker of a quotation, statement, or claim, especially surnames in speech attributions (e.g. "X said", "says X", "X added"). The name and the following reporting verb are both marked, with the strongest activation on the final part of the name.

45439.name: The token "vec"/"Vector" used as a code type or macro name, typically just before a dimension number (vec3, Vector2) or Rust's vec![ ] macro. Activation is highest for lowercase shader/glm-style vec2/vec3. Weak firing also appears on tokens that come right before a number or symbol ("of" before counts, spaces before ♋ signs, equation references like (2)).

45447.name: Separator tokens (mostly commas, also spaces, '=', '|', ':', '-') placed between numbers in numeric lists, arrays, coordinates, tuples and data tables, especially in code. Activation peaks in the middle of a sequence of numbers, where the next token is expected to be another number.

45457.name: The abbreviation "rel" (and its period), most strongly in the legal case-name phrase "ex rel." (ex relatione), as in "United States ex rel. X". Weaker activations appear on other connector words in formal names and citations ("ex" in botanical author citations, "of" in "Estate of" and "on Behalf of").

45461.name: Weak, diffuse activation on the predicate right after a subject (copulas, auxiliaries, main verbs and their complements such as 'be', 'was gone', 'are in intensive care', 'it's right there'). These spans describe the state, location or outcome the subject ends up in. They typically follow a setup clause (temporal, conditional or narrative lead-in such as 'once', 'if', 'at some point', 'soon').

Verb or predicate phrases stating the condition, activity or location a subject is in at a particular moment, such as 'we're in', 'he lay dying' or 'is now'. Activation is strongest right after an abrupt shift in time or circumstance, marked by words like 'later', 'the next', 'now', 'suddenly' or 'ended up'.

45505.name: Structural boundary tokens in scraped web pages, mostly newlines and punctuation-plus-newline, that separate boilerplate or header metadata (titles, bylines, dates, source tags, site descriptions) from the main body text. The strongest cases are Slashdot-style headers such as story titles, 'by user (id) on' bylines and 'writes "'.

45525.name: Tokens made of repeated semicolons (";;", ";;;", ";;;;"), often with a leading space or trailing newline. They show up as shell case terminators, the for(;;) loop idiom, config comments, and in garbled or noisy text. Single semicolons that end a line activate only weakly.

45531.name: Assignment/binding operators right after a variable or identifier name, mostly " =" in code (also R's "<-", type-annotation ":", keyword args, "from" in imports, and definitions in math or plain text). It marks the point where a name is about to be given its value, type, or definition.

45532.name: The word "option" in the standard open-source license boilerplate phrase "(at your option) any later version", mainly from GPL/LGPL headers in code comments. A few weak, unrelated activations occur on sentence-ending periods and stray tokens.

45544.name: Punctuation, newlines, and connectors that come right after a person's name (usually an author name or initial) in bylines, citations, and reference lists, marking where the name ends and the next element begins: commas, periods after initials, '.,', ' (' before a year, ' and', 'et al', semicolons, and line breaks before an affiliation or title. Activation is strongest after abbreviated initials in reference entries.

4555.name: Mostly the first element of a paired or structured value: the first number in coordinates, dimensions (A x B), scores, ratios, ranges, intervals, array indices and function arguments, especially just after an opening parenthesis/bracket or before a separator such as a comma, x, dash or colon. Strongest on numeric coordinate arguments like moveTo(0, …) and the (1.7, 0) point. Weak, sparse firings also appear on miscellaneous tokens in code and technical text.

45568.name: Separator and connector tokens right before the next item or noun phrase begins. It fires most strongly on semicolons that split items in an enumerated list, as in a legal disclaimer of damages. It fires weakly on function words like "or", "such as", "a", "those" and "les" that introduce the following element.

45600.name: Mentions of Bitcoin (and its ticker BTC), with weaker activation on generic "cryptocurrency/cryptocurrencies" and other crypto-related names like Ethereum or Satoshi.

45603.name: The word "peptide(s)", whether as a whole token or as the "ptide(s)" suffix in polypeptide, neuropeptide or dipeptide. It fires most strongly on standalone "peptide(s)" after a describing word (small, antimicrobial, synthetic, cyclic). It responds weakly to similar biochemical suffixes like oligonucleotide, oligosaccharide and epitope.

4561.name: Tokens within lists of person names, mostly author bylines of academic papers and citations. It fires on first names, initials, surname fragments and the separating commas or affiliation markers, and is strongest in the middle of long comma-separated author lists.
