45625.name: The ".id" token immediately following "R" in Android Java resource references (R.id.xxx), typically inside findViewById() calls. Other R resource types such as ".string" activate weakly. Scattered weak activations on unrelated prose tokens appear to be noise.

45626.name: Generic, usually plural head nouns (things, issues, processes, properties, experiences, components) that close a noun phrase following a quantifier or adjective such as some, several, many, various, new, or other. They denote vague collections of items or abstractions.

45645.name: Primarily the " class" keyword right after "public" in Java class declarations (following package/import/comment headers). Weaker scattered hits on a word that completes a fixed phrase or compound (e.g. "camera bag", "Gold Plus", ".cls", "Meta-Analysis", "compatible with", "affirmed by").

45651.name: A diffuse feature with low, fairly uniform activations. It fires mostly on predictable tokens inside repetitive or templated text: unit-conversion pages, tables, lists, code, date sequences and repeated headings such as 'Fuel Cost from' or 'Angle Unit Converter'. The marked token typically continues a pattern already seen earlier in the context, which suggests copying or induction rather than any specific meaning.

A diffuse feature that fires mostly on tokens inside structured, repetitive or templated text, especially arithmetic and math notation (numbers, operators, parentheses, "% of … is", Q:/A: pairs, function calls like suma(…)) and repeated boilerplate phrases. It favors positions where the next token follows predictably from an established pattern.

45657.name: Acknowledgment, funding and author-affiliation boilerplate in papers and reports, such as "This work was supported by", "We are grateful to", "would like to thank", "Funding:" and "Acknowledgements". Activation is strongest on the key verbs and the prepositions after them (supported/funded/grateful/thank + by/to), just before the funder or thanked person is named.

45662.name: A single long whitespace token (a run of many spaces or tabs) used as padding or indentation. It shows up in code, tables, logs, ASCII art and garbled or noisy text, often right after a newline or a word and before more whitespace or content.

45694.name: Words expressing co-residence or joint partnership, chiefly "together" after living/staying/moving (couples cohabiting) and "filing jointly/joint" after married. Weak, scattered activations also appear on punctuation, citation commas and other function words.

45715.name: The word "blank", strongest by far as the value of an HTML link attribute target="_blank" (open in new tab/window). Weaker on stray "blank" in garbled or code-like text, and faint on other web/markup tokens.

45738.name: Fires mostly in code and technical or synthetic text. The strongest cases are the first token of a new statement, usually leading indentation whitespace, the next keyword or variable, or an assignment '='. These often follow a comment line, especially in Python try/except fallback blocks around imports. It also fires on scattered syntax tokens (brackets, braces, parentheses, '=') and on words that start the next clause in prose.

45750.name: Diffuse, low-level activation on reproductive and fertility content. The strongest spots are fertility treatments, donor semen, embryos being implanted, cloning and egg donation, and trying to conceive. Weaker activation spreads to nearby words in medical and biotech procedure contexts (injection, in vitro, testing, dose).

45764.name: Weak, diffuse activation in biological/biomedical contexts about living organisms, microbes, viruses and their manipulation, especially words describing an organism's state or type (live, virulent, mutant, irradiated, infectious, modified organisms, cultures, fungi, vectors, natural enemies).

45769.name: Mentions of the "Standard Model" of particle physics, strongest on "Model" and its abbreviation "SM". Weaker activation falls on other names for established physical theories or frameworks, such as quantum mechanics/theory, GR, QED and "science", and on the generic word "model" after "standard".

45798.name: A diffuse, boundary-oriented feature. It fires on tokens sitting at transitions between structural units, most strongly in LaTeX/math, where braces fuse with the backslash of the next command ('}\', '_\') or a closing '$' or ')' ends inline math. Weaker hits include markdown/HTML closers (')**', 'strong>'), newlines after date headers or code lines, list bullets and dashes, and words directly preceding a multi-word term or name ('a' whitelist, 'online' casinos, 'Research' Ecologist).

4584.name: The "flare" part of Cloudflare. It fires most strongly on the ".cloudflare" token in CDN script URLs (cdnjs.cloudflare.com) and weakly on "flare" in mentions of Cloudflare or similar names.

45842.name: Structural break points inside formulaic, templated or boilerplate text, where what follows is predictable. Examples are newlines in web boilerplate ("Custom Essay Specifically⏎For You", list items, metadata fields), ">⏎" after HTML table tags, the hyphen in the middle of DOI numbers, commas in stock phrases ("Early version, also known as"), and LaTeX command boundaries.

45868.name: Space-prefixed delimiter or symbol tokens that begin the next item in a repetitive, list-like or markup sequence of non-prose text. Typical cases are the leading backslash of a LaTeX command, an opening bracket, an emoji colon, "http", or bare whitespace separators. Activation is strongest where the same item-start token repeats many times, as in chained LaTeX macros.

45880.name: The "asm" subword following "pl", chiefly in "plasmid(s)" (strongest) and more weakly in "plasmalemma", "plasmacytoid" and "plasmodesmata"; the trailing "id/ids" is weaker. Weak activation also appears on related molecular-biology terms such as cloning/expression "vector(s)", "episomal", "mobile genetic elements" and "horizontal gene transfer".

45885.name: Line breaks and punctuation, mostly double newlines, that close a header or metadata line (title, date, byline, citation, breadcrumb, section number) right before the main body text starts.

45887.name: Fires on the word "serum" in lab and biology writing, most strongly in cell-culture supplement phrases like "fetal bovine/calf serum" and its abbreviation FBS. It also responds weakly to other reagent and medium components such as BSA/albumin, glycerol, methanol, NaCl, sulfate, glucose and yeast extract.

A diffuse feature with no clear unifying concept: it fires most strongly on the biomedical term "serum" in a list of biological factors. It fires weakly on scattered structural or function tokens in technical or formatted text. These include markdown table separator pipes, code-comment markers, punctuation in math derivations, and determiners.

45900.name: The word "cold" (and capitalized "Cold") in every sense: low temperature (cold water, weather, air), the illness ("a cold"), figurative coldness, and fixed names and phrases (Cold War, cold callers, cold emailing, Captain Cold). Weaker activation goes to synonyms such as "chilly" and foreign words for cold.

45952.name: Indentation whitespace and opening tag pieces (" <", "li", "a", "><") at the start of lines in nested HTML markup, strongest on repeated sibling elements such as nav links and list items. It also fires weakly on other code-structure tokens like indentation, separators and punctuation.

45968.name: Terms tied to physical and mechanical properties, materials, and biomedical/engineering concepts, such as forces, stresses, loads, friction, tension, structure, substrates, devices, polymers, and coatings, especially in scientific or technical contexts. Activation is strongest for mechanical stress and load and for substrates.

45991.name: The "-Co" token right after a hyphen in compound terms, strongest for SARS-CoV(-2). It is moderate in acetyl-/acyl-CoA and weak in chemical cobalt (Cu-Co, Sm-Co, WC-Co) or place and name compounds. A similar hyphenated-fragment case ("-se" in ChIP-seq/RNA-seq) and other scattered tokens activate only faintly.

46008.name: Middle subword pieces inside rare technical or scientific words, mostly Latin or Greek taxonomic names of organisms (genera, families such as -idae or -oid forms, e.g. ixodid, Phytoseiulus, Pheidole, Bacillariophyceae) and other specialised terms. Activation is strongest on fragments within the word rather than at its start. There are occasional weak hits on ordinary words.

46029.name: Fires in AI-assistant/code-explanation text, mainly on "Let"/"let" in "Let's…" and "Let me know…" phrases that open a new step or close a response. Weaker hits are argument-separating commas in function calls and exclamation marks ending friendly closing sentences.

46030.name: Tokens inside LaTeX math notation, mostly the subscript/superscript operators ("_{", "^", "_\") and the \partial command, especially in partial derivatives (\partial_x, \partial^2). Weaker hits on similar structural symbols in code, such as Rust lifetime apostrophes (&'a) and C++ template brackets.

46039.name: Verbs (and nearby particles like 'for', 'whether', 'at') for checking, testing, detecting, monitoring, searching, or analyzing something to determine its state or a condition. Activation is strongest for 'check'/'checks', especially in code comments and procedural contexts.

46068.name: Fires mainly on the word "Runtime", strongest when it is a metadata label before a colon ("Runtime: 120 minutes" for films, "Runtime: 92 ms" for code results), and also inside software names like "OpenJDK Runtime" and "RuntimeError". Weaker hits land on similar header or label words ("Error", "Registration", "pts"), on "players" in "Australian players", and diffusely on separators such as commas and spaces in structured text.

46073.name: Final word of a person's title or rank that comes after a name, especially "Judge" in "Senior Circuit/District Judge" and "itus" in "Educator Emeritus" in user profile lines. Weak, scattered activations also appear on sentence-ending periods and on verbs that follow a subject.

46088.name: The preposition "at" (sometimes "on" or a colon) used to point to where something can be found online, mostly just before a URL or site name, as in "Available at:", "Share at Facebook", "online at www…". It also fires weakly on separators such as double newlines after headings and commas in keyword lists.

46089.name: The token that names a previously mentioned or defined entity being acted upon, typically the object noun of a verb or preposition ("submit your application", "after running the command", "the questions above"). It is strongest for code variables passed as arguments that were defined earlier ("init(settings", "Open filename", "searchPaths", "tempString"). The feature marks the head of an anaphoric reference that completes a phrase, just before punctuation or the next clause.

Nouns (or noun-like tokens and code variables) that refer back to a previously described or prepared entity, typically the object of an action, e.g. 'the mixture', 'the ingredients', 'this code', 'the questions above', 'the marked length'. Especially strong in recipes ('mixture', 'batter', 'ingredients') and in code arguments (site, builder, expr, _color).

46096.name: The object noun (almost always "file", sometimes "work") right after "you may not use this" in software license boilerplate, mainly the Apache 2.0 header. Weak, sporadic activations appear on unrelated tokens elsewhere.

46130.name: Token immediately following "log"/"Log" (or a log-related word like Syslog, audit, Logger) that continues a logging library or function name, most strongly the "4" in log4j/Log4J, plus suffixes like back (logback), uru (loguru), 2/10 (log2, log10), Handler.

46138.name: The first token (often a word-initial fragment) of a place name, usually a city, district, street or institution name, inside an address or affiliation line in academic or business text. It fires most strongly on city names that come right after a comma, postal code or institution name.

4615.name: Weak activation on short connective or structural tokens in bibliographic, legal and metadata-style text. These are small function words or abbreviations that link or separate fields: "v." between case parties, "et al", "vol./no./n", "by/to/of/AND" between title-page or author blocks, list numbers, and separators between citation parts or names.

46158.name: The word "judiciary" (and its pieces like "Jud-iciary" and "judici-aries"), meaning the court system. It fires most strongly on capitalized "Judiciary" in committee names such as House or Senate Judiciary Committee, and less on lowercase general references to the judicial branch. Unrelated function words get only weak activation.

46166.name: Sentence-ending punctuation (period, often fused with a paragraph break, or a closing parenthesis or bracket) at the end of a paragraph or section. It fires most strongly in scientific and methods-style writing, where the next text starts a new section, heading or step, such as Results or a methods subheading.

46185.name: The ".security" token in Java-style package and import paths (java.security, javax.security, org.springframework.security, and project packages). It fires most strongly on standard library and Spring imports and more weakly on custom package names. Activations elsewhere are faint and scattered, such as the French "sécurité" and random punctuation.

46209.name: The ".blogspot" token within URLs/domain names (e.g., name.blogspot.com), right after the blog's subdomain name; weak, sporadic activation on unrelated tokens like "of" or a bare "spot".

46217.name: The token "sys" in C/C++ #include directives, strongest for system headers like <sys/types.h> and weaker for local includes such as "sys.h". Activations on other text are negligible.

46231.name: The property or field name part of a setter method in code (the token(s) right after "set", e.g. setNeighbours, setId, setReduction), plus its parameter type and name. Weaker hits land on other method or field names and assignment parts of property setters.

46258.name: Subword tokens inside gene and protein names in biomedical text, mostly the middle or final fragments of symbols like Pitx3, KLF5, OLIG2 and Sox9. It fires most strongly on transcription factors, and also on related words such as "factor" in "transcription factor". Weaker activations appear on other name fragments and newlines.

46270.name: Concepts tied to cloning and cellular reprogramming, such as cloning/cloned, Dolly, nuclear transfer, reprogramming, iPS cells, immortalized cell lines and pluripotency. The strongest signal falls on word pieces like "iPS" and "reprogramming". There is also weak, spurious firing on the "iP" in iPads and other scattered tokens.

46272.name: Mostly fragments of biochemical signaling-molecule names, firing most strongly on "AMP" in cyclic AMP / cAMP, with weaker hits on related cyclic-nucleotide pathway terms. Related terms include GMP, c-di-GMP, phosphate, AMPK, PDE, adrenergic, second messenger, forskolin and theophylline. Weak, scattered activations also occur on lookalike acronyms (GMP certification, Accelerated Mobile Pages) and on paragraph breaks.

46286.name: Diffusely activates on tokens in contexts about challenges, puzzles, contests, and submissions, such as competitive-programming sites (HackerRank, 'Problem D', solved-problem tables), homework or math problems, game jams, competitions, rankings, and site boilerplate around them. The strongest hits are words like 'Problem', 'solution', 'find', 'submission', 'Runtime' and 'however'.

46325.name: The operand or object that completes a mathematical or computational relation, i.e. the variable, noun or pronoun after words like "divided by", "less than", "to the", "of" or "divides". It appears mostly in math problems and code, marking the end of an expression or argument slot such as "5 ÷ m", "divisible by tot", "from 0 to x" or "the average edge weight".

46326.name: The determiner "the" (sometimes "a" or a space) right before an expected ordinal, position or superlative, mostly after "is in" / "which is" in logic-puzzle clues ("is in the first house") and quiz questions ("which is the greatest"). It marks the spot where a position or answer is about to be given.

46328.name: The "tom" token beginning "tomography", firing hardest after "computed" in medical imaging contexts (CT, PET, OCT). It fires more weakly on quantum tomography, on the abbreviation "CT", and on "tom" in "tombs".

The token "tom" as the first piece of "tomography" (computed/computerized tomography, CT imaging), firing most strongly after "computed" or "computerized". It fires weakly on "tom" in other words (tombs, the name Tom) and on nearby "CT" mentions. The remaining activations are faint and scattered across punctuation and table separators.

46358.name: Key-value/associative data structures in code: type names like HashMap, Map, Dict, Dictionary, BTreeMap, defaultdict, HashSet, and empty or opening dict literals ({}, = {, {$). These fire most strongly on map type annotations, with weaker activation on tuple/collection openers and on prose words like "mapping" or "from" that describe a mapping.

46364.name: The word "Mississippi", whether it names the U.S. state or the river. Weaker activations come from related forms like "MS", "Ole Miss", and Mississippi town names (Tupelo, Vicksburg).

46371.name: The ".test" token joined to a preceding identifier, firing most strongly in Java package/import paths (especially org.springframework.test / boot.test). It also fires on .test method calls (regex .test(), R poisson.test/cor.test, algo.test). Weak activations land on leader dots in tables of contents and on stray punctuation or spaces.

46383.name: Mostly the minus sign starting a negative number inside a list or sequence of values, such as array literals, input lines, matrices and multiple-choice options, usually right after a comma or separator. It is strongest in comma-separated arrays mixing positive and negative numbers. Weaker hits go to other mid-sequence elements: individual numbers, decimal points, nested brackets and repeated letters.

46387.name: Fires overwhelmingly on " BASIS" in the Apache License boilerplate "AS IS" BASIS. Much weaker activation appears on tokens inside other stock web and code boilerplate, such as "Skip to content", comment-form notices ("Required fields", "campos", "поля"), "Back to Top" line breaks and DEFAULT_SIZE.

46419.name: Whitespace-only tokens (runs of spaces, tabs and newlines) that make up blank or empty lines, especially between sections, after colons that introduce code or formulas, and within long repeated stretches of blank lines.

46433.name: Tokens that finish a journal name or its abbreviation, usually the last word or letter fragment of a journal title. These often appear inside DOIs or URLs (e.g. the code after "10.3390/" like ijerph, nu, ijms) or in citations (PLoS ONE, HESS, Journal of … Research). The strongest activations are on the abbreviation fragments in DOI strings.

46445.name: Citation and reference numbers in text, mostly the numeral inside brackets/parentheses or as a superscript after a sentence (e.g. [15], (11), .[3]), plus the final digit of years in author–year citations (Rogers, 1983).

Citation and reference markers: footnote/endnote numbers placed after a claim, often inside brackets or parentheses or as superscripts after punctuation (e.g. [5], .3, (98), *, ii), plus the final digit of years in author-year citations and figure/exhibit labels. Weaker activation on a few unrelated tokens.

46447.name: The backslash or ")\" token that starts the next item in a sequence of LaTeX-formatted citation/superscript markers (e.g. after "\(^1\)," or "\cite{..},"), i.e. the separator position between consecutive reference numbers or LaTeX commands in a list. The strongest activations come on the second and later superscript citations after commas or dashes. Weak, sporadic activations appear on other list separators and word fragments.

46460.name: The word "liability"/"liabilities" in legal disclaimer boilerplate, especially after "damages or other" in software license or indemnity clauses. It fires weakly on unrelated tokens such as "weight" in "weight loss" and sentence punctuation.

4648.name: A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires on scattered tokens in ordinary prose, code and lists. The strongest hits tend to be the word or subword piece that completes a term, name or list item, where the continuation is highly predictable. Examples include "he-ifer", "mesol-imbic", "Inequal-ities", "missile attack" and "blackjack". It also fires weakly on function words and list separators.

46482.name: The ":name" token in namespaced attribute syntax, especially Android XML manifests (android:name in uses-permission/meta-data tags); weaker on other XML/schema ":name" uses and assorted low-weight code or metadata tokens.

46510.name: The word "style" and related CSS terms in code and markup, most strongly the HTML <style> tag opening an embedded stylesheet. It also fires on style.css filenames, style properties, "css" code-block labels and style-definition comments.

46525.name: Names and terms tied to software frameworks, tools and web-dev tooling, especially PHP/web frameworks (strongest on "Laravel") and database-migration vocabulary (migrate, migrations, Migration, settings). Also fires weakly on completions of tech product and library names (Metasploit, Tailwind, Alamofire, OpenFOAM, PHP-FPM, Joomla) and framework identifiers in code (.Router, create_app, .Set, Application_Start).

Tokens forming framework/library command or API names in code contexts, chiefly Django-related: " start" in "python manage.py startapp", "-admin" in django-admin (strongest), and Migration, plus similar framework identifiers like tf.keras and model.fit.

46594.name: The first numeric operand in a pair or list of numbers, usually a function argument (e.g. add(3, 5), gcd(54, 24)), the first of "between X and Y", or the first value in a set/input line. It fires on the number that comes right after an opening parenthesis, bracket, "between" or "from" and before a comma or a second number, mostly in code examples and math problems.

46658.name: Keywords that open a function or method definition in code, such as def, fn, func, function, sub, and return types or modifiers like void, public, private, and static. They fire right before the function name, typically at the start of a new declaration line. Activation is strongest on return types like 'void' after an access modifier. Weak activations appear on other declaration openers (class, const, let) and occasionally on unrelated prose.

46659.name: Units of measurement (often the first token of an abbreviated or spelled-out unit) that directly follow a numeric value, especially scientific/physical units such as kg, km, mm, eV, kcal and compound units like km/s or g/dl. Activation is strongest on the unit's first token.

Units of measurement (often the first token of an abbreviated or compound unit like ft, g/dL, mm Hg, km, MB, per) that come right after a numeric value. Activation is strongest for physical and scientific units.

46678.name: Namespace or prefix identifiers right before a colon (or other separator) in code and markup, e.g. XML/XAML tag prefixes (c:, asp:, s:) and RDF/OWL prefixes (rdf:, owl:, rdfs:). Activation is strongest on these prefix tokens and weaker on other tokens that come before qualifiers or delimiters.

4670.name: Words expressing being outside, exterior to, or beyond some boundary or scope, chiefly "outside (of)" and "beyond". Weaker activations appear on related exclusion or separation terms such as "other than", "except", "external", "outdoor", "unrelated", "independent", "escape" and "away from".

46705.name: The token "-transform" attached as a hyphenated suffix within code identifiers, such as CSS properties (text-transform, -webkit-transform) and package names (plugin-transform, sentence-transformers). It fires most strongly in CSS style contexts.

46708.name: Section headings in documents, especially academic papers, patents and reports, usually written in all caps (INTRODUCTION, ABSTRACT, MATERIALS AND METHODS, METHODOLOGY, ACKNOWLEDGMENTS, REFERENCES). The feature fires on the first token or word-piece of the heading, typically right after a line break or a section number such as "1." or "I.". It is strongest for "INT" in INTRODUCTION and "ATERIAL" in MATERIALS.

46710.name: Author surnames (mostly their continuation subword tokens) and the tokens that follow them, such as "et", commas, spaces and years, inside academic citations. These appear as parenthetical (Author et al., Year) references, LaTeX \cite keys and bracketed reference codes. Author names in paper bylines and affiliations also activate.

46711.name: Mentions of Florida, strongest on the word "Florida" itself (also in university and institution names), weaker on Florida cities such as Tampa and Orlando and on abbreviations like FL/Fla. Unrelated tokens that start with "FL" (FLV, FLUENT, FLAT) also activate weakly.

46718.name: First names, or the middle subword pieces of them, belonging to foreign political leaders and other prominent figures, especially Middle Eastern and authoritarian heads of state (Bashar, Jong, Salman, Recep Tayyip, Muammar, Hosni). It fires most strongly on "Bashar" after "President" and "Jong" in Kim Jong-un. The token usually comes right after a title such as President, leader or King, and just before the surname.

46727.name: Fires on the token right after a clause break (a comma, period, opening parenthesis or "or") that begins a supplementary or explanatory aside. The token is usually an article ("a", "The", "An"), a parenthesis, or the first word of the aside. The pattern shows up mostly in boilerplate such as copyright takedown notices, license text, library contact info and instructions, where the text starts adding clarifying detail.

46757.name: Assignment and equality operators ("=", "}=", "=>", ":" in lambdas) in code and math, plus the tokens right after them where the right-hand expression or value begins, such as "$", "\frac" or "(". Activation is strongest on the "=" itself. Weaker hits fall on other expression connectors and openers like commas, opening parentheses, "return", "is"/"be" before a formula, and list bullets.

46759.name: The "US" country abbreviation, chiefly the ".S" piece of "U.S.", firing hardest in patent citations ("U.S. Pat. No.", "U.S. Provisional Application"). It is moderate in patent metadata such as "U.S. Cl." and "U.S. PATENT DOCUMENTS", and weak in general "U.S."/"US" mentions. In the patent-citation cases the trailing period also fires.

46762.name: Words that introduce or name the venue where something is published or appears. This is mostly the preposition "in" (also "on", "the", or an opening asterisk) right before a journal, report series, or outlet name, as in "published in" or "appear in a". Parts of the venue name itself also fire, e.g. "Report Series", "Research" Explorer, "Version of Record". Found in academic and publication boilerplate.

46785.name: Tokens within technical specification details, chiefly in scientific methods sections and product or catalog listings: reagent purities (e.g., 99%), catalog, model and part numbers, manufacturer or brand fields after colons, antibody and reagent descriptions, and instrument settings. Activation is weak and diffuse, with the strongest values on purity numbers, catalog codes and reagent names.

46809.name: Tokens that come right after a number, or begin a new field, in structured reference or tabular text. The strongest case is the reporter abbreviation letter after a volume number in legal case citations (the " S" in "199 S.W.3d", the " N" in "N.W.2d"/"N.J.", the " A" in "A.D.2d", the " P" in "P.2d"). Weaker cases include street-address directions ("135 N."), HTML table cell tags (<th>, <td>), and units after numbers.

46830.name: The word "capita" (or its "ita" fragment) in the phrase "per capita", with weaker firing on other nouns completing a "per ___" rate expression (per unit, per person). Faint, scattered activations also appear on separators like •, - and < in spam product-title lists.

46841.name: Page numbers and other citation locators that come right after a quotation or reference, especially in parenthetical citations like (p. 50), (Loughran 250), (123) and in footnote brackets. Weaker activations fall on years, table-of-contents page numbers, and the speaker/attribution words or name endings that close a quote (e.g., "said").

46874.name: A diffuse, weak feature that fires on tokens inside fixed names, titles and identifiers in structured or boilerplate web text, such as site or product names, section headers, menu items, URL path segments, DOI prefixes and code strings. It often lands on the first word of a heading or name, or on a line break right after one, where the following text is a predictable fixed label rather than free prose.

46888.name: Names of pointer/drag events in code, chiefly "mouseover"/"mouseenter" and their parts (e.g. "Over" after "mouse", "enter" after "drag"). Activation peaks on whole tokens like "mouseenter" and "mouseover" used as event strings or handlers.

46922.name: The HTML definition-list tag name "dt" (and, more weakly, "dl"/"dd") in opening and closing tags like <dt> and </dt>. Activation peaks on the opening <dt> tag, is slightly lower on the closing tag, and is weak elsewhere, such as other definition/term-like markup (details, definition) or stray "dt"/"dl" letter sequences.

46939.name: Names of API documentation and testing tools, chiefly Swagger (especially "io.swagger" in Java imports), OpenAPI, and Postman (the "man" in Post-man). It responds more weakly to the ordinary word "swagger" meaning a confident strut. Other API terms such as "Documentation" or ControllerBase get only weak, scattered activation.

46940.name: Fires most strongly on the "10" in ZIP code 02110 within the boilerplate Free Software Foundation address (51 Franklin Street, Boston, MA 02110-1301) of GPL license headers. It also fires weakly on highly predictable tokens in other boilerplate, such as the line break after "Leave a Reply/Comment" before "Your email address will not be published", and digits in DOIs and dates.

46943.name: Mostly diffuse and weak. The strongest firing is on runs of dashes followed by newlines, which act as separators or row and section dividers in tables, data dumps and markdown. Weaker firing falls on mid-sentence tokens, usually function words or modifiers such as 'the', 'their', 'called', 'into' and 'strong', that lead into a following noun phrase or fixed expression.

46956.name: Fires most strongly on " at" in Apache license boilerplate ("You may obtain a copy of the License at"), the token just before a line break and the URL. Weaker activation goes to other tokens preceding a break or continuation, such as trailing spaces after a sentence-ending period before a paragraph break, newlines, and LaTeX braces.

46980.name: Mostly the space token placed right before the second number in a math operation or comparison (e.g., after "and", a comma, "of", or "="), where the model is about to predict a numeric operand. It fires most strongly in min/max and pairwise-number contexts. Weaker activations land on punctuation just before a predicted continuation.

46984.name: The "iggs" token completing the name "Higgs", firing most strongly in particle-physics contexts (Higgs boson, field, doublet, mass). It fires weakly for other "-iggs" surnames (Myers-Briggs, Griggs, Riggs), and there is faint, scattered noise on unrelated tokens.

46987.name: Interior connecting subword fragments (mostly "oc", also "ob", "ov", "os", "oid") that sit at the joint between two combining forms in compound biomedical terms, e.g. aden-oc-arcinoma, Strept-oc-occus, Enter-ob-acter, aden-ov-irus, hepat-oc-ellular, hemat-oc-rit. Activation is strongest for adenocarcinoma.

46995.name: Column headers and field labels in tables and structured data, such as HTML <th> cells, markdown table headers, and flattened header rows like "Name District" or "Term Explanation". The latent fires on the header words and on the surrounding header markup that separates columns.

Column headers and field labels in tables and structured data, most strongly the HTML <th> header cells (names like Parameter, Compound, Measures) and the tags around them. It also fires weakly on plain-text header rows ("Item Price", "Type | Null | Key") and on label words at the start of list or metadata fields.

Column headers and field labels in tables and structured data: words naming a column, attribute or category (e.g. "Size", "Speaker Title", "Components | Volume", "HTTP request", "Value"), plus the surrounding header markup such as <th>, </th> and |. Activation is strongest on header rows of tables. It is weaker on label-like nouns that introduce key–value pairs ("Price:", "Study ID") or on parameter names in code.

47003.name: Fires most strongly on the SVG attribute token "viewBox", especially inside <svg> tags right after width/height or xmlns and before ="0 0 N N". It fires weakly on other graphics dimension parameters such as matplotlib's "(figsize" in plt.figure(...), and faintly on scattered code and prose tokens.

47008.name: In source code, the whitespace indentation (or line-ending newline/semicolon) that starts the line right after a variable is initialized to an empty or zero value (x = 0, [] , {}, set(), ""). It fires most strongly when a loop (for/while) that uses that variable comes next, marking the transition from setup to loop body.

47015.name: Exception/error type names in code signatures, especially Java "throws" clauses. The strongest is IOException right after "throws" or "ServletException,". Weaker on other exception classes and "Exception" suffixes (SQLException, ConfigException), Rust Result error types, and a few unrelated tokens.

47016.name: Final class-name segments in Java import statements that name annotations (Spring, Lombok, JPA, Servlet, ButterKnife), especially Spring's ".Autowired", which fires strongly every time. Other annotation imports such as .Component, .Column and .AllArgsConstructor give weak activations. Non-import text produces only rare, faint hits.

47060.name: The Latin abbreviation "et al." placed after an author's surname in a citation. It fires most strongly in patent references (e.g. "issued to X et al." and patent number listings) and more weakly in ordinary academic citations.

47070.name: Numeric tokens in math contexts, especially perfect squares and powers (9, 25, 49, 81, 225, 441, 256, 125/625, 216) and computed results or answers (after '=' or 'result in'). The strongest activations fall on final digits of multi-digit numbers in number-pattern puzzles. Scattered weak activations on unrelated words are noise.

47073.name: Trailing-space line breaks (Markdown hard-break style "  ⏎"), firing most strongly after author names, list entries and table-of-contents lines. Weaker activation on superscript/subscript characters such as affiliation markers (¹, ²) and chemical or unit subscripts, and on accented or split word fragments (faç, ô, ṣ).

Tokens made of two trailing spaces followed by a newline (the Markdown hard line break, sometimes with extra newlines). They appear at the end of a line of prose, code, lists or tables. Activation is weak on other formatting tokens such as bold "**" markers and superscripts.

47078.name: Words for helping or being complicit in wrongdoing, firing most strongly on "abetted", "accessory to" (murder), and "aid and comfort" (to enemies), and more weakly on "assisting" and "assistance". Elsewhere there are faint, scattered activations on structural or punctuation tokens in math and dialogue text (colons, periods, "'s", list markers).

47081.name: Boilerplate directive and attribute tokens in code and HTML: mainly the linter-suppression comment "noqa" (e.g. "# noqa: E501"), HTML rel values "nofollow" and "noopener", and the "cdn.jsdelivr" CDN domain in script and link URLs. Weaker activations on "# type: ignore" and stray tokens in noisy text.

47119.name: Fires densely across runs of generic expository or descriptive prose, strongest in SEO-style, marketing or article-spinner text with awkward synonym swaps (e.g. "video clip poker", "good mobile discussion", tire product blurbs) and in encyclopedic summary sentences. Activation spans whole clauses of content words and function words rather than single tokens. Elsewhere it fires only weakly on scattered words.

47128.name: Statement boundary tokens. These are mostly periods that end a sentence, clue or problem statement, or that follow a list number ("3."). Code statement terminators like ";" and ");" behave the same way, as do the spaces or comment markers (#, //) that come right after a code line. In each case the token marks the end of one item or premise before the next begins. Activation is strongest in structured puzzle clues and math word problems.

47146.name: Tokens that complete a highly predictable, templated or boilerplate fragment in web or technical text: header labels like "News Feed Item", site names (allnurses), repository citation phrasing ("and the [... Commons]"), man-page references ("(3)"), date and spec fields, and spam keyword strings. The activating token often ends a short segment just before a line break.

47168.name: Terms for stellar types, stages and life cycles in astrophysics: dwarfs and giants (strongest on "dwar" in "white dwarfs" and "red giants"), main-sequence, stellar progenitors, core-collapse, mass-loss, evolution models, variable stars and supernovae. It fires more weakly on the same words in other settings, such as fantasy dwarves, volcanoes and eruptions, and geological periods.

47186.name: Numeric locants within names of phosphoinositide-signaling molecules, most strongly the "3" in PI3K / phosphoinositide 3-kinase. It also fires on related numbers and fragments such as the "3" in IP3, the "1" and "4" in inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate, and "osphate". Weaker hits occur on numbers in other gene or protein names (PAR6, G6PD, SH3).

47188.name: Descriptive phrases in technical specifications, especially programming problem statements, API docs and math (often in English or Chinese), that define what an input, parameter or object is. Activation peaks on spans like "the argument z of the function", "represents a valid tree", "the size of the grid" and "the rows of the table", particularly around "of the" + noun constructions.

47197.name: The word "code" (any casing, or as part of compounds like codebase, CodeForge, codeless, /code), mostly in the programming/source-code sense but also other meanings (code of ethics, code names). It also fires on cross-lingual equivalents (代码, código) and related symbols like 💻.

47217.name: The fragment "trans" (mostly the split piece "rans") inside long scientific compound words, with the strongest activations in enzyme names such as aminotransferase; it also fires on evapotranspiration, cotransporter, biotransformation and related tokens like "transfer", "amin" and "phosph-at-ase". There is weak firing on the blank line after "Leave a Reply" in blog comment footers.

47238.name: Boilerplate and metadata in academic repository or web pages: newline breaks (often double) after URLs, IDs, dates and citation fields, separating sections such as "Submitted on", rights, permissions and citation info. The strongest activation is "contact" in the repository phrase "For more information, please contact ...", along with the email's ".edu".

47245.name: Mostly fires on website boilerplate and user-directed calls to action, such as navigation and UI labels (Read more, Previous, Articles, Reviews), sign-up and subscription prompts, cart and stock notices, and offers of help ("we've got the right solution for you", "find answers... here"). Activation peaks on the key words or phrase endings of these promotional or instructional snippets. Weaker activations land on the final words or punctuation of list-ending or sentence-ending phrases in ordinary prose.

47250.name: Variable-interpolation and template-placeholder openers (e.g. $, ${, $(, %(, <, {) glued directly onto a preceding path, filename or string fragment, often fused with a separator like /, _, . or -. Activation is strongest in shell and file paths such as /$, _${ and /${.

47260.name: Boilerplate and metadata in scraped web pages, such as forum, Q&A, freelance and research-database pages. The strongest tokens are counts that come right before or after labels like "freelancers are bidding", "comments", "views", "Citations" or "results". Other hits are UI and template fragments, such as "peer-review", "improve this question", "Reply to" and "further replies". Some are line breaks or spaces in these templates, and the highest are pieces of blogger.com email or ID strings.

47307.name: The first token of a speaker's or subject's name (usually a surname, often split into subword pieces) appearing right after a quotation or clause boundary, typically in quote attributions like '" X said' or 'said X'. Activation is strongest on the opening subword of unusual surnames and weaker on titles or generic roles such as 'the official' or 'spokesman'.

The first token (often a word fragment) of a person's surname or name, especially when it starts a speaker attribution right after a closing quotation mark (e.g., ',” [Name] said'). Activation is strongest on the initial subword of multi-token, unusual surnames, and weaker on titles like 'Mr', on whole common names, and on organization names.

47313.name: Mostly fires in source code (especially Rust, C++, Python) on syntactic and structural tokens where a statement or expression continues: assignment and comparison operators (' =', ' =='), leading indentation whitespace, control keywords ('else', 'let', 'for'), and method-chain pieces (the 'ok' in ok_or/ok_or_else, '()', '.is', '_mut'). It also fires weakly and diffusely on prose tokens, often sentence-ending punctuation or newlines and mid-sentence function words, with no clear semantic theme.

Mostly code, firing hardest on tokens in value comparison, type-checking and type-conversion logic: equality and inequality tests, conditional checks such as `i == reflect.Func || i == ...`, `.Equals(...)`, assertion calls, `reflect.ValueOf(...).Kind()`, and type-mismatch error messages like "want ..., got %T". Lower activations appear on general code structure (if, return, indentation, operators) and on scattered words in prose.

47350.name: Functions and properties that measure or aggregate something, such as len, sum, size, .shape, .length, gcd and max, especially when called on a collection in code. In prose it picks up the matching measure phrases ("length of", "number of", "deviation of", "multiplicity of") and the "of" that links a quantity to what it describes. Activation is strongest for len/sum used as divisors and for size().

4736.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly in code and math. Its strongest activations are on identifiers and arguments that reuse a name already introduced in the context, such as returning a previously assigned variable ("hashed"), passing "salt", "self.", repeated "knobs", or "col.gameObject". Elsewhere it gives scattered low activations on formatting tokens, numbers, and line breaks.

47375.name: Tokens within dates, years, and citation/reference numbers, chiefly the space, slash, or digit chunk right before a year or volume number (e.g., "June 1942", "7/1921", legal citations like "47 So. 274 (Ala. 1908)"). It peaks in legal and patent citations and is weak and scattered on ordinary prose words.

47387.name: The word "Question" used as a label beginning a reading-comprehension Q&A segment ("Question: ... Answer: ..."), appearing right after a blank line that follows a passage of text.

4739.name: Numerals that act as structural labels or indices rather than quantities: page numbers in tables of contents, section, equation, figure and list numbers, post/day counters, and numeric parts of IDs or filenames. Activation is usually on the number token that ends the label. Occasionally it fires on other boundary tokens in structured or formatted text, such as table tags, line breaks, or arrows.

47393.name: Tokens describing an opposing or rival party, especially a sports opponent: its name, its record or condition (e.g. win-loss record, struggles, strengths), and the verbs that state that condition (are, has, had, was). Activation is strongest in sports previews and match reports. It fires weakly on subjects and predicates that characterize a third-party entity in other contexts.

47403.name: The "@" symbol, often merged with a preceding quote, parenthesis or space, that begins a scoped package or path name in code (e.g. from '@angular/core', require("@mux/..."), npm i @types/...). Activation is strongest in JS/TS import and require statements and weaker for Android resource refs (@color/...), annotations, decorators and handles. Weak activations on unrelated tokens are noise.

47441.name: Function words (mostly auxiliaries and copulas like "are", "is", "be", "shall be", "should be", plus commas and "and") that come right after a subject or condition phrase and begin the predicate. They are strongest in formulaic, rule-like statements about what is permitted or will happen, such as copyright and permission notices ("Reproduction is authorised, provided..."), "papers published after 2023 are currently being built", and "A null value is permitted, and indicates...".

47483.name: The second or later operand in an arithmetic expression or argument list, usually a numeric literal right after an operator (+, /, *, =) or comma in code or math, e.g. the "2" in "1 + 2". Occasionally it fires on a variable or a word in similar trailing-operand positions.

47489.name: Words describing color and visual appearance, such as color modifiers and shade words (pale, deep, dark, pitch, jet, sandy, metallic, matte, vibrant), hue/shade/tone/complexion nouns, and color-change phrasing ("turned from... to...", "from pale... to deep navy"). Activation is usually on the modifier or descriptor slot just before a color word and is strongest in explicit color-gradient or shade descriptions.

Descriptive words for visual and sensory qualities, chiefly color and its intensity or tone (deep, muted, light, pale, vivid, dull, neon, coral, lavender, ivory, cobalt), along with framing phrases that introduce a color ("shades of", "in", "a"). Texture and finish words (glossy, velvety, brushed, matt) also activate. The strongest activations fall on color shade modifiers and named hues.

47496.name: Fires mostly at structural boundaries in formulaic web boilerplate, where the next chunk of text is a predictable template continuation. The strongest cases are a sentence-final period plus paragraph break just before a new heading, FAQ question or section (e.g., "…suitable for kids and friends." before "Quick Jump To"). It also fires on the space before a date or year in "Last update on" and copyright lines. Weaker hits fall on mid-word fragments in lists of usernames and scattered function words.

47500.name: Leading whitespace or indentation tokens at the start of a line, right after a newline, usually preceding indented content such as code lines, table-of-contents subsections (e.g. "2.1"), list items or continuation lines. Strongest for indented subsection entries in tables of contents and nested code. Occasionally fires on other line-initial markers (bullets, dashes, quotes) or trailing spaces before a newline.

47507.name: The word "auto" as a value or keyword in code, strongest for the CSS centering idiom "margin: 0 auto". It fires weakly on SQL AUTO_INCREMENT and editor-mode settings, and barely at all on unrelated tokens.

47514.name: Structural boundary tokens in code and structured text: leading indentation whitespace at the start of a new line, especially before CSS selectors/closing braces (strongest in CSS/style blocks), plus line-ending tokens like ';}⏎', '}⏎⏎', ' */⏎', and list dashes after newlines. Weak, scattered firing on punctuation in garbled multilingual text.

47545.name: Line-initial structural tokens at the start of a new line, mostly after a newline or heading: indentation whitespace, list bullets/dashes, quote markers '>', table pipes, '###', '\[' math openers. They mark the formatting prefix that begins a block or list item. Strongest on leading indentation spaces before code or commands.

Line-initial formatting tokens that open a new line's content, mostly leading whitespace/indentation, bullets (•, -, *), blockquote '>', list numbers or LaTeX '\[', typically right after a newline (often following a header, colon, or comment marker) and just before the line's first real word. Activation is strongest for code indentation.

Line-initial formatting tokens that open a new line of content: leading indentation whitespace, bullet markers (•, -), email quote markers (>), LaTeX display delimiters (\[), opening quotes, and similar prefix punctuation, typically right after a newline or heading/colon that introduces a list, quote, code, or equation block.

47568.name: Tokens in math expressions or code, most often the last operand (number or variable) just after an operator, and especially in a denominator or after a division slash inside parentheses (e.g. "/(7/3", "(c - d)", "/N"), often right before a closing parenthesis. Weak activations on other punctuation and code tokens.

47571.name: Highly predictable tokens inside formulaic or templated text, mostly website boilerplate and document metadata in many languages. Examples include repository and journal page text ("Hier finden Sie…", "Persistent URL hdl.handle", Korean comment-form notices), freelancer bid listings ("Değerlendirme", "Ulasan"), and academic paper scaffolding (line breaks after "Received …" dates, "Abstract" or "Keywords", citation brackets, "Department of"). Common function words in stock phrases also activate.

47576.name: Mostly scientific and technical text. The marked words name an external input, source or stimulus that acts on a system: an applied field, voltage or current, an incident or pump laser beam, light, pressure, an input signal. They tend to follow phrases such as "presence of", "applying", "subjected to" or "external". The strongest cases are applied external fields and currents.

47578.name: The token "Mount"/"Mt" and its variants (mount, MT, mt), firing most strongly when it begins a proper name of a mountain or a place, school or station named after one (Mount Olympus, Mt. Ararat, Mount St. Helens). It fires more weakly for the verb or noun "mount" (mounting, mounts) and for unrelated MT/mt abbreviations.

The token "mount" and its variants (Mount, Mt., Mont, mounting, mounted). It fires most strongly on "Mount"/"Mt." as part of proper place names (mountains, towns, universities), more weakly on the verb "mount" and "mounting" (escalating), and weakest on look-alike strings such as "MT"/"mt" abbreviations.

4758.name: Fires on the final term of a mathematical expression, most strongly on the constant term that closes a polynomial after a + or − sign (e.g. the 8 in 7n^2−10n−8). It also fires weakly on the last number in lists, tuples and code arguments, and on trailing digits of long numbers. Isolated non-math tokens show only faint, noisy activation.

The final operand or constant term in a math or code expression, usually the number or variable right after '+', '=', or another operator at the end of an equation or formula (e.g. the 'c' in 'ax^2 + bx + c', the '1' in '... + 1;'). It fires most strongly on constant offsets added at the end of a formula.

47587.name: Words for sexual violence, mainly "rape" and its verb forms (strongest, even for the rapeseed plant sense). Weaker activation goes to "assault", "abuse" and "violence", especially when they follow "sexual".

47593.name: The words "citation" and "cite" (sometimes split as C+itation) in repository and publication front-matter boilerplate, such as "Citation for published version" and "To cite this version". Activation is strongest for "Recommended Citation", the standard header on institutional repository pages. Related boilerplate words (version, APA, Posts, Content, bib) activate weakly.

47602.name: The final digit of a year in a citation, most strongly in taxonomic authority citations that follow a species or genus name (e.g., "Bleeker, 1854", "Linnaeus, 1758"). It also fires more weakly on years in ordinary literature citations and dates, and occasionally on the end of an author name in such citations.

4762.name: Completion tokens of proper names, chiefly author surnames in academic citations (e.g. the final word-piece of a surname, the following "et" of "et al.", and the space or opening digits of the year). It is strongest in parenthetical or bracketed references like "(Name et al., 2003)" or "[Va20]". There are weaker hits on the trailing pieces of other names, brands and titles.

47621.name: The "http"/"https" token that starts a URL placed directly after a timestamp in RSS/feed metadata, such as "+0000" or "GMT". It is strongest for WordPress "?p=" permalinks. Weak activations appear on other structural boundaries in scraped web or feed text, such as "/read" URL path segments, double newlines after headings, and navigation words.

47692.name: Punctuation and function-word tokens (commas, periods, colons, spaces, opening parentheses, prepositions and conjunctions) at phrase or clause boundaries, where a new segment such as a name, number, list item or clause is about to begin.

47709.name: Very long runs of whitespace (a single 128-space token), usually showing up in garbled, degenerate, or code-like text, often right before a newline or right after a previous run of spaces. Short ordinary tokens barely trigger it.

47710.name: Tokens in the middle of long runs of repeated identical tokens or symbols, such as dash or asterisk separators, big blocks of whitespace, daggers, quote marks, dots, zeros, repeated table cells or matrix entries. Activation peaks deep inside decorative or filler repetition, especially symbol-based separators.

Tokens inside long runs of the same repeated character, symbol, or short pattern (e.g. OOOO, ßßß, | | |, 0,0,0, *\*\, ```). It fires mid-sequence on the repetitive or degenerate token, often in garbled, filler, or array-like text, and gets stronger as the repetition continues.

47720.name: The keyword "derive" in Rust #[derive(...)] attribute macros (strongest), plus related auto-deriving/annotation constructs like Haskell "deriving", Python decorators, Java Lombok annotations, and #[allow]; faint activations on boilerplate web-page whitespace/formatting tokens.

47724.name: The token that completes a proper name or multi-token named entity, mostly the final piece of an author surname, institution, publisher or place (e.g. 'University', 'Press', 'Technology', 'iedo'), often in citations, affiliations or bylines. It also fires on the closing digit of years, phone numbers and reference indices. Weaker activations land on other phrase-final nouns.

47731.name: Slash-prefixed subword tokens (especially "/ms", also "/windows") glued onto preceding text, as in URL paths or garbled, run-together words. They fire most strongly when the fragment is out of place, e.g. "is/ms" standing in for "Ms". A closing bracket after an array index in code activates weakly.

47737.name: The word "Free" in "Free Software Foundation", especially in GPL license boilerplate ("write to the Free Software Foundation"), activating most strongly right after "the". It fires weakly on the first word of other organization or brand names that follow "the" (e.g. "Better" in BetterHelp).

47777.name: Index or label numbers (usually "1", sometimes 0, 2, 3, etc.) placed inside square brackets or after caret/footnote markers, such as footnote and reference markers ([1], [^1]), Jupyter prompts (In [1]:), link references, and array indices. The number right after an opening bracket fires most strongly.

47811.name: Words tied to handling errors, failures and risk, especially "handling"/"handled" after error or exception, and also catch, recover, troubleshooting, debugging, contingency, incident response and risk management. Weak activations also fire on unrelated software or web-UI terms such as search, page and folders.

Words tied to catching, handling, or guarding against errors, exceptions, and unexpected cases, most often in programming ("error handling", "handled by", "exceptions", "edge cases", "default to handle everything else", "catchall"). It also fires on the literal verb "catch"/"capture" and on related protection, recovery, or coping words. Activation is strongest on "handling"/"handled" after "error"/"exception".

47813.name: Tokens that continue a repetition or a pattern already set up in the context: repeated words, characters or punctuation ("hehe hehe", "six! six!", "♣♣♣", "!!!!"), reprised phrases ("A Shooting Is A Shooting", "I'll always stand"), and the later items of a list or sequence (here, here and here; N–P–K; 1/2/3/4; fifties, forties, thirties). Activation is strongest on the repeated content word itself.

47818.name: A variable or subject that is repeated from earlier in the same expression, typically the left operand of a second comparison joined by &&, ||, and, or (e.g. "c >= 'a' && c <= 'z'", "ans == 'n' or ans == 'N'"). The strongest activations are on code and math conditions. It fires weakly on repeated subjects or words in prose ("no man living and no man dead", "it never rains but it pours").

47826.name: Discourse framing in academic or expository writing, especially introduction and literature-review language. It fires on section openings such as "Introduction" headers and the line breaks after them. It also fires on references to prior work ("et al.", "previous studies", "existing works", "this review", "the authors", "Researchers"). Further triggers are transitional or framing phrases like "However", "In recent times,", "We will show that" and "was presented in". Activation is strongest where a sentence pivots to situate or survey research.

47827.name: The first operand (number) of an arithmetic expression, especially right before a multiplication sign, in math/calculation contexts. It fires on the leading space, digits, decimal point, or opening symbol ($, (, **) that begins the expression, often just after '=' or ':'.

47829.name: The token "meta" (or "Meta"), mostly as the prefix of "meta-analysis" and related research-synthesis terms (meta-review, meta-synthesis). Activation peaks in scientific and medical contexts on aggregating studies; it is weaker for other senses of "meta" (gaming meta, meta-heuristic, usernames) and for related pooling words ("pooled", "umbrella review", "combined analysis").

47848.name: Prepositions (mostly "in", also "on"/"for") that come right after a verb or noun of copying or distributing in copyright and license boilerplate, as in "reproduction in any medium" or "post on servers". They introduce the medium, form or scope of the permitted or prohibited use.

47851.name: Tokens in academic paper front-matter and citation boilerplate, especially MDPI-style headers. The strongest are the "ence" in "* Correspondence:", journal names (Sensors, Sustainability, Diversity, Molecules), the comma after the year, the 10.3390 DOI prefix, author-affiliation asterisks, and "Keywords".

47862.name: Long runs of the same token repeated over and over, such as dashes, spaced dots, ";amp", ";\", repeated letters, or empty table cells. Activation rises the deeper it is into the repetitive run. Ordinary prose tokens get only weak activation.

Tokens inside long runs of one repeated token or character: whitespace, backticks, dashes, pipes, symbols, escaped asterisks, repeated letters. It fires partway through the run, after the repetition is established, marking degenerate repetitive text rather than meaningful content.

47903.name: Mostly fires on structural, boilerplate, highly predictable tokens: chiefly the line break after a "Leave a Reply/Comment" heading just before the template line "Your email address will not be published". It also fires on formatting tokens such as indentation and list bullets in menus, and on fixed pieces of citations and code ("L.R.", "K.R.S.", "public class", "https" in URLs, LaTeX braces).

47915.name: Word-final inflectional suffixes (case, number, gender, definiteness endings) completing words in non-English languages, especially Slavic, Scandinavian, Germanic, Romance and Semitic text. Activation is strongest on Russian/Ukrainian case endings and Scandinavian definite-article suffixes, with weak scattered hits on English text.

Word-final subword pieces (often inflectional endings) that complete a multi-token word, especially foreign or non-English words (German, Russian, Estonian, Latin, Greek, etc.) and names, typically right at a phrase or sentence boundary, often just before the text switches to English. Occasionally whole English nouns at the end of a clause.

47930.name: Activates on the first digit chunk (or the space or separator just before it) of numbers embedded in structured or reference metadata: page numbers, URL and record IDs, citation pages, timestamps, statute and section numbers, patent paragraph numbers. The token marks where a multi-token number begins, often a number that continues an earlier, similar number in the text.

47959.name: The namespace token "UnityEngine" in C# "using UnityEngine;" import lines at the top of Unity scripts (also "UnityEngine.UI"), plus mentions like "UnityEngine.Random". Other tokens fire only weakly and appear to be noise.

47983.name: Special reserved identifiers and keywords in code that refer to the current context or module: mostly Python dunder names (__main__, __name__, __file__, __class__), Rust "use super::", os.getcwd/"current directory", ThisWorkbook, and the blog "<!--more-->" marker. Activation falls on the keyword itself, strongest for dunder names.

48003.name: The "d" in legal reporter citations like "P.2d" (Pacific Reporter, Second Series), sitting between a volume number and a page number. Other tokens, such as ordinary words, newlines and digits in ISSN numbers, fire only weakly and inconsistently.

48008.name: Arbitrary identifier fragments, mostly numbers and alphanumeric strings embedded in filenames, URLs, IDs, code variable names, log entries, and section/theorem numbers. These are low-semantic, hard-to-predict tokens inside technical or structured text (e.g., IMG_ numbers, hashes, user IDs, array indices).

48009.name: The pronoun "it" after "modify" in the boilerplate free-software license phrase "you can redistribute it and/or modify it under the terms of..." (GNU GPL/LGPL, Perl license headers). Other weak activations are scattered, unrelated tokens.

48010.name: Mid-phrase connector tokens that bind the preceding word to an obligatory continuation: prepositions, articles, operators (*, +), suffixes and mid-sentence line breaks. They occur where a phrase or expression is incomplete and the next token is strongly expected (e.g., 'A Study of …', 'one mole of a …', 'flow⏎between', 'menghasil-kan').

48029.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires mainly in scientific and technical writing about searching for, detecting, surveying or cataloguing populations of objects (pulsars, radio sources, planets, craters, dust grains, fires, database entries). The strongest activations fall on words tied to discovery and survey work, such as 'sources', 'density', 'survey', 'pulsars', 'discovered' and 'we have studied'. Weaker hits are scattered over nearby function words and punctuation.

48089.name: The word "license"/"licence" (the noun for a legal usage/copyright license), firing most strongly in boilerplate copyright text like "this license", "the licence" and "terms of the license". It also fires weakly on stray tokens in SEO-spam page titles, such as separators before site names.

48094.name: Backslashes and math delimiters ($$, \[, \() that open a LaTeX math expression. The strongest activation is on the first backslash of a command (\frac, \sum, \mathcal, \varepsilon) that follows directly after an opening delimiter, most often in display math after $$.

48109.name: Newline and formatting tokens that close a markdown-style heading or section label (e.g. "Problem", "Description", "Background", "Question") and lead into the body text below it. Strongest on the line break right after headers like "Problem:" and "Problem Description". Weaker on other boundary tokens such as list markers, bold markers, and the "e.g.," punctuation.

48123.name: The keyword "do" that opens a code block in programming. It fires most strongly on Ruby block syntax ("do |x|" after method calls like .each or File.open) and more weakly on loop "do" in shell for/while scripts and similar languages.

48147.name: Structural and formatting tokens in academic and bibliographic metadata, such as citation punctuation (periods, commas, colons, page ranges, years), DOI and URL fragments (pubmed/, doi), journal names, and section headers like Keywords, References, Abstract, and author lines. Activation is strongest inside reference-style citations (journal abbreviation, year, page numbers, 'doi').

Structural punctuation, newlines and field labels in bibliographic or metadata-style text (citations, author/journal/DOI listings, email archive headers, abstract headings). The strongest responses are on boundaries between metadata fields and the start of main content, e.g. 'ABSTRACT:', 'Learn More' followed by a newline, or a bracket followed by a newline.

Weak activations scattered over the structural parts of bibliographic and metadata text: citations, journal names and abbreviations, author lists, page ranges, DOI/PMC/PubMed identifiers and URLs. They fall mainly on separators and boundary tokens such as periods, colons, commas, newlines and slashes. The strongest cases are periods inside journal abbreviations or DOIs and the end pieces of citation fields.

48176.name: Boilerplate notices and disclaimers about a document: version-of-record and author-manuscript statements, copyright and takedown notices, transcript-error warnings, and instructions to cite, contact, or consult the publisher. The feature fires on the function words and phrase heads of these formulaic sentences ("Please", "is available", "may differ from the", "contact the author for the final version", "refer to the", "providing") rather than on the content nouns.

Mainly a standalone space token that comes between an arithmetic operator (such as / or x) and the number after it, in code or in math factorizations. It can also fire on a word continuing a garbled technical sentence, such as "require".

48211.name: Structural boundary tokens in noisy, garbled or code-like text: newlines (especially double newlines), whitespace/indentation runs, and closing punctuation or brackets (periods, colons, parentheses, quotes, braces) that end a line, segment or field before new content begins.

48213.name: The distinguishing token that follows a repeated prefix or stem in parallel or list-like structures, i.e., the varying part of a repeated name or label (escalaX→escala Y, Temperature F→Temperature C, petal_length→petal_width, VG-BART→VG-T5, snake→snake2/3, Tank→Tank(Clone)). It is common in code identifiers, specs, file lists and enumerations.

48256.name: Comment delimiters in code, mainly the '#' and '//' tokens (also '/*', '/**', ';', '\\', '*') that start a line or inline comment. Activation is strongest when the marker opens a comment line at the start of a code block after prose. Weaker activations occur on similar separator symbols in non-code text.

48272.name: The word "survival" (and its pieces like "surv" + "ival", occasionally "survivor") across all contexts. Activation is strongest in medical and biological uses such as median survival, post-operation survival, and cell or bacterial survival.

48281.name: Fires in noisy, code-like, or structured data text (logs, number lists, pseudo-code, garbled prompts), mostly on separator or boundary tokens such as colons, spaces, newlines, opening quotes and print( that come right before a value, answer or output is written (e.g. 'response:', 'Output Format:', 'set: ', 'print("'). It also picks up some odd fragment tokens inside such strings.

48284.name: Sub-word fragments inside odd, opaque or unpredictable strings, such as random IDs, URL hashes, ticker symbols, model numbers, variable names, acronyms, and transliterated or misspelled words. It fires on pieces of letter strings that are not ordinary English words.

4829.name: The parameter name "savedInstanceState" following "Bundle" in Android Java lifecycle method signatures (onCreate, onCreateView, onCreateDialog). Other weak activations are incidental.

48316.name: Tokens inside boilerplate metadata such as copyright notices, publisher/organization names, citation lines, and publication timestamps. It fires mainly on the publisher or company name and the punctuation, suffixes (Inc., AG), years, and times that close these lines, rather than on article content.

48322.name: Tokens right after a multiplier or fraction word (half, twice, double, times, one-third, quarter, percent, fraction). They are usually the determiner or preposition that begins the quantified noun phrase ("the", "of the", "of all", "their", "this", "as") and sometimes the noun being scaled (amount, number, size, cost). The strongest activations fall on "the" after twice, double, or half.

48328.name: Words for generosity (generous, generously, generosity, the "ously" of "Generously"), strongest in sponsor/donor acknowledgments such as "Hosting generously sponsored by" or "thanks to the generosity of". There is weak, scattered firing on other tokens, such as list-indent spaces and adverbs.

48332.name: Names of estimated statistical or model quantities, mostly regression and effect parameters such as coefficient, slope, odds or log-odds, logit, effect size, ratio, rate, beta, lift, AUC and reproduction number. These appear in stats text and in code like coef_. Activation peaks on "coefficient(s)", "odds", "lift" and "effect size".

48347.name: The token "http"/"HTTP". It fires most strongly when HTTP is discussed as a protocol in technical text (status codes, headers, HTTP/1.1, protocol lists). It fires weakly when http is just the start of a URL. There are occasional weak hits on unrelated tokens.

The token "http"/"HTTP" (including fused variants like ".http", "(http", "ttp"), mostly starting URLs. Activation is strongest when HTTP is used as a word for the protocol in prose ("HTTP server", "HTTP cookie", "HTTP logs", "non-http requests") rather than as a URL prefix, which fires only weakly. Occasional weak hits on other capitalized prefixes before hyphens ("HTML-", "Anglo-").

48367.name: Highly predictable tokens that complete a formulaic or repeated pattern, often echoing earlier context (e.g., 'close your eyes' after eyes are mentioned, the space after 'given:' in repeated forum stat lines, the word after a repeated 'forced', a paragraph-ending break).

48381.name: The definite article "the" following a preposition or verb (in, into, of, to, through, across) and preceding a noun naming a physical location, body system, anatomical structure, or environment (bloodstream, brain, soil, respiratory tract, atmosphere). Activation is strongest in scientific/biomedical contexts, especially for anatomical or biological targets reached by movement or injection.

The definite article "the" right after a preposition or verb, opening a noun phrase for a concrete, well-known entity or location. It fires most strongly when that entity is a body part or organ (heart, eyes, abdomen, human body), and also before systems and places such as the Earth, the cloud, the server or the periodic table.

48391.name: In academic citations, the separator right after the author name(s) (e.g. "Smith,", "et al.", "Lee & Kim"), just before the year or locator. It fires mostly on the space or opening parenthesis preceding the year, sometimes on the comma or the last year digit.

48409.name: Tokens right after a number or entity in structured reasoning text, mostly units, nouns, and relational words ("years older than", "minutes", "students in", "more than", "directly left of") in math word problems and logic puzzles. It also fires on pipe characters at the start of markdown table separator rows and on some repeated tokens in garbled text.

48418.name: Separators and connectors (mostly commas, plus words like "in", "at the", "of", and venue words such as "Center" or "Base") inside formal location or venue strings in addresses, affiliations, event listings and citations. Typical spots are the comma between a city and its state or country, and the links between a venue and its city.

48436.name: The opening word of a generated question, almost always "What" (sometimes the "is" after it) right after a "Question:" label that follows a passage, as in synthetic reading-comprehension Q&A. Weaker hits fall on list bullets that begin a summary line, such as "-" or "**".

Function words that open or link a following phrase, such as question words starting a question (often in quiz or exam-style text), prepositions like "with" or "than" that require a complement, and list-separating commas. The token sets up a continuation rather than carrying content itself.

48447.name: Mostly fires on small two-digit numbers (10–12, especially "11") that sit inside dates, DOIs, manuscript IDs or issue/volume numbers, usually between hyphens or periods. It peaks on day/month fields such as the "11" in 25-11-2020. Weaker, noisier activations land on month names and on structural tokens in list-like or bibliographic text, such as double newlines after titles and commas.

48449.name: Numeric coordinate values and the separating spaces/commas inside long sequences of numbers, strongest in SVG path data (e.g. "C31 21.8623 28.662..."), canvas bezier calls, and cubic-bezier() parameters. The fractional digits of decimals and the space after a number are the most likely to be marked. Weaker hits fall on other inline numbers such as q=0.9 and math expressions.

48462.name: Opening quote marks in code that begin a short string literal used for comparison or as a mode/type argument. Activation is strongest after typeof checks with == or === (e.g. 'object', 'undefined', 'number') and weaker for file-open modes ('rb', 'w') and other comparisons.

48477.name: Mathematical and physical terms for singular or pathological behavior, where a quantity blows up, breaks down or becomes ill-defined. The strongest cases are singularity, divergence/divergent, pole, and infinity/∞. Weaker cases include discontinuity, boundary layers, convergence issues, unboundedness, shocks, jumps, zero denominators, outliers, and whether something exists.

48504.name: A diffuse feature firing on mid-clause tokens (function words like 'and', 'of', 'to', 'him', verbs, and punctuation) where the sentence continues an action. It is strongest in classical Chinese biographical text and fires broadly on historical or biographical narrative about officials, emperors and generals, and on translated Chinese web-novel prose. It shows weak, scattered activation elsewhere, including scientific text, code and citations.

48551.name: The word "injury" and its variants (injuries, injured, split forms like "In|juries"), meaning physical harm or tissue damage. Activation is strongest in medical and biological contexts such as nerve, liver, or spinal cord injury, and weaker for generic mentions in news or accident reports. Related harm terms like "infection" activate only faintly.

The word "injury" and its variants (injuries, injured, split "in-jury"), strongest when used in a medical, physical-harm sense (e.g., knee/brain/nerve injury, acute injuries); weaker on odd contexts and occasional unrelated punctuation or conjunctions.

48554.name: The uppercase " HTML" token immediately after "<!DOCTYPE" in document type declarations, strongest at the beginning of a text. It is weaker when the declaration appears mid-text or follows other content, and shows only faint activation on scattered code tokens such as closing backticks.

486.name: Phrases in technical or instructional text that spell out what an operation or task does and what it acts on, such as its object, target, range or parameters. Activation is strongest in code comments, docstrings and log messages describing a function's action (e.g. 'summarize points based off of HexID', 'for tickers, in date range… pull into a dataframe', 'adds an event binding to label one'). Weaker activation appears on similar descriptive object or argument phrases in programming questions, math problems and how-to steps.

Natural-language descriptions of what code or a technical procedure does, strongest in inline code comments that state an operation's purpose (e.g. 'Create nodes for…', 'Find one record', 'for file stream open/close'). It fires across the whole verb or noun phrase naming the action and the data it acts on. Weaker activation appears on similar functional descriptions in technical prose, such as specs, docs and problem statements.

48607.name: The first word of an instruction or question in a problem or exercise, usually an imperative verb (Find, Calculate, Determine, Write, Show) or a question word (What, How, Which). It typically comes right after the setup or given information, often in math or science homework text. Weaker activations occur on similar sentence-initial directive words in other contexts (Share, See, Assume, Consider).

48620.name: Word-piece suffixes (most often "ella") that complete Latin-style scientific genus/species names, especially bacterial pathogens (Salmonella, Legionella, Brucella, Campylobacter, Vibrio). Activation is strongest for well-known pathogenic bacteria and weaker for the same suffix in personal names, fungi, or unrelated words.

48631.name: The division separator in a fraction, sitting between numerator and denominator: the slash in plain-text fractions like "1/2" or "4/3", and the "}{" in LaTeX \frac{a}{b}. Activation is strongest for simple numeric fractions. Weak firing also occurs on other ratio-like connectors, such as "in" in "1 in 10" and "-t" in "one-tenth".

The division/fraction separator between a numerator and denominator: the slash in fractions like 1/2, the LaTeX "}{" in \frac{a}{b}, ⁄ and ÷ symbols, and occasionally words expressing ratios ("out of", "divide by"). Activation is strongest for simple numeric fractions, especially those with a numerator of 1.

The separator between numerator and denominator in a fraction: the slash in plain-text fractions like 3/4, the fraction slash ⁄, and the "}{" (or \over) in LaTeX \frac expressions. It also fires weakly on similar ratio tokens such as "in" in "three in five" and "d" in dice notation.

48640.name: Fires mainly in technical and mathematical prose on the words that open or qualify a noun phrase naming a class of objects. Typical spots are restricting adjectives and determiners such as 'a finite reflexive' (digraph), 'a closed, orientable' (manifold), 'such' (logics), 'infinite' (trees), 'binary' (codes) and 'single' (lossy lines).
