It also fires on the connectors leading into them ('of', 'with', 'for two', 'and/or' between contrasted properties). The strongest signal is on property-specifying modifiers inside definitions or statements of hypotheses.

48662.name: Weak, diffuse activations on function words and continuation tokens in promotional or review-style descriptions of places and businesses, especially hotels, hostels, guest houses and other venues. The strongest firing comes right after a venue is named, as the text goes on to describe what it offers or how it is experienced (e.g., 'hotel hosts', 'specializes in', 'with easy access').

48682.name: Separator tokens inside structured identifiers, mostly the slash in URLs and file paths (also ::, _, -, ., :). It fires on the delimiter that comes just after one path or name segment and before the next, often merged with the first letters of that next segment ("/d", "/p", "_N"). It is strongest in URLs and file paths.

48752.name: Word-initial subword fragments of long medical or scientific words that are split across tokens, most often the prefix "antim" in antimicrobial. Weaker cases include "antib" (antibacterial, antibiotic, antibody), "colore" (colorectal), and the "ib", "if", "im" fragments after "ant". The token is the incomplete start of the word, before its completion.

48757.name: The second (losing or trailing) number in a score or tally, especially after a hyphen in sports results (e.g., 77-72, 31-28), along with similar opposing figures in vote counts, percentages and p-values. Activation is highest for close final game scores.

48766.name: The word "Question" opening a synthetic reading-comprehension Q&A block ("Question: ... Answer:") that follows a passage after a blank line; there are a few weak unrelated hits.

48777.name: Whitespace-only tokens (indentation spaces/tabs combined with newlines) forming blank or trailing-whitespace lines, especially between blocks of code (methods, statements) and occasionally in prose. Weak, sporadic activation on boilerplate tokens such as HTML closing tags and repeated page-template words.

48813.name: The hyphen (and the first characters right after it) that opens the fourth group of a UUID/GUID, i.e. the separator after the 8-4-4 portion and the start of the variant group (often 8, 9, a, b). It fires weakly on similar separators in other long hex strings, such as IPv6 addresses and PGP fingerprints.

48820.name: Numeric digits of a secondary or uncertainty value, firing most strongly on the number after ± (standard deviation or error margin) and also on standard errors, confidence bounds and tolerances. It fires weakly on other numbers that follow a primary value, such as the second column of a table or a percentage change.

48854.name: Opening curly braces (often fused with a quote, key, or parenthesis, like ' {"', ' {'', '({', '},{') that begin a new object/dict literal, especially a repeated element in a list of similar objects in code or JSON. The strongest cases are later entries in an array of records. It fires weakly on other repeated list-item starts such as '[' or indentation.

48887.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly at the start of a new clause, on the subject or relativizer that comes just before its verb. It is strongest on person nouns and relative pronouns introducing a clause, especially with past perfect 'had': 'officer who had served', 'the person had committed', 'the other party had reached', 'those that my…'. It also fires weakly on clause-initial pronouns (I, you, he, she) and on sentence boundaries or periods where a new clause begins.

48913.name: Line boundaries in code just before a new statement begins: closing tokens with a newline (")⏎", ");⏎", "))⏎") and leading indentation whitespace (or comment markers). Activation is strongest when the next line repeats a similar statement, especially consecutive print/assert/EXPECT/println calls.

48943.name: Tokens inside formulaic phrases and collocations whose next word is highly predictable, especially words that call for a following preposition or infinitive marker such as "to", "of" or "with". Examples include "allow you (to)", "so as (to)", "in addition (to)", "managed (to)", "taking into (account)", "in light (of)", "one (of)", "along (with)", "take care (of)" and "on the other hand". Discourse connectives like "However" and "Therefore" also trigger it weakly.

Words inside stock phrases and collocations whose next word is highly predictable, usually a preposition or complement: 'in addition (to)', 'the fact (that)', 'opportunity/intended/aspire/enables you (to)', 'synonymous/compliance (with)', 'result/field/occasion/full/lots (of)', 'as follows', 'for example', 'look forward (to)'. Discourse connectives such as 'However', 'Therefore', 'but also' and 'even if' also fire. Activations are weak overall.

48973.name: Mainly JavaScript anonymous callback openers, i.e. the "function" / "(function" / "() =>" / "{" tokens right after a call such as $(...), .ready(, addEventListener(..., or .onload =, with the strongest activations on jQuery document-ready wrappers like $(function(){ and .ready(function(){. It fires more weakly on "while True" loops and on prose transition openers such as "However,", "In addition," and "One of", which likewise introduce a following block or clause.

49001.name: Tokens inside highly repetitive, periodic sequences: the first token of a unit that repeats over and over (numbers, symbols, escape codes, code fragments, or repeated words), firing once the repetition pattern has been established and the token is predictable from earlier copies.

49026.name: CSS and style-sheet code, chiefly property names (margin, padding, border, font-size, background, color) along with their colons, values and semicolons inside selector braces. The strongest activations are on layout and spacing properties like margin and border. It fires weakly on similar layout or formatting terms in prose and other code, such as size, margins, font and time listings.

CSS style declarations, especially the opening of a body/selector rule block: the brace, indentation, and property names and values like font-family, margin, padding, line-height, color (strongest on "font", "margin", "0", ";"). It fires weakly on other styling or layout code such as background, size, colors, and canvas or plot settings, and on stray code formatting tokens.

49049.name: The command or operator that opens a regex substitution/transliteration in code: mostly the "s" of sed/Perl "s/…/…/" expressions (strongest right after sed '), plus related tokens such as "tr", "m/", the "//" of shell ${var//…}, and re.sub/gsub/preg_replace( calls.

49050.name: Closing brackets, mostly ")" but also "]", "}", and LaTeX \right, that end a parenthesized or bracketed group. They fire most strongly when the group closes an arithmetic or code expression, such as (v * 100.0) or (1 + max * 2), before an operator or cast follows. Weaker activations occur on closing parentheses in prose, phone area codes, and citations.

49071.name: Command-line program or tool names, typically the first word of a shell command a user is told to type or run, and most often a package manager or build tool followed by a subcommand like "install" (npm, go, composer, pod, pip, make, rails). Weaker activations fall on other command-like tokens: subcommands, flags, SQL keywords, menu commands and code identifiers.

49072.name: Leading whitespace/indentation tokens at the start of a line, typically right after a newline and just before a bullet point (•), numbered list item or indented code/config line. Occasional weak hits on separators like commas, "and", "by" or quote-reply markers.
Whitespace tokens that indent the start of a line, right after a newline. They usually come before list items ("1.", "•"), code lines, traceback entries, or other indented structured text.

49136.name: Fires on the token that completes a highly predictable, formulaic phrase or structure, usually in web or document boilerplate: "Flag as inappropriate", "Synonyms", "cite it", "referring to" and "marked *". The most frequent case is the ">" plus newline that closes an HTML "<thead>" tag before a table header row. Activation lands at the natural end of a templated segment, often just before a line break or a new section.

49138.name: The word "Plaintiff" naming a party in legal case captions (e.g., after a party name or case number, before "v." or "-Appellee"). Other activations are weak and scattered over function words and list items in structured text.

49156.name: The word "Received" (and occasionally "Published" or the French "reçu le") that opens a scholarly article's manuscript history and comes right before the submission date. It typically appears after the author affiliation or email lines, with a colon following it in some cases.

49204.name: Mid-sentence function words and phrase pieces in sports-news style reporting, especially football transfer, injury and match prose. It peaks on stock journalistic phrases about player status, timeframes and competitions, such as "until the end of the season", "out of action for", "will link up with", "on loan" and "in all competitions". It fires weakly on scattered tokens in other genres.

49216.name: Mid-phrase tokens that sit just before a highly predictable continuation. Most are function or filler words, especially the spurious inserted " typically" before "the" in spun, SEO-style gambling or tech articles, plus words like " together" (with), " addition" (to), " the", " to" and " can". It also fires on section numbers ("Section 2", "sec2") and on the second syllable of the Korean search term 검색.

49245.name: Tokens that complete or continue the names of institutions and organizations, mostly research bodies, universities, academies, labs and government agencies (e.g. 'Academy of Sciences', 'CNRS', 'NASA', 'Fraunhofer Institute'). They typically appear in author affiliations, addresses and URLs. Activation is strongest on the later parts of these multi-token names and their acronyms.

Mainly fires on tokens that complete names of research, academic or government institutions, especially acronym pieces and final name words (Chinese Academy of Sciences/CAS, MRC, CNR, National Natural Science Foundation of China, ETH, NHS, OWASP, Fédérale). It also fires on the "py" in __init__.py filenames. Elsewhere there is only weak, diffuse activation on function words, parentheses and indentation inside code comments and explanations.

49248.name: In code, the token right after a newly declared/defined identifier (variable, parameter, macro, class, or member) that begins its type, initializer, base class, constructor argument, array size, or macro expansion, e.g. 'var u user', 'x: Component', 'class Dog(Animal', 'vector<int> root(n', '#define pb push'. It fires weakly on a few non-code analogues.

49304.name: Fires mainly on sentence-final periods and newline tokens that close a sentence or field in formulaic boilerplate, such as NASA STI notices, copyright/permission statements, disclaimers, thesis declarations, safety data sheets and report form fields. These mark the boundary before the next predictable section. Weaker hits fall on predictable next words inside stock phrases or spam text (e.g., "weight loss", "male enhancement", "in addition").

49313.name: Words that frame a quantity or measurement as extreme or measured against a reference point, such as superlatives and record language (all-time highs, record, unprecedented, peak, maximum, near-record low), intensifiers (whopping, massive, impressive, staggering) and comparison baselines (current, average, planned, levels). These usually come right before a number or the thing being measured.

49322.name: A token that completes a highly predictable collocation or set phrase, typically the object or function word right after a verb or preposition, as in “lose weight”, “contact with skin” and “known as”.

49352.name: A diffuse feature that fires most strongly on mid-phrase tokens in formulaic boilerplate, such as cookie and privacy policy notices, software license text, website help or footer instructions, and job-ad disclaimers, across several languages. The marked word is usually a predictable continuation of the stock phrase (e.g. 'Cookie Policy and', 'The exception… is', 'innan du går'). Weaker activations fall on scattered tokens in ordinary prose.

49378.name: A broad structural-boundary feature in math, code and task-prompt text. It fires mainly on the first token of a new line or statement: the left-hand side of an equation (0 =, 4 =, x =, result =) and the indentation before code statements like try or print. It also fires on the final period, newline or punctuation that ends a problem or instruction prompt. Small numeric constants such as 0 or 1 inside expressions trigger it too.

4939.name: A diffuse, weakly-firing feature with no single trigger token. It is strongest in biographical or news-style passages about a specific named person, often a celebrity, such as Bowie, Madonna ("Madge"), Kanye West or Obsidian. There it fires on the person's name, possessives, and pronouns or phrases referring to them and their circle ("his crew", "her father", "you"). Elsewhere it shows only scattered low activations on function words and punctuation.

49406.name: Comma (occasionally the noun right before it, or a following "then") that closes a fronted introductory phrase or subordinate clause (time, cause, condition, context, e.g. "After deployment," "Since August 1998,"), marking where the main clause begins.

49417.name: Sentence-ending punctuation (periods, often merged with following newlines as ".⏎⏎") that closes a sentence or paragraph, especially at the end of a descriptive/bio-style passage (affiliations, credentials, organization descriptions) right before a topic shift or new section; strongest at the boundary into a new section or author/contributor block.

Sentence-final punctuation (periods, often merged with newlines) ending descriptive or biographical statements, especially closing an author/company bio or 'about' blurb, i.e. the boundary where a profile or description segment ends and new content begins.

49449.name: Words or values describing a hidden, concealed, disabled, or inactive state, such as hidden, none, off, concealed, collapsed, blank, false/true flags, or protected. These appear in both prose and code/CSS property settings, and are strongest for 'display: none' and 'hidden'.

49460.name: Methods-style descriptions of data and samples, as in research papers, dataset documentation or data-processing code. It fires on words that say how data were selected, gathered or combined, such as sample sizes ("n =", "N=933"), "included", "were included", "select a sample", date ranges ("for the years 2000 to 2010") and "This dataset tracks". Activations are weak and spread across the function words of these phrases.

4949.name: Words for touring or itinerant series of appearances or performances, peaking on "tour" (book tour, speaking tour, 19-city sold-out European tour) and related terms like circuit, campaign trail, concert, live set, stint and rollout. Activation is weak and diffuse on other tokens.

49566.name: Tokens inside website navigation or link boilerplate, mostly the word right after "Go" ("Go to", "Go Annotations", "Go to author profile"), plus similar UI labels like "Favorite Authors" and "nav_menus". A few weaker activations fall on scattered tokens inside lists or index-like text.

49601.name: Words naming distant or foreign places and destinations, such as countries, cities, regions, overseas or other-world locations, usually after travel or location prepositions (to, in, from). It also often fires on the word that follows them (for, when, where, a comma). There is weaker activation on broader 'elsewhere' domains like markets, industry, territory, another dimension, or a martian base.

49608.name: Spread thinly across mixed text, but strongest in legal, copyright and permission boilerplate that sets out prohibitions. It fires on the verb phrase after "may" or "should", especially "not be" and the passive verb that follows ("may not be created/offered/reproduced"). It also fires weakly on nouns like "name" or "term" in trademark-restriction text, and on scattered function words and punctuation elsewhere.

49614.name: Mainly fires on file-extension tokens in filenames inside error logs and stack traces (".cpp", ".kt", ".py", ".scr"), which give the strongest activations. It also fires weakly on opening bold markdown markers (" **") placed mid-sentence just before an emphasized phrase, and on table pipe separators.

49652.name: Name fragments of online document repositories, archives and hosting platforms (HAL, DSpace/eSpace, Wikisource, SlideShare, StudyMode, DOI, ORCID, open access), mostly inside URLs or the boilerplate repository notices in scraped academic documents. Activations are weak.

49662.name: Verbs, mostly participles, that come right after a noun and tell where it comes from or what causes it. "arising" is by far the strongest, especially in legal and liability wording like "damage arising out of" or "claims arising from". Weaker hits include "resulting", "stemming", "occurring", "originating", "derived" and forms of "arise", usually followed by "from".

49680.name: Nouns for the party who owes money or a financial obligation, strongest for "debtor" (including the "ors" in "debtors"), weaker for borrowers, taxpayers, the bankrupt and the "ent" in decedent; often preceded by "the"/"a" in legal or financial contexts. Scattered weak hits on unrelated tokens.

49689.name: Language that predicts or describes doom, ruin, decline, or catastrophic outcomes (death, collapse, destruction, being lost forever, societal or institutional downfall). It fires most strongly on the build-up to the disaster, such as 'we will all be', 'headed for a new ice age', 'net neutrality dies, they'll be', and 'societal collapse'.

Words in phrases describing a slide or trajectory toward a dire, extreme, or irreversible outcome (e.g., "headed for a bailout", "point of no return", "pretty soon there will be no choice but", "will be really rough", "become unhealthy", "edge of"). They mark warnings about where a trend or situation is going: escalation, catastrophe, loss, or becoming obsolete. The strongest firing is on the future and transition verbs (will be, become, lead to, end) and on the bad end state itself.

4969.name: A diffuse feature that fires on highly predictable continuations of fixed phrases, boilerplate and templates, such as web UI text ('Forgot your password', 'improve this', 'otherwise noted', '[top]'), code keywords following modifiers ('public abstract', 'Public Const', 'overloads the ... methods'), and set expressions ('longer than usual', 'came time'). It is strongest on programming-language declarations.

Java/OOP method declarations, especially the modifiers and return type after an annotation like @Override (e.g., "public void onCreate", "public abstract"). Weak, scattered activations on unrelated tokens (e.g., "time to", "SKU", "protected", "overridden", separators) appear to be noise.

49695.name: Fires on delimiter/separator tokens that introduce the next segment, most consistently the colon after a "User" speaker label at the start of a chat transcript. It also fires on lone spaces between citation or number fields, list dashes, arrows, hyphens, and abbreviation periods.

49746.name: Separator or operator tokens (=, :, ':, ',', ->, =>, -=, '(', '.') that come right after an index, key or counter in repetitive, enumerated sequences such as code assignments, dictionary entries, numbered lists and tuples. The model is predicting the value that follows the label. Activation tends to rise as the repeated pattern continues.

49756.name: Weak, diffuse activation on word-internal subword fragments, mostly in non-English or non-Latin scripts (Cyrillic, Hebrew, Arabic, Bengali, Japanese, Korean, Turkish, Polish, diacritic-heavy transliterations) and in rare or nonsense English words. It also fires on long runs of dot leaders in tables of contents. The common thread is low-frequency, mid-word tokenization in unfamiliar or noisy text.

49811.name: Mostly fires at structural or discourse boundaries: the word "Guide" closing the "Universe Guide" page header (strongest), trailing spaces right before paragraph breaks or equation numbers, dashes introducing a quote attribution, and sentence-initial transitions like "However". It also fires weakly on scattered mid-sentence words, often modifiers just before the noun they describe ("light sleepers", "side branch", "standard conditions").

49817.name: Color names used as arguments inside LaTeX/markup color commands (e.g. \color{red}, \blue{...}) activate strongly. Weaker, scattered activations fall on tokens inside code or markup syntax (class names, braces, enumerated option labels like "A.", "e.g.,") and on assorted function words.

49818.name: Function words and connectives (of, the, in, to, and, can be, as) inside expository scientific prose, especially descriptions of physical emission and signals (light, radio waves, spectra, luminescence, synchrotron emission, echoes). It fires most strongly in astrophysics passages explaining how emission is produced or modeled.

49838.name: Closing tokens that end a source file's import/use block and the newlines after it (strongest on Go's closing ')' of import(...) followed by blank lines; weaker on Rust '};', Java/Python import line endings). Also fires weakly on the first token after imports, such as 'pub' or indentation.

49933.name: Tokens containing the "ugh"/"ough" letter sequence (or the related "augh" sound, as in Vaughan), mostly in proper names and surnames (Hugh, Hughes, Dougherty, Greenough, Mughal, Baughman). Activation is strongest on "Hugh"/"Hughes". A few weak hits fall on paragraph breaks in web boilerplate such as "Leave a Reply".

49944.name: The opening quote token, often fused with a path start like "/", "<" or "./", that follows "File" in Python traceback lines (File "path", line N) and begins the file path. Activation is strongest when a Unix absolute path "/" follows. Other contexts score near zero.

49958.name: The final token of a heading, label, URL, or sentence that comes just before a line break and the start of a new structured section (headers, lists, profiles, report contents) on web pages.

49959.name: Separator tokens (mostly colons, also commas, 'by', dashes, newlines) that come right before an organization or publisher name in citation/metadata contexts. The strongest cases are the colon in bibliographic references between the place of publication and the publisher (e.g. 'New York: Kodansha', 'Albuquerque: University Press'). Weaker cases include field labels like 'Manufacturer:' or 'Publisher:' and taxonomic order separators.

49972.name: Tokens marking the point right before a predictable, structured continuation begins. Most often this is "Answer" after the options of a multiple-choice question, just before the answer letter. It also fires on the language tag after code fences (```python) and on a few template-like positions, such as "to use" in legal text and "I am" in a dialogue.

50007.name: Fires mostly on the "Answer" label that comes right after the A–D options of a multiple-choice question, just before the answer letter is given. It also fires more weakly on tokens within question or problem text that lead up to an answer, such as "mentioned in the text", "is" and "help me".

50042.name: The "inheritdoc" token in code documentation comments (e.g., /// <inheritdoc/>, @inheritdoc, {@inheritdoc}). Other tokens show only negligible, unrelated activation.

50048.name: The division slash (or decimal point / LaTeX \frac separator) inside a fractional number, especially in fractional exponents like ^(1/2), ^{1/4}, ** 0.5 for roots; weaker on plain fractions like 1/4 in lists.

50050.name: Words just before a description of a study or work's type or design, mainly in scientific abstracts. Typical cases are the article or verb that sets up phrases like 'This was a cross-sectional study', 'Methods: A...', 'we conducted a...', 'is a ... protocol', and the commas between design adjectives ('randomized, multicenter'). It fires most strongly on 'This study was' and 'This was a' after a Methods heading.

50059.name: Attribute or parameter names (especially "id", also name, class, width, help) that come right after a previous quoted value inside HTML/XML tags or function calls, just before the "=" sign. Activation is strongest for "id" on input elements.

50062.name: Mainly the opening token of an inline citation or reference marker placed directly after a claim in academic text, such as "[", "(", "\" before \textsuperscript or \(^, and "(^". It fires on the token right where a sentence's content ends and the citation begins. Weaker, scattered activations appear at other boundary points, such as a field label like "Damage" or "Method:" in structured lists, and a few words in casual speech.

50076.name: Fires on the word "limitations" in the standard software license boilerplate phrase "governing permissions and limitations under the License". It also responds to similar nouns that complete a legal "X and Y" pair, such as "rights and restrictions". Other contexts produce only weak, scattered activations.

50089.name: Words expressing localized, restricted, or subset scope, i.e. something confined to a small region, part, or specific domain. The strongest cases are "local" and "focal" with their nouns (local anomaly, local color inconsistency, focal impairment). Weaker cases include "patch of", the prefixes "sub-" and "micro", "-specific", "personal", "custom" and "intracellular". Activations are generally weak and diffuse.

50114.name: Clause-ending punctuation (mostly commas, sometimes semicolons/colons) placed at the end of a complete clause where the sentence continues with a dependent or qualifying phrase, especially in formulaic license/permission text ("...to do so, subject to"; "...provided"; "...cited, in accordance") and archaic biblical prose. Strongest in MIT/CC-style license boilerplate.

50120.name: Structural tokens in repetitive, templated sequences (code output comments, step lists, Q&A blocks, logs) that mark where the next item in the pattern begins: newlines, colons, comment markers like # or //, closing parens, and repeated line labels such as "Current Letter", "Step", "Question" or "print". It is a predictor of the recurring format.

50143.name: Tokens that complete the custom organization or project name segment early in Java-style package paths (e.g. com.<org>, org.<project>) within import statements, typically the final subword of the second or third path component just before the next dot. Weak scattered activations appear on unrelated prose.

50157.name: Notation-introducing phrases, mainly in mathematical and technical writing, that define or name a symbol or term. The strongest are "denote (by)", "we define", "let", "will be abbreviated by", "we will call", "the notation" and "we say", especially right before a LaTeX symbol. Weaker activations land on related convention-setting text such as nomenclature lists, symbol tables, code comments and syntax explanations.

Tokens in technical, math or code contexts where a name, symbol or notation is being defined or introduced, e.g. typedef, #define, using, \newcommand, "we write/say/note", "notation", "variable", "referred to as". Activation peaks on the defining keyword or the delimiter right before the new symbol or definition.

50203.name: Words about crafted, decorative or artistic objects and how they are made or embellished: carving, inlay, weaving, painting, gilding, intricate patterns, artworks, posters, doodles, engravings and materials such as wood, ivory and enamel. The strongest activations fall on descriptions of ornate craftsmanship, e.g. "carved from wood", "inlaid with ivory, enamel", "carvings" and "elaborate painting".

Weak activation on words for crafted, artistic or decorative objects and materials and the techniques that make them (art, paintings, prints, carvings, tiles, embroidery, quilts, marble, bronze, dance or music performances). It peaks on descriptions of how a decorative piece is made or what it depicts (carved, incised, adorn, depict, composed of, cut outs).

50232.name: A weak, diffuse pattern. It fires most strongly in repetitive, structured text such as matrices, HTML tables, coordinate lists, subscripts, author-affiliation numbers and phone numbers. The marked token usually repeats or continues an element seen earlier in the sequence (e.g. repeated matrix entries, "1a", ">C", "blow", "(1,0)"). Elsewhere, scattered ordinary content words get low activations.

Tokens inside repetitive, cyclic or structured sequences (number lists, coordinates, code, repeated symbols) where the token echoes or returns to an earlier element. Examples include a loop closing back to its start (0 → 1 → 2 → 0, the (3,0) element closing a polygon, "back to unity"), reversed or mirrored series, and repeated variable names like start or Top. It is strongest when a sequence wraps around to its initial value.

50258.name: Words for raids and violent disorder, chiefly 'raid' (raids, raiders, raided), then 'riot', plunder, ransack and storm. It also fires weakly on 'ra'/'ri'-initial lookalikes such as raft, raunchy, raucous and Raoul.

50266.name: The second half of a doubled or paired term, where a symbol or word repeats or is mirrored by its partner. The strongest cases are in physics and chemistry notation: particle pairs and collisions (pp, γγ, c c̄, D⁰–D̄⁰, A+A, gluon–gluon, proton–proton, ββ), diatomic subscripts (H₂, O₂) and conjugate pairs (Rᵀ R, ∂∂̄). It also fires on general repeated forms (A-A, NS-NS, Device-to-Device).

50280.name: A diffuse feature that is strongest on tokens inside mathematical expressions, such as fraction slashes and numerators ("1/7", ")/"), derivative notation "y'(", small numbers in exponents like ^{-1}, and LaTeX braces. It fires weakly on other structured or formulaic text: the parenthesis before an issue number in citations ("55(3)"), "contrib" in wiki edit logs, list separators and line breaks, and function words in garbled spam text.

50293.name: Separator punctuation (mostly "/", also ".", "-", ",") right after a four-digit year within dates, typically in URL paths (e.g. /2015/08/...), DOIs (j.cell.2016.10.026) and timestamps, at the point where the month or issue number comes next.

50326.name: Opening quotation marks (usually space-prefixed " or ') that begin a key or item in structured data such as JSON, Python dicts, or lists, typically following a comma or indentation. Activation peaks when the quote opens a dictionary key (e.g. "type", "value", "name"), and is weaker for plain list elements.

50331.name: Personal surnames (and name fragments), mostly as cited authors or researchers in academic-style references (e.g., "Heller, 1941", "Cottam et al."). Activation is strongest on the closing subword pieces of the surname, especially just before a year, "et al.", or a page number.

Personal surnames (and some given names or organization/brand names), with the strongest activation on the final subword pieces of multi-token names, especially names cited as sources, authors, or speakers (e.g., "X et al.", "X said", "according to X").

50332.name: Separator tokens (quote-colon, equals, colon, opening quote) between a key/attribute name and its value in code, HTML, JSON or HTTP headers, firing most strongly on the " content=" in HTML meta tags (name="description" content=) and on key-value pairs like "Referer": "https". Weak activation on other key:value or label: punctuation.

50340.name: Noun phrases naming the object or subject area of study or understanding, mostly in scientific and academic prose. They typically follow verbs or nouns like investigate, understand, insight into, shed light on, probe of, or knowledge of (e.g. 'the functions of phytohormones in…', 'an early stage of primate evolution'). Activation spans the whole object phrase, often including its internal 'of'/'in' links.

50346.name: The word "multipart" (and its pieces like "ultipart" in MIMEMultipart, or "Part" in MultiPart), mostly in code or HTTP/email contexts such as multipart/form-data and MIME messages. Related terms like FormData, boundary, and "-part" fire weakly.

50347.name: Mostly punctuation and short tokens at boundaries of assistant-style output, especially the closing '!' or '?' of helpful offer sentences ('happy to help!', 'How can I assist you today?'), 'Let' starting 'Let me know…' and markdown heading/bold markers ('###', '**') after '---' separators. Activation is strongest where a sentence, section, or title segment ends or a new one begins.

50377.name: Word-piece tokens inside a word that begins with "stre"/"Stre" or "St"+"re", firing strongest on "pt" in microbial and antibiotic names (Streptococcus, Streptomyces, streptozotocin, streptavidin, streptomycin). Weaker activations appear on other medical or biological word fragments, such as "ic" in penicillin, "pt" in Lepto-/tryptophan, and "fever", and on "stre" in strengthening or Streisand.

50378.name: Mostly fires in rule- or constraint-style text, on the words that tie a quoted or named term to a requirement about where or how it may be used. Typical cases are the "in" in "Do not include keywords [...] in the response", "must not be indicated in", "the term '...' for", "MUST be written" and "in the second sentence". Weaker activations land on scattered punctuation, quote marks and function words after a named item in code or technical text.

50408.name: The name "Carnegie", either as the whole token or the "egie" piece after "Carn", especially as the start of an institution's name (Carnegie Mellon University, Carnegie Hall, Carnegie Institution or Endowment). It also fires weakly on other "egie" word endings.

50409.name: Separators and positions inside enumerations: commas, "and", newlines, bullets, pipes and table tags that sit between items of a list or sequence (names, numbers, regions, table cells). Count words that announce how many items follow (three, four) also fire. The feature tracks position within a multi-item series.

50438.name: Weak, diffuse activation on technical/scientific notation, mainly the identifying parts of measurement or spectral labels: wavelengths and frequencies with units (730 nm, GHz), spectral lines and bands (H-alpha, [O III], Kα, Mg II h&k, red edge), isotope and element symbols, subscripts on variables (T_a, C_M), and specific rotation [α]D. Scattered function words in scientific prose also fire faintly.

50483.name: Single-letter variable names (x, n, k, p, t, etc.) at the point where they are introduced or defined in math, word problems, or code, e.g. after "let", "where", "an integer", "value of", or at a sympy symbol declaration. Weaker scattered activations fall on structural tokens in instructions, tables, and code.

50485.name: A diffuse, mostly weak feature with no single clear trigger. It fires most strongly on connective and function words inside formal expository sentences, such as prepositions, "was", "and", commas and colons (e.g. "Until the 19th century, geometry was the foundation of mathematics"). It also often fires on tokens within phrases or titles that repeat text seen earlier in the context, such as duplicated headlines, captions and repeated report lines.

50486.name: Tokens that open two or more nested parentheses at once ("((", " ((", "*((", " ((("), mostly in code and math expressions. Activation is strongest where the double paren begins a cast such as ((Type)obj), and is also high after return, if, or operators. There is weak activation on spaces before list numbers (" 1.", "No. 2").

50506.name: Standalone separator tokens: dashes (mostly "---" markdown horizontal rules, also single "-", em-dashes, pipes, soft hyphens) immediately followed by newline(s), dividing sections in markdown/LLM-style responses or garbled text. Strongest on isolated or repeated single-dash lines.

50520.name: Fires mostly on structural and boilerplate tokens in scraped or extracted documents rather than on content words. Typical cases are page and section headers, numbering punctuation and the first word after a list or section number ("3.", "5. Best", "Lesson 9"), dates and timestamps, URLs and file paths, title separators such as colons and dashes, and page markers. Activations elsewhere are weak and scattered.

50540.name: Official registration and identifier contexts, firing most strongly on clinical trial registrations (clinicaltrials.gov, NCT/ISRCTN/ACTRN codes, 'Trial registration number', 'pre-registered'). Weaker activation spreads to other registry-style ID text such as grant/agreement numbers, ISSN, CAS/EC/MDL numbers, company registration ('Registered in England & Wales') and the separators or digits of those IDs.

50546.name: Crystallographic orientation notation, chiefly Miller indices such as (001), (100), (110), (111), [001] and {01-12} written after material names or in surface/plane descriptions. Related crystal-geometry terms (axis, face, plane, cleavage, crystallographic, surfaces, grain boundaries, poles) activate weakly. Stray tokens like sentence ends and newlines show near-zero activation.

5056.name: Segments inside hierarchical names and paths, mostly in code: package, namespace, module and import paths (calculator.ast, DataLayer.Repositories, std::chrono, django.forms.models), plus URL/domain parts and file-path components. Weaker hits fall on parts of compound names, categories and titles.

50579.name: The noun "product(s)", especially in commercial disclaimer/endorsement boilerplate (e.g., "does not endorse any products", "reference to any specific commercial product"), strongest when it is the object of endorsement. There is weak, scattered activation on unrelated tokens.

50582.name: Highly predictable tokens inside fixed, boilerplate sequences, mostly in code: "ServletException" after "throws" in Java servlet methods, ".openapi" in package paths like com.intellij.openapi, and ".protocol" in location.protocol or web3j.protocol. It also fires on "eiusmod" in Lorem ipsum placeholder text. Activation is strongest where the token is nearly certain from context.

50611.name: Descriptions of performances, music and entertainment such as concerts, theatre, songs, singers, shows and the audience's experience of them. It fires most on the descriptive narration of a performance or its effect (e.g., 'she was convincingly angry', 'Both of these arias', 'musicians playing', 'want to hear'), with weak, diffuse activation elsewhere.

Fires most strongly on descriptions of lively musical or stage performances (concerts, duets, DJ sets, dancing, final chords), especially words that convey their energy and spirit, such as "energetic", "heartfelt" and "the whole time he's…". Weaker activations appear on structural boundaries like code line breaks, table separator pipes and sentence-ending punctuation.

50620.name: The word "how" (and close equivalents like "the way", "however", "which") introducing an embedded clause or question about manner or degree, typically after verbs like understand, remember, decide, choose, tell. It is strongest when "how" is the complement of such a verb or precedes "much/many/long/well". Weaker activation sometimes spreads to the following subject pronoun or auxiliary (it, they, I, do).

50634.name: The preposition "to" (sometimes with a following "the"/"their") right after verbs and nouns of contributing or adding, especially "contribute(s/d/ing)/contribution to", and more weakly "add to", "commitment to", "led to". It marks the slot where the thing being contributed to or affected comes next.

The preposition (mostly "to", sometimes followed by "the"/"this"/"its") that comes right after verbs and nouns of contributing, donating, adding or being integral, introducing the recipient or the outcome. Activation is strongest after "contribute/contribution" and weaker after "donate", "add", "integral" and similar words.

50675.name: File extensions in filenames, strongest for executable scripts that are being run (.sh, .py, .rb, .pl, .m, .php). Words that refer to running code, such as "script", "program", "run" and "make", also activate weakly.

50695.name: The capital letter "I" starting a new paragraph or section after a blank line. It fires most strongly when it is the Roman numeral of a first section heading ("I. INTRODUCTION"), typically just after an abstract, keywords list or DOI in academic papers. It fires weakly on a line-initial pronoun "I" and on a few scattered other tokens.

50709.name: The infinitive marker "to" (and sometimes the verb itself) that follows verbs of attempt or intention, chiefly "try/tried/trying" but also "attempt", "endeavour", "want", "promise" and "careful". It marks the point where a verb of effort is about to introduce the action being attempted.

50710.name: Multiplication and product concepts. It fires most strongly on "product of", on "multiply… together", and on × signs or equals signs in products such as "1 × 2 × 3 =" and "Z1 Z3 = Z2 Z4". It fires more weakly on related operations and terms like ratio, divided by, *= and Cartesian product, and faintly on unrelated tokens.

Fires on the concept of multiplication or combining two quantities: multiplication operators (*, *=, ')(', Times), 'multiplied by', 'product of', 'factor', and 'multiply the two equations'. It also fires on words tied to the other senses of 'product' and to bilateral exchange, such as 'Products', 'trade', 'free trade', 'Commerce', 'partnership', 'alliances' and 'business partners'. The strongest activations come from mathematical product contexts.

5079.name:
The first word(s) of a new segment that begins in lowercase where a capital letter might be expected: words right after a colon, an opening parenthesis, a line break or heading, or a sentence-ending mark. Typical cases are ": the/a/she", "(sometimes", "(a", "

by", "

hardback" and ". if the". Activation is strongest on lowercase sentence- or line-initial words that begin an explanation, definition or list item.

50800.name: Structural boundaries where a heading, title, closing tag, string, or statement has just ended and new content is about to begin. The active tokens are mostly newline-bearing ones such as '}⏎', '>⏎', '")⏎' and '⏎⏎', plus the indentation or opening token that follows ('\', ' <', spaces). This shows up across LaTeX section headers, HTML tags, code print statements and markdown titles. The strongest cases are HTML closing tags followed by indentation and a new opening tag.

Line-break tokens (often with leading indentation or a closing tag/quote/bracket/punctuation) that end a heading, title, tag or code statement and introduce the next line or block. Activation is strongest after closing HTML header tags (e.g. , ) followed by an indented new line and the next opening '<'.

50806.name: The word "sperm" and its fragments (sper, perm, spermat-), plus related male reproductive terms such as semen, seminal, gametes, ejaculation and fertility. Activation is strongest for the literal word "sperm" in reproductive contexts and stays high even in compounds like "sperm whale" or "spermatic".

50969.name: The word "behavior/behaviour" (and "behave/behaves/behaved") plus related terms for how something acts, operates, or responds (functionality, functioning, act strangely/differently, what happens, behave this way/fashion). It fires most strongly on the noun "behavior" when it refers to how a system, program, object, or phenomenon operates.

Words for how something acts or functions, chiefly "behavior/behaviour" and its verb forms (behave, behaves, behaving), plus near-synonyms like act, performance, treatment, response and fashion. Activation is highest for the noun "behavior" used in technical or analytical contexts, such as software behavior, the exact behaviour, qualitative behavior, or the behavior of a system.

50970.name: Tokens inside identifier-like strings such as filenames, image paths, URLs, DOIs and captions, mostly the final numeric suffix or last path/name segment (e.g. 'image1', '-1', '004') just before the extension or line break.

50982.name: Self-referential receiver keywords in code, chiefly Rust/Python "self"/"Self" (especially "(self" and "&mut self" in method signatures), plus "this"/"me"/"ThisWorkbook" in other languages and in `use x::{self, ...}` imports. There is weak, sporadic activation on self-referential "this" in prose and on assorted unrelated tokens.

50998.name: The noun (or first word of the noun phrase) right after a possessive determiner, especially "our", "your", "my" and "their". Activation is strongest for "our" plus a work or group noun, as in "our proposal", "our study", "our method" or "our company".

The noun (or noun phrase) that directly follows a possessive determiner such as "our", "your" or "my", i.e. the thing being possessed. Activation is strongest for organizational or technical possessions like company, team, servers, app and program.

51024.name: The first part of a multi-word proper name, a place or brand that comes right before the rest of the name. It fires most strongly on city or region names in front of a sports team name (New York Jets, Houston Rockets, Los Angeles Kings, Tampa Bay Buccaneers). It fires more weakly on company or brand names in front of a product (Amazon Echo, Nintendo Switch, Toyota Supra) and on place names in front of organizations or newspapers.

51075.name: The variable token right after a numeric coefficient in algebraic equations being solved (e.g. the "x" in "2x = 6", "-9*m"). It is strongest for the "*m"/"*p" multiplication form in "Solve ... for m" problems. Activations elsewhere are weak and scattered.

51120.name: Mostly code decorator, annotation and attribute names: the module or namespace parts after @ or #[ (e.g. asyncio, scrapy, winapi::, pytest.mark, tf.keras). It also fires on the ".," in "e.g.," and weakly on function words that come right before a noun phrase in prose.

51143.name: The word "being" and closely related welfare terms: strongest on "-being" completing "well-being" (and "wellbeing"/"wellness"). It fires more weakly on "being(s)" as a noun for an entity or existence ("human beings", "living beings", "state of being") and on "welfare".

The word "being" used as a noun, peaking in "well-being"/"wellbeing" (health, welfare sense). It also fires more weakly on "being(s)" meaning an entity or existence (human beings, magical beings, one's being) and on related welfare words like "wellness" and "welfare".

51199.name: Fires on the ".math" token that names a math module or domain, strongest in Java-style package imports (java.math, gdx.math, lang3.math) and weaker in URLs like www.math.* and math macros (_MATH, RhinoMath). Other tokens show only negligible noise.

51206.name: Mid-word subword pieces, mainly "opo" in "hematopoietic"/"haematopoietic", plus related "o"/"iet" in erythropoiesis/erythropoietin and thrombopoietin. Weaker on "op" in myeloproliferative, on "opo" in other words and names (Jacopo, Limpopo, Mythopoetic), and on medical suffixes such as "-ogenesis".

51228.name: Words inside parenthetical, non-restrictive modifiers that interrupt a main clause: tokens just after a noun followed by a comma (appositives, 'which/who' relative clauses, participial phrases like 'used in', 'based in', 'inspired by'). Activation peaks at the start of the inserted descriptive clause (verbs, prepositions, adjectives) before the sentence returns to its main predicate.

51232.name: Citation and reference markers in academic or encyclopedic prose: the opening bracket/parenthesis and the digits of reference numbers (e.g. [13], (2), .[19]) and of author–year citations (e.g. (Mark, 1985; ...)), firing most strongly on the final year digit. It also fires weakly at points where a statement ends and a source or attribution follows, such as punctuation before a speaker's name or words like "previously" and "below".

Citation and attribution markers right after a claim or statement: academic references (opening parentheses, author-year dates, et al., bracketed footnote numbers like [5] or .[3]), plus similar source cues such as "according to", "he said", closing quote-comma before a speaker, and URL fragments. The year digit or footnote number activates most strongly.

51236.name: Biting, pest and disease-carrying arthropods, mosquitoes above all, plus flies, ticks, fleas and moths, often split mid-word (e.g. "quito", "opheles"). It also fires on disease-vector vocabulary such as "vector", "-borne", "reservoir", "biting" and "bitten". Activation is strongest for mosquitoes in malaria and disease-transmission contexts.

51243.name: Initial subword fragments of proper names that are split across tokens and need a continuation, especially surname or given-name stems like "Kauf" (Kaufmann/Kaufman) and "Humph" (Humphrey/Humphries), with weaker activation on similar fragments ("Guth", "auf" in Beaufort, "ph" in Umphrey's).

51279.name: The preposition completing a source-attribution phrase, mainly "to" in "According to" and also "per" in "As per" or Dutch "volgens". It is strongest when "According to" opens a sentence and introduces a named source such as a person, organization or publication, and weaker after a lowercase mid-sentence "according".

51291.name: Mainly a coordinating conjunction ('and'/'or') linking two alternative formats, media or representations (fraction and decimal, microfilm and electronically, electronic or paper, numerals and words). It fires weaker on other connective tokens inside a list or phrase that predict a parallel continuation (commas in lists, '->', 'the' after a preposition).

51295.name: The word "label" as an HTML tag name inside form markup, firing hardest on the opening <label> tag (often before for="...") and more weakly on the closing </label>. Weak activation on other UI label references (gr.Textbox label=, ttk.Label, JSX <Label>) and stray code tokens such as print.

51302.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires mostly on tokens that complete a phrase or clause, typically the head noun ending a noun phrase (e.g., platform, market, rotor, happiness), and on the punctuation that follows, such as periods, commas or newlines. Occasionally it spreads across short continuation spans right after a sentence boundary (e.g., "The chart suggests", "The benefits ... from CBD is greatly affected"), suggesting a general clause-boundary or phrase-closure signal.

A diffuse, weakly selective feature with no clear lexical target. It fires at low levels on scattered function words, sentence-ending punctuation (often a period before a line break), and occasional content nouns in ordinary running prose. Its strongest activations come as long contiguous spans across whole clauses in conversational, instructional or promotional sentences, for example 'colors for your convenience... are saved', 'conclude that if they can't finish it on normal mode' and 'is to be the leading trusted online source'.

51313.name: Separator or ellipsis tokens (especially "..", "...", "-", ":", ",") right after a number or item in a sequence, range, or enumeration (e.g. 0..7, 1-4, 1. , 1:). They mark the boundary where a list or range continues, mostly in noisy code-like text.

51324.name: Fires on clause/sentence boundaries (periods, commas, paragraph breaks, and the conjunction or pronoun starting the next clause) right after a statement about excess, avoidance or prevention. Typical preceding words are overload, overwhelmed, overboard, too much, avoid, prevent, waste and criticise. The feature marks the end of such a cautionary or limiting clause.

51329.name: Words about carrying, holding or transporting goods: cargo, freight, loads, contents, packing, containers and vehicles (trains, wagons, lorries, boxes, stuffed or full). Activation is strongest on "cargo", "load" and "full of".

51359.name: Comment markers (mostly "#", also "//", "///", "/*", "##") at the start of a line in code or scripts, usually right after a newline and often continuing a run of comments or following a shebang line. Weaker activation on other line-leading markers such as bullets, dashes and newlines.

51378.name: Diffuse, weak activations spread across scientific/technical prose (physics, plasma, astrophysics abstracts and reports). The highlighted tokens are mostly function words and generic noun-phrase pieces such as "the", "of", "amount of", "effect", "nature" and "confinement", often inside descriptive phrases about physical quantities and processes. There is no single specific word; the common thread is academic scientific register.

51380.name: Repeated structural filler tokens in ASCII tables, diagrams and box drawings: runs of dashes, box-drawing lines, pipes and padding whitespace that form row separators or column borders. Activation is strongest in the later parts of long horizontal rules and corners (e.g. ─, ---, +----+). It is weaker on stray symbols or words inside aligned columns.

51406.name: Structural and attribution tokens in news or journalistic prose: sentence and paragraph boundaries (period plus double newline, headline-ending newlines), the first word of a new paragraph, and reporting or attribution words such as "said", "according to", "announced", "stresses" and "found". It also fires on the punctuation around quotes, source names, datelines and photo credits. Activation is strongest on "said" after a quote and on paragraph breaks.

51409.name: Tokens right before an answer is given, mostly "Answer" and especially the colon after it in Q&A and multiple-choice quiz formats, predicting the answer that follows. Weaker hits on other spots just before an expected answer or continuation (e.g., "is ___" before a result, "Leave a Reply", cout <<).

51434.name: Tokens of code and markup syntax in noisy or garbled technical text: URI scheme separators and prefixes (javascript:, mailto:, file:///, urn:), format specifiers like {:?}, HTML attribute names (href, classid), command flags, and odd punctuation fragments (=_, ,_, =?). These are mostly glue tokens that sit inside URLs, code strings, or command lines.

51441.name: The JavaScript DOM method token "addEventListener" (usually ".addEventListener" after document, window, or an element variable) used to attach event handlers; strongest on document/window calls. Related "EventListener" in removeEventListener activates weakly.

51492.name: Text inside error, warning or status messages from software and systems (e.g. "No address found", "failed to destroy network for", "Access Denied", "Operation timed out", "Prototype mismatch"), especially quoted or logged failure strings. The strongest activations fall on the failure words themselves (found, failed, denied, mismatch). Many weak activations are scattered over unrelated technical or code tokens.

Text of error, warning and system status messages: words inside quoted or reported software errors and failure notices (e.g. "invalid input syntax", "could not connect", "no longer supported", "unable to save", "cannot be empty", "not found"). The strongest responses are on negations and failure terms ("not", "invalid", "error", "No"). There are weaker hits on boilerplate website notices ("you're using an unsupported browser", "you already have an account") and scattered technical tokens.

51505.name: Language that expresses predictions, expectations or intentions about future outcomes. It is strongest on modal and forward-looking phrasing such as "will/'ll be", "expect that", "hoping to get", "sure to", "promises to be" and "primed to", especially in sports previews and forecasts. Activation peaks on the auxiliary or infinitive "to" that sets up the anticipated event.

51536.name: The "cellul" / "ul" / "ulos" subword pieces of cellulose-family words (cellulose, hemicellulose, nitrocellulose, cellulosic, cellulase, celluloid, cellulite, cellulitis). It is strongest for " cellul" in cellulose. Other sugar or chemical fragments (xyl-, -lose) activate only weakly.

51541.name: Opening sigil tokens, mostly "%" (also "@", "{", "[", "«"), that begin a placeholder, variable, or format specifier in code or shell syntax, such as %VAR%, %s, %(name)s, %%I, "%~1" or @param. Activation is strongest in batch/shell-style variable references.

51568.name: The word "affair(s)" (incl. French "affaire", "Public/Home Affairs", "state of affairs", love affair, all-day affair) is the strongest trigger. Weaker hits go to near-synonyms for general domains or concerns after a modifier, such as matters, issues, business, relations and things.

The word "affair(s)" in all its senses: a domain or field (public, foreign, rural, world, current affairs, often in department or job titles), an event or occasion ("an all-European affair", "a messy affair"), and a romantic affair. It fires most strongly on "affairs"/"Affairs". Near-synonyms for a subject or business, such as matters, relations, liaison, business and fiasco, fire weakly.

51630.name: Separator or lead-in tokens (commas, 'and', 'or', pipes, table-cell tags, bullet/bold markers, newlines, indentation, 'The', 'a') that come immediately before the next item in an enumeration, glossary or definition list, especially one naming technical, programming or vocabulary terms (imports, keywords, language constructs, acronyms). The feature anticipates that a new term or list entry is about to be introduced.

51644.name: Internet laughter or reaction slang in casual writing, mainly "lol"/"LOL", along with "haha", "kek", "OMG" and emoticons. It fires most strongly on a standalone "lol" placed at the end of a clause or sentence. It also fires weakly on look-alike letter strings such as "Lol" in "Lollipop", "Lolwe", "Lollapalooza" and "LOL" as in League of Legends.

Internet slang laughter/reaction interjections in informal text, chiefly "lol"/"LOL" (strongest), plus variants like "lulz", "LMAO", "haha", "hehe", and weaker "OMG"; often the final token completing the acronym, typically placed at the end of a sentence or clause.

51663.name: Marks the point where a statistic's clause wraps up, usually the word "line"/"level" in "(at or below) the poverty line" or the comma that follows. Activation is strongest on "poverty line," right before another percentage figure. The same feature fires weakly on clause-ending commas after other percentage or statistic statements (e.g., "X% of voters think ... is hot," "not expected,").

51666.name: Word-final pieces of anatomical terms for the eye and its parts, chiefly "ocular" in intraocular/binocular/ocular and "reous" in vitreous. Others include intravitreal, choroid/choroidal, uveitis, iris, iritis and subretinal. Activation is strongest for intraocular (especially "intraocular pressure") and vitreous. Weak activation appears on non-eye lookalikes, such as choroid plexus and intra-articular, and on stray tokens.

51675.name: The subword token "del"/"Del" (and close variants like "dele", "delic", "deline", "el") at the start of a word that it only partially spells, as in delve, deliver, delirious, deleterious, delicacy, delineate, or names like Delphine, Delly and Delin. Activation is strongest for a capitalized " Del" beginning a proper name or sentence-initial "Delve"/"Delivered".

51693.name: Highly predictable continuation tokens in fixed formulaic or templated text. The strongest case is "Circuit" after an ordinal in U.S. Court of Appeals names (5th/Fourth Circuit). Weaker cases include the hyphen or digits inside DOI and ISSN codes, "Destination" after "Choose", "Asked" after a user name in Q&A listings, "_wallet" after "account_balance", and table markup.

51716.name: Fires at structural boundary tokens that end one segment and precede new content. These include question marks or newlines right before an answer, the period after a multiple-choice letter before the option value, and spaces or colons before a numeric value. It also covers paragraph breaks before a new heading or section, and web-page boilerplate labels such as "Leave a Reply", "Write a Review", "Sponsored", "BrainMass" and "Author".

51742.name: The '="' token that opens an attribute value in HTML/XML-like markup, most often right after 'class' or 'id' on div/span tags (e.g. class="container"). It is strongest on div class attributes and weaker on other markup openings such as ' <' before structural tags or other quote characters.

51799.name: The delimiter right after a creative work's title (mostly films, also books, shows, plays) or an author name, usually an opening parenthesis or bracket, that introduces a release year or similar annotation. Occasionally it is a space, dash, comma or "in" placed before a year, and it is strongest in lists of titles with years.

51801.name: Words naming the hoped-for, uncertain, or prospective outcome or endpoint of an action or process, usually verbs and nouns after modals, 'to', 'will', or 'able to'. Examples are success, conquer, save, be passed, get fixed, elect, failure, champion, and breakthrough. They mark the goal or result that might or might not be achieved.

51807.name: Continuation subword tokens inside proper names and foreign or uncommon words, especially personal names, places, institutions and non-English or non-Latin script terms. Activations are weak and diffuse; they are slightly stronger for distinctly foreign character sequences such as Czech, Polish, Russian, Chinese or Romanian.

51829.name: Tokens inside long runs of the same repeated token or short pattern, such as dashes, asterisks, quotes, stars or "true". Activation builds the longer the repetition continues, peaking in decorative separator lines. Ordinary prose words fire only weakly.

51832.name: The word "sustainable"/"sustainability" in any form, including other languages (German Nachhaltigkeit, Turkish sürdürülebilirlik). Weaker firing on related ethical or long-term terms such as responsible, renewable, holistic, inclusive, eco, lasting and security.

51837.name: Numbers that bound an age range (mainly the upper endpoint after a hyphen or 'to', as in '30-39 years'), often together with a following 'years'. Weaker activations appear on other numeric ranges such as year spans.

51850.name: Fires on tokens where a new item or condition is about to be added. These are mainly conjunctions ("and", "和"), commas, sentence starters ("If", "Each", "The") and list bullets ("- The") that introduce the next clause or requirement, often in technical definitions, specifications or problem statements. It also fires on monotonous repeated filler sequences such as runs of newlines, "|", "***" or repeating fragments.

51851.name: Tokens in code and command-line text that end an argument, string or path, mostly closing quotation marks (often fused with ')', ',' or ';'), closing brackets, file extensions like .zip/.yaml/.diff, and line-continuation whitespace. They fire where a literal or argument finishes and the next argument or code resumes.

51866.name: Repeated package-name tokens in sequential Java import lists, chiefly " android" (and the "import" before it) in Android import blocks. Activation builds the deeper into the list it gets, peaking around android.widget/android.view imports; it also fires weakly on the next "import" line once the android imports end. Weak scattered activations appear at list or section transitions, such as an abstract's closing period before its keyword list.

Structural punctuation and separator tokens (commas, spaces, '=', LaTeX '\(') in technical or structured text, such as code import lists, numbered Q&A, and math notation. It fires mainly where a token repeats an established pattern, e.g. later items in a comma-separated list, a second function definition, or a repeated 'Question N' header.

5188.name: Separator tokens (mostly a lone space, but also '.', '/', ':', '-') that come right before a multi-digit number in structured references: citation page/article numbers, DOI suffixes, suite numbers, timestamps ('at 14:25'), post/view counts and phone numbers.

51915.name: The first token of a direct object or argument: a determiner, opening quote or parenthesis, or the first piece of a multi-token name or identifier. It typically follows a verb, preposition, or function call (e.g. print(lst, open TEST, into conf, the + noun). Activation is weak and diffuse, and is somewhat stronger for code identifiers and function arguments.

Tokens that open a noun phrase or multi-part name/identifier right after a verb or preposition, where the following token completes a specific entity. These include determiners after instruction verbs in recipes ('add the', 'whisk together the', 'cutting your'), first subword fragments of names or codes ('Ch|aitanya', 'R|ijiju', 'K|ARB', 'i|Red', 'Sim|Cash'), hyphens inside alphanumeric labels ('RM-131', 'carbon-13') and labels like 'Step'/'Group' that precede an index.

51922.name: The word "enterprise(s)" (and cross-lingual equivalents like 企业, empres-), meaning a business or organization. It is strongest in the corporate IT/software sense of large organizations (enterprise applications, enterprise IT, Enterprise plan) and weaker for general business ventures, social enterprises, or company names.

51928.name: Sentence-ending punctuation (mostly periods, sometimes with newlines, colons, ?/!) at abrupt boundaries in incoherent, spammy or machine-generated text, where the next sentence is unrelated to the previous one. Activation is strongest after citation-like fragments (years, page numbers, journal references) that are followed by an unrelated topic.

51937.name: Biographical or profile-style text: fires at the points where a description of a person (or organization) moves on to the next fact about them, especially on the subject pronoun, name, or verb that opens a new clause or sentence ("He was", "She is", "who served as", "has been a", "I publish") and on articles introducing a role ("the author/director of").

51945.name: Fires on the first token of a new line or block after line breaks, especially in degenerate, whitespace-heavy or garbled text. It responds to runs of newlines and spaces, and to the first word or fragment, code comment marker (#, //, /*) or symbol that starts a new segment after a break.

51946.name: Mostly in code and math, fires on the token naming a function or operator right before its argument list or operand, i.e. a function name or name suffix just before "(" (f, func, add, _count, _function, rho, D), or an index/call bracket. It also fires weakly on operators (=, *) and punctuation that precede a computed expression.

51957.name: Diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires on connective tokens sitting just before the content that completes a phrase. These are mostly function words ("the", "by", "with"), bare spaces and punctuation, and the next token is usually a number or a key noun. Typical cases include the space between a month and a year, the space before the last number in a list, and "by" or "the" before an agent or object. A few hits fall on in-word or in-equation tokens instead.

51970.name: Mainly the word "verified" in the boilerplate "Short Answer / Expert verified" header of homework-help solution pages, which comes just before a worked answer. Weaker hits fall on scattered tokens in math, LaTeX and code text (operators, superscripts, indentation) with no clear shared meaning.

51971.name: A weak, diffuse signal over the core clause of normative, definitional or interpretive statements. It falls on copulas, modals (must, shall, should be, can be), negations and qualifiers in sentences that state a rule, principle, legal provision or how something should be understood. Typical contexts are legal and constitutional clauses, doctrinal or scriptural interpretation, and methodological principles.

51973.name: Tokens immediately preceding a multi-component value such as a coordinate pair, vector, tuple, dimensions (e.g. 640x480, 2.4m by 3.6m), grid size or array index. These are mostly opening brackets or parentheses ('[(', '((', '=[', ' (', 'vec![', 'new Point'), colons or spaces right before the first number of the group. The feature anticipates an upcoming tuple or dimension list of numbers.

51990.name: Minus signs (often fused with an opening parenthesis) that mark a negative number as the second operand of a multiplication or division, e.g. "* -1", "× (-3)", "/ -2". The strongest cases are products of negatives like "-3 * -3" or "inf * -1". There are weaker activations on other math and code operator tokens such as "*", "(", "=" and "/".

5200.name: Whitespace tokens (often unusual or non-breaking spaces) immediately preceding a special Unicode symbol such as an emoji, ℃, ω, ⌚ or ‹. More weakly, the feature fires on stray formatting and encoding artifacts like Â, €, BOM or directional marks, combining diacritics in kaomoji, bullets (•, ·, ●) and list-number punctuation.

Weak, diffuse activation on unusual or non-standard characters and encoding artifacts: special Unicode symbols (bullets, emoji, zero-width/invisible spaces, BOM, variation selectors, braille blank), odd whitespace before non-Latin text, mojibake fragments, HTML entities, and escaped unicode sequences.

52011.name: The capitalized token "Json" (mostly ".Json") in code, peaking in namespace/package imports such as Newtonsoft.Json, System.Text.Json and javax.json.Json. It fires more weakly on Json in class or identifier names (JsonUtil, JsonParser). Faint activations on unrelated function words and punctuation are noise.

The token "Json" (capitalized JSON), mostly embedded inside camel-case code identifiers, class or file names (e.g. DoseJson, Wiki2Json, SimpleJsonWSItem). It also fires weakly on a few unrelated tokens.

52035.name: The "/wp" path segment (WordPress) in URLs and file paths, usually right after a domain or directory and before "-content", "-includes" or "-json". Weaker on standalone "wp"/"WP" tokens (e.g., "wpb-js-composer" CSS classes) and other URL path segments like "/media", "/node" and "/product".

52043.name: Nouns naming a property or attribute category in descriptive or spec-style text, often as section headers (Personality, Screen, Voice, Inhalation, Spore Print). Activation is strongest for sensory terms, especially taste and smell (flavor, notes, inhale/exhale, odor, aroma, bite).

52046.name: Mostly code: the property or method name that comes right after an object or selector and sets an attribute, such as .setVisibility, .setImageResource or .DataSource. It also fires on CSS property names like background, font-weight and flex-wrap, and on hyphenated config keys like user-agent. Weak scattered activations appear on bullet-point indentation spaces and on some ordinary prose tokens.

52064.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens where the text becomes unexpected or incoherent. Typical triggers are spliced or spam-inserted phrases, duplicated words ('the the', 'like like'), typos ('firewords'), OCR and formatting artifacts (ligatures, broken citations, stray numbers or spaces) and abrupt topic shifts. It often lands on the noun or term right at the point of disruption.

52073.name: Tracks state that changes step by step, especially quantities being reduced over time. In code it fires on loop-state variables and their updates: while/if conditions, mutated variables (n /= i, x = x - 2, self.position +=) and the statements that follow them. In prose it fires on remaining or diminishing amounts, such as supply dwindling, the remaining error being smaller, days remaining, or 'this leaves eighteen'. Activations are mostly weak and diffuse.

52079.name: The ".slf" token in Java logging package paths (org.slf4j, lombok.extern.slf4j), especially in import statements. Related logging-package tokens like ".log" in org.apache.log4j get weak activation. Other tokens only fire faintly.

52115.name: The verb or predicate that follows a noun phrase naming a qualification, item or action and judges how desirable, required or acceptable it is, as in "is a plus", "would be desirable", "is a must", "preferred", "would be appreciated" or "can help". It is especially common in job requirement lists and in requests or guidelines. Activation is strongest on the copula or modal ("is", "would be") and on evaluative words like "plus" and "must".

52123.name: Empty parameter lists opening anonymous functions or lambdas in code, i.e. the "()" or "(()" token right before an arrow (=> or ->). It is strongest when it is passed as a callback argument, as in setTimeout(() =>, new Thread(() ->, or useFactory: () =>. It fires weakly on related placeholders such as "_" in for-loops, Rust "(move" closures and Fn() bounds, and on scattered commas in lists.

52142.name: Words about the release format, version, or edition of a media product, such as edition, version, copy, remake, re-release, HD, Blu-ray, resolution, recording, or review. Activations are weak and diffuse. They peak in product and review listing contexts like 'Review by', price lines, Blu-ray/720p, and remake.

52160.name: Separator or connective tokens in the middle of structured, formulaic sequences whose continuation is highly predictable. Most often this is the hyphen inside DOI, article and archive identifiers (e.g. s41561-018-0069, halshs-00007196) or page ranges, plus "al" in "et al." citations. Weaker cases include a space before a number, timestamp separators, and function words in prose.

52176.name: A diffuse feature that fires on the opening words of an expository sentence that comes right after a heading, bullet label, colon or title. It mostly lands on the subject and main verb or connective that introduces the description ("is believed to", "emphasizes that", "Go to", "is assigned to", "A one deck version"). In other words, it tracks the start of the body text that explains or defines the labelled item.

52201.name: Values assigned to a radius, above all the CSS "border-radius" property: the colon and pixel amount right after it (":5px", ": 35px") activate strongly. Weak activation also appears on tokens right after a mention of radius or a size in code and math ("radius is", "radius =", circle-drawing arguments) and on assorted formatting tokens.

52205.name: Incomplete word fragments, mostly stems or prefixes of longer, often technical or academic words, where the next token supplies a derivational suffix such as -ation, -ity, -ment, -ance or -ize (e.g. polar|ities, mobil|isation, reint|roduced, co|ales|cence). A few whole words that begin a compound or phrase also activate weakly.

52208.name: The opening brace plus newline, and the indentation that follows it, at the start of a struct or enum definition body (mostly Rust `pub struct/enum Name {`, also Go `type X struct {`), right before the first field or variant is listed. It fires weakly on other structural separators such as list indentation, colons, and table cells.

52226.name: Key content words that complete a domain-specific phrase, often the object or verb after a setup like 'motion to', 'applied for', 'sentence of' or 'a'. Activation is strongest for legal and judicial vocabulary such as dismiss, sued, affirmed, eviction, asylum and prison terms in years, with weaker, diffuse firing on technical or topical nouns in other domains.

52259.name: In scientific and technical prose, this fires weakly to moderately on words just before or between mentions of observation and measurement methods, especially imaging types and electromagnetic bands (radio, infrared, thermal, VHE emission, nm ranges, RF/IF, radiography vs sonography, fMRI). The activating tokens are often connectives and modifiers such as 'and', 'or', 'of', 'at', 'both', 'multiple', 'conventional' and 'functional'. The strongest case is 'observed at radio wavelengths at very late times'.

52293.name: Tokens that close a repeated entry in structured or tabular data, most often the unit after a number in conversion tables (miles, knots, hours, /s, ug/m3, t) and closing tags or brackets in HTML tables and code. These are mostly end-of-row items just before a newline. There are some weak unrelated activations in prose.

52300.name: Mostly fires on a middle chunk of digits inside long numeric identifiers, especially DOI suffixes (e.g. journal.pgen.100|498|5) and other ID codes, where the value is arbitrary and hard to predict. There are weaker activations on other unpredictable tokens, such as lorem-ipsum or nonsense words and the '>' plus newline after <thead in HTML tables.

52303.name: Separators between items in enumerated lists, especially keyword, tag, or synonym lists (commas, semicolons, bullets, dashes, slashes, 'or'). They fire on the delimiter that comes just before the next item, and are strongest in long keyword lists.

52325.name: Fires on the operand right after a relation or operator, chiefly the value on the right-hand side of an equation or inequality (after =, ≥, >). It peaks on constants in simple algebra like "x − 5 = 10" or "≥ 28". It also fires weakly on the object following comparison or operation words in code and prose ("greater than", "of a", "uninstall it").

52335.name: Fires at the very start of a document on leading boilerplate or list formatting: indentation spaces, bullet points (•) and numbering like "1.", plus the first word that follows. These are usually navigation menus, breadcrumbs and list items. It responds weakly to other opening structural markers such as runs of newlines, section commands, separator lines and stray header or menu words like "Stations".

52346.name: Tokens in scientific and technical writing, mostly abstracts and methods sections, that describe a material, device or method being made, prepared or studied. The strongest hits are the words that name or connect the material and its preparation, such as synthesis, polymer, nanoparticles, deposited, coated with, obtained by, and "the synthesis of a". Weaker hits fall on connectives and component lists in materials and method descriptions.

52360.name: The subword token "itone" inside words, firing most strongly in "peritoneum/peritoneal" (anatomy) and more weakly in "baritone", "tritone" and "Multitone". Faint activation also appears on bullet-point characters at the start of list lines.

5237.name: Numbers and operands (or the spaces before them) appearing in arithmetic expressions, especially the second operand right after an operator like ×, /, *, ^, = or a comma in function arguments, as in calculations, equations, code, and table cells. A few weak activations fall on unrelated words.

52374.name: The word "rehearse" and its forms (rehearsal, rehearsals, rehearsed, rehearsing), firing most strongly on the first subword piece " rehe"/" rehears". This covers performance, music and theatre practice as well as mental rehearsal. It fires weakly on look-alike pieces such as "reheated", "re-heating" and "heater".

5238.name: The word "New" (and equivalents like "new", "Nieuwe", "新"), strongest when capitalized as the first word of a multi-word proper name, especially places (New York, New Delhi, New Hampshire, New Zealand) or titles (New Labour, New Scientist, Newbery). It fires weakly on lowercase "new", code constructors (::new), and similar name-opening words like "Los" (Angeles), "Long" (Beach), and "Young".
