55519.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly on separator tokens (spaces, periods, commas, colons) inside structured or numeric text such as lists of numbers, decimals, times, dates, tables and DOIs, right before the next number or identifier part. The strongest hits are the periods in DOI/journal identifiers (e.g. PhysRevA.101) and the spaces before numbers in lists. It also fires faintly on code tokens (main, for) and on metadata labels (Created by, Answered by).

55526.name: Function words and punctuation (prepositions, commas, periods, 'does', 'to', 'the', 'with') at a boundary just before a new, often hard-to-predict content phrase or entity begins, such as a new topic noun, a name, or an inserted spam phrase like 'does rhino 5 male enhancement work'. The feature marks the slot where the upcoming key content is about to be introduced.

5553.name: Location-related words, mainly "where" (and somewhere/anywhere/wherever), plus the clause that follows them, such as "where the physician holds their" or "Where are they". Activation is strongest on "Where" opening direct or indirect questions about a place ("Where can I", "where to go with"). It is weaker on locative relative clauses and on other wh-question phrases.

The word "where" (and variants like Where, wherever, anywhere, somewhere) introducing a location clause or question, plus the clause words right after it (subject, verb, e.g. "where it was coming", "where my mom got"). It is strongest for "where" questions and indirect questions, and weak on related location or question words (places, when, how).

55531.name: Tokens that open a curly-brace placeholder or interpolation, strongest for "${" in shell, Makefile and template variable substitution (e.g. " ${", "=${", "(${"). It fires more weakly on "{" in C#/Python f-strings and format strings, and on "${" starting LaTeX inline math.

55536.name: Range or transition separators placed between two values, such as ".." in ranges (0..25, i0..j0, git diff hashes) and arrows (->, →) between version numbers or values. The strongest case is ".." in a git index hash line.

55542.name: The right-hand side of an assignment in code, i.e. the value or expression being stored into a variable, strongest on the variable name just after "=" (e.g. "= b;", "= score;", "= tt;"). Weaker activation appears on function arguments, indices and other operands that supply a value.

55569.name: Technical terms in scientific and laboratory writing that name experimental, analytical, or physical methods, instruments, materials, and processes (spectroscopy, chromatography, ionization, desorption, ablation, fragmentation, sample preparation, staining). Activation usually falls on the key word or word-piece of the method or process name.

55570.name: Whitespace (or comma) separators between coordinate pairs in numeric coordinate lists, especially SVG path data (e.g., between control points in C/Q commands like "7 30 9.79 30 13"). Strongest on the space separating one x,y pair from the next in dense SVG path strings.

Separator tokens (spaces, commas, brackets, "][", ",-", "$") positioned between repeated items in lists, sequences, or structured data, most often just before a number, where the next element follows a predictable pattern (coordinates, prices, fractions, navigation links).

55586.name: The subword token "aure"/"Aure", firing most strongly in the species name Staphylococcus aureus (including S. aureus), and weakly in other words built on it (Aurelius, Aurelia, aureole, Aurel).

55594.name: Past participles (and similar verbs) in passive constructions, often following 'is/was/be/can be' and preceding an agent or source phrase like 'by', 'in', 'from', 'through' (e.g. 'controlled by', 'appointed by', 'decided in').

55603.name: Names of terrorist, jihadist, and militant groups, strongest for ISIS / Islamic State / Daesh (including name-completing subword tokens like "esh", "ab", "aida"). It fires weakly on other extremist groups, rebels, cartels and cults, and on "Republic" after "Central African" or "Islamic". It also fires on "ISIS" even when it is an unrelated name, such as a particle accelerator.

55621.name: Separators inside long repetitive sequences, mostly the commas between numbers in number lists and arrays, plus spaces between numbers in columns or rows and repeated filler patterns like " -", "-*" and ";\". Activation is strongest midway through a long run of items, rather than at its start or end.

55634.name: Narrative or report descriptions of how a storm or other natural or physical event behaves and changes over time. The strongest cases are news-style tropical cyclone reports about a named storm's intensity, strength, sustained winds, movement and forecast track (e.g. "has weakened to", "maintained its strength", "forecast to move"). Weaker activation falls on verbs, auxiliaries and connectives describing the progression of fires, earthquakes, eruptions and similar events.

5565.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on awkward, non-native, machine-translated or SEO-spun English. It activates on tokens where the word choice or grammar is unnatural, such as redundant verbs, odd collocations and garbled phrasing. The strongest examples are spammy health copy and broken technical or product descriptions.

55661.name: Formal bureaucratic, legal and policy language, especially wording that describes mandates, authorizations and directives. It fires on words following verbs like directed, required, authorized, prohibits or tasked (often 'to' plus an action verb), on statutory section headings such as 'Declaration of a… emergency' and 'Authorization.--', and on official program or report titles.

55676.name: The word "current"/"currently" (and Current in identifiers like GetCurrent), meaning present or active state, especially in technical contexts (current location, time, buffer, session, directory). Weaker on other present-time words (now, today, right now) and look-alike tokens such as "content".

The word "current" (and "currently") used to mean the present or active instance of something. Activation is strongest in technical and software contexts such as the current document, file, domain, hour, speed or the currently playing station. Weaker activations come from related words like "present", "selected", "now" and "next", and from "Current" used as a name.

55677.name: The separator token (a space, hyphen, opening parenthesis, subscript marker, or similar) placed right after a name or noun and just before the number, label or parenthetical that tags it. Examples are patent reference numerals ("resonator 10", "medium 2"), model numbers (PPSh-41), citations ("et al. (2014)", "Fig. 1"), list items and math variables. Activation is strongest for the space before patent part numerals.

55678.name: The word "drawable", especially as a graphics or Android resource type (e.g., in resource paths like com.example:drawable/...). Other activations are weak and scattered across ordinary words (often function words or the word just after a verb or preposition).

55706.name: Mainly fires on the double newline right after a section heading (e.g. "\section{Introduction}" or "**BACKGROUND**"), just before the first sentence of body text in academic or technical writing. It fires more weakly on mid-sentence tokens where a predictable continuation follows ("by means of", "zur Verfügung gestellt").

55733.name: A diffuse feature that fires weakly on separator or boundary tokens in structured, machine-like text such as logs, code, HTML tables, LaTeX and numbered lists (spaces, punctuation, opening brackets, tag names, and the word starting the next field). It is strongest on the space or number that directly follows a timestamp in log-style lines. It also fires faintly on function words right after a verb in technical prose ("shows the", "equal to").

55745.name: Delimiter and punctuation tokens that close or terminate a structured sequence (a list, tuple, string, argument list, input block, or equation side), such as closing brackets, quotes, parentheses, newlines and code fences after example inputs, or the "=" after an expression. These mostly occur in code, math, and example input and output text. Activation is strongest at the boundary right after the last element of the sequence.

55748.name: Text that states what a system, device, or program displays, reports, or claims, such as error messages, status indicators, and warnings (e.g. "the password is incorrect", "invalid argument", "USB devices not recognized", "the folder is empty"). These usually come right after verbs like says, shows, is telling, or indicates, and are mostly found in tech troubleshooting text.

Text describing technical problems, chiefly error messages, system warnings and status notices from software or devices (e.g. 'unable to save display settings', 'invalid package file', CRYPTO_LIBRARY_INTERNAL_ERROR, 'marked as dirty'). Activation is highest on the quoted or named error and status text, and weaker on nearby troubleshooting terms such as loading, connection, update and powering issues.

55751.name: The space (or short function words) right after a label/colon and just before a predictable value is filled in, e.g. a number after "Kudos [?]:" or a time after "Local time in X:" in templated web text. It marks the slot where a specific value is expected next.

55755.name: Inner subword pieces of Latin-style scientific names, chiefly the species epithet of binomial nomenclature (e.g. falc-ip-arum, offic-in-ale, leg-uminos-arum). The middle fragments after the first piece of the word fire most strongly. Weaker hits come from other rare Latinate or foreign words split into odd subwords, such as medical terms and non-English names.

55775.name: The separator space token immediately preceding the second operand in an arithmetic expression (after ×, *, +, "by", "plus", "=", commas in number lists), i.e. the position just before a number is written, especially the right-hand operand of multiplication/addition; occasionally the decimal point within that number.

55797.name: Head nouns (often abstract or generic) that complete a noun phrase, typically after a determiner or modifier ("the", adjective, compound modifier) and often followed by "of", a preposition or punctuation. The feature fires on the main noun of a phrase rather than on any particular topic.

Generic common nouns that head a noun phrase, usually right after a determiner or preposition ("the", "a", "its", "an"). They name an entity whose specific identity comes from the surrounding context (the case, the deal, the crisis, an office, the program), and they are often followed by a period, comma or prepositional phrase.

55801.name: Names of commands and functions used to look up, check for, or load programs, modules and system information in shell scripts and code, e.g. `which`, `command -v`, `man`, `import`, `class_exists`, `getProperty`, `modprobe`/`insmod`, `killall`, `--version`. The strongest case is `which` used to check whether an executable exists.

55810.name: Terms from space and geophysical science, especially solar and plasma physics: the Sun, solar flares, sunspots, the corona, photosphere and atmospheric layers, radiation, auroras, fusion and tokamak plasmas, plus related Earth-science terms. Activation peaks on solar phenomena such as flares and sunspots.

55844.name: Option labels in multiple-choice questions, most strongly the final option letter ("D", sometimes "C") at the start of a line before its answer text, which is usually followed by "Answer:". Roman numeral item labels (I, III) also activate it. There is weaker activation on question words such as "Which" or "How" that introduce a choice, and on occasional connective words ("and", "to", "with") in lists or explanations.

5585.name: Temporal expressions, mainly the tokens that open a date or time reference: prepositions and words like "in", "since", "during", "while", "past", "last", month names and "Day", plus the space or leading digits of a year or day number (e.g. "in 201", "March 16", citation years). Activation is strongest on the space just before the day number after a month name.

55886.name: Fires on awkward, unidiomatic or incorrect word choices, typical of synonym-spun SEO text, machine paraphrasing or non-native grammar. Most often these are swapped prepositions or connectives ("within" for "in", "from"/"into" for "of"/"to", "plus" for "and", "along with", "which" for "that"). It also catches odd synonym substitutions ("returning" for "back", "fringe" for "edge", "prosperity" for "well-being", "likelihood" for "odds"). It marks the token where the phrasing deviates from what a fluent writer would say.

55889.name: Newline tokens closing a short metadata or header line, typically one ending in an ID/code number, phone number, date, location or 'n/a', just before a new field label, title or section begins. These occur in document front matter, listings and records. Weaker activations appear on paragraph breaks after a sentence.

55899.name: Fires in HTML boilerplate right after the opening <html> tag (or <html lang="en">) closes. It is strongest on the closing ">" plus newline, and weaker on the indentation and "<" that begin the <head> tag. These are the structural tokens that lead from the html tag into the head section. There is weak activation on a newline right after <!DOCTYPE html>.

55919.name: Multi-digit numbers inside citations or reference strings, firing most strongly on the volume number of a reporter in US legal case citations (e.g., the "523" in "185 Colo. 272, 523 P.2d"). Weaker activation appears on page numbers, address and coordinate digits, and other numeric IDs. Occasional faint activations land on scattered function words.

55955.name: Interior subword pieces of long biochemical compound names, especially glycan and lipid terms. The strongest hits are "ly" in glycosaminoglycan, proteoglycan, peptidoglycan and aminoglycoside. Weaker hits include "ip" in glycolipid/phospholipid, "onic" in hyaluronic, and "amin" in glycosaminoglycan. Scattered weak activations also fall on unrelated tokens such as newlines in bid listings.

55969.name: A diffuse, weakly-firing feature on ordinary mid-sentence tokens, mostly function words and verb-phrase pieces that continue a clause. It favors infinitive or modal-style predicates such as "able to act", "allows them to", "enough to", "must", "could" and "would", plus their objects or complements. It fires most strongly on an incongruous inserted phrase ("drive on" in spam text).

55985.name: Classifier modifiers that come right before the head noun and specify the type or format of a creative or professional work, most often music or film releases (studio, debut, sophomore, full-length, solo, feature, LP). They typically follow ordinals or possessives like "his third", "first", or "debut". Weaker hits are similar category modifiers such as head (coach), lead (role), original (articles), peer-reviewed and oil (paintings).

55993.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on words in phrases describing what something does, provides or contributes: its function, role, purpose or beneficial effect. Examples include 'play a role', 'creates jobs for', 'provide shelter and… while also offering', 'distribute heat, salt', 'feast on… specialize in consuming', 'tax revenues plus economic benefits' and 'committed to supporting'. It usually lands on the verbs, connectives ('and', 'while also', 'for', 'into') and nouns that link an entity to its impact, mostly in expository text.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no clear lexical trigger. It fires on ordinary mid-sentence tokens, mostly content nouns and verbs and short phrases that continue a clause, such as objects of prepositions and predicate phrases ("fund transfers", "memes can", "return to"). Occasional hits fall on code tokens or CJK characters. It is more common in noisy, garbled or synthetic-looking text, and seems to track generic continuation of the sentence rather than any specific meaning.

56007.name: The word "parking" (and related "parked"/"park"/"car park"), especially as a modifier before lot, garage, space, or area. Weaker activation on related vehicle and storage terms like car, vehicles, seat, and moored.

The word "parking" (and related forms like "Parking", "parked", car "park"), especially in "parking lot" and amenity listings (free/on-site parking). Weaker activation on related vehicle-storage terms (garage, car, moorage, lane, charging).

56009.name: Opening delimiters of shell command substitution, i.e. a backtick or "$(" that starts an embedded command, often fused with a preceding "=" or quote in variable assignments (VAR=`cmd`, VAR=$(cmd), "$(cmd)"). Activation is strongest for these assignment forms and weaker for a plain "$" variable reference, a bare "(" or stray backticks in non-shell contexts.

56011.name: Highly predictable tokens that complete formulaic or boilerplate web text: repeated templates such as quote-site headers, iTunes store blurbs, Korean site navigation and CSS theme class strings, plus stock collocations like "heart attack and stroke", "last minute" and "Similar movies". The feature tracks memorized or easily predicted continuations rather than any specific meaning.

56040.name: A diffuse, weak feature that fires on tokens naming quantities or values, mostly in math and code: variables and arguments in formulas (z^2, n, the index in a_{n+2}, L(x)), numeric literals, and struct fields or parameters (date->year, data.Length). It also fires faintly on measurable nouns in prose (density, tablets, tones) and on scattered word fragments.

56044.name: Line breaks (sometimes with trailing punctuation like '.', ')', '},' or a ' %' field delimiter) that end a metadata field, mostly an author affiliation or address line ending in a city/country, institution name, email, ISSN/DOI or venue name. They appear in academic paper headers and bibliographic records, where the next line starts another author, affiliation or section.

56056.name: Closing delimiters and terminators of markup, code, LaTeX, or link spans (closing braces, brackets, parentheses, quotes, backticks, $, %, >, file extensions like .png) that end an inline reference, label, filename, or formatted segment, usually inside noisy or garbled technical text.

56112.name: The token right before a written-out date's month name, e.g. "on" after filed/released/died/born, a day number before the month, or a colon, comma or semicolon before the date. It fires most strongly in patent filing phrases ("filed on Aug. 31") and Federal Register citations.

56142.name: Attribute syntax inside HTML <link rel="icon"> favicon tags, especially the closing quote and the following attribute names (href, type, sizes), the =" and URL parts (https://, image/ MIME types, .svg/.icon). Elsewhere activation is weak and scattered over miscellaneous tokens, slightly more on code and URLs.

56151.name: Tokens that name a data type or format spec, mostly in code or technical text: string (as in <string>), int/[int, str, %s, hex, number, integer, real, raw, text, Set, character. The '<string>' and '%s' cases fire most strongly. Weaker, scattered activations fall on function words like 'the', 'we', 'to' and 'a' in technical or instructional prose.

56166.name: Titles and roles of people who speak or give statements on behalf of an organization. The strongest cases are "spokesman", "spokesperson" and "spokeswoman", usually in attribution phrases like "said a spokesman". Weaker cases are related roles and sources such as representative, communications or PR officer, press secretary, source, and press service or agency.

56187.name: The word "Software" right after "Free" in "Free Software (Foundation)". It is strongest in the GPL license boilerplate ("write to the Free Software Foundation, Inc.") and weaker in ordinary prose mentions. Other tokens fire only faintly.

56205.name: The token that ends a return expression in code, usually the semicolon (or closing paren/newline) right after the returned value in short getter-style functions such as `return name;` and `{ return x; }`. Activation is strongest for simple getters returning a field and weaker for method-call returns and Rust/Python implicit returns. There are faint stray hits on line endings in non-code text.

56255.name: Names of laboratory culture media, buffers, and solutions that cells or samples are grown, bathed, or dissolved in (DMEM, Eagle's medium, PBS, saline, Ringer's, Hanks', broth, agar, media, solvents). It fires most strongly on the final token of the name or on the head noun 'medium'. There is weak spillover to other substrate or base nouns such as soil, diet, and Snapdragon chipsets.

56260.name: Low-level feature on connective tokens that introduce a source, specification or examples. Most often it fires on the "e" of a parenthetical "(e.g.," and on the ".," after "e.g". In code it fires on static factory, constructor or lookup method names that take what follows as input (.of, .from, arrayOf, dictionaryWith, getElementBy, find_element_by, ::new). Weaker hits are prepositions like "based on" and "to".

56270.name: Tokens inside formal citations and references, mostly numbers such as volume, page, year and case-report numbers (e.g., "233 CLR 162", "pp. 87–108", "201[6]"). Also fires more weakly on other pieces of citation strings like journal-name endings, dates, URLs, DOIs and HTML table tags.

56305.name: A diffuse, non-semantic feature that fires on single tokens in the middle of a running sequence, mostly where the next token is strongly predictable. These are often separators or connectors (commas, periods, spaces, table tags, digits before ",000") or partial words and phrase starts ("result" before "in", "how" before "well", "væ" before "kke"). It appears across prose, code, tables and non-English text.

56325.name: Boundary tokens just before the main propositional content of a sentence, most often in scientific or expository writing. These are mainly the complementizer "that" after reporting verbs (showed, suggests, indicate, conclude). They also include the comma after discourse connectives or introductory phrases (Thus, Moreover, Therefore, In contrast), plus colons and paragraph breaks after headings. Each marks the point where the new claim or finding begins.

56333.name: The complementizer "that" following a verb of saying or mentioning (e.g. "let us mention that"), which introduces a clause in formal mathematical prose.

56339.name:
Tokens inside repetitive, predictable runs of text, such as repeated words or phrases ("Image Image Image", "very, very", "Skip to"), repeated symbols or separator lines, and boilerplate markup like HTML table tags (, ⏎, ),
and blockquote ">⏎" lines. Activation increases the longer the same pattern keeps repeating.

Repeated tokens in degenerate, repetitive sequences, such as runs of newlines, whitespace, punctuation, code fences, symbols, or repeated words and fragments. Activation grows the longer the repetition continues and is strongest on structural or formatting tokens like blank lines, pipes, and closing tags.

Repeated, degenerate token sequences: the latent fires on tokens (often punctuation, separators, whitespace/newlines, slashes, dashes, brackets) that repeat a pattern already seen in the immediate context, growing stronger as the repetition continues in garbled or boilerplate text.

56360.name: Tokens in attribution contexts that link a person or claim to a source: prepositions and connectors like "of", "at", "by", "with" and "from" between a person's name and their organization or outlet, plus bylines ("By", "writes", "Review by"), appositive commas after names, and source or publication names. These appear in news, reviews and citations, signaling who said or published something and where.

56389.name: The word "except" in the Apache License 2.0 boilerplate phrase "you may not use this file except in compliance with the License" found in source code headers. Weak, scattered activations elsewhere on unrelated tokens (paragraph breaks after dates, an import keyword, name fragments).

56421.name: The letter sequence "roy"/"oy", strongest on the standalone first name "Roy" (e.g., Roy Rogers, Roy Blunt) and weaker on "roy" inside other words and surnames (McElroy, Rolls-Royce, royal, Troy, Fitzroy). It also fires weakly on other personal first names such as "Diana".

56422.name: The word "date"/"Date" used as a metadata field label or key (YAML front matter, JSON/TOML keys, bibliographic and repository records such as "Date Published"), usually right before a timestamp value. It fires most strongly at line-initial "date:" in blog-post headers.

56431.name: The letter "p"/"P" used as the p-value symbol in statistical reporting (e.g. "p < 0.05", "P = .003"), often in parentheses after results. The following "=" or "<" activates more weakly. Related statistical-significance terms ("significance", "p-value") and other statistic symbols (r, r², Ki) fire weakly, as does the "p" in "pH".

Statistical hypothesis-testing terminology, above all "p"/"P" in p-values (e.g. "p-value", "P=", "(p<0.05)"). Related terms such as "significance (level)", "alpha/α" and "probability" activate more weakly, and unrelated tokens only faintly.

56459.name: The ">" + newline token that closes an opening tag at a line end. It fires most strongly after "<summary" in C# XML doc comments ("/// <summary>") and weakly after HTML "<thead"/"<tbody" tags in tables.

56474.name: Opening tokens of in-text citations and reference markers in academic or encyclopedic writing, such as " [", ".[", " (", "\cite{", superscript markup and reference numbers, usually placed right after a claim or an author name like "et al.". The strongest activations are on " [" following author names or statements.

56509.name: Business and financial news context, especially funding, investment, contracts, deals and monetary amounts. Activation is weak and diffuse across function words, numbers and punctuation in such passages. It peaks on the key phrases describing money changing hands, such as "awarded a contract", "raised £270k in funding" and "amount invested was not disclosed".

56562.name: Past participle verbs in passive voice constructions (after "was/were/is/be/been"), especially in scientific and methods writing describing procedures that were performed (assessed, examined, investigated, measured). Activation is strongest for research-evaluation verbs.

56567.name: Separator and value-position tokens inside structured code data literals (dicts, tuples, arrays, object/config entries, tables). It fires mainly on commas, colons/equals signs, closing quotes, padding spaces and indentation, and on the short values that follow a key, such as true/false, numbers and strings. Typical contexts are lines like key: value, (a, b) tuples and list rows. Weak spillover appears in prose and markdown tables.

56579.name: Mentions of the U.S. state Idaho, most strongly the word "Idaho" itself, and more weakly its capital Boise or fragments like "aho"/"ise" in split or lowercase spellings of Idaho and Boise.

56609.name: Separator or connector tokens at the boundary between two parallel segments, marking where a second item, alias, gloss or field begins. Typical cases are opening parentheses before an explanation or alternate name, pipes, slashes, dashes, '#', ':', '; also' and 'or the'. Some hits also fall at the start of the next element in code, IDs, URLs or lists.

56611.name: Words in instructions to express, write, rewrite or convert something into a particular representation, mostly in math contexts. The strongest tokens are the prepositions and nouns naming the target form, as in "in the form of", "in terms of", "into … form" and "written as". Words like "expression", "write" and "using" also fire, and the target is often a notation or format such as standard, polar or scientific form.

56613.name: Separators between parts of postal or affiliation addresses (commas, newlines, the spaces after them, and country-code prefixes like "N-" or "CZ-"). Activation is strongest at the separator that comes right after a street address or PO box, just before the postal code.

56620.name: Introduction of a generic or variable entity in definitional/technical contexts: the noun or symbol being posited as the subject of a definition, statement, or argument (e.g., "Consider a linear operator L", "a category $C$", "an object $x$", "a function", "If z_0 is a point"), including math variables in LaTeX and function parameters in code. Strongest in formal math definitions and hypotheses.

56644.name: Tokens inside long runs of numeric coordinates, chiefly SVG path data and canvas drawing arguments (numbers, spaces, commas, decimal points between coordinate values). Weaker activation falls on the column-separator pipes in markdown table divider rows (|-----|-----|) and on other delimiters in structured numeric/code sequences.

56681.name: The word "Introduction"/"INTRODUCTION" as a section heading in academic papers, reports and tables of contents (e.g., after "1.", "I.", or in \section{}), often right after the abstract or keywords. Weaker activation on other front-matter headings like "Summary"/"Executive Summary".

56689.name: Organization or company names (Microsoft, Google, Oracle, AWS, Intel) appearing right after "by", "the", "with" or "in" in attribution or ownership phrases such as "provided by X" or "the X License". It also fires weakly on the token starting a phrase after such prepositions.

56691.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on mid-sentence continuation tokens in formal, expository prose (scientific, legal, technical, business writing). It mostly hits function words that extend a phrase, such as of, the, that, as, in, for, or, and including, especially right after a noun ("types of", "range of", "factors that are"). Less often it hits modifiers or content words inside an ongoing clause ("bulk", "heavy", "defective", "substances"). It tracks the elaboration of a noun phrase or clause rather than any specific meaning.

56702.name: Portable consumer electronic devices, most strongly mobile/cell phones, smartphones, handhelds and related wireless gadgets (iPod, PSP, DS, cameras, Bluetooth, Nokia/Blackberry). Weaker hits land on other carried or personal items and on fragments inside such terms.

Nouns for electronic devices and gadgets, especially mobile/cell phones and related wireless tech (cellular, Bluetooth, earbuds, radios/communicators, cameras, players), and to a lesser degree vehicles and other portable hardware. Activation peaks on "phone" and "cellular".

56721.name: The words that build a question asking for a computed answer, mostly "is" (and "the", "value of") right after "what" in math, logic or code problems ("what is the value of X?"), plus "how many"/"does". Weaker activation falls on instruction verbs (compute, create, check, print) and connectives in technical text.

56748.name: Structural delimiter tokens that open a new field or entry in structured, form-like text. The strongest case is an opening <td> cell tag at the start of a table row. It also fires on line breaks, bullets, dashes, list numbers and their periods, quotes, and brackets that come just before the next key or label (e.g. 'Terms of Use', 'Manuscript Type:', 'Department:').

56801.name: Terms for natural selection and related evolutionary or shaping forces, strongest on "selection" and "selecting for", also firing on fitness, selective force, adaptation, competition, reinforcement and similar mechanism and pressure words that favor or filter outcomes.

Terms tied to Darwinian evolution, chiefly the word "selection" in natural/sexual/artificial selection or "under selection", which fires strongest. Weaker hits include evolutionary pressure, survival of the fittest, fitness, Darwin, eugenics and intelligent design. Non-biological uses of "selection" or "pressure" (self-selection, team selection, selling pressure) fire weakly.

56829.name: Fires most strongly on the subword "oppel", especially in the legal term "estoppel", and more weakly in "doppelganger" and the surname "Koppel". Elsewhere it gives only weak, scattered activations on mid-sentence function words and punctuation (commas, "all", "in", brackets, bullets, Indic virama signs).

56850.name: Tokens within proper titles and names: words of capitalized title-like phrases for articles, books, pages, sections, products, laws or file names. They usually follow a cue such as 'see', 'read also:', 'in', 'our', or an opening quote, and the activations are weak overall.

56878.name: Courts and judicial decision-makers as the subject of a ruling, especially "court" in phrases like "the district court" or "High Court". Activation peaks when the court is followed by a ruling verb (ruled, found, concluded, granted). It fires more weakly on judges, juries and other authorities that issue decisions, such as committees, agencies and administrations.

56883.name: Nouns naming sports competitions, postseason events and titles, most often the final word of a multi-word event name (bowl, tournament, playoffs, championship, league, trophy, Final Four). The strongest responses are to "bowl" in college-football contexts such as "bowl eligible" and "Rose Bowl".

569.name: Content words and connectives inside formal, expository explanation, mostly in scientific, technical, business or educational prose. Activation is strongest on long stretches of explanatory clauses that state causes, requirements, consequences or mechanisms, such as 'leading to', 'due to the presence of', 'may be' and 'require'. Isolated words in casual or listing text activate only weakly.

Weak, diffuse activation across formal expository prose, such as academic abstracts, technical descriptions and SEO or marketing copy. It fires on mid-sentence spans of abstract, jargon-heavy phrasing: nominalizations ("use of…metabolism", "perception of quality of life", "diversity of ordered architectures"), connective prepositions and conjunctions (of, to, and, over), and purpose clauses ("to obtain", "to seamlessly integrate"). Activation is strongest inside long, formulaic descriptions of processes, relationships or goals, and is not tied to any specific word.

56905.name: Mentions of the fruit fly Drosophila, strongest on the "ros" subword of "Drosophila" (weaker on "ila"/"aster" of melanogaster), plus words like "fly"/"flies" (especially as model organisms) and occasionally other model organism name fragments; weak spurious activation on "<thead>" newline tokens in tables.

56913.name: The word "Question" used as a label right after a blank line following a passage, starting a reading-comprehension style Q&A ("Question: ... Answer: ...") about the preceding text.

56930.name: The verb "found" (occasionally "find", "located", "encountered"), chiefly as a passive participle meaning something exists or is present somewhere ("found in the petals", "can be found in", "ports found in a standard router"). It is strongest when the participle directly follows a noun and leads into an "in" location phrase.

56932.name: Tokens inside auto-generated, templated or SEO/spam web text, firing at the slots where variable content is filled in: the space within a phone number, a stuffed keyword like 'australia', separators in job-title lists, and digits in catalog IDs such as star names.

56939.name: Operands in math and code expressions, mainly variable names, symbols and numbers. It fires most strongly on the left-hand term just before an operator, relation or comparison ("n % i", "signature ==", "Y_test -", "1 \leq"). It also fires on a math variable and its closing delimiter before "is" ("\( K \) is"). Weaker activations occur on prose subject nouns just before a verb like "is" or "could".

56947.name: Symbols and letter-based names of subatomic particles and physical states, chiefly mesons, bosons and leptons (D⁰, B⁺, K, J/ψ, η′, Z/W bosons, Υ). Activation peaks on the particle letter or Greek name and its charge or superscript, often in LaTeX. Weaker activation appears on other physics notation such as molecular term symbols (Σ, Π), subscripts and isotope labels, plus occasional stray tokens like '(' after usernames.

56961.name: Medical surgical procedure terms, firing most strongly on the word part naming the intervention. Chiefly "replacement" after a body part or organ (joint, valve, knee, renal, hormonal), and the "pl" in arthroplasty or dysplasia. Also covers "oplast" in rhinoplasty/blepharoplasty, transplant/transplantation, bypass, fusion, implant and CABG. There are weak hits on non-medical replacements (roof, windshield).

56996.name: Fires most strongly on the token " NAV"/" nav", usually in uppercase as the start of words like NAVIGATING, NAVY, NAVSTAR or website navigation labels ("SKIP NAVI", "shulou NAV:"), and in lowercase as "nav" menus or bars. It fires weakly on scattered punctuation and spacing tokens, such as parentheses around Slashdot user IDs, periods in citations, and spaces before emoji.

57038.name: Words right after a reporting, testimony or recollection verb, or a source attribution (says, testified, reported, records, according to X), that open the reported content. Usually this is the complementizer "that", but it can also be a comma, "how", "when", or the speech verb itself ("said", "says", "remember") after a speaker's name. Activation is strongest for formal or legal testimony and for source attributions.

57043.name: Variable-name fragments, indices, subscripts and operators inside code or math expressions, especially where similar identifiers repeat in parallel with small variations (e.g., .x/.y/.z/.w, hj0/cj0/ck0, CLUSTERCAP5/6/7, t2=t3). The latent fires on the distinguishing part of a repeated identifier or index and on nearby operators. It also fires weakly on repeated nouns in prose, such as 'state' or 'plane'.

57045.name: The "#endif" preprocessor directive, strongest when it closes a header include guard at the very end of a C/C++ header file. Activation is weaker for mid-file #endif closing #ifdef/#else blocks and for template "endif" keywords in PHP or Django. Scattered weak hits on ordinary prose tokens are noise.

57125.name: Names of emerging/vector-borne infectious diseases, above all Zika and Lyme, plus chikungunya (the name or its final subword, e.g. "ika", "yme", "unya"). Activation is strongest on "Zika" in outbreak/virus contexts. "Lyme" fires even as a place name, though more weakly. Other weak hits are scattered noise.

57147.name: The word "Floor" after an ordinal (e.g. "Fifth Floor", "4th Floor"), mostly in street addresses. It fires by far the strongest in the Free Software Foundation license boilerplate "51 Franklin Street, Fifth Floor, Boston".

57162.name: The class/type name "Handler" in code, especially Android-style declarations and constructors like "private Handler handler = new Handler()", where it fires most strongly. Other type names in code (Widget, TimeUnit) get weaker activation, and scattered ordinary prose words get only faint, inconsistent activation.

57173.name: Patent application serial numbers and their lead-in phrases, e.g. "Ser. No.", "Appl. No.:", "Application Data" and "of application No.", along with the digits that follow. The strongest response falls on the "No" and its surrounding periods in "Ser. No.", plus the number parts like "14/612,460". There is weak, scattered activation on function words in other boilerplate or formulaic text.

57181.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly in code, markup, LaTeX and table text at structural transition points where a new construct begins and its continuation is predictable. The strongest cases are the start of function or constructor bodies, such as the opening brace after a signature, a local variable declaration, or a return statement. It also fires on assignment and comparison operators, argument delimiters, and the "<thead>" line break just before "<tr>".

57204.name: Words and phrases that set up a problem, difficulty, or confusing situation the writer is about to solve, often in a problem-then-solution or advice framing (e.g. "can be daunting", "a bit tricky", "overwhelmed", "unsure", "wondering", "confusion", "struggling to"). It responds to descriptions of hardship, uncertainty, or inconvenience, typically just before a reassuring turn like "but", "fortunately" or "here are some tips".

57221.name: No clear semantic theme. The feature fires on single connective or filler tokens in technical or explanatory prose, at points where a noun phrase is about to continue or be completed. Examples include "the" after a verb or preposition, a repeated list head such as "Battery Command", and the trailing space after a spec value.

57231.name: Diffuse, weak activation on framing language in journalistic and feature-style prose. It fires on verb and predicate phrases and evaluative transitions that set up a story's stakes, tension or significance, for example "leaves consumers in a quandary", "growing anger at the", "remains one of the most controversial topics", "researchers are again looking back" and "has yet to be carried out". These are typically clause-linking or main-predicate words in mid-sentence, pointing toward the article's key point.

57253.name: Coordinating conjunctions (mostly "or", sometimes "and") joining paired adjectives that modify the same noun, especially stock pairs like "express or implied", "explicit or implicit", "substantial or systematic". Weaker activations on other connective tokens such as separators, hyphens and commas.

57254.name: The final class name in Java import statements that bring in annotation types (e.g. Spring's Service/Controller/RestController/RequestMapping, JPA's Entity, Lombok's Data/NoArgsConstructor, JUnit's RunWith, WebServlet), which are later used as @-annotations. It fires most strongly on '.RunWith'. Rare weak activations appear on word endings in ordinary prose.

57328.name: Sports-venue and location terms about where a game is played, chiefly "home" and "road" (home game, road favorites, at home, on the road), along with "away", "visitors/visiting", "host" and stadium or city names. Weaker activations come from other sports and betting jargon such as derby, serve, blind, spread and bye.

Words marking where a sporting event takes place relative to the teams, i.e. home vs. away. The strongest activations are on "home", "away" and "road (trip)" in game contexts. Weaker activations fall on related venue and travel terms: at, travel to, visited, venue, host, hometown, neutral field, crowd, stadium.

57339.name: The word "pick" and its inflections (picks, picked, picking, picky, pick-up, nitpick), in every sense: choosing, lifting, collecting, increasing. It also fires on look-alike pieces such as 'iqu' in Piquette and the name Pickthall. Activation is strongest on the verb forms, especially 'picked/picks up'.

57356.name: Mostly fires on the " ::::::::" token in the ASCII-art "42" logo of 42-school C file header comments. It also fires weakly on assorted tokens in formulaic, templated, or oddly formatted text, such as citation markers, stray punctuation, URL path parts, and mid-phrase nouns.

57372.name: The word "schema", especially the "chema" piece after a split "s" (e.g. xsi:schemaLocation in XML, schema-free, db:schema). It is strongest in XML schemaLocation attributes and weak elsewhere, with only scattered faint activations on unrelated tokens.

57383.name: The ".href" property token in JavaScript/HTML code, especially after "location" (window.location.href, self.location.href). Unrelated prose words such as "However" or "you" show only faint activation.

5743.name: Tokens marking the end of a line, item, heading, or clause, usually a newline or terminal punctuation fused with a newline (".⏎", "?⏎", ":⏎"). They appear after list items, titles, questions, code comments, and table cells, at boundaries where one unit ends and the next begins. Activation is strongest at newlines closing code comments or declarations.

Tokens that close off a sentence, line, list item, heading or table cell: final punctuation fused with newlines (".⏎", ".⏎⏎", "?⏎⏎"), bare newlines after list items or code comments, and closing HTML tags ("</") that end cell or heading content. Activation is strongest where the end of one unit leads into another parallel item, such as numbered steps, bullets, enum variants or table cells.

Line-ending and segment-ending tokens (newlines, often fused with a period, question mark, colon or comma) that close a short self-contained unit such as a list item, heading, code comment, title or question, right before a new item, line or section starts. Activation is strongest after code comments and at line breaks within structured or list-like text.

57475.name: Tokens beginning with the sound/spelling "St(e)w" / "Ste…", most strongly the surname "Stewart" (also Stuart-like names); weaker on "steward(ship)", "stew", "Stuttgart", and the similar-sounding name "Seymour".

57508.name: Mainly the article "the" right after a preposition in license and copyright boilerplate, especially "distributed under the" (strongest in the Apache License header "software distributed under the License", weaker in open-access and Creative Commons notices). It also fires weakly on the "</" of the closing </thead> tag in HTML tables and on a few other predictable function words in formulaic text.

57515.name: Separator tokens (newlines, commas, periods/semicolons plus newline, closing quote/paren) that end one item in a list or enumeration and come right before the next item, especially bulleted or numbered lists. Activation is highest at separators in the middle of a list, where more items clearly follow.

Separators that end one item in a list or sequence of parallel entries, usually the newline (often with trailing punctuation like . ? ” ) >) that follows a list item, bullet, step, ingredient or domain name. It is strongest in long repetitive lists. Commas, semicolons or periods that separate items in inline enumerations activate it more weakly.

57519.name: Logical conjunction operators joining conditions, mainly "and" and "&&" (sometimes "or" or an opening parenthesis) inside if/while conditionals in code. Weaker activations come from prose "and" that joins conditional clauses ("if X and Y").

57529.name: Conditional or control-flow keywords that open a statement in source code, above all "if" (and "if (" / "if (!"), with weaker hits on while, elif, match, when and "if let". Activation is strongest when the keyword starts a new indented line at the top of a function or block body. Rare weak hits occur on prose "if" or other conditional-like words.

57567.name: Second-half completion of a hyphenated physicist name in physics terms, peaking on "instein" in "Bose–Einstein" (condensate/statistics), weaker for "Stokes–Einstein", "Hilbert–Einstein" and "ac" in "Fermi–Dirac". Faint activation on the space before a clock time ("The time now is 10:45") and other predictable continuations.

57569.name: The word "License"/"licence" that ends a named license, mostly Creative Commons Attribution boilerplate in open-access articles and wikis plus GNU/Mozilla Public License notices in code headers. Activation is highest when "License" opens a new line in a GPL/LGPL comment block. Scattered weak hits on unrelated tokens.

57575.name: The boundary token right after a formal named entity (an act, regulation, standard, institution, publication or ISSN line), most often an opening parenthesis or bracket, or a space before a number, that begins an abbreviation, citation, statute code (e.g. "(25 U.S.C.") or reference number. It is strongest before U.S. Code citations following an Act's name and weaker at other sentence or section breaks.

57585.name: The token ".Context" in code qualified names, strongest in the Java import "android.content.Context" and weaker in other packages (org.mozilla.javascript, org.apache.catalina, echo.Context, C# namespaces). Scattered prose tokens show only negligible activation.

57611.name: Weak, diffuse activations in news/commentary prose about revelations, controversy, scrutiny or accountability (investigations, conspiracies, disclosures, accusations, government failures). Fires on function words and key nouns/verbs in phrases about information coming to light or being questioned (e.g. 'asking for answers regarding', 'more sinister than we thought', 'broke the story', 'details emerged', 'knowledge of', 'accused of').

57643.name: Time-unit words that express age or duration after a number (year, years, months, weeks, days, -year-old, "old"), as well as their equivalents in other languages (岁, 月, वर्ष, лет) and the word "age" itself. Activation is strongest on the unit right after a numeral, especially in age phrases such as "two year old".

57644.name: Fires on the Android 'dimen' dimension-resource identifier, i.e. the 'imen'/'en' pieces of R.dimen and @dimen, and more weakly on related getDimension/getDimensionPixelSize calls. Activations on unrelated tokens elsewhere are faint and appear to be noise.

57655.name: The ".py" Python file extension token that completes a filename or path (scripts, modules, command-line invocations, code comments). It fires most strongly on clear file-reference contexts, weakly on bare "py" after a dot, and only marginally on a few unrelated tokens.

57659.name: Fires on the digit marking a square-root exponent: the "2" in 1/2 (as in ^(1/2), **(1/2), \frac{1}{2}) and the "5" in 0.5 (as in ** 0.5, pow(x, 0.5)), in both math notation and code. It also fires weakly on other tokens near square roots, such as the closing parenthesis of sqrt(...) or the brace after \sqrt, and on scattered section-break or formatting tokens in math and technical text.

57668.name: Paragraph/section break tokens (double newlines, often fused with a final period or other punctuation) that end a sentence, list, or block and come right before a new paragraph, heading or topic shift. Activation is strongest at section boundaries where the following text starts a new unit.
Paragraph-break tokens (double newline, often fused with a period or closing quote/punctuation) that end one text segment and precede a new section, often an abrupt topic or format shift.

57688.name: Weak, diffuse activation on historical and proper-noun tokens, peaking around conquest and medieval European history: Norman/Normandy, conquest, conquistadors, invasion, Mongols, Anglo-Saxon, Anjou, Boniface, 'de' in noble names, battles (the Somme, Manhattan). It often fires on name fragments such as surnames, places and historical figures, and sometimes on dates.

57728.name: Closing delimiter tokens, mainly doubled right brackets "]]" (often repeated or in garbled, code-like text) and closing code-fence backticks "```" that end a code block. Weaker hits are other closers like ")]", "}}" and "$$".

57736.name: Tokens that open a yes/no or true/false question, most often the auxiliary verb ("Is", "Does") right after a "Question:" label. Also covered are "whether" in "determine whether" and the colons, option letters and punctuation that set up a binary or truth-value judgment, including boolean code contexts.

57765.name: Separator tokens at boundaries between a heading or label and the boilerplate that follows it. Most often this is the double newline after "Leave a Reply"/"Leave a Comment" (also in other languages) before "Your email address will not be published". It also fires on the newline after "TABLE OF CONTENTS" or a table header, and on the ".," after abbreviated names and titles ("J.,", "M.D.,").

57772.name: CSS property names and their colons inside style declarations, especially inline HTML style="..." attributes (width, height, display, color, font-size, background-color, border, position). Values and units such as px get weaker activation, and the first property right after style=" activates most strongly. Similar styling or attribute keywords in other code (color, align, height) get weak activation.

57780.name: Function words, chiefly "of", directly following a plural noun and introducing its complement, as in "warranties of", "Schools of", "degrees of", "quantities of". Activation peaks on the license boilerplate "WARRANTIES OF" and the comment-prefix tokens on the next line. Other prepositions and connectives after nouns or verbs fire only weakly.

57797.name: Literal symbols, characters, operators and punctuation being referred to as objects in their own right (quoted operators/delimiters in code, math symbols, words naming symbols like "question mark", "semicolon", "asterisk", "minus"), with weaker activation on mentioned words and specific item nouns (card, vase).

57801.name: Separator (mostly a comma, sometimes a newline or semicolon) in postal addresses or affiliations that follows the city, region or postal code and comes just before the country name (USA, China, Canada, Germany, etc.). Activation is strongest after a postal code or city when the country is expected next.

57815.name: Separators between columns or fields in tabular and aligned text: HTML table cell tags ("<td", especially the opening tag of a second or later cell in a row), runs of spaces used to pad columns, and leader dots in tables of contents or forms that join an entry to its page number or value.

57827.name: Page ranges and issue/volume numbers in bibliographic citations. The strongest activations fall on the page-range portion: "pp.", "pages", "p.", or the colon/parenthesis before the start page, the starting page number, and the dash. Volume and issue numbers and other citation punctuation are weaker.

57846.name: The "i" token completing "Fermi", firing most strongly in solid-state physics terms like Fermi energy, level and surface, with weaker activation on the noun that follows (energy, level, function). Weaker activation also appears on related physics terms such as chemical/formal potential, E_F, HOMO/LUMO, Feynman and Debye. Faint activations on newlines in lists and spec sheets are noise.

57850.name: The `const` keyword opening a top-level constant declaration in source code, mostly Go and Rust. It fires most strongly on Go `const (` blocks or declarations that come right after the import section, and more weakly on Rust `const`/`pub const` items. The few non-code hits are weak and scattered.

57870.name: Tokens inside a condition being stated, mostly the subject or left-hand operand of a comparison or test right after 'if', 'while', 'whenever', 'when' or 'case' (e.g. "if (n > 10)", "if nums[mid] ==", "when the simulated value exceeds"). It fires most strongly on variables and operators in code conditionals, and weakly on the subject or verb of conditional and qualifying clauses in prose and math.

57871.name: Final letter(s) completing an abbreviated word, chiefly the "a"/"A" closing U.S. state abbreviations such as Fla., FLA., Ala., W.Va. and Ia., usually just before a period in legal citations, political party tags or datelines. It also fires weakly on word-final fragments elsewhere (Calif, Kindred, Belgium).

57907.name: Words naming a purpose, capability or suitability, mostly participles and adjectives like "adapted", "configured", "designed", "capable", "suited" and "prepared". They usually come right before "to" or "for" and a verb or noun saying what the thing is for. Activation is strongest for "adapted to" and "configured for" in patent-style technical writing.

57918.name: The subword "lign" starting words like lignin, lignocellulosic, lignans and lignite (wood/biomass chemistry). It fires most strongly on the word-initial " lign" token and weakly on "ign" pieces inside names (Lusignan, Puligny, Ligny).

57936.name: The word "claim(s)", firing most strongly in its patent sense: numbered patent claims, "N Claims, M Drawing Sheets" headers, "according to Claim 1" and "claims the benefit of priority". It fires weakly for other senses such as mining claims, JWT claims, discount claims and ownership claims, and occasionally on other patent boilerplate like "SUMMARY".

57952.name: Evaluative or critical judgments of a work, product or thing, as in reviews and critiques. It fires on the words that give a verdict on quality or merit (praise, faint praise, hedged or negative assessments such as 'just barely misses classic status', 'wasn't that great', 'was okay', 'brilliant movie') and on the framing words around them ('regard as', 'by no means a', 'but it certainly'). Activation is strongest on mixed or qualified appraisals.

57960.name: The repeated variable-name prefix (e.g. "x", "v", "arg", "num") in a run of sequentially indexed identifiers such as x1, x2, x3. It fires on the stem just before its number or subscript, mostly in code or math lists, and grows stronger as the sequential pattern continues.

57986.name: The first token right after a source file's package or namespace declaration, which opens the file body. In Java this is usually "import" (strongest), but can be "public", "/**", or the semicolon-plus-newlines that end the package line. In C# it is the newline or "{" after the namespace name. Weak activation also appears on "text" in "Sample/Example text" headers that mark where a document body begins.

5802.name: Words about strictness, rigidity and tightness versus their opposite, looseness or flexibility: strict, rigid, rigorous, tight, stiff, formal, restrictions, enforced, repression, discipline, flexible, tension. It extends to related senses of severity, constraint and exactness, such as technically, proper and abruptly. "Strictly" activates most strongly, followed by rigid, tight and rigorous.

Words about strictness, rigidity, and how tight or loose something is, in both a physical and a rule-based sense. The strongest hits are strict/stricter, stringent, tight/tighten and stiff. Weaker hits are related ideas such as enforcement, restrictions, formal, mandatory, harsh, uncompromising and meticulous, along with their opposites: loose, flexible, lenient and relaxation.

58022.name: Word-final suffix pieces (and some interior pieces) that complete multi-token names, overwhelmingly drug and chemical names: -ib, -ram, -ine, -amide, -ol, -mab, -ose, -ate. The strongest responses are on the characteristic pharmaceutical suffixes, such as -ib kinase inhibitors, -ram SSRIs and -ifene. Weak activations also occur on the final fragments of other rare, technical or proper-noun words.

Suffix or final subword pieces of drug, chemical and pharmaceutical names (e.g. -oxetine, -azine, -fen, -ify, -adalafil, -ab, -ol, -ium), usually inside noisy or garbled text. Activation is highest on drug-name endings, with weaker hits on element and compound names and a few unrelated tokens.

58041.name: The word "Question" used as a section label at the start of a new line (after a double line break) following a passage, opening a reading-comprehension Q&A block, typically formatted as "Question: … Answer:".

58048.name: The subword token "int" (any case: Int, INT, int) at the start of a longer word, e.g. INTRODUCTION, Introduce, Intense, Integrate, Intake, Intelligence, and the patent abbreviation "Int. Cl.". Activation is strongest when it is a word-initial fragment completed by a following subword. It is weaker for the standalone programming type "int" and for the whole word "International".

58074.name: Tokens inside highly formulaic, memorized boilerplate strings that the model can predict almost word for word. The strongest cases are "AppleWebKit" in browser user-agent strings and words in Lorem ipsum placeholder text (eiusmod, labore, dolore, veniam, odio, Duis). Weaker cases include "Nacional" after "Universidad" in affiliations, "Duis" in Duisburg, and stock web phrases such as "cookie policy".

58080.name: A separator plus the first fragment of an unusual or custom name that gets broken into pieces, such as a dot plus the opening letters of an uncommon Java package segment after "import com"/"org" (e.g. ".plan", ".y", ".m"), or a slash or dot plus the start of a URL path or domain. It also fires weakly on the backslash of \textsuperscript in affiliation lists.

58110.name: A generic head noun that comes right after a proper name, brand, acronym or other specific modifier, saying what kind of thing that name refers to (e.g. "Stinger project", "TeraShake simulation", "Data Access specification", "Bodele depression").

58131.name: Speaker attribution in news-style prose: the closing quote punctuation, speech verbs (said/says/explained), and especially the speaker's name plus the appositive title or role that follows it (e.g., ", director of…", ", lead author, who…"). The strongest activations come right after a quotation ends.

58135.name: Sentence boundaries where the period and the start of the next sentence are merged into one token because the space after the period is missing (e.g. ".The", ".In", ".A", ".B"). These fire most strongly. Weaker hits are other malformed boundaries: a missing period before the next sentence, merged punctuation like ".," or "..", stray spaces, and quote-plus-word tokens at a sentence start.

The start of a new sentence that directly follows the previous sentence's punctuation with no space, so the token fuses the period (or comma, quote, ellipsis) with the first letters or word of the next sentence (e.g. ".The", ".W"). Activation is strongest for these fused period+capital tokens and weaker for ordinary sentence-initial words after spaces, newlines or quotes.

58171.name: Conditional range and comparison logic, mostly in code: comparison and modulo operators, logical &&/and, and the numeric thresholds in if-conditions. It also fires on prose range boundaries such as 'between 0 and 4' or 'from 18 until 59'. Activation is far strongest on leap-year divisibility checks (year % 4 / 100 / 400); elsewhere it is weak and diffuse.

58189.name: In code, the separator between a function's first argument and the next one, peaking on the comma and opening quote just before a file-open mode string (e.g. open(file, "w"), fopen(path, "rb")). It responds more weakly to argument-separating commas and delimiters in other calls, especially ones that set modes or options.

58196.name: The word "optional" and its variants (Optional, optionally, 可选), which mark something as not required. It fires strongly in documentation, code and parameter lists, and on parenthetical "(Optional)" labels. Related words for non-mandatory choice, such as "voluntary", "elective" and "facultative", activate it weakly.

58201.name: Numeric digit tokens in nearly any setting: quantities, decimals, percentages, times, dates, prices, and IDs. The feature fires mostly on digits that follow or sit within an existing number, such as after a decimal point, colon, or other digits, rather than on the first digit of a number.

58202.name: The word "latent" (including the "ent" piece of a split "Lat-ent"), meaning hidden or dormant, in technical uses like latent variables/spaces, latent heat, and latent viral infections, plus figurative uses. The related words "latency" and "unobserved" fire only weakly.

58215.name: Physical or mathematical property terms in scientific (mostly physics and materials) text, usually the word or word-piece that completes a technical term naming a property, state or structure, e.g. "Fermi surface", "Goldstone bosons", "edge states", "sp2", "lossless", "light/massive", "curvature", "modulus". Activation is strongest on well-known condensed-matter terms like Fermi surface and Goldstone.

58222.name: The word "histone", with activation peaking on the "one"/"ones" piece that completes it ("hist" weaker). Histone names such as H3, H4, H2B and H2AX, and nucleosomes, also activate moderately in chromatin and epigenetics contexts. Other protein words fire only weakly.

58233.name: Syntax and delimiter tokens inside code, shell commands, markup and URLs, such as quote marks closing attribute values, opening angle brackets, command-line flag dashes, commas between arguments, colons, slashes, query separators (?, &) and opening parens or quotes. Prose tokens appear only weakly.

Weak, diffuse activations spread across many contexts. The clearest pattern is tokens that open or introduce a literal argument or specification, especially in code, shell commands and markup. Strongest are command-line flags ("-o", "-g", "-c") and tag/markup delimiters ("</", "<", "\", "{", quotes). Other examples are separators before a parameter or value (":", "=", "\",\n"). In prose, it fires faintly on words that introduce a means or condition, such as "using", "with", "by" and "set to".

58251.name: The word "lineup"/"line-up" and related ideas of arranging things in a row or a set of members (lineup, roster, matchup, formation, batting order). It also fires on the particle "up" after line/match/measure, as in "lined up" or "match up". Activation is strongest for "lineup" meaning a band's members, product range, team or roster.

The "up" in "line up"/"lineup" and similar phrasal-verb particles (lined up, stack up, match up, pair up), strongest on the noun "lineup"/"line-up" meaning an arranged set of performers, players, or products (roster, product lines, matchups).

The "up" particle in arrangement/alignment compounds and phrasal verbs, especially "lineup"/"line up" and also "matchup", "stack up", "shape up" and "next up". Activation is strongest on the noun "lineup" meaning a set of band members, products or shows, with the related word "roster" also firing. The common sense is arranging items or people in order or pairing them for comparison.

58252.name: Technical and scientific descriptions of physical experimental setups and methods, such as samples, apparatus, materials, dimensions, placement or mounting of objects, and measurement procedures. Activation spreads across whole clauses describing how something is prepared, positioned or configured (e.g. 'placing 10 μL on copper grids', 'glued to a 10mm-thick board', 'suspended in water'). Function words and prepositions in these descriptions fire along with the nouns, and spatial-relation words like 'near', 'under', 'through' and 'at' also activate weakly in other contexts.

58268.name: Website boilerplate and UI text at the very start of scraped web pages, before the main article content begins: navigation and accessibility links, post metadata, date parts, and media or share labels. The strongest activation is on "navigation" in "Skip navigation".

58277.name: The name "Dennis" and its variants (Denis, Denise, Denn-), firing on the name token or its suffix piece ("ennis", "is", "ise") after a split "D"/"Den". "Dennis" activates most strongly, while Denis and Denise (including place names like Saint-Denis and "Denisovans") activate moderately. Unrelated tokens show only faint activation.

The name "Dennis" (strongest), plus related or similar-sounding forms such as Denis, Denise, and Denny, including name fragments after "D"/"Den" ("enny", "ise"). Weaker activation appears on lookalike subwords like "ennis" in "Tennis" and "ener" in "Tenerife".

58296.name: Words and phrases expressing how a person or thing is regarded by others: public reputation, popularity, approval, support, esteem, or disdain (e.g. popular with, regarded, considered by many, respect, fans, icon, unpopular). Activation is strongest on the evaluative word plus the prepositions naming the audience ("popular with some", "among", "considered by many").

58301.name: The "on" token (often ".on" or " on") used in code for event handler registration or event attributes, e.g. jQuery/Node .on('event', ...), HTML onsubmit/onvalid, onView. It fires most strongly on method-call .on( chains and weakly on related event-binding terms such as .bind, .get, .signal, Handler, and event.

58304.name: Words that introduce the tool, method, technique, or data used to accomplish something: verbs like "use", "using", "utilize", "apply", "leverage" and "employ", plus the prepositions and articles that follow them ("make use of", "relies on", "based on", "by", "with"). The frequent setting is research or technical writing describing methodology.

58338.name: A diffuse, non-semantic feature that fires on a single mid-sentence token, usually a function word or the first word of a phrase or clause that follows a conjunction, verb or preposition (e.g. a subject after "because" or "swore", a determiner after "of" or "until"). The token signals that a continuation is coming, and the activating words share no clear topic.

58347.name: Code block openers: tokens that end a function/loop/conditional header and begin its body, e.g. a colon plus newline in Python, an opening brace plus newline in C-like languages, or a closing parenthesis, along with the indentation and first statement (often print) that follow. Activation is strongest right at the start of a new indented block. Activations on ordinary prose tokens are weak and sporadic.

58349.name: Abstract summary nouns (and their verb phrases) that refer back to a set of previously described aims, tasks or items. Typical examples are "objective(s)", "goals", "purpose", "aim", "duties", "aspects", "questions" and "reasons". They usually follow anaphoric or aggregating words like "these", "this", "other", "all" or "the aforementioned", as in "this object is achieved", "other duties as assigned" and "these and more". Activation is strongest on the patent-style phrase "object is achieved".

58351.name: Fires on connective or function tokens (prepositions, articles, conjunctions, newlines, verbs like 'finden'/'updated') inside formulaic, templated text such as web boilerplate, spec lists and stock phrases in many languages. These sit at mid-phrase points where the rest of the phrase is highly predictable and links into what follows.

58362.name: A sparse, diffuse feature firing on single tokens in varied contexts, usually mid-phrase in a predictable collocation or compound name ("try to", "College of", "high grade", "by email", "Chinese Communist"). It fires most strongly on forms of "appoint" (appointee, appointed, By Appointment) and on the query-like suffix ":true".

58384.name: Names of teams, armies, nations, or other groups and agents acting as one side in a competition or conflict (sports teams, military forces, countries, rival factions). The activation is strongest for sports teams mentioned as an opponent or as the side making a play in a game.

58394.name: Operations that pull a single element out of a collection or wrapper, chiefly in code: indexing brackets and the index itself ([0], [i], [row], .get(0)), and accessor methods such as .First(), .FirstOrDefault(), .unwrap(), .top(), .find(), random.choice, findAny().get() and Current. Activation is highest on these retrieval methods. A weaker version appears in prose that singles out one item from a group ("one of", "choose the", "the third intersection").

5840.name: Tokens right at the start of a document, usually the second or third token of an opening title, headline or first sentence. Often this is the word-completion piece after a split first word (e.g. "Ins|pection", "E|levated") or the word right after a first word like "How", "The" or "We". Activation is strongest near the very beginning and fades soon after.

Fires on the first few tokens at the very start of a document (titles, opening sentences, code headers), typically the token(s) right after the first token, often completing a split first word or continuing the opening phrase; position-based beginning-of-text detector rather than content-specific.

Tokens near the very beginning of a document, usually the second token or the next few that complete the first word or phrase of a title or heading (e.g. the rest of a split first word, or the word right after an opening word like "#include", "A", "#").

58400.name: Python traceback headers. Activation peaks on "back" in "Traceback", on the closing "):" of "(most recent call last):", and on the following indented "File" and its opening quote. Weak activation appears on other code/error contexts such as comment markers, imports and "Trace" in stack trace.

58407.name: Separators and connective words inside boilerplate web and repository text, such as headers, footers, metadata labels and attribution lines ("published by", "brought to you by", "Part of", "downloaded from", "General rights", "Server:"). Activation falls on the newline, colon or preposition right after a label or stock phrase, just before its value or the next section. It is strongest on "by" in attribution lines like "open access by".

58411.name: The "mitochond"/"ochond" word-piece within mitochondria/mitochondrial, most strongly in biology contexts. It also fires more weakly on the same "ochond" piece in other words, such as hypochondriac, endochondral and costochondral.

58417.name: Structural boilerplate in Flutter/Dart widget code, strongest on State class names, createState(), @override, and the braces and indentation around class declarations. It fires weakly on formatting delimiters such as opening square brackets, bold "**" markers and punctuation in messy or code-like text.

58429.name: Top-level domain suffixes in URLs and web addresses (".com", ".org", ".edu", country codes), right after the site name. It also fires weakly on nearby URL path pieces ("/article", "/master", ".php") and other separators marking the end of a name.

5845.name: Terms about how text and data are encoded or represented: character encodings and standards (UTF-8, ASCII, coding declarations), fonts, characters and alphabets, language and format codes, and numeric or binary representation. The strongest cases are explicit encoding terms such as UTF-8 and ASCII value. Activation is weak and diffuse on other technical or standard names, such as metric spaces, the Gregorian calendar, EPSG, ipv4 and HDR.

58462.name: The determiner "the"/"The" (and occasionally other subject-starting words) opening a new noun phrase, usually at the start of a sentence or clause right after a period, newline, comma or conjunction, where it refers back to something already mentioned.

5847.name: Final tokens of proper names and named entities, especially institutions, organizations, publications and place names (e.g. 'Institute in Boulder, Colo', 'University College London', 'Vanity Fair', 'Protection Agency'). Activation is strongest on the closing word of multi-word names and on location tags after affiliations, and also fires on name-completing subword pieces and unit or technical terms.

Tokens within specific factual details in news-style text, mostly the later parts of proper nouns and named entities (places, organizations, people, teams, products) such as name suffixes, city/state pairs, street addresses, and institution words like Center, University, Council, Corp. It also covers concrete specifics like dates, days, times, numbers and job titles.

58506.name: A weak, diffuse feature of news-article structure. It fires mostly at boundaries between a headline or lede and the body: the period or line break ending an opening sentence (".⏎⏎"), the first word of the next paragraph, and dateline, byline or source punctuation such as "(", ":" and "|". Activation is strongest within lede sentences that report an event with place and time details ("at an event at… Tuesday night.").

5851.name: A diffuse, low-level feature that fires across ordinary expository or narrative prose. It peaks mainly at clause boundaries such as commas and periods and on the connective words that continue a sentence ('and then', 'which means', 'when they', 'even if'), with weaker activation on content nouns inside these running clauses. It seems to track mid-sentence continuation and discourse flow rather than any particular topic.

58522.name: Physical locations and spatial settings in narrative or descriptive text: place nouns (area, bushes, center, forest, tunnel, coastline), named places, and the spatial prepositions and phrases that introduce them (in the middle of, outside the, at a bus stop on, through the, east of). Activation is strongest on the location head noun or the preposition that marks where an event or object is situated.

58527.name: The word "names" (occasionally "name"), mostly in the plural, usually as a noun in phrases like "the names of…", "other names", "trade names" or "click on their names". Rare weak hits land on unrelated function words.

58535.name: Minus signs marking negative numbers in math expressions, strongest in short algebra prompts like "Solve -96 = -9*p". It fires weakly on other negating or qualifying tokens such as "not" and "non".

58540.name: Boundary tokens at the junction between items or segments, mostly in list-like or structured text such as keyword lists, tag lists, table cells, and product listings. They are typically separators, line breaks, quotes, or short function words like "of" and "the" that sit right before a new term, name, or entry begins.

58560.name: The token right before a verdict is given, such as a yes/no, true/false, or correct/incorrect answer. It fires on "Answer:", "Output:", "The answer is", "is" before "false/wrong", code comments like "//" before true/false, and opening parentheses before "False". It anticipates an upcoming binary judgment.

58589.name: Commas in postal addresses and institutional affiliations that come right after a city or locality name and come before the larger region (state, province, country) or the postal code.

58591.name: The word "opposition" and related terms for groups or stances against an established power, such as the political opposition, minority party, challengers, dissidents, rebels, resistance and civil society. Activation is highest for the political sense (opposition parties versus a ruling government) and weaker for the general sense of being "in opposition to" something.

The word "opposition" and related nouns for opposing or rival groups. It fires most strongly on political opposition parties, leaders and groups, more weakly on opposition as resistance to a policy. Related words such as opponents, rivals, rebel, Minority (as in Senate or House Minority Leader), dissent and factions also activate it.

58615.name: Biology and genetics terms for invasive, inserted or self-copying entities, most strongly mobile genetic elements such as transposons, retrotransposons, LINEs, viral elements, prophages, plasmids and insertions. Weaker activation appears on invasive species and weeds, and on things intruding into something else, such as plutons and dikes.

58644.name: Assignment punctuation (colons, equals signs, opening quotes/parentheses) right after a font-related key (font-family, font=, Font(, family=) where a font name is about to follow. It is strongest for CSS "font-family:" and its opening quote, and weaker for the separators between listed font names and for similar string-valued parameters such as cmap, encoding and theme.

58646.name: The word-start token "progn" in "prognostic"/"prognoses"/"prognosticators", most strongly in medical "prognostic factor/value" contexts, often after "diagnostic and". The whole word "prognosis" and the split "gn" in "Prognosis" fire only weakly.

58654.name: The first letter(s) of a command-line flag or option right after a hyphen (e.g. -o, -f, -W, -X, -v), strongest for compiler warning flags like -W. Weaker on similar short prefix tokens in code, such as os.O_ / Errno::E constants and regex escapes.
