58661.name: Word-piece tokens at the start or middle of the species (second) part of Latin binomial names, strongest after an abbreviated genus like "S." or "P.". Weaker hits fall on fragments of other rare multi-token proper nouns and identifiers.

58666.name: The strict equality/inequality operators "===" and "!==" in code comparisons (mainly JavaScript/PHP conditionals), firing most strongly in if-statements and ternaries. It fires weakly on "==", on "==="-style wiki heading markers, and on other symbol tokens such as "####" and "→".

58718.name: Words expressing replacement or succession, where one person or thing takes the place, role, or position of another. Typical forms are "replaced (by/with/in)", "replacement for", "succeeded by", "take his place", "filled" (a role or vacancy), "successor"/"predecessor" and "stand-in". Activation is strongest on "replace"/"place"/"succeeded" forms and weaker on loosely related transition words such as "until", "after" and "new".

58728.name: Tokens inside fixed multi-word expressions (idioms, collocations, set phrases) where the next word is highly predictable from the phrase, e.g. "each [other]", "taken [place]", "in other [words]", "at the same [time]", "remains to be [seen]", "needless to [say]", "choose [from]".

58746.name: Auxiliary or copular verbs, mostly "was" (also is/are/been/has), coming right after a subject pronoun or name, usually in biographical or narrative text about a person or thing. Activation is strongest on "was" opening a past-tense passive or descriptive statement, such as "He was born", "was wounded" or "was a defender".

58752.name: A weak, diffuse feature. It fires on tokens that link a preceding subject or left-hand side to what comes next. The clearest cases are equals signs in code assignments and math equations, along with nearby variable names and numbers. In prose, it fires on verbs, auxiliaries and prepositions that directly follow a noun phrase (e.g. 'had', 'has', 'is moving', 'between', 'from the'). Activation is generally low, and slightly higher in code and math contexts.

58753.name: The token "usr" (or "/usr"), almost always as the Unix/Linux system directory in file paths such as /usr/bin, /usr/local and /usr/share. It fires most strongly in path contexts and only weakly on "usr" as a letter sequence inside words or names (e.g., "Susruta", "Nusrat"). Rare weak hits on commas, spaces and other stray tokens are noise.

58757.name: Words expressing decline or worsening of a condition or quality, peaking on the stem "deterior" (deteriorate, deteriorating, deterioration). Weaker activation on near-synonyms like degradation, degrade, decline, worsening, erode, disintegrate and detrimental.

58758.name: HTML/CSS stylesheet link boilerplate, strongest right after a Google Fonts/CDN CSS URL: the closing quote and the following ' rel="stylesheet">' tokens, plus nearby URL pieces (.com, &display=swap) and following <style>/font-family lines; weakly fires on other attribute syntax such as style=".

58771.name: The "Kle"/"Kl" letter sequence, mostly in surnames like Klein, Kleijn, Kline, Kleinke and other proper names (Kleene, Klebsiella, Kleavor). It fires on the " Kle"/" Klein" token or on the suffix that follows a split-off K ("lein", "line", "le"), and is strongest in author citations and personal names.

58779.name: The head noun (or final token of a multi-token word) that completes a noun phrase, often an abstract or general noun right after a determiner or modifier and frequently followed by a prepositional complement such as "of" or "in" (e.g., "the mass of", "the people of", "the C-terminus").

58781.name: The "leuk"/"leuc" word stem (Greek for white), most strongly as the token " leuk" in leukocyte/leukemia, and more weakly as the subword piece after "le" (uk, uc, uka) in leukemia, leucine, leucoderma, interleukin. It also fires weakly on "blood" in "white blood cells".

5879.name: Conditional clauses. Fires most on the word "if" (also "if possible", "see if", code `if(`) that starts a condition, and weakly on the subject/verb tokens inside an already-opened "If …" clause (e.g., "If the body…", "If your router has a…").

Weak, diffuse feature centered on words that introduce conditions, constraints or qualifications, mainly "if" (often sentence-initial), "unless", "as long as", "whether", "nor", and modal or limiting words such as "may", "must not" and "only". These appear in rule-like or instructional statements. It also fires on scattered function words inside such conditional or contrastive clauses.

58850.name: Proverbs, scripture and other moralizing or archaic text, especially Biblical verses and wise sayings ("better than", "the Lord is close to the brokenhearted", "thy lot"). It fires most on the content words of the quoted maxim or verse, plus related religious or moral vocabulary such as evil, mercy, heaven and wickedness.

58862.name: Predicate language that ranks or characterizes an entity (often a place, country, or organization) by its standing relative to others: superlatives and ranking phrases like "the highest/largest/best", "among the first", "number one", "the nation's largest", "one of the most". Strongest on the article and superlative right after the subject plus verb ("X has the...", "X is the...").

58871.name: Words for giving a talk or performing in front of an audience: presentations, talks, panel discussions, lectures, speakers, sessions, and verbs like present, speak about, share insights on, address. Activation is strongest on the event nouns (panel, presentation, speaker, talk) and the following 'on/about'.

58873.name: Asterisk (or similar star symbols like ∗, ⁎, often fused with a comma) placed right after an author's name or affiliation number in academic paper author lists, marking the corresponding author. Weak firing on other stray asterisks or bracket and label tokens that follow names.

58877.name: Separators and punctuation between items in a list of links, formats or labels, such as pipes, commas, semicolons, brackets, spaces, colons and closing parentheses. It fires on the delimiter right before the next item starts ("| [", "), [", "PDF | Word", "(b)").

5891.name: Attribution of information to a source, i.e. naming the person, institution, organization, publication or study behind a claim. It fires on phrases like "according to the…", "report from…", "a [job title] at [institution]", affiliations and locations ("University of…, Sweden", "NCAR in Boulder, Colorado"), author lists and citations, and "is a … tool that". Activation is strongest on the introducing words (from, according to, report, study, think tank) and on organization names.

58915.name: Continuation subword pieces that finish rare or multi-token words, mostly proper nouns such as personal names, places, brands, products, teams and mythological or historical names. Examples include Maxim-us, Ab-el-ton, Carth-aget, H-okusai and Na-utilus. It occasionally fires on a whole word that ends a name or title (e.g. Falls, Button, Shepard). Activations are weak overall.

Final tokens of proper names (brands, places, groups, titles, people), especially the subword pieces that finish an uncommon multi-token name like Cerber-us, Koy-ote or Mor-pheus. Activation peaks at the point where the name is completed.

58928.name: Middle-to-late terms of a descending sequence, mainly the low exponents (especially ^2, also ^3) and linear 'x' terms in polynomials written in decreasing-degree order, with strongest activation on the squared term. Weaker hits on other countdowns (5×4×3, 23…11, five/four/three) and indented rows of ASCII patterns that step down line by line.

58931.name: Nouns (and some verbs) naming the source or venue through which information is communicated, typically after 'in a', 'according to', 'based on': study, report, interview, presentation, survey, statement, meeting, data, post. Activation is strongest for research or press sources used to attribute a claim.

58954.name: A weak, diffuse feature with no clear single-token pattern. It fires mostly on generic, low-information filler in noisy web text such as SEO spam, scrambled or nonsensical sentences, code and number snippets, and templated boilerplate. It is strongest on corporate-buzzword placeholder text (e.g., 'Organically grow the holistic world view…') and on generic website promo copy ('If you are ready, you can play some other games').

58958.name: A diffuse feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires on single tokens in the middle of a sentence, either function words or content words, that begin or link a continuing phrase ("Once", "for", "the", "finding", the space before a number). It often appears in noisy, spun or boilerplate web text.

58960.name: Directory and path components at the start of file paths in Python traceback lines (File "..."), such as drive letters with :\ , /usr, /home, /tmp, /root, Users, lib, version numbers. The strongest activations fall on the first segments right after the opening quote, with weak, scattered activations elsewhere.

58977.name: Biblical and archaic scriptural prose (KJV-style narrative and verse), firing most on connective and function words like 'and', 'with', 'of', 'that', commas, colons and semicolons that chain the clauses together. Weaker, scattered activations land on clause boundaries and sentence-ending punctuation in ordinary text.

58986.name: The opening of a citation or reference marker placed right after a claim or sentence ends: an opening bracket or parenthesis, a reference number or superscript, or LaTeX \cite or \textsuperscript{. The strongest activations are on the opening " (" or " [" and the first number or author token of a parenthetical citation (e.g. "(reviewed in 2)", "(4)"). Weaker activations appear on related pointers such as "Figure", "See", and stray delimiters.

58993.name: Highly predictable continuation tokens that complete a fixed construction. The strongest case is "strict" in the JavaScript directive 'use strict'. Weaker cases complete set phrases ("such as", "hold their tongues", "don't") or are dash bullet markers in nested lists.

59.name: Formatting and punctuation tokens at structural boundaries, most often stray or extra whitespace (doubled spaces, indentation runs, newlines) along with list numbers, opening brackets/parentheses, quotes, dashes and garbled characters like '?s'. The activating tokens tend to be irregular, noisy or layout-related rather than ordinary words.

59005.name: Words marking that a statement applies jointly to several previously mentioned entities, or to what they share or how they compare. Typical cues are collective quantifiers and plural subjects with their verbs ("both", "all of these", "each with the same", "two models are", "alike", "also", "everyone else", "interchangeably"), as in "both have to do with" or "all three options would result".

59006.name: Hospital emergency departments and urgent acute-care settings, firing most strongly on "emergency department/room", "ER", "A&E" and "urgent care". Weaker activations come from other hospital units and service places named by a modifier plus a noun (operating room, maternity ward, pediatrics department, jail, food bank, service desk). Generic words like "emergency" or phrases such as "seek medical attention" also fire weakly.

59037.name: Tokens inside titles and headlines, mostly article or blog headings, product pages, breadcrumbs and section headers, and especially the first such heading near the start of a document or right after a paragraph break. The signal is spread weakly across the words of a headline, with peaks on colons, 'Is'/'Vs', 'Everything to know about'-style phrasing and subject names.

59044.name: A diffuse feature in technical text (math word problems, equations, code, logic puzzles). It fires on connective or structural tokens in the middle of a definition or specification, just before the key content arrives. Typical triggers are function words and operators such as "be" in "Let x be", "=", "(", ",", "a", "of", "the" and "years".

59058.name: A diffuse, mostly syntactic pattern with no clear topical theme. It fires on the token just before the key content of a phrase: articles, prepositions, relative pronouns, opening parentheses, a year prefix like "200" before its final digit, or a space before a number. The next token, typically a noun, name, number or argument, completes the phrase. Some hits fall on oddly chosen words in spun or garbled text.

59076.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens inside formulaic multiword expressions and predictable collocations, such as idioms, set phrases and discourse fillers ("of course", "in turn", "took place", "so far", "pretty much", "for what it's worth", "in pretty bad shape", "as if there is one"). It also fires on conversational clause starters like "I know what", "that's just", "this is" and "they're", mostly in informal or narrative prose. It responds most strongly where the phrase continuation is highly predictable.

59078.name: Tokens that link an expression or subject to its result, value, or explanation: equals signs and arrows in calculations, inline comment markers (#, //, <!--) after code, 'Output' headers, and predicate verbs like 'is/are', 'will', 'should be', 'that is' introducing what something equals or produces.

59122.name: Fires inside low-quality, templated or spammy web text (SEO keyword lists, product-page fields, lorem ipsum, DOIs, canned reviews). It peaks on tokens that complete a phrase repeated nearby, such as "male enhancement", "sixth mass extinction", "reading list not updating" and "questions related to this textbook", or on punctuation within such boilerplate.

59141.name: The "value" attribute/key token in code, strongest in HTML <option value=...> within select dropdowns (also input/radio value=, data-value, .value); weaker activation on separators that introduce the value of a labeled choice or field, like " (" before option ranges in input prompts, ")" after multiple-choice letters, and ":" after object keys.

5917.name: A diffuse, weakly firing latent with no single clear concept. It fires on tokens that complete a phrase, name or statement. In code, this is mostly the final piece of an identifier or expression: suffixes like Form, Marker, Parameter, ScrollBar, a variable reused from earlier, or closing ');', ')' or '];'. In prose, it fires on phrase-final nouns ('ingredients', 'expectations', 'Source'), on location words ('below', 'bottom', 'end'), and on sentence-ending punctuation or citation numbers. Activation is strongest in code, where the token is highly predictable from preceding context.

59176.name: The subword token "phil" (love/affinity root), firing most strongly in "hydrophilic" and other chemistry/solubility contexts (polar, water-soluble). It fires more weakly in other words such as philosophy, philanthropist, and taxon names, and faintly on unrelated tokens.

59193.name: Opening delimiter tokens that come right before a file path, URL or other reference value, such as =" in href/src/onclick attributes, (" in read_csv calls, ](, ://, ./ and \ref{. Strongest on href=".

59220.name: Function words and connective phrases in expository scientific/technical prose, peaking where a material or technology class (especially nanoparticles/nanomaterials/polymers) is being introduced, defined or characterized, e.g. "are one of the", "represent a captivating class of", "are being designed to". Activation is weak and diffuse elsewhere.

59238.name: Nouns naming formal institutional bodies, official documents, and expert proceedings, such as commissions, academies, consortia, summits, workshops, reports, resolutions, conventions, strategies, inquiries and recommendations. They usually appear as the head word of an organization or publication title (e.g. "National Academies", "Broadband Commission for"). Activation is strongest on the core institutional noun.

59249.name: Speech and attribution markers in reported speech or news style: verbs of saying (said, added, reported, wrote, explained), the speaker or source named near a quote (he, she, Moscow, the report), and source nouns such as statement, release, interview, survey or papers. They mostly appear just after a quotation or claim, or in 'according to' constructions. The strongest activations are on 'said' and on source nouns like 'report', 'statement' and 'release'.

59255.name: Tokens that close or finish an embedded span, such as a closing quote, bracket, brace, parenthesis, abbreviation period, or end of a code/math expression. These usually sit inside a parenthetical, argument list or citation, just before the outer context resumes (often right before a closing parenthesis or other delimiter).

59266.name: Tokens in assistant-style explanatory or math text that begin a new section or deliver a judgment. Most often this is the opening "**" of a bold markdown header after a blank line (Answer, Solution, Key Concepts, Step-by-Step). Strongest are verdict words such as False, No, Not or "but" that state whether something is correct; "e.g.," separators also fire.

59315.name: The abbreviation "Ct" for "Court" in legal citations, firing most strongly on the Supreme Court Reporter form "S. Ct." after a volume number. It fires more weakly on other court abbreviations (Cir. Ct., Eur. Ct., SUP. CT) and on nearby citation punctuation, with near-zero activation on unrelated tokens.

59330.name: Text about problems and preventing them, such as harm, disease, damage or deterioration, often in warning or advisory language. It fires most on conditional and consequence clauses ("if... persists", "without proper treatment", "it can be", "should be considered") that state risks, the need for intervention, or recommended preventive actions.

59350.name: Names of government tax and revenue authorities, mainly the IRS, "Revenue" in Internal Revenue Service and Canada Revenue Agency, and HMRC, plus weaker hits on other tax terms, tax laws, and federal or regulatory agencies such as the ATF, DMV, SSA and Treasury.

Names of tax authorities and related government revenue/regulatory agencies, chiefly the IRS ("Internal Revenue Service", "IRS", "irs"), with similar but weaker activation on other tax bodies (HMRC, ATO, Department of Revenue, Customs and Excise) and other federal agency names (ATF, USCIS, BMV). It also fires weakly on tax-related terms like taxman, tax code/rules/policy, audit and CPA. Activation is strongest on the distinctive word or acronym within the agency name, especially "Revenue".

59352.name: The word "to" right after a grant of rights in legal or licensing text ("permission to", "license to", "right to", "granted to", "without charge to"), which introduces either the permitted action or the person receiving it. It is strongest in the MIT License phrase "granted, free of charge, to". Other scattered tokens fire only weakly.

59365.name: Subword tokens that begin or form part of a multi-token word, where the next token completes it (e.g. "space" + "walk", "vapor" + "izers"). They often appear at the start of a sentence. The pattern is noisy: one case is a preposition leading into a hyphenated compound.

59371.name: The "d" in legal reporter citations for second/third series (e.g., "N.W.2d", "S.W.3d", "Wis. 2d"), which comes right before a page number. Other tokens show only weak, scattered activation.

59380.name: The "/licenses" path segment in the Apache License URL (http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0) within boilerplate license headers in code; weak, sporadic activation on articles/conjunctions elsewhere.

59397.name: The colon (occasionally a dash) that separates the hour from the minutes in a clock time. It appears in timestamps, log entries, ISO datetimes and chat transcripts, almost always right after the hour digits.

59402.name: Legal names of killing offenses, firing most strongly on "manslaughter" (including the split "laughter" token) and more weakly on "homicide" and "murder". Activation is highest when the word names a criminal charge, often after modifiers such as "second-degree", "negligent", "felony", or after "charged with" or "acquitted of". Weak activations on unrelated tokens look like noise.

59446.name: Python method decorators, mainly "staticmethod"/"classmethod" right after "@" and before a def, plus weaker hits on related class-level keywords like static, self in Ruby's "def self.", and ::. It also fires faintly on transitional or boilerplate tokens such as "However", "In addition" and "Leave a Reply".

5945.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on content nouns or noun modifiers naming the specific subject or setting being described, especially in scientific or descriptive prose. It is strongest on biological and natural-world terms: animals (turkey, sheep, goats, owls), body parts or tissues (pharyngeal, lymph, liver) and land or environment types (urban park, pasture, tillage). These words often act as the modifier in a compound, as in 'turkey farms', 'kidney transplant' and 'fatty liver'. It also fires lightly on other domain nouns and proper names such as places, teams and organizations.

59475.name: The token "init", mostly inside Python's double-underscore __init__ (constructor methods and __init__.py package files), plus related constructor/initializer names like New() and Model::new. It fires most strongly in tracebacks and file paths. Weak secondary hits fall on scattered punctuation in code and technical text, such as "e.g.,", colons and comment "#" markers.

59481.name: Fires on tokens in templated, boilerplate or repeated text where the continuation is highly predictable. These include HTML table-cell tags, URL pieces like "://" and hyphen-joined slug fragments, stray standalone space tokens inside blog-post titles ("Responses to …"), and " all"/" are" in duplicated instruction text. They often sit at odd tokenization boundaries partway through a structure.

59486.name: The word "district" (and its plural and capitalized forms, including split tokens like "istrict") in any sense: an administrative, electoral, school, water or military division, or a named urban or geographic area. It fires most strongly on lowercase uses after a place name or modifier ("school district", "Kajaki district"). Related area nouns like "city" activate only weakly.

59531.name: A diffuse feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires on single mid-sentence tokens that begin a predictable complement or continuation of the preceding word, such as 'equal to', 'need any', 'that not only', 'nicknamed '…'', 'via endogenous' and 'Damage level'. These are often function words or word-initial fragments that open a dependent phrase.

59540.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on content words (or word pieces) completing familiar fixed phrases: titles of works, idioms, catchphrases, quotes, and institutional names. Examples include "Gentlemen Prefer Blondes", "The Man Who Fell to Earth", "catch a falling knife", "the ultimate question of life, the universe and everything", and "Complementary and Integrative Health". It is strongest on the distinctive word in such set expressions.

59553.name: Mentions of Linux, especially "linux" as a path component in C #include headers (<linux/...>, include/linux, <sys/...>), plus related system/kernel terms (Linux kernel, android package imports). Activation is weak and sporadic elsewhere.

5960.name: The "<" symbol in any role: less-than comparisons in code and math, opening angle brackets for HTML tags, generics, email addresses and placeholders, or "less than" values such as <90. Weaker activations go to other opening or prefix symbols like "+", "[", "(", "*" and "<=".

59602.name: Tokens inside repetitive, enumerated, or list-like sequences (letters, numbers, citation brackets, repeated words/labels, separators, newlines) where an item follows the same pattern as earlier items. Activation is weak and strongest on items or delimiters in the middle of such predictable series, such as repeated 'Image' words, figure numbers, or citation indices.

59607.name: Fires most strongly on the token "libs" (" libs", "/libs"), the abbreviation for libraries, especially in code, path or garbled technical contexts. Weaker activations land on scattered tokens in code or noisy technical text, mostly function words and identifier fragments (" a", " next", " after", " with", "end", "depend").

59615.name: Words expressing participation or involvement of an entity in a process, chiefly "involved" (also involvement, participates, implicated, role, interact, contributes). Activation is strongest in biomedical and scientific contexts, as in genes or proteins "involved in" a biological process.

59630.name: Words marking the present moment or a recent update, most often "now", plus "today('s)", "recently" and "current". It also fires on present or present-perfect auxiliaries (is/are/has/have) right after a subject, typically in news-style sentences reporting a new development that contrasts with earlier background.

59685.name: Editor modeline settings in code comments (vim/vi ":set ts=4 sw=4 tw=…", emacs tab-width), strongest on the option names like ts/sw/sts and their "=" and numeric values. Weaker on similar key=value or label-number separators.

59689.name: Weak, diffuse activation centered on mathematical, code and formula syntax: assignment/equals signs, operators (+, ^, \in, \Rightarrow), function names and brackets (ln(, cos(, range(, gcd), variable names being defined, plus chemical formula fragments and unit abbreviations. It fires mainly on symbolic/technical notation, with scattered low activations on ordinary prose tokens.

59695.name: Descriptions of what someone perceives, usually seen, heard, felt or smelled, in narrative scenes. It fires on the object or phenomenon perceived (a figure, a voice, a flash of light, faint streaks, tiny dots, a smell) and on the perception verbs that introduce it (spotted, saw, hear, felt). It is strongest on sudden or vague sensory encounters, like hearing a familiar voice or a figure appearing.

Mentions of something perceived but vague or unidentified: a sudden or mysterious sensory phenomenon (a voice, a figure, a glow, a sound, a vibration, flickering form) emerging or being noticed, or noticing that something is off or unclear (garbled text, unfamiliar charges, 'something's off'). Strongest in narrative descriptions of an entity or perception appearing, e.g. 'a voice', 'something moves behind', 'a glow emerged from'.

59719.name: Pieces of graphics and statistics library names, mostly the suffix or prefix after "GL"/"gl" (glm, GLU, GLUT, GLFW, GLSL, glumpy, GLM models, OpenTK, SFML). The strongest cases are in C++/OpenGL code, such as glm:: types and include paths. Weak, sporadic activation appears on other code identifiers and random subword tokens.

59740.name: The word completing an abbreviated author/party list after one or more names, chiefly "al" in "et al." in citations, plus "others"/"Ors" in legal case names ("X and others v Y"). Activation is strongest in reference lists that name several authors.

59781.name: The word "agreed" in boilerplate legal/license text, overwhelmingly the Apache License phrase "Unless required by applicable law or agreed to in writing". It fires more weakly on similar stock formulas such as "All authors have read and agreed" and occasionally on other predictable function words in fixed phrases.

59830.name: Common or vernacular names of species and substances, especially when given alongside or as an alternative to a scientific or technical name (after "also known as", "or", or in parentheses after a Latin binomial, e.g. Large White, golden orfe, Early Bumble bee). Activation is strongest on the descriptive modifier words of the common name (colour, size, place) and on the connectors that introduce it.

Tokens that begin or form part of common, vernacular names of species and other entities, especially plants and animals, often given next to a scientific name or in lists of alternative names (e.g. "known as", "including"). Activation is strongest on descriptive modifiers such as place, color, or shape words ("Rocky Mountain", "long-finned", "mountain beech") and on the separators that introduce a new common name.

Common (vernacular) names of species, mostly plants and animals, and similar named varieties. It fires on the descriptive modifier words of the name (colors, places, body-part terms such as 'three-toed', 'whitetip', 'cranberry white') and on the connectors that introduce or list them ('known as', 'the', 'and', commas), often next to scientific binomials. It peaks in lists of several species or alternate names.

59840.name: The very first token of a document, firing most strongly when the text begins mid-stream with a bare number fragment (e.g. part of a phone number, ID, count or price like "869", "837", "051"). It fires more weakly on other opening fragments such as partial words, markdown hashes, newlines or punctuation.

59845.name: Words naming a recommended or desirable quality, behavior or manner, usually as the object or complement of advice, guidelines or prescriptive statements (e.g. treat with respect, be kind, write clean/maintainable code, stay active, remain vigilant, be properly cited). Often appears in imperative or "should/must" contexts describing good practice or virtuous conduct.

59873.name: Fires on structural/formatting tokens that begin a new segment or explanation, chiefly code comment markers (#) and indentation before explanatory comments, whitespace+newline tokens, and long runs of repeated filler symbols. It also fires weakly on words opening an instruction or derivation step in technical/math prompts (e.g., 'Solve', 'move', '=').

59894.name: The preposition "for" in the Apache License boilerplate phrase "See the License for the specific language governing permissions" found in code headers; weak activation on other prepositions/words that come before an expected, predictable continuation (e.g., "hooked up with", "rhymes with").

59897.name: Mainly fires strongly on the "for" attribute immediately after an HTML <label tag (label for="..."); also weakly on the first "def" following a Python import line (import math/random/re).

59924.name: The leading indentation whitespace right after a blank line that begins a numbered list, just before the first item number (usually "1."), typically following an introductory sentence ending in a colon. A few weak, scattered activations fall on unrelated mid-sentence tokens.

59927.name: Nouns naming bodies of prior precedent, evidence or reference material, i.e. things cited or consulted as authority. These include case law and legal cases, literature, research, references, sources, publications and precedents. Activation is strongest for legal "case law" and "cases".

Nouns naming documented precedents or bodies of evidence that can be cited, above all legal ones: case(s), decision(s), ruling, case law, jurisprudence, precedent, court. The feature is strongest in judicial contexts. It fires more weakly on research and reference nouns such as studies, research, article, citations, references, quote and observations.

59941.name: Words that mark a temporal (sometimes spatial) reference point from which later events proceed, especially the anaphoric word after "since"/"from"/"until" ("since then", "from there", "from now on", "since that time", "has since"). Activation is strongest on "then" in "Since then". Weaker hits fall on time spans ("years", "decade") and on commas closing an introductory time phrase.

59983.name: Final tokens (often the ending subword piece) of personal surnames, mostly author names in academic citations, reference lists and author bylines; strongest in parenthetical citations like (Name, year) or 'Name et al.'.

60004.name: Stock, formulaic web/document boilerplate: open-access license statements ("article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License"), copyright notices ("All rights reserved"), forum/blog UI text (Reply/Replies, bullets, post dates/times), calls to action ("Click here to", "Sign Up Now", "Please..."), and templated freelancer bid phrases ("I have X years of experience", "your project description"). Activation is strongest on the core words of the license phrase.

60013.name: Fires on the "Yugoslav" tokens (" Yugosl", " Yugoslavia"), most strongly in country and adjective uses, and on the matching "-osl-" and "-isl-" pieces inside Slavic names ending in "-slav" (Yaroslav, Stanislav, Branislav, Jaroslav, Miloslav). Weak firing on unrelated tokens is noise.

60026.name: Highly predictable tokens that complete a fixed, formulaic sequence, e.g. the second half of a split word (검→색 in 검색, Wein→berg, Aeros→mith, N.W.2→d) or a template-bound next token (public→class, State→University, time-limit 초, conjunctions in stock marketing prose). It fires on low-surprisal continuations rather than on any particular meaning.

60034.name: In source code, the line-ending tokens (closing quote/semicolon/paren plus newline, or bare newlines/indentation) that end a variable assignment or constant declaration, typically just before another assignment or declaration line begins. Strongest on string constant assignments.

60035.name: The word "License" in the standard Apache license boilerplate phrase "you may not use this file except in compliance with the License" found in source code headers; very weak, sporadic activation on unrelated tokens elsewhere.

60045.name: Tokens that are highly predictable from the preceding context, typically completing a fixed phrase or familiar pattern (e.g. 'As a result', 'in terms of', '{@link org'). Some also continue a topic or repetition already set up in the text (telecom, the numeric 'km/miles' table).

6005.name: Names of data containers and collections, mainly in code: dictionaries, maps, arrays, key lists and settings dicts (e.g. a variable indexed with brackets, a "dict" key, a DATABASES = { block). Activation is strongest on identifiers being indexed or assigned to and on the bracket or brace tokens around them. Prose words for stored data (database, payload, packages, parameters) activate weakly.

60050.name: Binary operators and connectors sitting between two operands, mostly arithmetic signs (+, -, /, //, %, <=, \frac's }{) in math, LaTeX, and code, especially + and - after a variable or subscript. It also fires weakly on word connectors with the same role, such as 'than', 'to' and 'by'.

60081.name: A diffuse feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires weakly on scattered, hard-to-predict tokens. It is strongest in noisy or mixed text such as garbled or mojibake characters, random URL or email fragments, mixed scripts and odd name pieces. It also fires at phrase or segment boundaries, like the first word after punctuation or a list marker, or a function word introducing a new noun phrase.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires near discourse boundaries in scraped web text. It peaks on the opening words of a new segment after a break: a new paragraph, header, caption, signature line or URL boundary. Examples include "Photos:", "Hotel features (", "MADNESS! A recurring", "*The" and "On behalf of". It also fires on the first content words that introduce a new topic or statement, with low activation elsewhere.

60093.name: Words that mark a person or thing as dead or gone, mostly modifiers placed before a noun: "late", "deceased", "dead", "fallen", "departed", "predeceased", "posthumously", "passed away". The strongest activations are for "deceased" and "late" describing a dead person. Weaker activations occur for related senses of removal or loss of status ("deposed", "disgraced", "extinct") and for non-death uses of "late" (e.g., "late '80s").

60109.name: Fires at the boundary right after a clause or phrase that is already grammatically complete, on the token that opens an add-on: a parenthetical, clarification, qualification or elaboration. Typical triggers are opening parentheses (strongest), dashes, colons, and connectives such as "including", "albeit", "except", "rather", "like", "but", "either" and "sometimes". It also fires weakly on sentence-ending punctuation at that same point. A secondary pattern is definitional phrasing (e.g., '“Elimination of contaminants” is defined as').

60137.name: Start of the next item in a parallel list of facts or statistics, mostly after a number or a comma, 'and', 'while', or a line break. Fires on the determiner or the opening noun ("the", "average", "maximum recommended", "range of", "Total") that introduces a new quantity, which is usually followed by another value.

60158.name: The ">" plus newline token that closes the final or cell of an HTML table row, just before . It marks the end of a row. Weaker activations occur on other boundaries where a list item, field or segment ends, such as line breaks after list items, closing parentheses, and sentence-final punctuation.

60185.name: Tokens that come right after a person's (or entity's) name and open supplementary identifying information about it, such as an alternate, maiden, or former name, a nickname, birth details, or a relation. Typical triggers are an opening parenthesis, a quotation mark, or words like 'born', 'called', 'formerly', 'name was'. Activation is strongest on 'née' and its variants ('neé', 'n’ee'), which introduce a maiden name.

60187.name: Sentence boundaries in scientific or technical abstract-style prose. Activation peaks on the period closing a sentence, especially the opening background or aim sentence. It continues onto the first words of the next sentence when that sentence moves into methods, data, or findings ("The study involved", "Data were from", "Methods: This was a", "We compared"). Weaker activation falls on method and reporting phrases and on parenthetical acronyms.

60208.name: Prefix tokens of member/field variable names in code, chiefly the Hungarian-style "m" (as in m_foo, mFoo) and the leading underscore (_foo), plus occasional "g" for globals. They usually come right after return, this->, an opening parenthesis/bracket, or at the start of an assignment line. Activation is strongest for "m" followed by an underscore.

60218.name: The token "io (with its opening quote) inside Go import blocks, i.e. the "io" or "io/ioutil" package import. It fires strongly and consistently there, with only negligible scattered activity on other tokens.

60238.name: Low-intensity activations in expository, encyclopedic or scientific prose that explains how something works, is structured or is made. They fall mostly on the verbs, prepositions and articles that link a subject to its mechanism or property, just before the key noun phrase (e.g. 'occurs via', 'regulated through', 'stored in', 'contains a', 'made of a', 'has an').

60282.name: Python import keywords ("import", "from", occasionally "class") at the start of a line in a file's header block, firing most strongly on the second or later import line right after an earlier import. A few weak hits land on boilerplate web text such as "Leave a Reply".

6029.name: A diffuse, weakly firing latent with no clear semantic trigger. It activates sparsely on scattered mid-sentence tokens, such as content nouns, verbs, numbers, punctuation and code operators. These appear mostly in expository, technical, scientific or code text, often where a clause continues or specifies details (e.g., 'is replicated', 'execution stayed, pending', '/= d;').

60315.name: The word "cut" and its inflections (cuts, cutting, Cut) in any sense: literal slicing, reducing costs or amounts, phrasal verbs (cut off/down/back), idioms (cutting-edge, cut corners), and even as part of names or compounds.

The word "cut" in any form (cut, cuts, cutting, Cut, CUT, -cut), whether literal (slicing, cutting out) or figurative (budget cuts, cut short, cut back, cutting-edge, cut through, cut to the chase). Activation is strongest on verb uses meaning reduce or stop and on idioms, and somewhat lower on 'cutting-edge' and literal slicing.

60336.name: The main verb or auxiliary right after a sentence's subject, especially when the clause opens with a time phrase ("Since 1993," "In recent years," "Now,"). It fires most strongly on present-perfect auxiliaries (has/have/been) and the participles that follow them, and more weakly on simple tense verbs (was, are, will) that mark the clause's tense or aspect.

60359.name: Line-initial structural keywords in code or formatted text that repeat the construct begun on the preceding line, such as nested or consecutive namespace and class declarations, repeated import, cd or print statements, and repeated URL path segments. Also fires on the "Answer" label after multiple-choice options. Strongest on stacked namespace and class declarations.

6036.name: Final subword pieces of proper names, especially author surnames and given names in author or citation lists (often followed by an affiliation number, comma or initial). Weaker activation falls on name-like endings in URLs and sources (".com") and on separators that end an entry, such as a comma, colon or paragraph break.

Fires on the token that completes a multi-token word or entity, most often the final subword piece of a person's name (surname or given name fragments like "eson", "gens", "uger", "ana"). It also fires on endings of other proper nouns, URLs, IDs and number strings. Weaker activations land on sentence-final periods or other tokens that close a unit just before a break such as a newline, citation or "Read More".

60373.name: Anonymous function or lambda definitions in code, mainly the JavaScript "function" keyword used as an expression (assigned to a variable, passed as an argument, or wrapped in parentheses as an IIFE). It also fires on the following "()" and opening brace, on arrow "=>" syntax, and on analogues like lambda, λ, Perl sub/eval blocks and Lisp let. Activation is strongest for "(function" right after an opening parenthesis.

6038.name: Words about renting, leasing, and temporary use or access to property and services. It is strongest on "rent" and "rent out", then "leasing", with weaker activation on related terms like lend, borrow, subscribe, own, vacancies, occupied, as-a-service and per month.

Words about renting, leasing, and temporary use of property or services. Rent/rental terms fire strongest, followed by lodging and booking words (hotel, booking, reservation, check-in, stay), lending and borrowing, and housing units. Weaker activations come from related service and transaction terms such as hiring, repair, licensing and providers.

60513.name: Nouns (and related verbs) naming a position, title or role held by a person, especially leadership or authority roles such as president, emperor, director, chairman, commander, prime minister, host. They typically follow words like "become", "named", "as" or "the next".

60517.name: The word "distributed" (often with "under") as a past-participle modifier after a noun in license boilerplate, strongest in the Apache License phrase "software distributed under the License" and weaker in "article distributed under the Creative Commons" text. Other reduced relative participles or prepositions after a noun ("born on", "returned") fire faintly.

60544.name: Words for physical restraint, peaking on "handcuff" and its forms (especially the "handc" token, with "uff/uffed/uffs" weaker). Weaker activation for related binding words such as shackled, chained, restraints, bound, tied and cuffed, including figurative uses like being handcuffed to a job.

60547.name: Math contexts where specific coefficient or variable values are being assigned, especially quadratic coefficients (a, b, c), with activation on the "=" sign, the space after it, and the first digits or minus sign of the value that follows. Weaker activation shows up on tokens that come right before a number or expression is stated ("is", ":", "to").

60549.name: The "-scale" token in HTML viewport meta tags ("initial-scale", "maximum-scale"). It fires weakly on "-width" in CSS media queries ("max-width") and on a few unrelated tokens.

60563.name: Metadata labels in file headers and document info, chiefly "Created" (as in "Created by"/"Created on"/"Created:") at the top of source-code comments, which fires most strongly. Similar provenance labels such as "Started", "DOI"/"doi" in citations, and "Commenced" fire weakly.

60566.name: The first token (subword fragment) of a multi-token proper name, typically a person's surname or given name (e.g. "Yak" in Yakaboski, "Fe" in Feustel, "Mark" in Markle), activating at the start of the name when it is being split into pieces. The strongest firing is on unusual or foreign names and on repeated mentions. It occasionally fires weakly on other word-initial fragments or ordinary words.

The first token or fragment of a proper name, mostly surnames of people, but also teams, places, products, split into subword pieces. It usually appears where the name is predictable from earlier context, often a repeat mention of an established subject.

60568.name: Line and phrase boundaries in song lyrics, poems, and verse. The strongest activations fall on line breaks, commas, and periods that close a lyric line, and on the last words of rhythmic lines or repeated refrains, as in Examples 18 and 22. Weaker activations appear on scattered punctuation in ordinary prose.

60578.name: Word-completion subword tokens in immune-suppression vocabulary. They fire most strongly on "uppress" in "immunosuppressive/immunosuppression". They also fire on the endings of immunosuppressant drug names (cyclosporine, mycophenolate, azathioprine, methotrexate) and other immuno- compounds (immunomodulatory, immunodeficient, inhibitor).

60589.name: Tokens that anticipate the naming of an academic degree or other qualification, chiefly verbs of obtaining (received, earned, holds, pursuing, obtained, completed) and the possessives or articles that follow them (his, her, a, an). The strongest activations come just before the degree name, as in "received her PhD" or "holds a B.A.". Weaker activations appear on degree-name fragments (B, M, Ph, "of" in "Master of") and on looser contexts of acquiring an award, credit or career.

Determiners, possessives, and verbs that come right before a mention of an academic degree, qualification, or career credential, such as "holds a", "earned a", "and an", "finished my", "pursue a", and "B"/"M" in BSc/MSc. Activation is strongest when a degree name (Master's, PhD, BFA, MSc) follows directly. It is weaker on similar slots before jobs, diplomas, reputations, or skills.

60602.name: A sparse, weak, largely nonspecific feature. Its strongest firing is on the "/LICENSE" path segment in a GitHub license URL (a predictable boilerplate completion). Elsewhere it fires weakly on scattered single tokens that typically follow a verb or preposition, such as articles ("an", "the"), pronouns, verbs, word suffixes and line breaks, with no clear shared meaning.

60631.name: The word "top" used as a positional or layout term, chiefly in code and markup (CSS margin-top/padding-top, style.top, top/left/right/bottom parameters, stack .top()) and in the website footer link "Scroll to Top". The strongest activations are on CSS "-top" properties.

60637.name: Fires inside formulaic, boilerplate web prose such as repository and copyright notices, privacy and data-safety text, takedown policies and corporate mission or marketing statements. It mostly activates on predictable connective points within these stock phrases, like commas, 'and', prepositions and the verb or clause continuation that comes next. Example phrases include 'documents, whether', 'recognise and abide', 'please let the Library know' and 'has long inspired our commitment to'.

Fires on assorted, non-specific tokens (function words, punctuation, single letters) inside dense technical or STEM content such as hashing and blockchain explanations, circuit equations in LaTeX, and code. The feature appears to track the technical/explanatory context rather than any particular word.

60667.name: The preposition "to" after a number or verb in rounding instructions ("Round 829 to the nearest hundred"), where it introduces the target precision. It fires weakly on other prepositions that link a verb or noun to its target ("exposed to", "visas for") and on scattered punctuation or whitespace.

60684.name: Fires on transition/boundary tokens that immediately precede a new chunk of content. Most often these are structural separators in list-like or web/document text: newlines, double newlines, bullets, dashes, colons after field labels, commas before dates, and sentence-ending punctuation before a new heading or entry. It also fires on mid-sentence function words (the, from, can, is, that, be, stay, click) just before the main content phrase begins.

60715.name: Fires strongly on the "/ajax" path segment following "ajax.googleapis.com" in script-src URLs that load jQuery. Everywhere else activation is only weak, scattered across highly predictable continuation tokens, such as the second word of place names (Los Angeles, Austin), punctuation and spaces inside citations.

60720.name: Numbers inside DOIs and academic URLs, especially the volume number or the final digit of the year (e.g. "201<<7>>", "vol<<46>>", "-<<11>>-"). A few weak hits are unrelated ordinary words.

60736.name: Continuation or final tokens of proper names (mostly surnames) used as citations, references, or eponyms in academic, legal, and technical text, especially author names in parenthetical citations and court case names (strongest on legal case names like Tinker v. Des Moines, Plyler v. Doe, Kitzmiller v. Dover).

60739.name: The prefix of a character escape or code-point notation, i.e. the token right after a backslash, "&#", or "U+" (u, x, xe, #, +, e) that introduces a hex/Unicode/HTML entity code in strings and code.

60777.name: Components of calendar dates in post/article timestamps and headers, mainly the month name or abbreviation, day number, separators, and final year digit that follow a weekday or day number.

60835.name: The ",v" suffix right after a filename in RCS/CVS $Id: or $FreeBSD: version header strings (e.g. "file.pl,v 1.9 2001/..."). It fires strongly in these revision-control tags and only weakly on other tokens.

60842.name: Negations and exclusions inside a condition, mostly in code. The strongest cases are operators and words like !, not, != and "not in" right after if, along with the thing being tested. Prose phrases of the same kind (unless, not yet, except, absence of, other than) activate weakly.

60844.name: Final digit(s) of numbers in citations and reference listings, firing most strongly on the page number that follows "S. Ct." in U.S. Supreme Court reporter citations. Weaker activation on trailing digits of years, volume/page numbers and post counts.

60854.name: The word "originally" or "Originally", firing hardest in forum quote attributions ("Originally Posted by …") and republication notes ("originally published/appeared in …"). It fires more weakly on sentence-initial "Originally" meaning "at first".

6087.name: A weak, diffuse feature that mostly fires on subword continuation tokens completing rare or unfamiliar names, acronyms and identifiers, such as the later pieces of personal names, product or company names, chemical labels and code variables. The piece is typically the second or later chunk of a word split into fragments. It occasionally fires on ordinary words or numbers in a noun phrase, with low activation.

60875.name: Expressions of possibility or potential: modal verbs (can, may, could, might) and the verbs/words right after them, along with words like "possible", "possibility that", "potential existence of", "in principle", that mark a hypothetical or capable outcome rather than a definite fact.

Expressions of possibility or potential: modal verbs (can, could, may, might, should) and the verbs right after them (be, happen, cause, occur), plus words like "possible", "possibility", "potentially", "theoretically" and upper-bound phrases ("up to"). Together they mark hypothetical or potential outcomes rather than definite facts.

60886.name: Weak, diffuse feature that fires in contexts of gathering or presenting people's perspectives, accounts and contributions: groups of people consulted, interviewed, invited, or featured (family, aficionados, founders, authors in this volume, members, professionals, artists), plus words for their testimony or output (eyewitness accounts, stories, reactions, proposals, anecdotal reports) and the surrounding function words or verbs (interview, asking, invited, highlight, reviews).

Words that set up reported speech or interviews, where someone is spoken to, interviewed or quoted: "spoke to", "interviewed … about", "said", "admitted on camera", "meet with experts", and opinion or testimonial headers such as "Voices:", "TESTIMONIALS", "Experts Weigh In" and "Profile:". Activation is strongest on "interviewed" and "We spoke to", and also falls on the sentence breaks just before such quotes.

60926.name: The offset and blur length values (e.g. "2px 8px", "0 10px") in CSS box-shadow and text-shadow declarations, peaking on the space between values and on the final "px". It responds weakly to other multi-value numeric arguments such as padding/margin shorthand or comma-separated function arguments.

60934.name: Fires on scattered single tokens in templated, auto-generated, or incoherent spam-like text (SEO keyword-stuffed articles, auto-filled location pages, garbled essays). It is strongest on the space or bracket token right before a number (times, doses, quantities) and on filler or keyword words that break the sentence flow.

60943.name: Whitespace, newlines, and structural delimiters (pipes, ampersands, backslashes, comment slashes, table cells) within spatially laid-out text such as ASCII diagrams, tables, LaTeX arrays/matrices, and figure labels. Activation is strongest on padding spaces and line breaks that align columns or box borders in multi-line 2D layouts.

Whitespace runs, newlines, and line-drawing characters (|, \, /, +, #, //) inside ASCII art, diagrams, box drawings, trees, grids, and aligned text layouts. It is strongest on the padding and vertical border pieces of box and flowchart diagrams, especially " |" followed by a newline and the long space runs that align columns.

61013.name: Closing tokens in code that end a function body or callback block, especially where the closing brace is immediately followed by invocation or further arguments: IIFE patterns like "})(" (strongest, e.g. "})(window,"), "}," before a trailing argument such as a timeout or flag, and "});". It also fires on a top-level "main()" call at the end of a script.

61019.name: Tokens naming globally/universally unique identifiers, chiefly "uuid"/"UUID" and "GUID"/"guid" (including code forms like uuid4, _uuid, randomUUID, NewGuid). Activation is weaker for related identifier terms (OID, IID, CLSID, DOI, ClientId, nonce), and nearly absent for unrelated words.

61024.name: The token right after an author surname in an academic citation, nearly always "et" in "et al.". It is strongest inside parenthetical in-text citations of the form (Surname et al., year). Weaker activations fall on other tokens that follow a cited author's name, such as "al", "and", or the comma before a year.

61029.name: Weak, diffuse activation across the text of plot summaries and story synopses (films, TV, books, fan fiction), describing what characters do and what happens to them: actions, relationships, settings and turns of events. It is strongest in dense stretches that narrate a sequence of events. Non-narrative text, such as instructions or business prose, gets only sporadic weak hits.

Tokens near the end of a clause that express temporal or forward-looking ideas, such as future time or final moments ("in the future", "last moments"), along with prepositions like "to" in expressions of holding on or persisting.

61036.name: The word "side" as a token, along with its variants (sides, sided, siding, sideways, sidetrack, sideburns) and compounds such as side effects, side dish, side by side, side to side, and side-channel. It also fires on look-alikes and translations like "Sid", "aside", Norwegian "siden" and French "côté". Activation is strongest for literal physical or positional senses (surfaces of objects, lateral position) and for set compounds.

61055.name: Function words inside meta-instructions that tell a model how to transform or format its output, such as translate, rewrite, convert or constrain a response. The feature peaks on the word right after the instruction verb and just before the target specification: "translate to/into", "翻译成中文", "convert to some professional", "at least 2", "If there are". It also fires on structural tokens that begin a templated field, such as " <" opening XML/tag lines, a leading quote before a JSON key, or "**" before "Model Response".

6107.name: Spans of news-report prose, most strongly local incident and disaster reporting (accidents, fires, shootings, storm damage, attacks), where officials or investigators describe what happened and what was affected. Activation peaks on the narrative clause right after a paragraph break, such as "Investigators say the accident involved a truck and two cars". Elsewhere it gives weak, diffuse activation on ordinary factual reporting.

61071.name: Text describing organized events such as conferences, workshops, symposia, forums, webinars, panels, meetings and round tables. Activation is strongest on the event nouns themselves ("conference", "workshop", "panels", "round table") and spreads weakly to surrounding logistics: dates, venues, "held from", "opened the meeting", "ends", and sentence boundaries.

61074.name: Subword fragments in the middle of rare, unfamiliar words, mostly foreign proper names (people, places, companies) and technical terms that the tokenizer splits into several pieces. The activating token is a non-initial chunk, typically the second or a later piece, that continues the word without completing it.

61078.name: The name "Scott" (most often as a first name in people's names, also as a surname or in compounds such as Azetsu-Scott). Similar strings like "ott", "Scot", "Scots", "Elliott" and "Scout" activate weakly. The period after a middle initial following Scott also activates moderately.

61084.name: Boundary tokens at the end of a text segment, just before a new section, post, comment, or list item begins. These are mostly sentence-final punctuation fused with newlines, bare newlines, the leading space or number of a new numbered entry, and the colon inside timestamps. Activation is weak.

Boundary tokens where a passage of text or code ends and a new synthetic Q&A or task section begins. The strongest are sentence-ending punctuation fused with a double newline (".

", "!

", "?

") right before "Question:". The colon after "Question" is weaker but consistent. Code-block closers and other answer, exercise, or section headers also fire weakly.

61099.name: Tokens tied to Windows/GUI programming concepts, especially Win32 window-handle identifiers such as win32"gui", hwnd, h"Instance", Window and ImGui, plus related ideas like giving a text box focus. It fires strongly even when such a token appears out of place (e.g. "hwnd" inserted into prose). Other activations are weak and scattered over unrelated text.

61104.name: Tokens inside highly repetitive, patterned sequences: separators (commas, pipes, dashes, operators, newlines) and repeated items in lists, tables, number series, and code. It is strongest where the next token can be predicted from the repeating structure.

61126.name: The word "limitations" in the standard Apache License boilerplate phrase "governing permissions and limitations under the License" found in source-code header comments; fires only weakly on other nouns.

61127.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature spread across generic web prose, mostly technology, software and service-marketing or tutorial text about tools, providers, platforms and solutions. It fires weakly on scattered function words, punctuation and filler phrases rather than on any specific content word. Examples include "you need to", "the right tools for the right task", "possible" and "even".

61133.name: Structural tokens in code and math, chiefly the opening-parenthesis-plus-argument token in function notation (f(n), P(t), Y(s), count(i)). Also fires on the "python" language tag after code fences, indentation whitespace at the start of loop or function bodies, opening braces in LaTeX, and bold "**" headers. These tokens mark points where a formal structure (argument, block, code) begins.

61168.name: The start of a new block or sentence, most often the first name or initial of a person's name at the beginning of an author, inventor, or attorney byline that follows a title or heading (e.g., paper authors, patent inventors, legal counsel). Weaker activations on sentence-initial words after a period.

61176.name: The '#' character used as a CSS/jQuery ID selector prefix (e.g. div #id, querySelector("#…"), $("#…")), often fused with a preceding quote, parenthesis, or space, right before an element ID name. It fires most strongly in CSS selector contexts and weakly on stray '#' or other tokens.

61181.name: Tokens in temporal phrases that mark an event, activity or process finishing or a point within its course, e.g. "end of", "after (the)", "when ... finished/completed", "following", "mid-way through", "the defense is about to rest". The token naming the endpoint or the event is what fires ("of", "finished", "closed", "rest", "proceedings", "innings"). The strongest case is legal and procedural language for concluding, such as "rest" a case.

61189.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens completing fixed boilerplate or metadata templates. Typical spots are the line break after a DOI in repository cover pages, the last digit of a copyright year, "Available On Air Stations" in radio-site headers, and comment-ID parentheses. It fires most strongly on "element"/"ELEMENT" in XML or DTD markup, class names and code (XmlRootElement, <!ELEMENT, elementor). Scattered weak hits also land on ordinary prose words.

61196.name: The word "html" as a markup/code token, mainly the root <html> tag that opens an HTML document (usually right after <!DOCTYPE html>), plus the ```html code-fence language label and related mentions like "html.parser" or html in CSS selectors.

61212.name: The "//" separator that follows the owner/organization name in formal public identifiers (e.g. "-//W3C//DTD" in DOCTYPE declarations, "PRODID:-//...//" in iCalendar headers). It fires most strongly in DOCTYPE strings; other tokens show only weak, scattered activation.

61230.name: Weak, diffuse activation on ordinary tokens in legal/regulatory or formal prose, strongest in passages about jurisdiction, territoriality, residency and where parties or businesses are located or operate (e.g., domestic vs. foreign, residents vs. non-residents, doing business in a district, legal ties to a state).

61247.name: Repeated punctuation/symbol tokens and whitespace in ASCII art, markdown table borders and grid-like layouts (pipes, slashes, hashes, dashes, underscores). It fires on the repeating structural elements mid-pattern, most strongly in dense ASCII drawings.

61262.name: Numeric components (mostly "0", sometimes "255") inside RGB/RGBA color tuples in code, especially later channels like green/blue/alpha in values such as (255,0,0) or rgba(0,0,0,0.x). The strongest activations are in black/shadow colors. A few weak activations fall on random words in prose.

61284.name: Tokens naming the input or object that an operation is applied to, most often function parameters and argument variables in code (e.g. (array, (a, b, value, string, text, data, number). It also fires in prose for the thing being acted on or entered, such as "a given integer", "the amount in", "a set of", "enter a number", and "the substrate".

61287.name: Structural tokens in error tracebacks and stack traces, mainly the indentation and the 'File "' / 'File "/' path opening, ', in' before a function name, and 'at' in JS/Java stack frames. Weaker activation on scattered code and prose tokens such as 'except', indentation and connective words.

61292.name: Words and phrases expressing spatial location, proximity, or distance relative to a reference point (e.g., "away", "nearby", "down the block", "next to", "across from", "opposite side", "10 meters away"). Activation peaks on the final word of such proximity or distance expressions, especially "away" and "block".

61317.name: Connector tokens that link one expression to its equivalent, result, or counterpart, mostly in math, unit-conversion, or code/technical text. Typical ones are '=', '=>', '->', '/', 'vs', '_', and the 'in' / 'how many' of conversion questions ('what in km/hour', 'equals how many centimeters'). They mark the pivot between the left-hand quantity and the answer or target. These tokens often appear in noisy or garbled text.

6132.name: Fires mainly on terms from endocrinology and physiology, most strongly on hormones and hormone-related words (estrogens, testosterone, hormone balance, hypothyroid, menstruation, glucocorticoids, adrenaline), often on word-piece subtokens. It also responds more weakly to other biomedical or anatomical fragments and to words like moon/lunar and feminine.

Hormone and endocrine terminology (hormone, hormonal, testosterone, thyroid, oxytocin, corticosteroids, T3/T4, HRT), which activates most strongly. Weaker activations come from loosely related concepts like femininity and masculinity, the moon or lunar cycles, goddesses, birth control, and body or medical terms.

61320.name: The "_INET" suffix in AF_INET (the IPv4 address-family constant in socket code), strongest in socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, ...) calls. It fires more weakly on similar socket identifiers like sockaddr_in and on stray "_INET" tokens in garbled text.

61325.name: Completion tokens of names of scientific instruments, experiments, detectors, observatories, space probes and research collaborations/teams (often acronym endings like CMS, Belle, OMEGA, RAVE, DESPEC experiment, magnetometer), plus words like 'instruments', 'experiment', 'detector'; weaker on author-name endings and line breaks in scientific paper headers.

Names of scientific missions, experiments, instruments and research projects (e.g. Curiosity Rover, Galileo, Rosetta, LIGO, LISA, ITER, Gaia, EDGES, New Horizons), firing on the completing token of the name or on head nouns like instrument, experiment, detector, study, group and institute. It responds weakly to unrelated tokens.

61371.name: Words in website boilerplate, navigation menus, metadata labels, and page headers (e.g., 'Sign Up', 'Item ID', 'Article INFO', 'Related Links', 'Now Reading', 'Home'), typically the second word of a short UI/label phrase rather than running prose.

61402.name: The name "Bloomberg" (whole token or the "loomberg" piece after "B"), strongest for the news/media outlet (e.g., "(Bloomberg) --", "according to Bloomberg") and also firing on other Bloomberg entities such as the School of Public Health or New Energy Finance.

61416.name: Sentence-final punctuation fused with a newline (".⏎", ".⏎⏎", or a bare newline) that closes a paragraph. It fires most strongly when the following text starts an unrelated new topic or a stitched-together snippet, as in scraped or concatenated web text. It fires weakly on other boundary tokens such as "search" in "Jump to: navigation, search".

61429.name: Function words (prepositions, articles, conjunctions, commas, list/example introducers like "such as", "like", "include") placed right before an upcoming content noun or name, i.e., the connective slot where the model predicts a specific entity, example item, or list member. Highest on example-introducing words ("like", "such as", "include") and "of" in noun phrases.

Function words (mostly prepositions like of/by/with/in/to, plus articles, 'and', and list commas) that introduce an upcoming noun phrase, typically a named entity, place, or descriptive complement in factual, encyclopedic or product-description prose; activation is on the connector just before the noun, strongest in dense descriptive lists or biographies.

61445.name: The token immediately following an author's surname in citations or bylines, overwhelmingly "et" in "et al.", but also commas, initials, superscript backslashes, brackets, or "on" after a username.

61455.name: Arithmetic and number-representation contexts, strongest on addition/sum words and plus signs, with weaker firing on base-conversion phrasing ("base N number", "equals") and on the space or token just before an operand.

61463.name: Newline tokens (often fused with punctuation such as ')', ':', '.', '>') that end short lines in structured, non-prose boilerplate such as metadata fields, web page headers and navigation, citation and publication info, contact lists, and table/markup rows, marking the boundary between one field or label and the next.

61495.name: Identifier numbers or letters that follow a reference label such as Figure, Section, Appendix, Eq., Vol., No., Chapter, issue #, or note, marking which item in a document or series is being cited.

61514.name: Fires on items late in a sequential enumeration, most strongly on the start numbers of the upper or final brackets of numeric class intervals or age ranges (e.g. "50 or older", "65-74", "75+", "95-99"). Weaker, scattered activation falls on list and table delimiters, array indices, option letters and opening parentheses within structured lists, tables, options or code.

61515.name: Fires most strongly on ".W" in the legal case citation "S.W.3d" (South Western Reporter). It fires weakly on the ">⏎" closing an HTML <thead> tag before <tr>, and faintly on scattered unrelated tokens.

61519.name: Numeric tokens (digits or digit chunks) inside dense sequences of numbers, such as data tables, code literals, version strings, dates, IDs, and lists of values. It fires mostly on mid-sequence or trailing numbers, including fragments of longer numbers, and occasionally on nearby non-numeric tokens in number-heavy contexts.

61533.name: Narratives of combat, warfare and violent or dramatic action, such as battles, attacks, shootings, captures, escapes, kills and military operations. Activation is strongest within descriptions of the action itself and at the sentence breaks between steps of the battle account. Weaker hits appear on related physical-action narration, like finding, seizing or rescuing someone, and sporadically elsewhere.

61550.name: Words expressing difference, distinctness, or sameness/comparison between things ("different", "differ", "unique", "same", "identical", "disparate", "distinction", "homogeneous"), plus tokens completing such comparisons ("from", "between", or the noun that follows). Strongest on "different" after an intensifier like "very" or "completely".

61599.name: Structural boundary tokens in news/web articles: double newlines, periods, colons, and stray spaces that separate headlines, datelines, bylines, and paragraphs. It is strongest on broadcast-media context such as "Radio", "GMT", station call letters, "By" bylines, and "produced/broadcast" credits.

A diffuse, mostly weak feature firing on structural boundary tokens that precede a new segment, such as the '#' starting an indented Python comment line (often after def main():), sentence-final periods, colons or closing brackets before line breaks, list dashes and code-block newlines. It also fires sporadically on parts of acronyms and names. The strongest isolated hit is the year digit in a '© 2024' copyright notice.

61614.name: Tokens that open a computation or a request for a result in code and math problems. In code, this means statement-starting keywords like print, return and if, assignment operators (=, ←), and the indentation before an executed call. In math word problems, it means directive or question words such as "Determine", "calculate", "How many", and "the number of". Activation is strongest on print( and return.

61630.name: Tokens inside titles and headings (article, book, game, film and product names, section headers, course or document labels), usually on their own line after a line break. The feature fires on parts of these title-like phrases, often internal words, prepositions or word fragments, rather than on running prose.

61634.name: The middle number segment of dotted classification codes, most strongly the second two-digit field of PACS physics codes (e.g. the "75" in 89.75.Hc). Activation is weaker on similar segments in OCIS, MSC, ACM, EC and industry codes, IP addresses and arXiv IDs.

61662.name: Women's first names (and full-name pieces) in family or relationship contexts, e.g. a wife, mother, sister, girlfriend or the second parent in "X and Y". Activation is strongest on the mother's or wife's name after "and" in parent or couple listings. Words like "wife" and "lady" fire weakly, as do a few unrelated name-like word pieces.

61672.name: Language about filling official positions through appointment, nomination, selection or election. The strongest hits are words like "appointed by", "nominee(s)/nomination" and "selected". It also fires on the officeholders and offices involved, such as judges, justices, secretary, minister, director and administration, and on confirmation hearings. Unrelated tokens get only weak, scattered activations.

61677.name: A diffuse, multilingual latent with no clear semantic theme. It mostly fires on a token that completes a partly built word or unit, such as a word-final suffix (chiropr→actic, 마지→막), the second half of a brand name (Mobo→Reader), or a number inside an amount (€200k). It occasionally fires on function or punctuation tokens at phrase boundaries (" two" before "terminals", a sentence-ending period).

61707.name: Fires at the boundary where a long, complex subject noun phrase ends and its main predicate begins. This is usually the main verb ('is', 'are', 'is an') or a closing parenthesis just before the verb. It is strongest in formal rule, disclaimer or policy statements (e.g., '…use of a veterinary medicine is an offence', '…statement made against a nation is a punishable offense', 'References for papers… are'). Other activations are weak and scattered.

61709.name: Shell output-redirection operators, especially ">&" in "2>&1" or ">&2" and ">/" in ">/dev/null", that send stdout/stderr to another stream or discard it. Related stream-handling code such as stdout=subprocess and /stdin fires weakly.

61721.name: Strongest on supersymmetry labels in physics notation, such as the "𝒩=4" or "𝒩=(2,2)" count ("N", "=", the number) and the word "supersymmetric"/"super". Weaker activation falls on "=" in quantum-number assignments (S=1/2, I=…, n=…), along with assorted math and LaTeX tokens and scattered formatting whitespace.

61749.name: The word "month" (and its variants "months", "monthly", "Month") as a time-unit noun, most strongly in singular references to a specific or recurring month ("last month", "this month", "every month", "per month"). Plural counts ("three months", "months ago") and other time units like week, day and hour activate more weakly.

The word "month" (and variants like months, monthly, Month) as a time unit, especially singular "month" in relative time phrases like "last/this/earlier this month" or "per month"; weaker on plural "months" and other time units (weeks, hour, tomorrow).

61758.name: Personal names of researchers and authors, especially in academic author bylines, citations, and reference lists. It fires on name pieces such as initials, given names, and surname-ending subword tokens, and on the separators between names (commas, 'and', affiliation superscripts and markers). It is strongest near the end of a name or author list, just before affiliations or the year. It also fires weakly on academic role words like 'professor' or 'senior author'.

Tokens of personal names, especially surnames, initials, and the separating commas and "and" in author lists of citations and bylines. Activation is strongest in long, repetitive bibliographic author sequences and weaker for single names attributed to quotes or credits.

61763.name: Fires on a token that ends a formulaic lead-in and comes right before an inserted or templated item. The strongest case is "Question" after a programming-language tag in scraped Q&A headers ("user - time ago - Python Question"), just before the question title. Another strong case is the punctuation closing boilerplate spam phrases like "visit this external resource.", right before an inserted URL or keyword. There are also weaker, scattered activations on function words in ordinary prose.

61767.name: Mid-path segments inside highly predictable technical identifiers, chiefly ".bind" in Java/Spring package imports (org.springframework.web.bind.annotation, javax.xml.bind) and socket .bind calls. Also matches "/latest" in AWS documentation URLs, header names like <iomanip>, and acronym fragments (HTLV, AFJROTC). Weak activity on whitespace and newlines in templated bid listings and on ordinary function words.

61784.name: The subword token "orig" inside words, strongest in "tumorigenesis/tumorigenic" and also in "origins", "original", "aborigines", "Dorigo". Weak firing on other mid-word fragments such as "rogen" (chondrogenic) and "raft" (xenograft).

61798.name: Formatting and structural tokens in tables, code, and other structured text: row-ending pipes plus newlines, indentation and alignment whitespace, line breaks, and separators that mark cell, line, or column boundaries ahead of the next aligned item.

61810.name: The standalone digit "0" used as a numeric value, most often in code and math (return values, function arguments, comparisons, assignments, binary 0/1 outcomes). Activation is strongest where 0 is a result or output value, as in "returns 0" or "print(0)".

61815.name: Fires weakly on segment boundaries, mostly sentence-final punctuation fused with paragraph breaks (".⏎⏎", "⏎⏎", ":⏎⏎", "...⏎⏎") where a paragraph, heading, title or list item ends and a new section or topic begins. It also fires occasionally on tokens near the very start of a document or line.

Segment boundaries in messy, often prompt-like or chat/system text. It fires mostly on line-break tokens (newlines, often followed by punctuation, closing brackets or code fences) that end one block and begin another. It also fires on instruction or system-prompt phrases that open a new section, such as "You are a helpful AI assistant", "rewrite it to...", "Below is", or Chinese request phrases.

61824.name: Boundaries in SEO spam and keyword-stuffed web text (gambling, pills, essay-writing, downloads, link farms). It fires on punctuation, line breaks, commas between keyword phrases, and tokens like " https", " online", " download", " visit", and " link", right where a junk keyword string or inserted URL begins or ends.

61840.name: The "test"/"Test" token that begins a unit test function or method name in code, right after a keyword like func, def, fn, or public void (e.g. Go's func TestX, Python's def test_x). It fires most strongly in Go. It also fires weakly on other tokens at the start of test definitions, such as test attributes, return types, or the first word of a descriptive test name.
